1.0.oldText: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner well known in our district in his own day, and still remembered among us because of his grim and tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I'll describe in its proper place. For now I'll only say that this "landowner"—for that's what we used to call him, though he barely spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange character, yet one fairly common: a type that was abject and vicious and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless people who are perfectly capable of managing their worldly affairs, and, it seems, nothing else. Fyodor Pavlovitch, for instance, began with almost nothing; his estate was tiny; he ran around dining at other men's tables and attached himself to them as a hanger-on, yet when he died it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in hard cash. At the same time, he was all his life one of the most senseless, absurd fellows in the whole district. I repeat, it wasn't stupidity—most of these absurd fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough—but pure senselessness, and a peculiarly Russian brand of it.

1.1.oldText: He was married twice and had three sons: the eldest, Dmitri, by his first wife, and two more, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, belonged to a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, the Miüsovs, who were also landowners in our district. How it came about that an heiress—a beauty, and on top of that one of those spirited, intelligent young women so common in this generation but occasionally found in the last—could have married such a worthless, puny weakling, as we all called him, I won't even try to explain. I once knew a young lady of the last "romantic" generation who, after several years of an enigmatic passion for a gentleman whom she could easily have married at any moment, invented insurmountable obstacles to their union, and ended up throwing herself one stormy night from a high bank—almost a cliff—into a deep and rushing river, perishing purely to satisfy her own whim, and to imitate Shakespeare's Ophelia. If that cliff, her chosen and favorite spot, had been less picturesque, if a prosaic flat bank had stood in its place, the suicide would most likely never have happened. This is a fact, and there have probably been more than a few similar cases in the last two or three generations. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov's action was, no doubt, a similar echo of other people's ideas, born of the irritation caused by a lack of mental freedom. She wanted, perhaps, to assert her feminine independence, to defy class distinctions and the despotism of her family. And a pliable imagination persuaded her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, despite his parasitic status, was one of the bold and ironic spirits of that progressive age—though he was in fact nothing more than an ill-tempered buffoon. What gave the marriage its flavor was that it was preceded by an elopement, and this greatly captivated Adelaïda Ivanovna's imagination. Fyodor Pavlovitch's situation at the time made him unusually eager for any such adventure, since he was desperate to make his way in the world one way or another. Attaching himself to a good family and getting his hands on a dowry was a tempting prospect. As for mutual love, it apparently didn't exist, either in the bride or in him, despite Adelaïda Ivanovna's beauty. This was perhaps a unique episode in the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was always of a voluptuous temperament and ready to chase any skirt on the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the only woman who made no particular impression on his senses.

1.2.oldText: Right after the elopement Adelaïda Ivanovna realized in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. So the marriage showed its true colors with extraordinary speed. Although the family accepted the event pretty quickly and handed over the runaway bride's dowry, husband and wife began to lead a thoroughly disorderly life, and there were endless quarrels between them. It was said that the young wife showed incomparably more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch, who, as is now known, got hold of all her money—up to twenty-five thousand roubles—as soon as she received it, so that those thousands were lost to her forever. The little village and the rather fine town house that were part of her dowry he did his utmost for a long time to transfer into his own name by means of some deed of conveyance. He would probably have succeeded, simply through her moral exhaustion and her desire to be rid of him, and from the contempt and loathing his persistent, shameless badgering stirred in her. But fortunately Adelaïda Ivanovna's family stepped in and thwarted his greed. It's known for a fact that frequent fights broke out between husband and wife, but rumor had it that Fyodor Pavlovitch did not beat his wife—she beat him, for she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. Finally she left the house and ran off from Fyodor Pavlovitch with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a child of three, in her husband's hands. Immediately Fyodor Pavlovitch introduced a regular harem into the house and gave himself over to drunken orgies. In between, he drove all over the province, tearfully complaining to everyone about Adelaïda Ivanovna having left him, going into details too disgraceful for a husband to mention about his own married life. What seemed to gratify him most and flatter his self-love was to play the ridiculous role of the injured husband and parade his suffering with embellishments.

1.3.oldText: "Fyodor Pavlovitch, one would think you'd just gotten a promotion, you look so pleased in spite of your sorrow," the scoffers said to him. Many even added that he was delighted by this new comic part in which to play the buffoon, and that he pretended to be unaware of his absurd position simply to make it funnier. But who knows—maybe it was genuine simplicity. At last he managed to track down his runaway wife. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had gone with her divinity student and had thrown herself into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once began bustling about, making preparations to go to Petersburg—for what purpose he couldn't have said himself. He might actually have gone; but having decided on the trip, he felt immediately entitled to fortify himself for the journey with another bout of reckless drinking. And just at that moment his wife's family received news of her death in Petersburg. She had died quite suddenly in a garret, according to one story, of typhus, or, as another version had it, of starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife's death, and the story goes that he ran out into the street and began shouting with joy, raising his hands to heaven: "Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace," but others say he wept uncontrollably like a little child, so much so that people felt sorry for him despite the repulsion he inspired. It's entirely possible that both versions were true—that he rejoiced at his release and at the same time wept for the one who had released him. As a rule, people, even the wicked, are far more naïve and simple-hearted than we imagine. And so are we ourselves.

2.0.oldText: You can easily imagine what sort of father a man like that could be and how he'd raise his children. His behavior as a father was exactly what you'd expect. He completely abandoned the child of his marriage with Adelaïda Ivanovna, not out of malice, nor because of his marital grievances, but simply because he forgot him. While he was wearing everyone out with his tears and complaints, and turning his house into a sinkhole of debauchery, a faithful family servant, Grigory, took the three-year-old Mitya into his care. If he hadn't looked after him, there wouldn't have been anyone even to change the baby's little shirt.

2.1.oldText: It also happened that the child's relatives on his mother's side forgot him at first, too. His grandfather was no longer living, his widow—Mitya's grandmother—had moved to Moscow and was seriously ill, and his daughters were married, so Mitya remained for nearly a whole year in old Grigory's care, living with him in the servants' cottage. But even if his father had remembered him (he couldn't have been entirely unaware of his existence), he would have sent him back to the cottage, since the child would only have gotten in the way of his debaucheries. Then a cousin of Mitya's mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, happened to return from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at the time was still a young man, distinguished among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had been in the capitals and abroad. Toward the end of his life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over the course of his career he had come into contact with many of the most Liberal men of his time, both in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally, and in his later years was very fond of describing the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he himself had almost taken part in the fighting on the barricades. This was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He had an independent property of about a thousand souls, to count in the old style. His splendid estate lay on the outskirts of our little town and bordered on the lands of our famous monastery, with which Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit, almost as soon as he came into the estate, about fishing rights in the river or timber rights in the forest, I don't know exactly which. He considered it his duty as a citizen and a man of culture to open an attack on the "clericals." Hearing all about Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom of course he remembered and in whom he had at one time been interested, and learning of Mitya's existence, he stepped in, despite all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He made Fyodor Pavlovitch's acquaintance for the first time and told him straight out that he wanted to take charge of the child's upbringing. He used to tell, long afterwards, as a characteristic touch, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch looked for some time as though he didn't understand what child he was talking about, and even seemed surprised to hear that he had a little son in the house. The story may have been exaggerated, but it must have been something close to the truth.

2.2.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch loved theatrics all his life—suddenly playing some unexpected part, sometimes without any motive whatsoever, and even to his own direct disadvantage, as in the present case. This habit, however, is characteristic of a great many people, some of them very clever ones, unlike Fyodor Pavlovitch. Pyotr Alexandrovitch pushed the business through vigorously and was appointed, along with Fyodor Pavlovitch, joint guardian of the child, who had a small property—a house and land—left to him by his mother. Mitya did indeed pass into this cousin's keeping, but since the cousin had no family of his own and, after securing the revenues of his estates, was in a hurry to return to Paris, he left the boy with one of his cousins, a lady living in Moscow. It so happened that, having settled permanently in Paris, he too forgot the child, especially when the February Revolution broke out, leaving an impression on his mind that he remembered all the rest of his life. The Moscow lady died, and Mitya passed into the care of one of her married daughters. I believe he changed homes a fourth time later on. I won't expand on that now, because I'll have much to tell later about Fyodor Pavlovitch's firstborn, and for now I must stick to the essential facts about him, without which I couldn't begin my story.

2.3.oldText: To start with, this Mitya—or rather, Dmitri Fyodorovitch—was the only one of Fyodor Pavlovitch's three sons who grew up believing that he had property and would be independent when he came of age. He spent an irregular boyhood and youth. He didn't finish his studies at the gymnasium, got into a military school, then went to the Caucasus, was promoted, fought a duel, was demoted to the ranks, earned promotion again, led a wild life, and spent a good deal of money. He didn't begin to receive any income from Fyodor Pavlovitch until he came of age, and until then he piled up debts. He saw and knew his father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the first time when he came of age and traveled to our neighborhood specifically to settle the matter of his property with him. He seems not to have liked his father. He didn't stay long and hurried to get away, having only managed to obtain a sum of money and entering into an agreement for future payments from the estate, whose revenues and value he was unable (a fact worth noting), on that occasion, to get any account of from his father. Fyodor Pavlovitch remarked for the first time then (this too should be noted) that Mitya had a vague and inflated idea of his property. Fyodor Pavlovitch was very well satisfied with this, since it fit in perfectly with his own plans. He gathered only that the young man was frivolous, unruly, of violent passions, impatient, and dissolute, and that if he could just get some ready cash he would be content—for a short time, of course. So Fyodor Pavlovitch began to take advantage of this, sending him small handouts from time to time, installments. In the end, when four years later Mitya, losing patience, came a second time to our little town to settle things with his father once and for all, it turned out, to his amazement, that he had nothing—that it was even hard to get an account, that he had already received the full value of his property in sums of money from Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was perhaps even in debt to him; that by various agreements he had, of his own accord, entered into at various previous times, he had no right to expect anything more, and so on, and so on. The young man was stunned, suspected deceit and cheating, and was almost beside himself. And indeed this circumstance led to the catastrophe whose account forms the subject of my first introductory story—or rather, the external side of it. But before I move on to that story, I must say a little about Fyodor Pavlovitch's other two sons, and where they came from.

3.0.oldText: Very soon after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married a second time. His second marriage lasted eight years. He took this second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, also a very young girl, from another province, where he had gone on some small bit of business in the company of a Jew. Though Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, he never neglected to invest his capital, and managed his business affairs very successfully—though, no doubt, not especially scrupulously. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon, and had been left an orphan from childhood, with no relatives. She grew up in the house of a general's widow, a wealthy old lady of good position, who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I don't know the details, but I've heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a halter in which she was hanging from a nail in the loft—so terrible were her sufferings from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who apparently wasn't bad-hearted, but had become an insufferable tyrant through sheer idleness.

3.1.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch made her an offer; inquiries were made about him, and he was refused. But again, as in his first marriage, he proposed an elopement to the orphan girl. There's very little doubt she would never have married him under any circumstances if she'd known a little more about him in time. But she lived in another province; besides, what could a little girl of sixteen know about it, except that she would be better off at the bottom of the river than remaining with her benefactress? And so the poor child exchanged a benefactress for a benefactor. This time Fyodor Pavlovitch did not get a penny, because the general's widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he had not been counting on a dowry; what lured him was the remarkable beauty of the innocent girl, above all her innocent appearance, which had a peculiar attraction for a vicious profligate who until then had admired only the coarser types of feminine beauty.

3.2.oldText: "Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor," he used to say afterwards, with his loathsome snigger. In a man so depraved this might, of course, mean no more than sensual attraction. Since he had received no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her "from the halter," he didn't stand on ceremony with her. Making her feel that she had "wronged" him, he took advantage of her phenomenal meekness and submissiveness to trample on the elementary decencies of marriage. He gathered loose women into his house and carried on orgies of debauchery in his wife's presence. To show how bad things had become, I should mention that Grigory—the gloomy, dim, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna—took the side of his new mistress. He championed her cause, abusing Fyodor Pavlovitch in a manner hardly befitting a servant, and on one occasion broke up the revels and drove all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end this unhappy young woman, kept in terror from her childhood, fell into that kind of nervous disease most often found in peasant women who are said to be "possessed by devils." At times, after terrible fits of hysterics, she even lost her reason. Yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey, the eldest in the first year of marriage and the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year, and, strange as it seems, I know that he remembered his mother all his life—like a dream, of course. At her death, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as had happened to their elder brother, Mitya. They were completely forgotten and abandoned by their father. They were looked after by the same Grigory and lived in his cottage, where they were found by the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother. She was still alive and had not, in all those eight years, forgotten the insult done to her. All that time she had been obtaining exact information about her Sofya's way of life, and, hearing of her illness and hideous surroundings, she declared aloud two or three times to her servants:

3.3.oldText: "It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude."

3.4.oldText: Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna's death, the general's widow suddenly appeared in our town, and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. She spent only half an hour in town, but she accomplished a great deal. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom she had not seen for those eight years, came in to her drunk. The story goes that the instant she saw him, without any sort of explanation, she gave him two good, ringing slaps on the face, seized him by a tuft of hair, and shook him three times up and down. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. Seeing at a glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, she promptly gave Grigory, too, a box on the ear, and announcing that she was taking both children away, she wrapped them up just as they were in a rug, put them in the carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory accepted the blow like a devoted slave, without a word, and when he escorted the old lady to her carriage, he made her a low bow and pronounced impressively that "God would repay her for the orphans." "You're a blockhead all the same," the old lady shouted at him as she drove away.

3.5.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch, thinking it over, decided it was just as well, and did not refuse the general's widow his formal consent to any arrangement regarding his children's education. As for the slaps she had given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

3.6.oldText: It so happened that the old lady died soon after this, but she left the boys a thousand roubles each in her will "for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so apportioned as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them." I haven't read the will myself, but I hear there was something odd of the sort, whimsically worded. The principal heir, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, turned out, however, to be an honest man. Writing to Fyodor Pavlovitch, and realizing at once that he could extract nothing from him for his children's education (though the latter never refused outright, but only procrastinated, as he always did in such cases, and was, in fact, at times effusively sentimental), Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the orphans. He became especially fond of the younger, Alexey, who lived for a long time as one of his family. I beg the reader to note this from the start. And to Yefim Petrovitch, a man of a generosity and humanity rarely to be met with, the young men owed their education and upbringing more than to anyone else. He kept the two thousand roubles left to them by the general's widow intact, so that by the time they came of age their portions had been doubled by accumulated interest. He educated both of them at his own expense, and certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each of them. I won't go into a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, and will mention only a few of the most important events. Of the elder, Ivan, I will only say that he grew up into a somewhat morose and reserved, though far from timid, boy. By the age of ten he had realized that they were living not in their own home but on other people's charity, and that their father was a man of whom it was disgraceful to speak. This boy began very early, almost in his infancy (so they say at least), to show a brilliant and unusual aptitude for learning. I don't know exactly why, but he left the family of Yefim Petrovitch when he was barely thirteen, entering a Moscow gymnasium and boarding with an experienced and celebrated teacher, an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say afterwards that this was all due to the "zeal for good works" of Yefim Petrovitch, who was captivated by the idea that the boy's genius should be trained by a teacher of genius. But neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was living when the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university. Since Yefim Petrovitch had made no provision for the payment of the tyrannical old lady's legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two, it was delayed, owing to the formalities inevitable in Russia, and the young man was in serious straits for his first two years at the university, since he was forced to support himself the whole time he was studying. It must be noted that he didn't even try to communicate with his father, perhaps out of pride, out of contempt for him, or perhaps out of his cool common sense, which told him that from such a father he would get no real help. However that may be, the young man was by no means discouraged and managed to find work, at first giving cheap lessons and later getting paragraphs on street incidents published in the newspapers under the signature of "Eye-Witness." These paragraphs, it was said, were so interesting and piquant that they were soon snapped up. This alone showed the young man's practical and intellectual superiority over the masses of needy, unfortunate students of both sexes who hang around the offices of the newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless entreaties for copying and translations from the French. Having once made contact with the editors, Ivan Fyodorovitch always kept up his connection with them, and in his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, so that he became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly manage to attract the attention of a far wider circle of readers, so that a great many people noticed and remembered him. It was a rather curious incident. When he had just left the university and was preparing to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, Ivan Fyodorovitch published in one of the more important journals a strange article that attracted general notice, on a subject of which he might have been supposed to know nothing, since he was a student of natural science. The article dealt with a subject that was being debated everywhere at the time—the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After discussing several opinions on the subject, he went on to explain his own view. What was most striking about the article was its tone, and its unexpected conclusion. Many of the Church party regarded him unquestioningly as on their side. And yet not only the secularists but even the atheists joined in the applause. Finally, some shrewd persons concluded that the article was nothing but an impudent, satirical burlesque. I mention this incident particularly because this article reached the famous monastery in our neighborhood, where the inmates, being particularly interested in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, were completely bewildered by it. Learning the author's name, they took an interest in the fact that he was a native of the town and the son of "that Fyodor Pavlovitch." And just then the author himself made his appearance among us.

3.7.oldText: Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come among us, I remember asking myself at the time with a certain uneasiness. This fateful visit, which was the first step leading to so many consequences, I never fully explained to myself. It seemed strange on the face of it that a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so cautious, should suddenly visit such an infamous house and a father who had ignored him all his life, hardly knew him, never thought of him, and would under no circumstances have given him money, though he always feared that his sons Ivan and Alexey would also come to ask him for it. And here the young man was staying in the house of such a father, had been living with him for two months, and they were on the best possible terms. This last fact was a particular cause of wonder to many others besides me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, of whom we've already spoken, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, happened to be in the neighborhood again on a visit to his estate. He had come from Paris, which was his permanent home. I remember he was more surprised than anyone when he made the young man's acquaintance, who interested him extremely, and with whom he sometimes argued and, not without an inner pang, compared himself in accomplishments.

3.8.oldText: "He is proud," he used to say, "he'll never be short of money; he has enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Everyone can see he hasn't come for money, since his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink and dissipation, and yet his father can't do without him. They get on so well together!"

3.9.oldText: That was the truth; the young man had an unmistakable influence over his father, who actually seemed to be behaving more decently and even appeared at times ready to obey his son, though he was often extremely, even spitefully, perverse.

3.10.oldText: It was only later that we learned that Ivan had come partly at the request of, and in the interests of, his elder brother, Dmitri, whom he saw for the first time on this very visit, although before leaving Moscow he had been in correspondence with him about an important matter of more concern to Dmitri than to himself. What that business was the reader will learn fully in due course. Yet even when I knew of this special circumstance, I still felt Ivan Fyodorovitch to be an enigmatic figure, and thought his visit rather mysterious.

3.11.oldText: I should add that Ivan appeared at the time in the role of a mediator between his father and his elder brother Dmitri, who was in open quarrel with his father and was even planning to bring an action against him.

3.12.oldText: The family, I repeat, was now united for the first time, and some of its members were meeting for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us for a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It is of that brother Alexey that I find it most difficult to speak in this introduction. Yet I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one odd fact—namely, that I have to introduce my hero to the reader wearing the cassock of a novice. Yes, for the last year he had been in our monastery, and seemed willing to be cloistered there for the rest of his life.

4.0.oldText: He was only twenty, his brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, while their elder brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First of all, I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was not a fanatic, and, in my opinion at least, was not even a mystic. I might as well give my full opinion from the start. He was simply an early lover of humanity, and that he adopted the monastic life was simply because at the time it struck him, so to speak, as the ideal escape for his soul, which was struggling out of the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. And the reason this life struck him this way was that he found in it, as he thought, an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, to whom he became attached with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. But I don't dispute that he was very strange even then, and had been so from his cradle. I've mentioned already, by the way, that although he lost his mother in his fourth year he remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, "as though she stood living before me." Such memories can persist, as everyone knows, from an even earlier age, even from two years old, but they rarely stand out through a whole lifetime like spots of light out of darkness, like a corner torn from a huge picture which has faded and disappeared except for that fragment. That is how it was with him. He remembered one still summer evening, an open window, the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all); in a corner of the room the holy image, before it a lighted lamp, and on her knees before the image his mother, sobbing hysterically with cries and moans, snatching him up in both arms, squeezing him close till it hurt, and praying for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms to the image as though to put him under the Mother's protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother's face at that moment. He used to say that it was frenzied but beautiful as he remembered it. But he rarely cared to speak of this memory to anyone. In his childhood and youth he was by no means expansive, and spoke very little, but not from shyness or a sullen unsociability; quite the contrary, from something different, from a kind of inner preoccupation entirely personal and unconcerned with other people, but so important to him that he seemed, as it were, to forget others because of it. But he was fond of people: he seemed his whole life to put implicit trust in people, yet no one ever looked on him as a simpleton or a naïve person. There was something about him that made one feel at once (and it remained so all his life afterwards) that he didn't care to be a judge of others—that he would never take it upon himself to criticize, and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, indeed, to accept everything without the least condemnation, though often grieving bitterly; and this was so much the case that no one could surprise or frighten him even in his earliest youth. Coming at twenty to his father's house, which was a very sink of filthy debauchery, he—chaste and pure as he was—simply withdrew in silence when to look on was unbearable, but without the slightest sign of contempt or condemnation. His father, who had once been in a dependent position and so was sensitive and quick to take offense, met him at first with distrust and sullenness. "He doesn't say much," he used to say, "and thinks all the more." But soon, within a fortnight in fact, he took to embracing him and kissing him terribly often, with drunken tears, with sottish sentimentality, and yet he evidently felt a real and deep affection for him, such as he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

4.1.oldText: Everyone, indeed, loved this young man wherever he went, and it had been so from his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the entire family, so that they treated him as their own child. Yet he entered the house at such a tender age that he could not have acted from calculation or artfulness in winning affection. So that the gift of making himself loved directly and unconsciously was inherent in him, in his very nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed like exactly the sort of child who would be distrusted, sometimes ridiculed, and even disliked by his classmates. He was dreamy, for instance, and rather solitary. From his earliest childhood he was fond of creeping into a corner to read, and yet he was a general favorite the whole time he was at school. He was rarely playful or merry, but anyone could see at a glance that this was not from any sullenness. On the contrary, he was bright and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his classmates. Perhaps because of this, he was never afraid of anyone, yet the boys understood at once that he was not proud of his fearlessness and seemed unaware that he was bold and courageous. He never resented an insult. It might happen that an hour after the offense he would address the offender or answer some question with as trustful and candid an expression as though nothing had happened between them. And it wasn't that he seemed to have forgotten or intentionally forgiven the affront, but simply that he didn't regard it as an affront, and this completely conquered and captivated the boys. He had one trait that made all his classmates, from the bottom class to the top, want to mock him, not out of malice but because it amused them. This trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He couldn't bear to hear certain words and certain conversations about women. There are "certain" words and conversations, unfortunately, impossible to eradicate in schools. Boys pure in mind and heart, almost children, are fond of talking in school among themselves, and even aloud, of things, pictures, and images of which even soldiers would sometimes hesitate to speak. What's more, much that soldiers have no knowledge or conception of is familiar to quite young children of our intellectual and higher classes. There is no moral depravity, no real corrupt inner cynicism in it, but there is the appearance of it, and it is often looked upon among them as something refined, subtle, daring, and worth imitating. Seeing that Alyosha Karamazov put his fingers in his ears when they talked of "that," they used sometimes to crowd around him, pull his hands away, and shout nastiness into both ears, while he struggled, slid to the floor, tried to hide himself, without uttering one word of abuse, enduring their insults in silence. But at last they left him alone and gave up taunting him with being a "regular girl," and, what's more, they looked on it with compassion, as a weakness. He was always one of the best in the class, but was never first.

4.2.oldText: At the time of Yefim Petrovitch's death, Alyosha had two more years to complete at the provincial gymnasium. The inconsolable widow went almost immediately after his death for a long visit to Italy with her whole family, which consisted only of women and girls. Alyosha went to live in the house of two distant relations of Yefim Petrovitch, ladies whom he had never seen before. On what terms he lived with them he did not know himself. It was very characteristic of him, in fact, that he never cared at whose expense he was living. In that respect he was a striking contrast to his elder brother Ivan, who had struggled with poverty for his first two years at the university, had supported himself by his own efforts, and had from childhood been bitterly conscious of living at the expense of his benefactor. But this strange trait in Alyosha's character must not, I think, be judged too severely, for at the slightest acquaintance with him anyone would have seen that Alyosha was one of those youths, almost of the type of religious enthusiast, who, if they were suddenly to come into possession of a large fortune, would not hesitate to give it away for the asking, either for good works or perhaps to a clever swindler. In general he seemed scarcely to know the value of money, not, of course, in a literal sense. When he was given pocket money, which he never asked for, he was either terribly careless with it, so that it was gone in a moment, or he kept it for weeks together, not knowing what to do with it.

4.3.oldText: In later years Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, a man very sensitive on the subject of money and bourgeois honesty, pronounced the following judgment, after getting to know Alyosha:

4.4.oldText: "Here is perhaps the one man in the world whom you might leave alone without a penny, in the center of an unknown city of a million inhabitants, and he would come to no harm, he would not die of cold and hunger, because he'd be fed and sheltered at once; and if he weren't, he'd find shelter for himself, and it would cost him no effort or humiliation. And to shelter him would be no burden, but, on the contrary, would probably be considered a pleasure."

4.5.oldText: He did not finish his studies at the gymnasium. A year before the end of the course, he suddenly announced to the ladies that he was going to see his father about a plan that had occurred to him. They were sorry and unwilling to let him go. The journey was not an expensive one, and the ladies would not let him pawn his watch, a parting present from his benefactor's family. They provided him liberally with money and even fitted him out with new clothes and linen. But he returned half the money they gave him, saying he intended to travel third class. On his arrival in the town, he made no answer to his father's first inquiry about why he had come before completing his studies, and seemed, so they say, unusually thoughtful. It soon became clear that he was looking for his mother's grave. He practically acknowledged at the time that that was the only purpose of his visit. But it can hardly have been the whole reason. It is more likely that he himself didn't understand, and couldn't explain, what had suddenly risen up in his soul and drawn him irresistibly onto a new, unknown, but inevitable path. Fyodor Pavlovitch could not show him where his second wife was buried, because he had never visited her grave since he had thrown earth on her coffin, and over the years had entirely forgotten where she was buried.

4.6.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch, by the way, had not been living in our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife's death, he had gone to the south of Russia and finally turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. He made the acquaintance at first, in his own words, "of a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins," and ended by being received by "Jews high and low alike." It may be presumed that during this period he developed a peculiar talent for making and hoarding money. He finally returned to our town only three years before Alyosha's arrival. His former acquaintances found him looking terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man. He behaved not so much with more dignity as with more effrontery. The former buffoon showed an insolent tendency to make buffoons of others. His depravity with women was not simply what it used to be, but even more revolting. In a short time he opened a great many new taverns around the district. It was clear that he had perhaps a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many of the inhabitants of the town and district were soon in his debt, and, of course, had given good security. Lately, too, he looked somehow bloated and seemed more irresponsible, more erratic; he had sunk into a kind of incoherence, used to begin one thing and go on with another, as if he were letting himself go altogether. He was drunk more and more often. And if it hadn't been for the same servant Grigory, who by then had also aged considerably, and who sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor, Fyodor Pavlovitch might have gotten into terrible scrapes. Alyosha's arrival seemed to affect even his moral side, as though something had awakened in this prematurely old man that had long been dead in his soul.

4.7.oldText: "Do you know," he used often to say, looking at Alyosha, "that you are like her, 'the crazy woman'"—that was what he called his dead wife, Alyosha's mother. It was Grigory who pointed out the "crazy woman's" grave to Alyosha. He took him to our town cemetery and showed him, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone, cheap but decently kept, on which were inscribed the name and age of the deceased and the date of her death, and beneath it a four-line verse, of the kind commonly used on old-fashioned middle-class tombs. To Alyosha's amazement, this tomb turned out to be Grigory's doing. He had put it up at his own expense on the poor "crazy woman's" grave, after Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he had often pestered about the grave, had gone to Odessa, abandoning the grave along with all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother's grave. He only listened to Grigory's detailed and solemn account of the erection of the tomb; he stood with bowed head and walked away without uttering a word. It was perhaps a year before he visited the cemetery again. But this little episode was not without an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for the soul of his wife; but not for the second, Alyosha's mother, the "crazy woman," but for the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, who used to thrash him. That same evening he got drunk and abused the monks to Alyosha. He himself was far from religious; he had probably never placed a penny candle before the image of a saint. Strange impulses of sudden feeling and sudden thought are common in such types.

4.8.oldText: I've mentioned already that he looked bloated. His face at this time bore traces of something that unmistakably testified to the life he had led. Besides the long, fleshy bags under his little, always insolent, suspicious, and ironic eyes; besides the multitude of deep wrinkles in his little fat face, the Adam's apple hung below his sharp chin like a great, fleshy goiter, which gave him a peculiar, repulsive, sensual appearance; add to that a long, rapacious mouth with full lips, between which could be seen little stumps of black, decayed teeth. He slobbered every time he began to speak. He was fond, in fact, of making fun of his own face, though I believe he was quite satisfied with it. He used particularly to point to his nose, which was not very large, but very delicate and noticeably aquiline. "A regular Roman nose," he used to say, "with my goiter I've got the face of an ancient Roman patrician from the decadent period." He seemed proud of it.

4.9.oldText: Not long after visiting his mother's grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were willing to receive him as a novice. He explained that this was his strong desire, and that he was solemnly asking his consent as his father. The old man knew that the elder Zossima, who was living in the monastery hermitage, had made a special impression on his "gentle boy."

4.10.oldText: "That's the most honest monk among them, of course," he observed, after listening in thoughtful silence to Alyosha, and seeming scarcely surprised at his request. "Hm!... So that's where you want to be, my gentle boy?"

4.11.oldText: He was half drunk, and suddenly he grinned his slow, half-drunken grin, which was not without a certain cunning and tipsy slyness. "Hm!... I had a premonition you'd end up in something like this. Would you believe it? You were heading straight for it. Well, to be sure you have your own two thousand. That's a dowry for you. And I'll never desert you, my angel. And I'll pay what's needed for you there, if they ask for it. But, of course, if they don't ask, why should we trouble them? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. Hm!... Do you know that near one monastery there's a place outside the town where every baby knows there are none but 'the monks' wives' living, as they're called. Thirty women, I believe. I've been there myself. You know, it's interesting in its own way, of course, as a variety. The worst of it is it's awfully Russian. There are no French women there. Of course they could get them fast enough, they have plenty of money. If they get word of it, they'll come. Well, there's nothing of that sort here, no 'monks' wives,' and two hundred monks. They're honest. They keep the fasts. I admit it.... Hm.... So you want to be a monk? And do you know I'm sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I've really grown fond of you? Well, it's a good opportunity. You'll pray for us sinners; we've sinned too much here. I've always been wondering who would pray for me, and whether there's anyone in the world to do it. My dear boy, I'm awfully stupid about that. You wouldn't believe it. Awfully. You see, however stupid I am about it, I keep thinking, I keep thinking—from time to time, of course, not all the while. It's impossible, I think, for the devils to forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. Then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? Made of what? Iron hooks? Where do they forge them? Do they have a foundry there of some sort? The monks in the monastery probably believe that there's a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I'm ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. It makes it more refined, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And, after all, what does it matter whether it has a ceiling or not? But, you know, there's a damnable question bound up in it. If there's no ceiling there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks it all breaks down, which is unlikely in turn, because then there'd be no one to drag me down to hell, and if they don't drag me down, what justice is there in the world? Il faudrait les inventer, those hooks, on purpose for me alone, because, if only you knew, Alyosha, what a blackguard I am."

4.12.oldText: "But there are no hooks there," said Alyosha, looking gently and seriously at his father.

4.13.oldText: "Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That's how a Frenchman described hell: 'J'ai vu l'ombre d'un cocher qui avec l'ombre d'une brosse frottait l'ombre d'une carrosse.' How do you know there are no hooks, darling? When you've lived with the monks you'll sing a different tune. But go and find out the truth there, and then come and tell me. It's easier going to the other world, anyway, if one knows what's there. Besides, it will be more seemly for you with the monks than here with me, with a drunken old man and young harlots ... though you're like an angel, nothing touches you. And I dare say nothing will touch you there. That's why I let you go, because I'm counting on that. You've got all your wits about you. You'll burn and you'll burn out; you'll be healed and come back again. And I'll wait for you. I feel you're the only creature in the world who hasn't condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can't help feeling it."

4.14.oldText: And he even began blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.

5.0.oldText: Some of my readers may imagine my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, poorly developed creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. On the contrary, Alyosha was at this time a well-built, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, radiant with health. He was very handsome too—graceful, moderately tall, with hair of a dark brown, a regular, rather long, oval face, and wide-set, dark gray, shining eyes; he was very thoughtful, and apparently very serene. It will perhaps be said that red cheeks are not incompatible with fanaticism and mysticism; but I suspect Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt, in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but in my view miracles are never a stumbling block to the realist. It is not miracles that dispose realists to belief. The genuine realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and the capacity to disbelieve in the miraculous, and if he is confronted with a miracle as an irrefutable fact, he would rather disbelieve his own senses than admit the fact. Even if he admits it, he admits it as a natural fact that was until then unknown to him. Faith does not, in the realist, spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once the realist believes, he is then bound by his very realism to admit the miraculous as well. The Apostle Thomas said he would not believe until he saw, but once he did see he said, "My Lord and my God!" Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not; he believed solely because he wished to believe, and possibly he already believed fully in his secret heart even when he said, "I do not believe till I see."

5.1.oldText: I may be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, didn't finish his studies, and so on. That he didn't finish his studies is true, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I'll simply repeat what I've said above. He set out on this path only because, at that time, it alone struck his imagination and presented itself as the ideal means of escape for his soul from darkness to light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a youth of our latest epoch—that is, honest by nature, desiring the truth, seeking it and believing in it, and seeking to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul, seeking immediate action and ready to sacrifice everything, life itself, for it. Though these young men unfortunately fail to understand that the sacrifice of life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices, and that to sacrifice, say, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set before them as their goal—such a sacrifice is utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose lay in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he reflected seriously he was convinced of the existence of God and immortality, and at once he instinctively said to himself: "I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise." In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question; it is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form taken by atheism today, the question of the Tower of Babel built without God, not to reach heaven from earth but to set up heaven on earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: "Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect."

5.2.oldText: Alyosha said to himself: "I can't give two roubles instead of 'all,' and only go to mass instead of 'following Him.'" Perhaps his childhood memories brought back our monastery, to which his mother may have taken him to mass. Perhaps the slanting sunlight and the holy image to which his poor "crazy" mother had held him up still worked on his imagination. Brooding over these things, he may have come to us merely to see whether here he could sacrifice all or only "two roubles," and in the monastery he encountered this elder. I must digress to explain what an "elder" is in Russian monasteries, and I'm sorry that I don't feel particularly competent to do so. I'll try, however, to give a superficial account of it in a few words. Authorities on the subject assert that the institution of "elders" is of recent date, not more than a hundred years old in our monasteries, though in the Orthodox East, especially in Sinai and Athos, it has existed for over a thousand years. It's claimed that it also existed in ancient times in Russia, but through the calamities that overtook Russia—the Tatars, civil war, the interruption of relations with the East after the destruction of Constantinople—this institution fell into oblivion. It was revived among us toward the end of the last century by one of the great "ascetics," as they called him, Païssy Velitchkovsky, and his disciples. But to this day it exists in only a few monasteries, and has sometimes been almost persecuted as an innovation in Russia. It flourished especially at the celebrated Kozelski Optin Monastery. When and how it was introduced into our monastery I can't say. There had already been three such elders, and Zossima was the last of them. But he was almost dying from weakness and disease, and they had no one to take his place. The question for our monastery was an important one, because until then it had not been distinguished by anything in particular: they had neither relics of saints, nor wonder-working icons, nor glorious traditions, nor historical exploits. It had flourished and been celebrated throughout Russia because of its elders, to see and hear whom pilgrims had flocked for thousands of miles from all parts.

5.3.oldText: What was such an elder? An elder was one who took your soul, your will, into his soul and his will. When you choose an elder, you renounce your own will and yield it to him in complete submission, complete self-abnegation. This novitiate, this terrible school of self-abnegation, is undertaken voluntarily, in the hope of self-conquest, of self-mastery, in order, after a life of obedience, to attain perfect freedom—that is, freedom from self; to escape the fate of those who have lived their whole life without finding their true selves within themselves. This institution of elders is not founded on theory, but was established in the East from the practice of a thousand years. The obligations due to an elder are not the ordinary "obedience" that has always existed in our Russian monasteries. The obligation involves confession to the elder by all who have submitted themselves to him, and an indissoluble bond between him and them.

5.4.oldText: The story is told, for instance, that in the early days of Christianity one such novice, failing to fulfill some command laid on him by his elder, left his monastery in Syria and went to Egypt. There, after great feats, he was at last found worthy to suffer torture and a martyr's death for the faith. When the Church, regarding him as a saint, was burying him, suddenly, at the deacon's exhortation, "Depart all ye unbaptized," the coffin containing the martyr's body left its place and was cast out of the church, and this happened three times. And only at last was it learned that this holy man had broken his vow of obedience and left his elder, and therefore, despite his great deeds, could not be forgiven without the elder's absolution. Only after this could the funeral take place. This, of course, is only an old legend. But here is a recent instance.

5.5.oldText: A monk was suddenly commanded by his elder to leave Athos, which he loved as a sacred place and a haven of refuge, and to go first to Jerusalem to do homage to the Holy Places and then to travel to the north, to Siberia: "There is the place for thee, and not here." The monk, overwhelmed with sorrow, went to the Ecumenical Patriarch at Constantinople and begged him to release him from his obedience. But the Patriarch replied that not only was he unable to release him, but there was not, and could not be, any power on earth to release him except the elder who had himself laid that duty on him. In this way elders are vested, in certain cases, with unbounded and inexplicable authority. That is why in many of our monasteries the institution was at first resisted almost to the point of persecution. Meanwhile the elders at once began to be held in the highest esteem among the people. Masses of the common folk, as well as distinguished men, flocked, for instance, to the elders of our monastery to confess their doubts, their sins, and their sufferings, and to ask for counsel and guidance. Seeing this, the opponents of the elders declared that the sacrament of confession was being arbitrarily and frivolously degraded, though the continual opening of the heart to the elder by the monk or the layman had nothing of the character of the sacrament. In the end, however, the institution of elders has been retained and is becoming established in Russian monasteries. It is true, perhaps, that this instrument, which has stood the test of a thousand years for the moral regeneration of a man from slavery to freedom and to moral perfectibility, may be a double-edged weapon, and it may lead some not to humility and complete self-control but to the most Satanic pride—that is, to bondage and not to freedom.

5.6.oldText: The elder Zossima was sixty-five. He came from a family of landowners, had served in the army in his early youth, and served in the Caucasus as an officer. He had, no doubt, impressed Alyosha by some peculiar quality of his soul. Alyosha lived in the cell of the elder, who was very fond of him and let him wait on him. It should be noted that Alyosha was bound by no obligation and could go wherever he pleased and be absent for whole days. Though he wore the monastic dress, it was voluntarily, simply to avoid being different from the others. No doubt he liked to do so. Possibly his youthful imagination was deeply stirred by the power and fame of his elder. It was said that so many people had for years come to confess their sins to Father Zossima, and to entreat him for words of advice and healing, that he had acquired the keenest intuition and could tell from an unknown face what the newcomer wanted and what suffering lay on his conscience. He sometimes astonished and almost alarmed his visitors by his knowledge of their secrets before they had spoken a word.

5.7.oldText: Alyosha noticed that many, almost all, went in to the elder for the first time with apprehension and uneasiness, but came out with bright and happy faces. Alyosha was particularly struck by the fact that Father Zossima was not at all stern. On the contrary, he was almost always cheerful. The monks used to say that he was more drawn to those who were more sinful, and the greater the sinner, the more he loved him. There were, no doubt, up to the end of his life, some among the monks who hated and envied him, but they were few in number and they were silent, though among them were some of great dignity in the monastery—one, for instance, of the older monks, distinguished for his strict keeping of fasts and vows of silence. But the majority were on Father Zossima's side, and very many of them loved him with all their hearts, warmly and sincerely. Some were almost fanatically devoted to him, and declared, though not quite aloud, that he was a saint, that there could be no doubt of it, and, seeing that his end was near, they anticipated miracles and great glory to the monastery in the immediate future from his relics. Alyosha had unquestioning faith in the miraculous power of the elder, just as he had unquestioning faith in the story of the coffin that flew out of the church. He saw many who came with sick children or relatives and begged the elder to lay hands on them and pray over them, return shortly afterwards—some the next day—and, falling in tears at the elder's feet, thank him for healing their sick.

5.8.oldText: Whether they had really been healed or were simply better in the natural course of the disease was a question that did not exist for Alyosha, because he fully believed in the spiritual power of his teacher and rejoiced in his fame, in his glory, as though it were his own triumph. His heart throbbed, and he seemed to beam all over when the elder came out to the gates of the hermitage into the waiting crowd of pilgrims of the humbler class who had flocked from all parts of Russia expressly to see the elder and receive his blessing. They fell down before him, wept, kissed his feet, kissed the earth on which he stood, and wailed, while the women held up their children to him and brought him the sick "possessed with devils." The elder spoke to them, read a brief prayer over them, blessed them, and dismissed them. Lately he had become so weak from attacks of illness that he was sometimes unable to leave his cell, and the pilgrims waited for him to come out for several days. Alyosha did not wonder why they loved him so, why they fell down before him and wept with emotion merely at seeing his face. Oh, he understood that for the humble soul of the Russian peasant, worn out by grief and toil, and still more by the everlasting injustice and everlasting sin, his own and the world's, it was the greatest need and comfort to find someone or something holy to fall down before and worship.

5.9.oldText: "Among us there is sin, injustice, and temptation, but yet, somewhere on earth there is someone holy and exalted. He has the truth; he knows the truth; so it is not dead upon the earth; so it will come one day to us too, and rule over all the earth according to the promise."

5.10.oldText: Alyosha knew that this was exactly how the people felt and even reasoned. He understood it, but that the elder Zossima was this saint and custodian of God's truth—of that he had no more doubt than the weeping peasants and the sick women who held out their children to the elder. The conviction that after his death the elder would bring extraordinary glory to the monastery was even stronger in Alyosha than in anyone there, and, lately, a kind of deep flame of inner ecstasy burned more and more strongly in his heart. He was not at all troubled that this elder stood as a solitary example before him.

5.11.oldText: "No matter. He is holy. He carries in his heart the secret of renewal for all: that power which will, at last, establish truth on the earth, and all men will be holy and love one another, and there will be no more rich nor poor, no exalted nor humbled, but all will be as the children of God, and the true Kingdom of Christ will come." That was the dream in Alyosha's heart.

5.12.oldText: The arrival of his two brothers, whom he had not known until then, seemed to make a great impression on Alyosha. He made friends more quickly with his half-brother Dmitri (though he arrived later) than with his own brother Ivan. He was extremely interested in his brother Ivan, but when the latter had been in the town for two months, though they had met fairly often, they were still not intimate. Alyosha was naturally silent, and he seemed to be expecting something, ashamed about something, while his brother Ivan, though Alyosha noticed at first that he looked at him long and curiously, seemed to have soon left off thinking of him. Alyosha noticed it with some embarrassment. He attributed his brother's indifference at first to the disparity of their age and education. But he also wondered whether the absence of curiosity and sympathy in Ivan might be due to some other cause entirely unknown to him. He kept imagining that Ivan was absorbed in something—something inward and important—that he was striving toward some goal, perhaps very hard to attain, and that that was why he had no thought for him. Alyosha wondered, too, whether there wasn't some contempt on the part of the learned atheist for him—a foolish novice. He knew for certain that his brother was an atheist. He could not take offense at this contempt, if it existed; yet, with an uneasy embarrassment which he himself did not understand, he waited for his brother to come closer to him. Dmitri used to speak of Ivan with the deepest respect and with a peculiar earnestness. From him Alyosha learned all the details of the important affair that had lately formed such a close and remarkable bond between the two elder brothers. Dmitri's enthusiastic references to Ivan were all the more striking in Alyosha's eyes since Dmitri was, compared with Ivan, almost uneducated, and the two brothers were such a contrast in personality and character that it would be difficult to find two men more unlike.

5.13.oldText: It was at this time that the meeting—or rather, gathering—of the members of this inharmonious family took place in the cell of the elder who had such an extraordinary influence on Alyosha. The pretext for this gathering was a false one. At this time the discord between Dmitri and his father seemed at its most acute stage and their relations had become insufferably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to suggest, apparently in jest, that they should all meet in Father Zossima's cell, and that, without appealing to his direct intervention, they might more decently come to an understanding under the conciliating influence of the elder's presence. Dmitri, who had never seen the elder, naturally supposed that his father was trying to intimidate him, but, since he secretly blamed himself for his outbursts of temper with his father on several recent occasions, he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that, unlike Ivan, he was not staying with his father, but living apart at the other end of town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at the time, eagerly seized on the idea. A Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and atheist, he may have been led on by boredom or the hope of frivolous diversion. He was suddenly seized by the desire to see the monastery and the holy man. Since his lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, he made it the pretext for seeing the Superior, in order to try to settle it amicably. A visitor coming with such laudable intentions might be received with more attention and consideration than one who came out of simple curiosity. Influences from within the monastery were brought to bear on the elder, who lately had scarcely left his cell and had been forced by illness to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he consented to see them, and the day was fixed.

5.14.oldText: "Who has made me a judge over them?" was all he said, smilingly, to Alyosha.

5.15.oldText: Alyosha was much troubled when he heard of the proposed visit. Of all the wrangling, quarrelsome party, Dmitri was the only one who could take the interview seriously. All the others would come from frivolous motives, perhaps insulting to the elder. Alyosha was well aware of that. Ivan and Miüsov would come out of curiosity, perhaps of the coarsest kind, while his father might be planning some piece of buffoonery. Though he said nothing, Alyosha thoroughly understood his father. The boy, I repeat, was far from being as simple as everyone thought him. He awaited the day with a heavy heart. No doubt he was always pondering in his mind how the family discord could be ended. But his chief anxiety was for the elder. He trembled for him, for his glory, and dreaded any affront to him, especially the refined, courteous irony of Miüsov and the supercilious half-utterances of the highly educated Ivan. He even thought of venturing to warn the elder, to tell him something about them, but, on second thoughts, said nothing. He only sent word the day before, through a friend, to his brother Dmitri, that he loved him and expected him to keep his promise. Dmitri wondered, for he could not remember what he had promised, but he answered by letter that he would do his utmost not to let himself be provoked "by vileness," but that, although he had a deep respect for the elder and for his brother Ivan, he was convinced the meeting was either a trap for him or an unworthy farce.

5.16.oldText: "Nevertheless I would rather bite out my tongue than be lacking in respect for the saintly man whom you revere so highly," he wrote in conclusion. Alyosha was not much cheered by the letter.

6.0.oldText: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The interview with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors did not take part in the service, but arrived just as it was ending. First an elegant open carriage, drawn by two valuable horses, drove up with Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. This young man was preparing to enter the university. Miüsov, with whom he was staying at the time, was trying to persuade him to go abroad to the university of Zurich or Jena. The young man was still undecided. He was thoughtful and distracted. He was nice-looking, strongly built, and rather tall. There was a strange fixity in his gaze at times. Like all very absent-minded people, he would sometimes stare at a person without seeing him. He was silent and rather awkward, but sometimes, when he was alone with someone, he became talkative and effusive, and would laugh at anything or nothing. But his liveliness vanished as quickly as it appeared. He was always well and even elaborately dressed; he already had some independent fortune and expectations of much more. He was a friend of Alyosha's.

6.1.oldText: In an ancient, jolting, but roomy hired carriage, drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses, a long way behind Miüsov's carriage, came Fyodor Pavlovitch, with his son Ivan. Dmitri was late, though he had been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriages at the hotel outside the precincts and went to the gates of the monastery on foot. Except for Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of the party had ever seen the monastery, and Miüsov had probably not been to church for thirty years. He looked around him with curiosity and an assumed ease. But apart from the church and the domestic buildings, which were ordinary enough, he found nothing of interest in the monastery's interior. The last of the worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded and crossing themselves. Among the humbler people were a few of higher rank—two or three ladies and a very old general. They were all staying at the hotel. Our visitors were at once surrounded by beggars, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov, who took a ten-copeck piece out of his purse, and, nervous and embarrassed—God knows why!—hurriedly gave it to an old woman, saying, "Divide it equally." None of his companions made any remark about it, so he had no reason to be embarrassed; but, noticing this, he was even more overcome.

6.2.oldText: It was strange that their arrival did not seem expected, and that they were not received with any particular honor, though one of them had recently made a donation of a thousand roubles, while another was a very wealthy and highly cultured landowner, on whom everyone in the monastery was in a sense dependent, since a decision in the lawsuit might at any moment put their fishing rights in his hands. Yet no official personage met them.

6.3.oldText: Miüsov looked absent-mindedly at the tombstones around the church, and was about to remark that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right of lying in this "holy place," but refrained. His liberal irony was rapidly changing almost into anger.

6.4.oldText: "Who the devil is there to ask in this imbecile place? We must find out, because time is passing," he observed suddenly, as if to himself.

6.5.oldText: All at once a bald-headed, elderly man came up, with ingratiating little eyes, wearing a full summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself with a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner of Tula. He at once grasped our visitors' difficulty.

6.6.oldText: "Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, apart, four hundred paces from the monastery, on the other side of the copse."

6.7.oldText: "I know it's on the other side of the copse," observed Fyodor Pavlovitch, "but we don't remember the way. It's been a long time since we've been here."

6.8.oldText: "This way, by this gate, and straight across the copse ... the copse. Come with me, won't you? I'll show you. I have to go.... I'm going there myself. This way, this way."

6.9.oldText: They came out of the gate and turned toward the copse. Maximov, a man of sixty, was practically running rather than walking, turning sideways to stare at them all, with an incredible degree of nervous curiosity. His eyes looked like they were starting out of his head.

6.10.oldText: "You see, we have come to the elder on business of our own," observed Miüsov severely. "That personage has granted us an audience, so to speak, and so, though we thank you for showing us the way, we cannot ask you to accompany us."

6.11.oldText: "I've been there. I've been already; un chevalier parfait," and Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.

6.13.oldText: "The elder, the splendid elder, the elder! The honor and glory of the monastery, Zossima. Such an elder!"

6.14.oldText: But his incoherent chatter was cut short by a very pale, wan-looking monk of medium height, wearing a monk's cap, who overtook them. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.

6.15.oldText: The monk, with an extremely courteous, profound bow, announced:

6.16.oldText: "The Father Superior invites all of you gentlemen to dine with him after your visit to the hermitage. At one o'clock, not later. And you as well," he added, addressing Maximov.

6.17.oldText: "That I certainly will, without fail," cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, hugely delighted at the invitation. "And, believe me, we've all given our word to behave properly here.... And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go, too?"

6.18.oldText: "Yes, of course. What have I come for but to study all the customs here? The only obstacle is your company...."

6.19.oldText: "Yes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch is non-existent as yet."

6.20.oldText: "It would be a capital thing if he didn't turn up. Do you suppose I like all this business, and in your company, too? So we will come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior," he said to the monk.

6.21.oldText: "No, it is my duty now to conduct you to the elder," answered the monk.

6.22.oldText: "In that case, I'll go straight to the Father Superior—to the Father Superior," babbled Maximov.

6.23.oldText: "The Father Superior is engaged just now. But as you please—" the monk hesitated.

6.24.oldText: "Impertinent old man!" Miüsov observed aloud, while Maximov ran back to the monastery.

6.25.oldText: "He's like von Sohn," Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.

6.26.oldText: "Is that all you can think of?... In what way is he like von Sohn? Have you ever seen von Sohn?"

6.27.oldText: "I've seen his portrait. It's not the features, but something indefinable. He's a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy."

6.28.oldText: "Ah, I dare say you're a connoisseur in that. But, look here, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you said just now that we had given our word to behave properly. Remember it. I advise you to control yourself. But if you begin to play the fool I don't intend to be associated with you here.... You see what a man he is"—he turned to the monk—"I'm afraid to go among decent people with him." A fine smile, not without a certain slyness, came to the pale, bloodless lips of the monk, but he made no reply, and was evidently silent from a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned more than ever.

6.29.oldText: "Oh, devil take them all! An outer show elaborated over centuries, and nothing but charlatanism and nonsense underneath," flashed through Miüsov's mind.

6.30.oldText: "Here's the hermitage. We've arrived," cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. "The gates are shut."

6.31.oldText: And he repeatedly made the sign of the cross to the saints painted above and on the sides of the gates.

6.32.oldText: "When you go to Rome you must do as the Romans do. Here in this hermitage there are twenty-five saints being saved. They look at one another and eat cabbages. And not one woman passes through this gate. That's what's remarkable. And that really is so. But I did hear that the elder receives ladies," he remarked suddenly to the monk.

6.33.oldText: "Women of the common people are here too now, lying in the portico there waiting. But for ladies of higher rank two rooms have been built adjoining the portico, but outside the precincts—you can see the windows—and the elder goes out to them by an inner passage when he is well enough. They are always outside the precincts. There is a Harkov lady, Madame Hohlakov, waiting there now with her sick daughter. Probably he has promised to come out to her, though lately he has been so weak that he has hardly even shown himself to the common people."

6.34.oldText: "So there are loopholes, after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don't suppose, holy father, that I mean any harm. But do you know that at Athos not only are the visits of women forbidden, but no creature of the female sex—no hens, nor turkey-hens, nor cows."

6.35.oldText: "Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you I shall go back and leave you here. They'll throw you out when I'm gone."

6.36.oldText: "But I'm not interfering with you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look," he cried suddenly, stepping within the precincts, "what a vale of roses they live in!"

6.37.oldText: Though there were no roses now, there were numbers of rare and beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was space for them, and evidently tended by a skillful hand; there were flower-beds around the church, and between the tombs; and the one-story wooden house where the elder lived was also surrounded with flowers.

6.38.oldText: "And was it like this in the time of the last elder, Varsonofy? He didn't care for such elegance. They say he used to jump up and thrash even ladies with a stick," observed Fyodor Pavlovitch, as he went up the steps.

6.39.oldText: "The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a great deal of what's told about him is foolishness. He never thrashed anyone," answered the monk. "Now, gentlemen, if you will wait a minute I'll announce you."

6.40.oldText: "Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time, your compact, do you hear? Behave properly or I will pay you out!" Miüsov had time to mutter again.

6.41.oldText: "I can't think why you're so agitated," Fyodor Pavlovitch observed sarcastically. "Are you uneasy about your sins? They say he can tell from one's eyes what one has come about. And what a lot you think of their opinion! you, a Parisian, and so advanced. I'm surprised at you."

6.42.oldText: But Miüsov had no time to reply to this sarcasm. They were asked to come in. He walked in, somewhat irritated.
