34.2.oldText: “Let me have some soup, and tea afterward — I'm hungry,” Alyosha said cheerfully.

34.3.oldText: “And cherry jam? They have it here. Do you remember how you loved cherry jam when you were little?”

34.4.oldText: “You remember that? Let me have jam too — I still like it.”

34.5.oldText: Ivan rang for the waiter and ordered soup, jam, and tea.

34.6.oldText: “I remember everything, Alyosha. I remember you up until you were eleven — I was nearly fifteen. There's such a difference between fifteen and eleven that brothers are never companions at those ages. I don't even know whether I was fond of you. When I went away to Moscow, for the first few years I didn't think of you at all. Then when you came to Moscow yourself, we only met once, somewhere, I think. And now I've been here more than three months, and so far we've barely said a word to each other. Tomorrow I'm leaving, and I was just sitting here thinking how I might see you to say goodbye, and just then you walked by.”

34.7.oldText: “Were you really that eager to see me, then?”

34.8.oldText: “Very. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. And then to say goodbye. I believe it's always best to get to know people just before you leave them. I've seen how you've been looking at me these last three months. There's been a constant look of expectation in your eyes, and I can't stand that. That's why I've kept away from you. But in the end I've come to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. I may be laughing, but I'm serious. You do stand firm, don't you? I like people who stand firm like that, whatever it is they stand for, even if they're just such little fellows as you are. Your expectant eyes stopped annoying me — I grew fond of them in the end, those expectant eyes. You seem to love me for some reason, Alyosha?”

34.9.oldText: “I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you — Ivan is a tomb! I say: Ivan is a riddle. You're a riddle to me even now. But I understand something in you, and I didn't understand it until this morning.”

34.11.oldText: “You won't be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.

34.13.oldText: “That you are just as young as any other young man of twenty-three — that you're just a young and fresh and nice boy, green, in fact! Now, have I insulted you horribly?”

34.14.oldText: “On the contrary, I'm struck by a coincidence,” Ivan cried, warmly and good-humoredly. “Would you believe that ever since that scene with her, I've thought of nothing but my own youthful greenness — and just as though you guessed it, you bring it up. Do you know I've been sitting here thinking: even if I didn't believe in life, if I lost faith in the woman I love, lost faith in the order of things, were in fact convinced that everything is a disorderly, damnable, and perhaps devil-ridden chaos, if I were struck by every horror of man's disillusionment — still I would want to live, and having once tasted the cup, I wouldn't turn away from it until I'd drained it! At thirty, though, I'm sure to set down the cup, even if I haven't emptied it, and turn away — where, I don't know. But until I'm thirty, I know that my youth will triumph over everything — every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I've asked myself many times whether there is any despair in the world that could overcome this frantic, and perhaps unseemly, thirst for life in me, and I've come to the conclusion that there isn't — at least not until I'm thirty, and then I'll lose it on my own, I suspect. Some driveling consumptive moralists — and poets especially — often call that thirst for life base. It's a Karamazov trait, this thirst for life regardless of everything; no doubt you have it too — but why is it base? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. Though I may not believe in the order of the universe, still I love the sticky little leaves as they open in spring. I love the blue sky, I love certain people — people one sometimes loves, you know, without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though perhaps I've long ceased to have any faith in them; still, out of old habit one's heart treasures them. Here, they've brought your soup — eat it, it'll do you good. It's first-rate soup; they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha; I'll set off from here. And yet I know I'm only going to a graveyard — but it's a most precious graveyard, that's what it is! Precious are the dead who lie there; every stone over them speaks of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, and their science, that I know I'll fall to the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them — even though in my heart I'm convinced that it's long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won't weep out of despair, but simply because I'll be happy in my tears — I'll steep my soul in that feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky — that's what it is. It's not a matter of intellect or logic; it's loving with one's insides, with one's gut. One loves the first strength of one's youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan suddenly laughed.

34.15.oldText: “I understand it only too well, Ivan. One longs to love with one's insides, with one's gut. You put that so well, and I'm awfully glad that you have such a longing for life,” Alyosha cried. “I think everyone should love life above everything else in the world.”

34.17.oldText: “Absolutely — love it regardless of logic, as you say; it has to be regardless of logic, and only then will one understand its meaning. I've thought so for a long time. Half your work is done, Ivan — you love life; now you only have to try the second half, and you're saved.”

34.18.oldText: “You're trying to save me, but perhaps I'm not lost! And what do you mean by your second half?”

34.19.oldText: “Why, one has to raise up your dead, who perhaps haven't died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I'm so glad we're talking, Ivan.”

34.20.oldText: “I see you're feeling inspired. I'm awfully fond of such _professions de foi_ from such — novices. You're a steadfast person, Alexey. Is it true you mean to leave the monastery?”

34.21.oldText: “Yes, my elder is sending me out into the world.”

34.22.oldText: “Then we'll see each other in the world. We'll meet before I'm thirty, when I'll start turning away from the cup. Father doesn't want to turn away from his cup till he's seventy; he dreams of hanging on to eighty, in fact — so he says. He means it all too seriously, buffoon though he is. He stands on a firm rock too — he stands on his sensuality, though after thirty, indeed, there may be nothing else to stand on.... But to hang on to seventy is vile; better to stop at thirty — one could retain ‘a shadow of nobility’ by deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?”

34.23.oldText: “No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” and Alyosha quickly but in detail described his encounter with Smerdyakov. Ivan began listening anxiously and questioned him.

34.24.oldText: “But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he'd told me about him,” Alyosha added. Ivan frowned and thought it over.

34.25.oldText: “Are you frowning because of Smerdyakov?” Alyosha asked.

34.26.oldText: “Yes, because of him. Damn him — I really did want to see Dmitri, but now there's no need,” Ivan said reluctantly.

34.27.oldText: “But are you really going so soon, brother?”

34.29.oldText: “What about Dmitri and father? How is it going to end?” Alyosha asked anxiously.

34.30.oldText: “You're always harping on that! What do I have to do with it? Am I my brother Dmitri's keeper?” Ivan snapped irritably, but then suddenly gave a bitter smile. “Cain's answer about his murdered brother, wasn't it? Perhaps that's what you're thinking at this moment? Well, damn it all, I can't stay here to be their keeper, can I? I've finished what I had to do, and I'm going. Do you think I'm jealous of Dmitri — that for the past three months I've been trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna? Nonsense, I had business of my own. I finished it. I'm going. I finished it just now — you were a witness.”

34.32.oldText: “Yes, and I've set myself free once and for all. And after all, what do I have to do with Dmitri? Dmitri doesn't enter into it. I had my own business to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know, on the contrary, that Dmitri behaved as if there were some understanding between us. I never asked him to do it, but he solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. The whole thing is absurd. Ah, Alyosha, if you only knew how light my heart is now! Would you believe it, I was sitting here eating my dinner and was on the verge of ordering champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Tfoo! It's been going on nearly six months, and all at once I've thrown it off. Even yesterday I'd never have guessed how easy it would be to put an end to it if I wanted to.”

34.34.oldText: “About my love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady, I tormented myself over her, and she tormented me. I sat brooding over her ... and all at once it collapsed! I spoke this morning with inspiration, but then I left and roared with laughter. Would you believe it? Yes, it's the literal truth.”

34.35.oldText: “You seem very cheerful about it now,” observed Alyosha, looking into his face, which had suddenly brightened.

34.36.oldText: “But how could I know that I didn't care for her in the slightest? Ha ha! It turns out that after all, I didn't. And yet how she drew me! How attractive she was just now when I made my speech! And do you know, she attracts me terribly even now — and yet how easy it is to leave her. Do you think I'm bragging?”

34.38.oldText: “Alyosha,” Ivan laughed, “don't philosophize about love — it doesn't suit you. How you plunged into the discussion this morning! I forgot to kiss you for it.... But how she tormented me! It really was sitting at the side of a ‘laceration.’ Ah, she knew how I loved her! She loved me, not Dmitri,” Ivan insisted gaily. “Her feeling for Dmitri was simply a self-laceration. Everything I told her just now was perfectly true — but the worst of it is, it may take her fifteen or twenty years to realize that she doesn't care for Dmitri and loves me, whom she torments — and perhaps she'll never realize it at all, despite the lesson she got today. Well, it's better this way; I can simply go away for good. By the way, how is she now? What happened after I left?”

34.39.oldText: Alyosha told him she had become hysterical, and that he'd heard she was now unconscious and delirious.

34.42.oldText: “I'll have to find out. Nobody dies of hysterics, though. It doesn't matter. God gave women hysterics as a relief. I won't go to her at all. Why push myself forward again?”

34.43.oldText: “But you told her that she'd never cared for you.”

34.44.oldText: “I did that on purpose. Alyosha, shall I call for champagne? Let's drink to my freedom. Ah, if you only knew how glad I am!”

34.45.oldText: “No, brother, we'd better not drink,” Alyosha said suddenly. “Besides, I feel somehow depressed.”

34.46.oldText: “Yes, you've been depressed for a long time; I've noticed.”

34.47.oldText: “So you've decided to leave in the morning, then?”

34.48.oldText: “Morning? I didn't say I was going in the morning.... But perhaps I will. Would you believe it, I only dined here today to avoid dining with the old man — I loathe him so much. As far as he's concerned, I'd have left long ago. But why are you so worried about my leaving? We've got plenty of time before I go — an eternity!”

34.49.oldText: “If you're leaving tomorrow, what do you mean by an eternity?”

34.50.oldText: “But what does that matter to us?” Ivan laughed. “We've got enough time for our talk, for what brought us here. Why do you look so surprised? Answer me: why have we met here? To talk of my love for Katerina Ivanovna, of the old man and Dmitri? Of foreign travel? Of the fatal position of Russia? Of the Emperor Napoleon? Is that it?”

34.52.oldText: “Then you know what for. It's different for other people, but we — in our green youth — have to settle the eternal questions first of all. That's what we care about. Young Russia is talking about nothing but the eternal questions now. And just when the old folks are all taken up with practical questions. Why have you been looking at me expectantly for the last three months? To ask me, ‘What do you believe, or don't you believe at all?’ That's what your eyes have been meaning for these three months, isn't it?”

34.53.oldText: “Perhaps so,” Alyosha smiled. “You're not laughing at me now, are you, Ivan?”

34.54.oldText: “Me, laughing? I don't want to wound my little brother, who's been watching me with such expectation for three months. Alyosha, look me straight in the eye! Of course I'm just such a little boy as you are, only not a novice. And what have Russian boys been doing up to now — some of them, I mean? In this stinking tavern, for instance — right here — they meet and sit down in a corner. They've never met before in their lives, and when they leave the tavern, they won't meet again for forty years. And what do they talk about in that brief pause in the tavern? About the eternal questions — about the existence of God and immortality. And those who don't believe in God talk about socialism or anarchism, about transforming all humanity on a new pattern — so it all comes to the same thing; they're the same questions turned inside out. And masses, masses of the most original Russian boys do nothing but talk about the eternal questions! Isn't it so?”

34.55.oldText: “Yes, for true Russians the questions of God's existence and of immortality, or, as you say, the same questions turned inside out, come first and foremost, of course, and so they should,” Alyosha said, still watching his brother with the same gentle, inquiring smile.

34.56.oldText: “Well, Alyosha, it's sometimes very unwise to be Russian at all — but you can hardly imagine anything stupider than the way Russian boys spend their time. Yet there's one Russian boy named Alyosha whom I'm awfully fond of.”

34.57.oldText: “How nicely you slipped that in!” Alyosha laughed suddenly.

34.58.oldText: “Well, tell me where to begin — give the orders. The existence of God, eh?”

34.59.oldText: “Begin wherever you like. You declared yesterday at father's that there is no God.” Alyosha looked searchingly at his brother.

34.60.oldText: “I said that yesterday at dinner on purpose, to tease you, and I saw your eyes glow. But now I've no objection to discussing it with you, and I say that very seriously. I want to be friends with you, Alyosha, because I have no friends and want to try having one. Well, just imagine — perhaps I too accept God,” Ivan laughed; “that's a surprise to you, isn't it?”

34.61.oldText: “Yes, of course, if you're not joking now.”

34.62.oldText: “Joking? I was told at the elder's yesterday that I was joking. You know, dear boy, there was an old sinner in the eighteenth century who declared that if God didn't exist, He would have to be invented. _S'il n'existait pas Dieu, il faudrait l'inventer._ And man has indeed invented God. And what's strange — what would be marvelous — is not that God really exists; the marvel is that such an idea, the idea of the necessity of God, could enter the head of such a savage, vicious beast as man. So holy it is, so touching, so wise, and such a credit to man. As for me, I long ago resolved not to think about whether man created God or God man. And I won't go through all the axioms laid down by Russian boys on the subject, all derived from European hypotheses — because what's a hypothesis there is an axiom for the Russian boy, and not only for the boys but for their teachers too, since our Russian professors are often the very same boys themselves. So I skip all the hypotheses. What are we aiming at now? I'm trying to explain to you as quickly as possible my essential nature — that is, what kind of man I am, what I believe in, and what I hope for. That's it, isn't it? And so I tell you that I simply accept God. But mark this: if God exists and if He really did create the world, then, as we all know, He created it according to the geometry of Euclid and the human mind with the conception of only three dimensions in space. Yet there have been, and still are, geometers and philosophers, even some of the most distinguished, who doubt whether the whole universe — or, to put it more broadly, the whole of being — was created only in Euclid's geometry; they even dare to dream that two parallel lines, which according to Euclid can never meet on earth, may meet somewhere in infinity. I've come to the conclusion that since I can't understand even that, I can't expect to understand about God. I humbly acknowledge that I have no faculty for settling such questions; I have a Euclidian, earthly mind, and how could I solve problems that aren't of this world? And I advise you never to think about it either, my dear Alyosha — especially about God, whether He exists or not. All such questions are completely out of place for a mind created with an idea of only three dimensions. And so I accept God, and am glad to, and what's more, I accept His wisdom, His purpose — which are utterly beyond our understanding; I believe in the underlying order and in the meaning of life; I believe in the eternal harmony in which, they say, we'll one day be blended together. I believe in the Word to which the universe is striving, and which Itself was ‘with God,’ and which Itself is God, and so on, and so on, to infinity. There are all sorts of phrases for it. I seem to be on the right path, don't I? And yet would you believe it, in the final result I don't accept this world of God's, and although I know it exists, I don't accept it at all. It isn't that I don't accept God — you must understand — it's the world created by Him that I don't and can't accept. Let me make this clear. I believe like a child that suffering will be healed and made up for, that all the humiliating absurdity of human contradictions will vanish like a pitiful mirage, like the despicable fabrication of man's impotent and infinitely small Euclidian mind — that in the world's finale, at the moment of eternal harmony, something so precious will come to pass that it will suffice for all hearts, for the consolation of all resentments, for the atonement of all the crimes of humanity, of all the blood they've shed; that it will make it not only possible to forgive, but to justify, all that has happened with men — but even though all that may come to pass, I don't accept it. I won't accept it. Even if parallel lines do meet, and I see it myself, I'll see it and say they've met, but still I won't accept it. That's what's at the root of me, Alyosha; that's my creed. I'm serious about what I say. I began our talk as stupidly as I could on purpose, but I've led up to my confession, because that's all you want. You didn't want to hear about God, but only to know what the brother you love lives by. And so I've told you.”

34.63.oldText: Ivan concluded his long tirade with marked and unexpected feeling.

34.64.oldText: “And why did you begin ‘as stupidly as you could’?” Alyosha asked, looking dreamily at him.

34.65.oldText: “First of all, for the sake of being Russian. Russian conversations on such subjects are always carried on with inconceivable stupidity. And secondly, the stupider one is, the closer to reality. The stupider one is, the clearer one is. Stupidity is brief and artless, while cleverness wriggles and hides itself. Cleverness is a knave, but stupidity is honest and straightforward. I've brought the conversation around to my despair, and the more stupidly I've presented it, the better for me.”

34.66.oldText: “You'll explain why you don't accept the world?” Alyosha said.

34.67.oldText: “Of course I will — it's no secret; that's what I've been leading up to. Dear little brother, I don't want to corrupt you or to shake you from your stronghold; perhaps I want to be healed by you.” Ivan smiled suddenly, exactly like a little gentle child. Alyosha had never seen such a smile on his face before.

35.0.oldText: “I have to make one confession,” Ivan began. “I could never understand how anyone can love their neighbors. It's precisely one's neighbors, to my mind, that one can't love — though one might love those at a distance. I once read somewhere of John the Merciful, a saint, that when a hungry, freezing beggar came to him, he took him into his bed, held him in his arms, and began breathing into his mouth, which was putrid and loathsome from some terrible disease. I'm convinced he did that out of ‘self-laceration,’ out of the self-laceration of falsity, for the sake of the charity imposed by duty, as a penance laid on him. For anyone to love a man, the man has to be hidden — because the moment he shows his face, love is gone.”

35.1.oldText: “Father Zossima has talked about that more than once,” Alyosha observed. “He, too, said that a man's face often prevents many people — people not practiced in love — from loving him. But still, there's a great deal of love in humanity, almost Christ-like love. I know that myself, Ivan.”

35.2.oldText: “Well, I know nothing of it so far, and I can't understand it, and the countless mass of humanity is with me on that. The question is whether it's due to men's bad qualities or whether it's inherent in their nature. To my mind, Christ-like love for men is a miracle impossible on earth. He was God. But we are not gods. Suppose I, for instance, am suffering intensely. Another person can never know how much I suffer, because he is another and not I. And what's more, a man is rarely ready to admit another's suffering (as if it were some kind of distinction). Why won't he admit it, do you think? Because I smell unpleasant, because I have a stupid face, because I once stepped on his foot. Besides, there is suffering and suffering; degrading, humiliating suffering that humbles me — hunger, for instance — my benefactor will perhaps tolerate; but when you come to higher suffering — for an idea, for instance — he'll very rarely admit it, perhaps because my face strikes him as not at all what he imagines a man suffering for an idea ought to look like. And so he instantly withdraws his favor, and not at all from any badness of heart. Beggars, especially genteel beggars, should never show themselves; they should ask for charity through the newspapers instead. One can love one's neighbors in the abstract, or even at a distance, but up close it's almost impossible. If it were like on the stage, in the ballet, where beggars come in wearing silken rags and tattered lace and beg for alms dancing gracefully, then one might enjoy looking at them. But even then we wouldn't love them. But enough of that. I simply wanted to show you my point of view. I meant to speak of the suffering of humanity in general, but we'd better confine ourselves to the sufferings of the children. That reduces the scope of my argument to a tenth of what it would be. Still, we'd better stick to the children, even if it weakens my case. But, in the first place, children can be loved even at close quarters, even when they're dirty, even when they're ugly (though I think children are never ugly). The second reason I won't talk about grown-up people is that, besides being disgusting and unworthy of love, they have a compensation — they've eaten the apple and know good and evil, and they've become ‘like gods.’ They go on eating it still. But children haven't eaten anything, and they are so far innocent. Are you fond of children, Alyosha? I know you are, and you'll understand why I prefer to speak of them. If they, too, suffer horribly on earth, it must be for their fathers' sins, they must be punished for their fathers, who have eaten the apple; but that reasoning belongs to another world and is incomprehensible for the human heart here on earth. The innocent must not suffer for another's sins — and especially such innocents! You may be surprised at me, Alyosha, but I'm awfully fond of children, too. And notice — cruel people, the violent, the rapacious, the Karamazovs, are sometimes very fond of children. Children, while they're still quite small — up to seven, for instance — are so remote from grown-up people; they are, as it were, different creatures, of a different species. I knew a criminal in prison who, in the course of his career as a burglar, had murdered whole families, including several children. But in prison he developed a strange affection for them. He'd spend all his time at his window watching the children playing in the prison yard. He trained one little boy to come up to his window and became great friends with him.... You don't know why I'm telling you all this, Alyosha? My head aches and I'm sad.”

35.3.oldText: “You speak with a strange air,” Alyosha observed uneasily, “as though you weren't quite yourself.”

35.4.oldText: “By the way, a Bulgarian I met recently in Moscow,” Ivan went on, seeming not to hear his brother's words, “told me about the crimes committed by Turks and Circassians all over Bulgaria out of fear of a general Slavic uprising. They burn villages, murder, rape women and children, they nail their prisoners by the ears to the fences, leave them that way until morning, and in the morning hang them — all kinds of things you can't imagine. People sometimes speak of bestial cruelty, but that's a great injustice and an insult to the beasts; a beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. The tiger only tears and gnaws — that's all he can do. He'd never think of nailing people by the ears, even if he could. These Turks also took pleasure in torturing children — cutting the unborn child from its mother's womb, tossing babies into the air and catching them on the points of their bayonets before their mothers' eyes. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the amusement its zest. Here's another scene I found very interesting. Imagine a trembling mother with her baby in her arms, surrounded by a circle of invading Turks. They've planned a little diversion: they pet the baby, laugh to make it laugh. They succeed; the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk points a pistol four inches from the baby's face. The baby laughs with delight, holds out its little hands to the pistol, and he pulls the trigger in the baby's face and blows out its brains. Artistic, wasn't it? By the way, Turks are particularly fond of sweet things, they say.”

35.5.oldText: “Brother, what are you driving at?” Alyosha asked.

35.6.oldText: “I think that if the devil doesn't exist but man has created him, then he has created him in his own image and likeness.”

35.7.oldText: “Just as he did God, then?” Alyosha observed.

35.8.oldText: “‘It's wonderful how you can turn words,’ as Polonius says in _Hamlet_,” Ivan laughed. “You turn my words against me. Well, I'm glad. Yours must be a fine God, if man created Him in his image and likeness. You asked just now what I was driving at. You see, I'm fond of collecting certain facts, and would you believe, I even copy down anecdotes of a certain kind from newspapers and books, and I already have a fine collection. The Turks, naturally, have made it in, but they're foreigners. I have specimens from home that are even better than the Turks. You know we prefer beating — rods and scourges — that's our national institution. Nailing ears is unthinkable for us, because after all, we're Europeans. But the rod and the scourge are always with us and they cannot be taken from us. Abroad now they hardly do any beating at all. Manners are more humane, or laws have been passed, so they don't dare to flog men anymore. But they make up for it in another way, just as national as ours is. And so national that it would be practically impossible among us — though I believe we're being inoculated with it, ever since the religious movement began in our aristocracy. I have a charming pamphlet, translated from the French, describing how, quite recently, five years ago, a murderer named Richard was executed — a young man, I believe, of twenty-three, who repented and was converted to the Christian faith on the very scaffold. This Richard was an illegitimate child who was given away by his parents at the age of six to some shepherds in the Swiss mountains. They brought him up to work for them. He grew up like a little wild beast among them. The shepherds taught him nothing and hardly fed or clothed him, but sent him out at seven to herd the flock in cold and wet, and none of them hesitated or scrupled to treat him that way. Quite the contrary, they thought they had every right, because Richard had been given to them as a piece of property, and they didn't even see the need to feed him. Richard himself describes how in those years, like the Prodigal Son in the Gospel, he longed to eat the mash given to the pigs, which were being fattened for sale. But they wouldn't even give him that, and beat him when he stole from the pigs. And that was how he spent his whole childhood and youth, until he grew up and was strong enough to run away and become a thief. The savage began to earn his living as a day laborer in Geneva. He drank what he earned, he lived like a brute, and finally killed and robbed an old man. He was caught, tried, and condemned to death. They're not sentimentalists there. And in prison he was immediately surrounded by pastors, members of Christian brotherhoods, philanthropic ladies, and the like. They taught him to read and write in prison and expounded the Gospel to him. They exhorted him, worked on him, drummed at him incessantly, until at last he solemnly confessed his crime. He was converted. He wrote to the court himself that he was a monster, but that in the end God had granted him light and shown him grace. All of Geneva was in an uproar over him — all of philanthropic and religious Geneva. All the aristocratic and well-bred society of the town rushed to the prison, kissed Richard and embraced him: ‘You are our brother, you have found grace.’ And Richard does nothing but weep with emotion: ‘Yes, I've found grace! All my youth and childhood I was glad of pigs' food, but now even I have found grace. I'm dying in the Lord.’ ‘Yes, Richard, die in the Lord; you have shed blood and must die. Though it's not your fault that you didn't know the Lord when you coveted the pigs' food and were beaten for stealing it (which was very wrong of you, because stealing is forbidden) — but you've shed blood and you must die.’ And on the last day, Richard, perfectly limp, does nothing but cry and repeat every minute: ‘This is my happiest day. I am going to the Lord.’ ‘Yes,’ cry the pastors and the judges and philanthropic ladies. ‘This is the happiest day of your life, because you're going to the Lord!’ They all walk or drive to the scaffold in procession behind the prison van. At the scaffold they call out to Richard: ‘Die, brother, die in the Lord, for even you have found grace!’ And so, covered with his brothers' kisses, Richard is dragged to the scaffold and led to the guillotine. And they chopped off his head in brotherly fashion, because he had found grace. Yes, that's characteristic. That pamphlet has been translated into Russian by some Russian philanthropists of aristocratic rank and evangelical aspirations, and distributed free of charge for the enlightenment of the common people. The case of Richard is interesting because it's national. Though it's absurd to us to chop off a man's head because he's become our brother and found grace, we have our own specialty, which is almost worse. Our historical pastime is the direct satisfaction of inflicting pain. There are lines in Nekrasov describing how a peasant lashes a horse on the eyes, ‘on its meek eyes’ — everyone must have seen it. It's peculiarly Russian. He describes how a feeble little nag has collapsed under too heavy a load and can't move. The peasant beats it, beats it savagely, at last beating it without even knowing what he's doing in the intoxication of cruelty, thrashing it mercilessly over and over. ‘However weak you are, you must pull, even if it kills you.’ The nag strains, and then he starts lashing the poor defenseless creature on its weeping, on its ‘meek eyes.’ The frantic beast tugs and drags the load, trembling all over, gasping for breath, moving sideways, with a sort of unnatural spasmodic action — it's horrible in Nekrasov. But that's only a horse, and God gave horses to be beaten. So the Tatars taught us, and they left us the knout as a remembrance of it. But men, too, can be beaten. A well-educated, cultured gentleman and his wife beat their own child with a birch rod — a little girl of seven. I have an exact account of it. The papa was glad that the birch was covered with twigs. ‘It stings more,’ he said, and so he began stinging his daughter. I know for a fact that there are people who get worked up with every blow, worked up to sensuality, to literal sensuality that increases progressively with each blow they inflict. They beat for a minute, for five minutes, for ten minutes, more and more often, more and more savagely. The child screams. At last the child can't even scream, it just gasps, ‘Daddy! daddy!’ By some diabolical, grotesque chance the case was brought into court. A lawyer was engaged. The Russian people have long called a barrister ‘a conscience for hire.’ The counsel protests in defense of his client. ‘It's such a simple thing,’ he says, ‘an everyday domestic event. A father corrects his child. To our shame be it said, it has been brought into court.’ The jury, convinced by him, returns a favorable verdict. The public roars with delight that the torturer has been acquitted. Ah, what a pity I wasn't there! I'd have proposed raising a subscription in his honor! Charming little pictures.

35.9.oldText: “But I have still better things about children. I've collected a great, great deal about Russian children, Alyosha. There was a little girl of five who was hated by her father and mother, ‘most worthy and respectable people, of good education and breeding.’ You see, I must say it again: in many people there is this peculiar trait, this love of torturing children, and children only. Toward every other kind of person these torturers behave mildly and benevolently, like cultivated and humane Europeans; but they're very fond of tormenting children — even fond of children themselves in that sense. It's the very defenselessness of the child that tempts the tormentor, the very angelic trust of the child who has no refuge and no one to appeal to, that sets his vile blood on fire. In every man, of course, a demon lies hidden — the demon of rage, the demon of lustful heat at the screams of the tortured victim, the demon of lawlessness let off its chain, the demon of the diseases that follow vice, gout, kidney disease, and so on.

35.10.oldText: “This poor child of five was subjected to every possible torture by those cultivated parents. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason until her body was one bruise. Then they refined their cruelty further — they shut her up all night in the cold and frost in a privy, and because she didn't ask to be let out in the night (as if a child of five, sleeping its angelic, sound sleep, could be trained to wake up and ask), they smeared her face and filled her mouth with excrement — and it was her mother, her own mother, who did it. And that mother could sleep, hearing the poor child's groans! Can you understand why a little creature, who can't even understand what's being done to her, should beat her little aching heart with her tiny fist in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to dear, kind God to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious and humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy must exist and is permitted? Without it, I'm told, man could not have existed on earth, because he could not have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil when it costs so much? Why, the whole world of knowledge is not worth that child's prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing of the sufferings of grown-up people — they've eaten the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I'm making you suffer, Alyosha, you aren't yourself. I'll stop, if you like.”

35.11.oldText: “Never mind. I want to suffer too,” Alyosha muttered.

35.12.oldText: “One picture, just one more, because it's so curious, so characteristic, and I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities. I've forgotten the name — I must look it up. It was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! There was in those days a general of aristocratic connections, the owner of great estates, one of those men — somewhat exceptional, I believe, even then — who, retiring from the service into a life of leisure, are convinced they've earned absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So our general, settled on his property of two thousand souls, lives in pomp and domineers over his poor neighbors as though they were his dependents and buffoons. He has kennels of hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys — all mounted and in uniform. One day a serf boy, a little child of eight, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general's favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone that injured the dog's paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looked the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ He was taken — taken from his mother and kept shut up all night. Early the next morning the general rides out with the hounds, his dependents, dog-boys, and huntsmen, all mounted around him in full hunting parade. The servants are summoned for their edification, and in front of them all stands the mother of the child. The child is brought from the lock-up. It's a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day — a perfect day for hunting. The general orders the child to be undressed; the child is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to cry.... ‘Make him run,’ the general commands. ‘Run! run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he sets the whole pack of hounds on the child. The hounds catch him and tear him to pieces before his mother's eyes!... I believe the general was afterward declared incapable of administering his estates. Well — what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot for the satisfaction of our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”

35.13.oldText: “To be shot,” Alyosha murmured, lifting his eyes to Ivan with a pale, twisted smile.

35.14.oldText: “Bravo!” Ivan cried, delighted. “If even you say so.... You're a fine monk! So there's a little devil sitting in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”

35.16.oldText: “That's just the point — that ‘but’!” Ivan cried. “Let me tell you, novice, that the absurd is only too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and perhaps nothing would ever have come to pass in it without them. We know what we know!”

35.18.oldText: “I understand nothing,” Ivan went on, as if in a delirium. “I don't want to understand anything now. I want to stick to the fact. I made up my mind long ago not to understand. If I try to understand anything, I'll be unfaithful to the fact, and I've determined to stick to the fact.”

35.19.oldText: “Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried with sudden distress. “Will you say what you mean at last?”

35.20.oldText: “Of course I will; that's what I've been leading up to. You are dear to me — I don't want to let you go, and I won't give you up to your Zossima.”

35.21.oldText: Ivan fell silent for a moment, and his face suddenly became very sad.

35.22.oldText: “Listen! I took the case of children only to make my case clearer. Of the other tears of humanity with which the earth is soaked from its crust to its center, I'll say nothing. I've narrowed my subject on purpose. I am a bug, and I recognize in all humility that I can't understand why the world is arranged as it is. Men are themselves to blame, I suppose; they were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, though they knew they would become unhappy — so there's no need to pity them. With my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian understanding, all I know is that there is suffering and that there is no one guilty; that cause follows effect, simply and directly; that everything flows and finds its level — but that's only Euclidian nonsense, I know, and I can't consent to live by it! What comfort is it to me that no one is guilty and that cause follows effect simply and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I'll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and space — but here on earth, and that I could see for myself. I've believed in it. I want to see it, and if I'm dead by then, let me rise again, because if it all happens without me, it will be too unfair. Surely I haven't suffered simply so that I, my crimes and my sufferings, may manure the soil of future harmony for somebody else. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. All the religions of the world are built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children — and what am I to do about them? That's a question I can't answer. For the hundredth time I repeat, there are countless questions, but I've only taken the children, because in their case what I mean is so unanswerably clear. Listen! If all must suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what have the children to do with it, tell me, please? It's beyond all comprehension why they should have to suffer, and why they should pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, furnish material to enrich the soil for the harmony of the future? I understand solidarity in sin among men. I understand solidarity in retribution, too; but there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it's really true that they must share responsibility for all their fathers' crimes, then such a truth is not of this world and is beyond my comprehension. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned — but you see, he didn't grow up; he was torn to pieces by the dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I'm not blaspheming! Of course I understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be when everything in heaven and earth blends in one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘Thou art just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will be reached and all will be made clear. But here's what pulls me up short: I can't accept that harmony. And while I'm still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to that moment, or rise again to see it, I, too, may cry aloud with the rest, looking at the mother embracing the child's torturer, ‘Thou art just, O Lord!’ — but I don't want to cry that aloud then. While there's still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn't worth the tears of that one tortured child who beat itself on the breast with its little fist and prayed in its stinking outhouse, with its unexpiated tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn't worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They must be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How are you going to atone for them? Is it possible? By their being avenged? But what do I care for avenging them? What do I care for a hell for oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want any more suffering. And if the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings that was needed to pay for truth, then I declare in advance that the truth is not worth such a price. I don't want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants; let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her mother's heart. But she has no right to forgive her tortured child's sufferings; she dare not forgive the torturer, even if the child itself were to forgive him! And if that's so, if they dare not forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there in the whole world a being who would have the right to forgive and could forgive? I don't want harmony. Out of love for humanity, I don't want it. I would rather be left with unavenged suffering. I would rather remain with my unavenged suffering and unsatisfied indignation, _even if I'm wrong_. Besides, too high a price is being asked for harmony; it's beyond our means to pay so much to enter into it. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket, and if I'm an honest man I'm bound to give it back as soon as possible. And that is what I'm doing. It isn't God I don't accept, Alyosha — only I most respectfully return Him the ticket.”

35.24.oldText: “Rebellion? I'm sorry you call it that,” Ivan said earnestly. “One can hardly live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you — answer: imagine that you are creating the fabric of human destiny with the aim of making men happy in the end, of giving them peace and rest at last, but that it was essential and inevitable to torture to death only one tiny creature — that very baby beating its breast with its fist, for instance — and to found that edifice on its unavenged tears — would you consent to be the architect on those conditions? Tell me, and tell the truth.”

35.25.oldText: “No, I wouldn't consent,” Alyosha said softly.

35.26.oldText: “And can you admit the idea that the men for whom you are building it would agree to accept their happiness on the foundation of the unexpiated blood of a little victim? And that accepting it, they would remain happy forever?”

35.27.oldText: “No, I can't admit it. Brother,” Alyosha said suddenly, his eyes flashing, “you said just now — is there a being in the whole world who would have the right to forgive and could forgive? But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You've forgotten Him, and on Him is built the edifice, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘Thou art just, O Lord, for Thy ways are revealed!’”

35.28.oldText: “Ah! the One without sin and His blood! No, I haven't forgotten Him; on the contrary, I've been wondering all this time why it took you so long to bring Him in, because usually every argument on your side puts Him in the foreground. Do you know, Alyosha — don't laugh! — I made up a poem about a year ago. If you can waste another ten minutes on me, I'll tell it to you.”

35.30.oldText: “Oh, no, I didn't write it,” Ivan laughed, “and I've never written two lines of poetry in my life. But I made this poem up in prose and I remembered it. I was carried away when I made it up. You'll be my first reader — that is, listener. Why should an author forgo even one listener?” Ivan smiled. “Shall I tell it to you?”

35.32.oldText: “My poem is called ‘The Grand Inquisitor’; it's a ridiculous thing, but I want to tell it to you.”

36.0.oldText: “Even this has to have a preface — a literary preface, that is,” Ivan laughed, “and I'm poor at making them. You see, my action takes place in the sixteenth century, and in those days, as you probably learned in school, it was customary in poetry to bring heavenly powers down onto the earth. Not to mention Dante — in France, clerks, as well as the monks in the monasteries, used to put on regular performances in which the Madonna, the saints, the angels, Christ, and even God himself were brought onto the stage. In those days it was done in all simplicity. In Victor Hugo's _Notre Dame de Paris_ an edifying, free entertainment was presented for the people at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris in the reign of Louis XI, in honor of the birth of the dauphin. It was called _Le bon jugement de la très sainte et gracieuse Vierge Marie_, and she herself appears on the stage and pronounces her _bon jugement_. Similar plays — mostly from the Old Testament — were occasionally performed in Moscow, too, up to the times of Peter the Great. But besides plays, there were all sorts of legends and ballads scattered about the world in which the saints and angels and all the powers of Heaven took part when required. In our monasteries the monks busied themselves translating, copying, and even composing such poems — even under the Tatars. There is, for instance, one such poem (from the Greek, of course), _The Wanderings of Our Lady through Hell_, with descriptions as bold as Dante's. Our Lady visits hell, and the Archangel Michael leads her through the torments. She sees the sinners and their punishment. Among others, she sees one notable set of sinners in a burning lake; some of them sink so deep into the lake that they can't swim out, and ‘these God forgets’ — an expression of extraordinary depth and force. And so Our Lady, shocked and weeping, falls before the throne of God and begs for mercy on all in hell — on all she has seen there, without distinction. Her conversation with God is immensely interesting. She beseeches Him, she will not desist, and when God points to the hands and feet of her Son, nailed to the Cross, and asks, ‘How can I forgive His tormentors?’ she bids all the saints, all the martyrs, all the angels and archangels to fall down with her and pray for mercy on all without distinction. It ends with her winning from God a reprieve from suffering every year from Good Friday until Trinity Day, and the sinners at once raise a cry of thankfulness from hell, chanting, ‘Thou art just, O Lord, in this judgment.’ Well, my poem would have been of that kind, if it had appeared back then. He comes onto the scene in my poem, but He says nothing — only appears and passes on. Fifteen centuries have passed since He promised to come in His glory, fifteen centuries since His prophet wrote, ‘Behold, I come quickly’; ‘Of that day and that hour knoweth no man, neither the Son, but the Father,’ as He Himself predicted on earth. But humanity awaits Him with the same faith and the same love. Oh, with even greater faith — because it's been fifteen centuries since man has ceased to see signs from heaven.

36.1.oldText: No signs from heaven come today To add to what the heart doth say.

36.2.oldText: Nothing was left but faith in what the heart doth say. It's true there were many miracles in those days. There were saints who performed miraculous cures; some holy people, according to their biographies, were visited by the Queen of Heaven herself. But the devil didn't slumber, and doubts were already arising among men about the truth of these miracles. And just then there appeared in the north of Germany a terrible new heresy. ‘A huge star like to a torch’ (that is, a church) ‘fell on the sources of the waters and they became bitter.’ These heretics began blasphemously denying miracles. But those who remained faithful burned all the more ardently in their faith. The tears of humanity rose up to Him as before; they awaited His coming, loved Him, hoped for Him, yearned to suffer and die for Him as before. And for so many ages mankind had prayed with faith and fervor, ‘O Lord our God, hasten Thy coming,’ so many ages had called upon Him, that in His infinite mercy He deigned to come down to His servants. Before that day He had come down already; He had visited some holy men, martyrs, and hermits, as is written in their lives. Among us, Tyutchev, with absolute faith in the truth of his words, bore witness that

36.3.oldText: Bearing the Cross, in slavish dress, Weary and worn, the Heavenly King Our mother, Russia, came to bless, And through our land went wandering.

36.4.oldText: And that certainly was so, I assure you.

36.5.oldText: “And so, He deigned to appear for a moment to the people — to the tortured, suffering people, sunk in iniquity but loving Him like children. My story is set in Spain, in Seville, in the most terrible time of the Inquisition, when fires were lit every day to the glory of God, and ‘in the splendid _auto da fé_ the wicked heretics were burnt.’ Oh, of course this isn't the coming in which He will appear according to His promise at the end of time in all His heavenly glory, which will be sudden ‘as lightning flashing from east to west.’ No, He visited His children only for a moment, and in the very place where the flames were crackling around the heretics. In His infinite mercy He came once more among men in that human shape in which He had walked among men for three years fifteen centuries earlier. He came down to the ‘hot pavements’ of the southern town where the day before nearly a hundred heretics had, _ad majorem gloriam Dei_, been burnt by the cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, in a magnificent _auto da fé_, in the presence of the king, the court, the knights, the cardinals, the most charming ladies of the court, and the whole population of Seville.

36.6.oldText: “He came softly, unobserved — and yet, strange to say, everyone recognized Him. That might be one of the best passages in the poem. I mean, why they recognized Him. The people are irresistibly drawn to Him; they surround Him, they flock to Him, follow Him. He moves silently in their midst with a gentle smile of infinite compassion. The sun of love burns in His heart, light and power shine from His eyes, and their radiance, shed upon the people, stirs their hearts with answering love. He holds out His hands to them, blesses them, and a healing virtue flows from contact with Him, even with His garments. An old man in the crowd, blind from childhood, cries out, ‘O Lord, heal me and I shall see Thee!’ and, as it were, scales fall from his eyes and the blind man sees Him. The crowd weeps and kisses the earth under His feet. Children throw flowers before Him, sing, and cry hosanna. ‘It is He — it is He!’ all repeat. ‘It must be He — it can be no one but Him!’ He stops at the steps of the Seville cathedral at the moment when weeping mourners are bringing in a little open white coffin. In it lies a child of seven, the only daughter of a prominent citizen. The dead child lies hidden in flowers. ‘He will raise your child,’ the crowd shouts to the weeping mother. The priest, coming out to meet the coffin, looks perplexed and frowns, but the mother of the dead child throws herself at His feet with a wail. ‘If it is Thou, raise my child!’ she cries, holding out her hands to Him. The procession halts, the coffin is set down on the steps at His feet. He looks on her with compassion, and His lips once more softly pronounce, ‘Maiden, arise!’ — and the maiden arises. The little girl sits up in the coffin and looks around, smiling with wide-open, wondering eyes, holding the bouquet of white roses they had put in her hand.

36.7.oldText: “There are cries, sobs, confusion among the people, and at that moment the cardinal himself, the Grand Inquisitor, passes by the cathedral. He is an old man, almost ninety, tall and erect, with a withered face and sunken eyes in which there is still a gleam of light. He isn't dressed in his gorgeous cardinal's robes, as he was the day before when he was burning the enemies of the Roman Church — at this moment he is wearing his coarse, old monk's cassock. At a distance behind him come his gloomy assistants and slaves and the ‘holy guard.’ He stops at the sight of the crowd and watches it from a distance. He sees everything; he sees them set the coffin down at His feet, sees the child rise up, and his face darkens. He knits his thick gray brows, and his eyes gleam with a sinister fire. He holds out his finger and bids the guards take Him. And such is his power, so completely are the people cowed into submission and trembling obedience to him, that the crowd instantly makes way for the guards, and in the midst of deathlike silence they lay hands on Him and lead Him away. The crowd immediately bows down to the earth, like one man, before the old Inquisitor. He blesses the people in silence and passes on. The guards lead their prisoner to the close, gloomy, vaulted prison in the ancient palace of the Holy Inquisition and shut Him inside. The day passes and is followed by the dark, burning, ‘breathless’ night of Seville. The air is ‘fragrant with laurel and lemon.’ In the pitch darkness, the iron door of the prison is suddenly opened, and the Grand Inquisitor himself comes in with a light in his hand. He is alone; the door is closed at once behind him. He stands in the doorway and for a minute or two gazes into His face. At last he goes up slowly, sets the light on the table, and speaks.

36.8.oldText: “‘Is it Thou? Thou?’ — but, receiving no answer, he adds at once, ‘Don't answer, be silent. What canst Thou say, indeed? I know too well what Thou wouldst say. And Thou hast no right to add anything to what Thou hadst said of old. Why, then, art Thou come to hinder us? For Thou hast come to hinder us, and Thou knowest it. But dost Thou know what will be tomorrow? I know not who Thou art and care not to know whether it is Thou or only a semblance of Him — but tomorrow I shall condemn Thee and burn Thee at the stake as the worst of heretics. And the very people who today have kissed Thy feet, tomorrow at the faintest sign from me will rush to heap up the embers of Thy fire. Knowest Thou that? Yes, perhaps Thou knowest it,’ he added with thoughtful penetration, never for a moment taking his eyes off the Prisoner.”

36.9.oldText: “I don't quite understand, Ivan. What does it mean?” Alyosha, who had been listening in silence, said with a smile. “Is it simply a wild fantasy, or a mistake on the old man's part — some impossible _quiproquo_?”

36.10.oldText: “Take it as the latter,” Ivan said, laughing, “if you've been so corrupted by modern realism that you can't stand anything fantastic. If you prefer it to be a case of mistaken identity, let it be so. It's true,” he went on, laughing, “that the old man was ninety, and he might well be crazy over his fixed idea. He might have been struck by the appearance of the Prisoner. It might, in fact, simply be his ravings, the delusion of an old man of ninety, overexcited by the _auto da fé_ of a hundred heretics the day before. But does it really matter to us whether it was mistaken identity or a wild fantasy? All that matters is that the old man should speak out, should speak openly of what he has thought in silence for ninety years.”

36.11.oldText: “And the Prisoner is silent too? He looks at him and doesn't say a word?”

36.12.oldText: “That's inevitable in any case,” Ivan laughed again. “The old man has told Him He has no right to add anything to what He had said of old. One might say that is the most fundamental feature of Roman Catholicism, in my opinion at any rate. ‘All has been given by Thee to the Pope,’ they say, ‘and all, therefore, is still in the Pope's hands, and there is no need for Thee to come now at all. At least, Thou must not meddle for the time being.’ That's how they speak and write, too — the Jesuits at any rate. I've read it myself in the works of their theologians. ‘Hast Thou the right to reveal to us one of the mysteries of that world from which Thou hast come?’ my old man asks Him — and answers the question for Him. ‘No, Thou hast not; for Thou mayest not add to what has been said of old, and mayest not take from men the freedom which Thou didst exalt when Thou wast on earth. Whatsoever Thou revealest anew will encroach on men's freedom of faith, for it will be manifest as a miracle, and the freedom of their faith was dearer to Thee than anything in those days fifteen hundred years ago. Didst Thou not often say then, “I will make you free”? But now Thou hast seen these “free” men,' the old man adds suddenly, with a pensive smile. ‘Yes, we've paid dearly for it,’ he goes on, looking sternly at Him, ‘but at last we have completed that work in Thy name. For fifteen centuries we have been wrestling with Thy freedom, but now it is ended and over for good. Dost Thou not believe that it's over for good? Thou lookest meekly at me and deignest not even to be wroth with me. But let me tell Thee that now, today, people are more convinced than ever that they have perfect freedom — and yet they have brought their freedom to us and laid it humbly at our feet. But that has been our doing. Was this what Thou didst? Was this Thy freedom?’”

36.13.oldText: “I don't understand again,” Alyosha broke in. “Is he being ironic? Is he joking?”

36.14.oldText: “Not in the least! He claims it as a merit for himself and his Church that at last they have vanquished freedom, and have done so to make men happy. ‘For now’ (he's speaking of the Inquisition, of course) ‘for the first time it has become possible to think about the happiness of men. Man was created a rebel; and how can rebels be happy? Thou wast warned,’ he says to Him. ‘Thou hast had no lack of admonitions and warnings, but Thou didst not listen to those warnings; Thou didst reject the only way by which men might be made happy. But, fortunately, departing Thou didst hand on the work to us. Thou hast promised, Thou hast established by Thy word, Thou hast given to us the right to bind and to unbind, and now, of course, Thou canst not think of taking it away. Why, then, hast Thou come to hinder us?’”

36.15.oldText: “And what does ‘no lack of admonitions and warnings’ mean?” Alyosha asked.

36.16.oldText: “Why, that's the chief part of what the old man has to say.

36.17.oldText: “‘The wise and dread spirit, the spirit of self-destruction and non-existence,’ the old man goes on, ‘the great spirit talked with Thee in the wilderness, and we are told in the books that he “tempted” Thee. Is that so? And could anything truer have been said than what he revealed to Thee in three questions — which Thou didst reject, and which in the books are called “the temptation”? And yet if there has ever been on earth a real, stupendous miracle, it took place that day — the day of the three temptations. The very statement of those three questions was itself the miracle. If it were possible to imagine, simply for the sake of argument, that those three questions of the dread spirit had perished utterly from the books, and that we had to restore them and invent them anew, and that to do so we'd gathered together all the wise men of the earth — rulers, chief priests, learned men, philosophers, poets — and set them the task of inventing three questions that would not only fit the occasion but express, in three words, in three human sentences, the whole future history of the world and of humanity — dost Thou believe that all the wisdom of the earth combined could have invented anything equal in depth and force to the three questions which were actually put to Thee then by the wise and mighty spirit in the wilderness? From those questions alone, from the miracle of their formulation, we can see that we are dealing here not with fleeting human intelligence but with something absolute and eternal. For in those three questions the whole subsequent history of mankind is, as it were, gathered together into a single whole and foretold, and in them are united all the unsolved historical contradictions of human nature. At the time it couldn't have been so clear, since the future was still unknown; but now that fifteen hundred years have passed, we see that everything in those three questions was so justly divined and foretold, and has been so truly fulfilled, that nothing can be added to them and nothing taken away.

36.18.oldText: “‘Judge Thyself who was right — Thou, or he who questioned Thee then? Remember the first question; its meaning, in other words, was this: “Thou wouldst go into the world, and art going with empty hands, with some promise of freedom which men in their simplicity and their natural unruliness cannot even understand, which they fear and dread — for nothing has ever been more unbearable for a man and a human society than freedom. But seest Thou these stones in this parched and barren wilderness? Turn them into bread, and mankind will run after Thee like a flock of sheep, grateful and obedient, though forever trembling lest Thou withdraw Thy hand and deny them Thy bread.” But Thou wouldst not deprive man of freedom, and didst reject the offer, thinking: what is that freedom worth, if obedience is bought with bread? Thou didst reply that man does not live by bread alone. But dost Thou know that for the sake of that earthly bread the spirit of the earth will rise up against Thee, and will strive with Thee and overcome Thee, and all will follow him, crying, “Who can compare with this beast? He has given us fire from heaven!” Dost Thou know that the ages will pass, and humanity will proclaim by the lips of their sages that there is no crime, and therefore no sin; there is only hunger? “Feed men, and then ask of them virtue!” — that's what they'll write on the banner they will raise against Thee, and with which they will destroy Thy temple. In the place where Thy temple stood a new building will rise; the terrible tower of Babel will be built again, and though, like the one of old, it will not be finished, yet Thou mightest have prevented that new tower and have cut short the sufferings of men for a thousand years; for they will come back to us after a thousand years of agony with their tower. They will seek us out again, hidden underground in the catacombs, for we shall again be persecuted and tortured. They will find us and cry out to us, “Feed us, for those who promised us fire from heaven have not given it!” And then we shall finish building their tower, for he finishes the building who feeds them. And we alone shall feed them in Thy name, declaring falsely that it is in Thy name. Oh, never, never can they feed themselves without us! No science will give them bread so long as they remain free. In the end they will lay their freedom at our feet and say to us, “Make us your slaves, but feed us.” They will understand at last that freedom and bread enough for all are inconceivable together, for they will never, never be able to share between them! They will be convinced, too, that they can never be free, for they are weak, vicious, worthless, and rebellious. Thou didst promise them the bread of Heaven, but, I repeat again, can it compare with earthly bread in the eyes of the weak, ever sinful, and ignoble race of man? And if for the sake of the bread of Heaven thousands shall follow Thee, what is to become of the millions and tens of thousands of millions of creatures who won't have the strength to forgo earthly bread for the sake of the heavenly? Or dost Thou care only for the tens of thousands of the great and strong, while the millions, numerous as the sands of the sea, who are weak but love Thee, must exist only for the sake of the great and strong? No, we care for the weak too. They are sinful and rebellious, but in the end they too will become obedient. They will marvel at us and look on us as gods, because we are ready to endure the freedom which they have found so dreadful, and to rule over them — so awful will it seem to them to be free. But we shall tell them that we are Thy servants and rule them in Thy name. We shall deceive them again, for we won't let Thee come to us again. That deception will be our suffering, for we shall be forced to lie.

36.19.oldText: “‘This is the significance of the first question in the wilderness, and this is what Thou hast rejected for the sake of that freedom which Thou hast exalted above everything. Yet in this question lies hidden the great secret of this world. Choosing “bread,” Thou wouldst have satisfied the universal and everlasting craving of humanity — to find someone to worship. So long as man remains free he strives for nothing so incessantly and so painfully as to find someone to worship. But man seeks to worship what is established beyond dispute, so that all men would agree at once to worship it. For these pitiful creatures are concerned not only to find what one or another can worship, but to find something that all would believe in and worship; what is essential is that all may be _together_ in it. This craving for _community_ of worship is the chief misery of every man individually, and of all humanity from the beginning of time. For the sake of common worship they've slain one another with the sword. They've set up gods and challenged each other: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we'll kill you and your gods!” And so it will be to the end of the world, even when gods disappear from the earth; they'll fall down before idols just the same. Thou didst know, Thou couldst not but have known, this fundamental secret of human nature — but Thou didst reject the one infallible banner which was offered Thee to make all men bow down to Thee alone — the banner of earthly bread; and Thou hast rejected it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Behold what Thou didst further. And all again in the name of freedom! I tell Thee, man is tormented by no greater anxiety than to find someone quickly to whom he can hand over that gift of freedom with which the ill-fated creature is born. But only one who can appease their conscience can take over their freedom. In bread Thou wast offered an invincible banner; give bread, and man will worship thee, for nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gains possession of his conscience — oh! then he will cast away Thy bread and follow after him who has ensnared his conscience. In that Thou wast right. For the secret of man's being is not only to live, but to have something to live for. Without a stable conception of the object of life, man would not consent to go on living, and would rather destroy himself than remain on earth, even though he had bread in abundance. That is true. But what happened? Instead of taking men's freedom from them, Thou didst make it greater than ever! Didst Thou forget that man prefers peace, and even death, to freedom of choice in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing is more seductive for man than his freedom of conscience, but nothing is a greater cause of suffering. And behold, instead of giving a firm foundation for setting the conscience of man at rest forever, Thou didst choose everything that is exceptional, vague, and enigmatic; Thou didst choose what was utterly beyond the strength of men, acting as though Thou didst not love them at all — Thou who didst come to give Thy life for them! Instead of taking possession of men's freedom, Thou didst increase it, and burdened the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings forever. Thou didst desire man's free love, that he should follow Thee freely, enticed and taken captive by Thee. In place of the rigid ancient law, man must hereafter decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, having only Thy image before him as his guide. But didst Thou not know that he would at last reject even Thy image and Thy truth, if he were weighed down by the fearful burden of free choice? They will cry aloud at last that the truth is not in Thee, for they could not have been left in greater confusion and suffering than Thou hast caused, laying upon them so many cares and unanswerable problems.

36.20.oldText: “‘So that, in truth, Thou didst Thyself lay the foundation for the destruction of Thy kingdom, and no one is more to blame for it. Yet what was offered Thee? There are three powers, three powers alone, able to conquer and hold captive forever the conscience of these impotent rebels for their happiness — those forces are miracle, mystery, and authority. Thou hast rejected all three and hast set the example for doing so. When the wise and dread spirit set Thee on the pinnacle of the temple and said to Thee, “If Thou wouldst know whether Thou art the Son of God, then cast Thyself down, for it is written: the angels shall hold him up lest he fall and bruise himself, and Thou shalt know then whether Thou art the Son of God and shalt prove then how great is Thy faith in Thy Father” — but Thou didst refuse and wouldst not cast Thyself down. Oh, of course, Thou didst proudly and well, like God; but the weak, unruly race of men — are they gods? Oh, Thou didst know then that in taking one step, in making one movement to cast Thyself down, Thou wouldst be tempting God and have lost all Thy faith in Him, and wouldst have been dashed to pieces against that earth which Thou didst come to save. And the wise spirit that tempted Thee would have rejoiced. But I ask again: are there many like Thee? And couldst Thou believe for one moment that men, too, could face such a temptation? Is the nature of men such that they can reject miracle, and, at the great moments of their lives, at the moments of their deepest, most agonizing spiritual difficulties, cling only to the free verdict of the heart? Oh, Thou didst know that Thy deed would be recorded in books, would be handed down to remote times and the utmost ends of the earth, and Thou didst hope that man, following Thee, would cling to God and not ask for a miracle. But Thou didst not know that when man rejects miracle he rejects God too; for man seeks not so much God as the miraculous. And since man cannot bear to be without the miraculous, he will create new miracles of his own, and will worship deeds of sorcery and witchcraft, though he be a hundred times a rebel, a heretic, and an infidel. Thou didst not come down from the Cross when they shouted to Thee, mocking and reviling Thee, “Come down from the cross and we will believe that Thou art He.” Thou didst not come down, because once again Thou wouldst not enslave man by a miracle, and didst crave faith given freely, not based on miracle. Thou didst crave free love, not the base raptures of the slave before the might that has overawed him forever. But Thou didst think too highly of men in this, for they are slaves, of course, though rebellious by nature. Look round and judge; fifteen centuries have passed, look upon them. Whom hast Thou raised up to Thyself? I swear, man is weaker and baser by nature than Thou hast believed him! Can he, can he do what Thou didst? By showing him so much respect, Thou didst, as it were, cease to feel for him, because Thou didst ask far too much from him — Thou who hast loved him more than Thyself! Respecting him less, Thou wouldst have asked less of him. That would have been more like love, because his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and vile. So what if he's everywhere now rebelling against our power, and proud of his rebellion? It is the pride of a child and a schoolboy. They are little children rioting and barring the teacher out of school. But their childish delight will end; it will cost them dear. They will cast down temples and drench the earth in blood. But they will see at last, the foolish children, that, though they are rebels, they are impotent rebels, unable to keep up their own rebellion. Bathed in their foolish tears, they will recognize at last that He who created them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say this in despair, and their utterance will be a blasphemy which will make them more unhappy still, for man's nature cannot bear blasphemy, and in the end always avenges it on itself. And so unrest, confusion, and unhappiness — that is the present lot of man after Thou didst bear so much for their freedom! The great prophet tells in vision and in image that he saw all those who took part in the first resurrection, and that there were twelve thousand of each tribe. But if there were so many of them, they must have been not men but gods. They had borne Thy cross, they had endured scores of years in the barren, hungry wilderness, living on locusts and roots — and indeed Thou mayest point with pride at those children of freedom, of free love, of free and splendid sacrifice for Thy name. But remember that there were only a few thousand of them; and what of the rest? And how are the other weak ones to blame, because they could not endure what the strong endured? How is the weak soul to blame that it is unable to receive such terrible gifts? Canst Thou have simply come to the elect and for the elect? But if so, it's a mystery, and we cannot understand it. And if it's a mystery, then we too have a right to preach a mystery, and to teach them that it's not the free judgment of their hearts, not love that matters, but a mystery which they must follow blindly, even against their conscience. That is what we have done. We have corrected Thy work and have founded it upon _miracle_, _mystery_, and _authority_. And men rejoiced that they were again led like sheep, and that the terrible gift that had brought them such suffering was, at last, lifted from their hearts. Were we right in teaching them this? Speak! Did we not love mankind, so meekly acknowledging their feebleness, lovingly lightening their burden, and permitting their weak nature even to sin with our sanction? Why hast Thou come now to hinder us? And why dost Thou look silently and searchingly at me with Thy mild eyes? Be angry. I don't want Thy love, for I love Thee not. And what use is it for me to hide anything from Thee? Don't I know to whom I am speaking? All that I can say is already known to Thee. And is it for me to conceal from Thee our mystery? Perhaps it is Thy will to hear it from my lips. Listen, then. We are not working with Thee, but with _him_ — that is our mystery. It has been a long time — eight centuries — since we have been on _his_ side and not on Thine. Just eight centuries ago, we took from him what Thou didst reject with scorn, that last gift he offered Thee when he showed Thee all the kingdoms of the earth. We took from him Rome and the sword of Caesar, and proclaimed ourselves sole rulers of the earth, though so far we have not been able to complete our work. But whose fault is that? Oh, the work is only beginning, but it has begun. It has long to await completion, and the earth has yet much to suffer, but we shall triumph and shall be Caesars, and then we shall plan the universal happiness of man. But Thou mightest have taken even then the sword of Caesar. Why didst Thou reject that last gift? Hadst Thou accepted that last counsel of the mighty spirit, Thou wouldst have accomplished all that man seeks on earth — that is, someone to worship, someone to keep his conscience, and some means of uniting all in one unanimous and harmonious ant-heap; for the craving for universal unity is the third and last torment of men. Mankind as a whole has always striven to organize a universal state. There have been many great nations with great histories, but the more highly they were developed, the more unhappy they were, for they felt more acutely than other peoples the craving for worldwide union. The great conquerors, the Timurs and Genghis Khans, whirled like hurricanes over the face of the earth, striving to subdue its peoples — and they too were but the unconscious expression of the same craving for universal unity. Hadst Thou taken the world and Caesar's purple, Thou wouldst have founded the universal state and given universal peace.
