For who can rule men if not he who holds their conscience and their bread in his hands? We have taken the sword of Caesar, and in taking it, of course, have rejected Thee and followed _him_. Oh, ages are yet to come of the confusion of free thought, of their science and cannibalism. For having begun to build their tower of Babel without us, they will end, of course, in cannibalism. But then the beast will crawl to us and lick our feet and spatter them with tears of blood. And we shall sit upon the beast and raise the cup, and on it will be written, “Mystery.” But then, and only then, the reign of peace and happiness will come for men. Thou art proud of Thine elect, but Thou hast only the elect, while we give rest to all. And besides, how many of those elect, those mighty ones who could have become elect, have grown weary waiting for Thee, and have transferred, and will transfer, the powers of their spirit and the warmth of their hearts to the other camp, and will end by raising their _free_ banner against Thee. Thou didst Thyself lift up that banner. But with us all will be happy, and will no more rebel or destroy one another as under Thy freedom. Oh, we shall persuade them that they will only become free when they renounce their freedom to us and submit to us. And shall we be right, or shall we be lying? They will be convinced that we are right, for they will remember the horrors of slavery and confusion to which Thy freedom brought them. Freedom, free thought, and science will lead them into such straits, will bring them face to face with such marvels and insoluble mysteries, that some of them, the fierce and rebellious, will destroy themselves; others, rebellious but weak, will destroy one another; while the rest, weak and unhappy, will crawl fawning to our feet and whine to us: “Yes, you were right, you alone possess His mystery, and we come back to you — save us from ourselves!”

36.21.oldText: “‘Receiving bread from us, they will see clearly that we take the bread made by their own hands from them, in order to give it to them, without any miracle. They will see that we do not change stones into bread, but in truth they will be more thankful for taking it from our hands than for the bread itself! For they will remember too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they have come back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. All too well will they know the value of complete submission! And until men know that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame for their not knowing it? — speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it astray on unknown paths? But the flock will come together again and will submit once more, and then it will be once and for all. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures such as they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them at last not to be proud, because Thou didst lift them up and thereby taught them to be proud. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are only pitiful children, but that childlike happiness is the sweetest of all. They will become timid and will look to us and huddle close to us in fear, as chicks to the hen. They will marvel at us and be awe-stricken before us, and will be proud that we are so powerful and clever, that we have been able to subdue such a turbulent flock of thousands of millions. They will tremble impotently before our wrath, their minds will grow timid, they will be quick to shed tears like women and children, but they will be just as ready at a sign from us to pass to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall set them to work, but in their leisure hours we shall make their life like a child's game, with children's songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall allow them even sin — they are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we allow them to sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for, if it is done with our permission, that we allow them to sin because we love them, and the punishment for these sins we take upon ourselves. And we shall take it upon ourselves, and they will adore us as their saviors who have taken their sins upon themselves before God. And they will have no secrets from us. We shall allow or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, to have or not to have children — according to whether they have been obedient or disobedient — and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience — all, all — they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for everything. And they will be glad to believe our answer, because it will save them from the great anxiety and terrible agony they endure at present in making a free decision for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, we who guard the mystery, shall be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken upon themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Thy name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall lure them with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for the likes of them. It is prophesied that Thou wilt come again in victory, Thou wilt come with Thy chosen, the proud and strong, but we will say that they have saved only themselves, but we have saved all. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, and holds in her hands the _mystery_, shall be put to shame, that the weak will rise up again and will rend her royal purple, and will strip naked her loathsome body. But then I will stand up and point out to Thee the thousand millions of happy children who have known no sin. And we who have taken their sins upon ourselves for their happiness will stand up before Thee and say: “Judge us if Thou canst and darest.” Know that I do not fear Thee. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, I too have lived on roots and locusts, I too prized the freedom with which Thou hast blessed men, and I too was striving to stand among Thy elect, among the strong and powerful, thirsting “to make up the number.” But I awoke, and would not serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Thy work_. I left the proud and went back to the humble, for the happiness of the humble. What I say to Thee will come to pass, and our dominion will be built up. I repeat — tomorrow Thou shalt see that obedient flock who at a sign from me will hasten to heap up the hot cinders about the pile on which I shall burn Thee for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is Thou. Tomorrow I shall burn Thee. _Dixi._’”

36.22.oldText: Ivan stopped. He had been carried away as he talked, and had spoken with excitement; when he had finished, he suddenly smiled.

36.23.oldText: Alyosha had listened in silence; toward the end he'd been greatly moved and seemed on the point of interrupting several times, but restrained himself. Now his words came in a rush.

36.24.oldText: “But ... that's absurd!” he cried, flushing. “Your poem is in praise of Jesus, not in blame of Him — as you meant it to be. And who will believe you about freedom? Is that the way to understand it? That's not the idea of it in the Orthodox Church.... That's Rome — and not even the whole of Rome; that's false — those are the worst of the Catholics, the Inquisitors, the Jesuits!... And there couldn't be such a fantastic creature as your Inquisitor. What are these sins of mankind they take upon themselves? Who are these keepers of the mystery who have taken on some curse for the happiness of mankind? When have they ever been seen? We know the Jesuits; they are spoken ill of, but surely they aren't what you describe? They aren't that at all, not at all.... They are simply the Roman army for the future earthly sovereignty of the world, with the Pontiff of Rome for Emperor ... that's their ideal, but there's no sort of mystery or lofty melancholy about it.... It's simple lust for power, for filthy earthly gain, for domination — something like a universal serfdom with themselves as masters — that's all they stand for. Perhaps they don't even believe in God. Your suffering Inquisitor is a mere fantasy.”

36.25.oldText: “Wait, wait,” Ivan laughed, “how worked up you are! A fantasy, you say — let it be so! Of course it's a fantasy. But let me ask you: do you really think that the Roman Catholic movement of the last centuries is actually nothing but a lust for power, for filthy earthly gain? Is that Father Païssy's teaching?”

36.26.oldText: “No, no — on the contrary, Father Païssy did once say something rather similar to what you said ... but of course it wasn't the same, not a bit the same,” Alyosha hastily corrected himself.

36.27.oldText: “A precious admission, despite your ‘not a bit the same.’ Let me ask you: why have your Jesuits and Inquisitors joined forces simply for vile material gain? Why can't there be among them one martyr oppressed by great sorrow and loving humanity? You see, only suppose that there was one such man among all those who desire nothing but filthy material gain — if there's only one like my old Inquisitor, who had himself eaten roots in the desert and made frenzied efforts to subdue his flesh to make himself free and perfect. But throughout his life he loved humanity — and suddenly his eyes were opened, and he saw that it is no great moral blessedness to attain perfection and freedom, if at the same time one is convinced that millions of God's creatures have been created as a mockery, that they will never be capable of using their freedom, that these poor rebels can never turn into giants to complete the tower, that it was not for such geese that the great idealist dreamed his dream of harmony. Seeing all that, he turned back and joined — the clever people. Surely that could have happened?”

36.28.oldText: “Joined whom? What clever people?” Alyosha cried, completely carried away. “They have no such great cleverness, no such mysteries and secrets.... Perhaps nothing but atheism — that's all their secret. Your Inquisitor doesn't believe in God, that's his secret!”

36.29.oldText: “What if it is so! At last you've guessed it. It's perfectly true, it's true that's the whole secret — but isn't that suffering, at least for a man like that, who has wasted his whole life in the desert and yet could not shake off his incurable love of humanity? In his old age he reached the clear conviction that nothing but the counsel of the great dread spirit could build any tolerable kind of life for the feeble, unruly, ‘incomplete, empirical creatures created in jest.’ And so, convinced of this, he sees that he must follow the counsel of the wise spirit, the dread spirit of death and destruction, and therefore accept lying and deception, and lead men consciously toward death and destruction, deceiving them all the way so that they may not notice where they are being led — so that the poor blind creatures may at least on the way think themselves happy. And note, the deception is in the name of Him in whose ideal the old man had so fervently believed all his life long. Isn't that tragic? And if only one such man stood at the head of the whole army ‘filled with the lust of power only for the sake of filthy gain’ — wouldn't even one such be enough to make a tragedy? More than that — one such man standing at the head is enough to create the actual leading idea of the Roman Church, with all its armies and Jesuits, its highest idea. I tell you frankly, I firmly believe there has always been such a man among those who stood at the head of the movement. Who knows — there may have been some such even among the Roman Popes. Who knows — perhaps the spirit of that accursed old man, who loves mankind so obstinately in his own way, is to be found even now in a whole multitude of such old men, existing not by chance but by agreement, as a secret league formed long ago for the guarding of the mystery — guarding it from the weak and the unhappy, so as to make them happy. Doubtless it is so, and so it must be. I imagine that even among the Masons there's something of the same mystery at the bottom of things, and that this is why the Catholics so detest the Masons — as rivals breaking up the unity of the idea, when it is so essential that there should be one flock and one shepherd.... But from the way I defend my idea, I might be an author impatient of your criticism. Enough of it.”

36.30.oldText: “You're perhaps a Mason yourself!” Alyosha suddenly blurted out. “You don't believe in God,” he added, speaking this time very sorrowfully. He imagined, besides, that his brother was looking at him ironically. “How does your poem end?” he asked, suddenly looking down. “Or was that the end?”

36.31.oldText: “I meant to end it like this. When the Inquisitor stopped speaking, he waited some time for his Prisoner to answer him. His silence weighed him down. He saw that the Prisoner had listened intently the whole time, looking gently into his face and evidently not wishing to reply. The old man longed for Him to say something, however bitter and terrible. But in silence He suddenly approached the old man and softly kissed him on his bloodless aged lips. That was all His answer. The old man shuddered. His lips moved. He went to the door, opened it, and said to Him: ‘Go, and come no more ... come not at all, never, never!’ And he let Him out into the dark alleys of the town. The Prisoner walked away.”

36.33.oldText: “The kiss glows in his heart, but the old man holds to his idea.”

36.34.oldText: “And you with him — you too?” Alyosha cried mournfully.

36.36.oldText: “Why, it's all nonsense, Alyosha. It's only a senseless poem by a senseless student who could never write two lines of verse. Why do you take it so seriously? You don't really suppose I'm going straight off to the Jesuits, to join the men who are correcting His work? Good Lord, it's no business of mine. I told you, all I want is to live to thirty, and then ... dash the cup to the ground!”

36.37.oldText: “But the little sticky leaves, and the precious tombs, and the blue sky, and the woman you love! How will you live? How will you love them?” Alyosha cried sorrowfully. “With such a hell in your heart and your head, how can you? No, that's exactly what you're going away for — to join them ... if not, you'll kill yourself, you can't endure it!”

36.38.oldText: “There's a strength to endure everything,” Ivan said with a cold smile.

36.40.oldText: “The strength of the Karamazovs — the strength of the Karamazov baseness.”

36.41.oldText: “You mean to sink into debauchery, to stifle your soul with corruption — yes?”

36.42.oldText: “Possibly even that ... only perhaps till I'm thirty I'll escape it, and then —”

36.43.oldText: “How will you escape it? By what means? That's impossible with your ideas.”

36.45.oldText: “‘Everything is lawful,’ you mean? Everything is lawful — is that it?”

36.47.oldText: “Ah, you've picked up yesterday's phrase, the one that so offended Miüsov — and which Dmitri pounced on so naïvely and paraphrased!” he smiled oddly. “Yes, if you like, ‘everything is lawful,’ since the word has been said. I won't deny it. And Mitya's version isn't bad.”

36.49.oldText: “I thought that in going away from here I'd have you at least,” Ivan said suddenly with unexpected feeling; “but now I see that there's no place for me even in your heart, my dear hermit. The formula, ‘all is lawful’ — I won't renounce it; will you renounce me for that, yes?”

36.50.oldText: Alyosha got up, went over to him, and softly kissed him on the lips.

36.51.oldText: “That's plagiarism,” Ivan cried, highly delighted. “You stole that from my poem. Thank you, though. Get up, Alyosha — it's time we were going, both of us.”

36.53.oldText: “Listen, Alyosha,” Ivan began in a resolute voice, “if I really am able to care for the sticky little leaves, I shall only love them while remembering you. It's enough for me that you're somewhere here, and I shall not lose my desire for life yet. Is that enough for you? Take it as a declaration of love if you like. And now you go to the right and I to the left. And it's enough, do you hear — enough. I mean, even if I don't go away tomorrow (though I think I certainly shall go), and we meet again, don't say a word more on these subjects. I ask that particularly. And about Dmitri, too, I specially ask you, don't speak to me again,” he added, with sudden irritation; “it's all exhausted, it has all been said over and over, hasn't it? And I'll make you one promise in return. When at thirty, I want to ‘dash the cup to the ground,’ wherever I am I'll come back to have one more talk with you, even from America — you may be sure of that. I'll come on purpose. It'll be very interesting to take a look at you, to see what you'll be by then. It's rather a solemn promise, you see. And we really may be parting for seven years or ten. Come, go now to your Pater Seraphicus; he's dying. If he dies without you, you'll be angry with me for having kept you. Good-bye — kiss me once more; that's right, now go.”

36.54.oldText: Ivan turned suddenly and went his way without looking back. It was just as Dmitri had left Alyosha the day before, though the parting had been very different. The strange resemblance flashed like an arrow through Alyosha's mind in the distress and dejection of that moment. He waited a little, looking after his brother. He suddenly noticed that Ivan swayed as he walked, and that his right shoulder looked lower than his left. He had never noticed that before. But all at once he, too, turned and almost ran to the monastery. It was nearly dark, and he felt almost frightened; something new was growing up in him for which he could not account. The wind had risen again as on the previous evening, and the ancient pines murmured gloomily about him as he entered the hermitage copse. He almost ran. “Pater Seraphicus — he got that name from somewhere — where from?” Alyosha wondered. “Ivan, poor Ivan — and when shall I see you again?... Here is the hermitage. Yes, yes, that's who he is, Pater Seraphicus — he will save me — from him, and forever!”

36.55.oldText: Several times afterward he wondered how, on leaving Ivan, he could so completely have forgotten his brother Dmitri, when only a few hours earlier, that morning, he'd so firmly resolved to find him and not give up trying, even if it meant not returning to the monastery that night.

37.0.oldText: After parting from Alyosha, Ivan headed home to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. But, strange to say, he was overcome by an unbearable depression, which grew greater with every step he took toward the house. There was nothing strange about him being depressed; what was strange was that Ivan couldn't have said what was causing it. He had often been depressed before, and there was nothing surprising about him feeling that way at such a moment, when he had just broken with everything that had brought him here, and was preparing that very day to make a new start and enter on a new, unknown future. He would be solitary again, and though he had great hopes — and great, too great, expectations of life — he couldn't have given any definite account of his hopes, his expectations, or even his desires.

37.1.oldText: Yet at that moment, though apprehension of the new and unknown certainly had a place in his heart, what was worrying him was something quite different. “Is it loathing for my father's house?” he wondered. “Quite likely; I'm so sick of it; and though it's the last time I'll cross its hateful threshold, still I loathe it.... No, it isn't that either. Is it the parting with Alyosha and the conversation I had with him? For so many years I've been silent with the whole world and haven't deigned to speak, and all of a sudden I reel off a rigmarole like that.” It might well have been the youthful vexation of youthful inexperience and vanity — vexation at having failed to express himself, especially with a person like Alyosha, on whom his heart had certainly been counting. No doubt that came in, that vexation; it must have. But still, that wasn't it — that wasn't it either. “I feel sick with depression, and yet I can't tell what I want. Better not think, perhaps.”

37.2.oldText: Ivan tried “not to think,” but that was no use either. What made his depression so vexing and irritating was that it had a kind of casual, external character — he could feel it. Some person or thing seemed to be standing out somewhere, just the way something will sometimes obtrude itself on the eye, and though one may be so busy with work or conversation that for a long time one doesn't notice it, yet it irritates and almost torments one until at last one realizes what it is and removes the offending object — often quite a trifling and ridiculous one — some article left in the wrong place, a handkerchief on the floor, a book not returned to the shelf, and so on.

37.3.oldText: At last, feeling very cross and ill-humored, Ivan arrived home, and suddenly, about fifteen paces from the garden gate, he realized what had been fretting and worrying him.

37.4.oldText: On a bench by the gateway sat the valet Smerdyakov, enjoying the coolness of the evening, and at the first glance at him Ivan knew that it was the valet Smerdyakov who was on his mind, and that it was this man that his soul loathed. It all dawned on him suddenly and became clear. Just before, when Alyosha had been telling him about his meeting with Smerdyakov, he'd felt a sudden twinge of gloom and loathing that had immediately stirred answering anger in his heart. Later, as he talked, Smerdyakov had been forgotten for the time being; but he'd still been in his mind, and as soon as Ivan parted with Alyosha and was walking home, the forgotten sensation had begun to obtrude itself again. “Is it possible that a miserable, contemptible creature like that can worry me so much?” he wondered, with unbearable irritation.

37.5.oldText: It was true that lately Ivan had come to feel an intense dislike for the man, especially in the last few days. He had even begun to notice in himself a growing feeling that was almost like hatred for the creature. Perhaps this hatred was sharpened by the fact that when Ivan first arrived in the neighborhood he had felt quite differently. Then he had taken a marked interest in Smerdyakov, and had even thought him quite original. He'd encouraged him to talk to him, although he'd always been struck by a certain incoherence, or rather restlessness, in his mind, and couldn't understand what it was that so continually and insistently worked on the brain of ‘the contemplator.’ They discussed philosophical questions, and even how there could have been light on the first day when the sun, moon, and stars weren't created until the fourth day, and how that was to be understood. But Ivan soon saw that, though the sun, moon, and stars might be an interesting subject, to Smerdyakov they were quite secondary, and that he was looking for something altogether different. In one way and another, he began to betray a boundless vanity — and a wounded vanity at that — and Ivan didn't like it. It was what first gave rise to his aversion. Later there was trouble in the house. Grushenka had come onto the scene, and there were the scandals with his brother Dmitri — they discussed that, too. But though Smerdyakov always talked about that with great excitement, it was impossible to tell what he wanted to come of it. There was, in fact, something surprising in the illogicality and incoherence of some of his desires, accidentally let slip and always vaguely expressed. Smerdyakov was always inquiring, putting certain indirect but obviously premeditated questions — but what his object was he didn't explain, and usually at the most important moment he'd break off and relapse into silence, or switch to another subject. But what in the end most irritated Ivan and confirmed his dislike for him was the peculiar, revolting familiarity that Smerdyakov began to show more and more markedly. Not that he forgot himself and became rude; on the contrary, he always spoke very respectfully — and yet he had obviously begun to consider (goodness knows why!) that there was some sort of understanding between himself and Ivan Fyodorovitch. He always spoke in a tone suggesting that the two of them had some kind of compact, some secret between them, that had at some point been expressed on both sides, known only to them and beyond the comprehension of those around them. But for a long while Ivan didn't recognize the real cause of his growing dislike, and only lately had he realized what was at the root of it.

37.6.oldText: With a feeling of disgust and irritation he tried to pass through the gate without speaking or looking at Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov rose from the bench, and from that action alone Ivan knew instantly that the man particularly wanted to talk to him. Ivan looked at him and stopped, and the fact that he did stop, instead of walking past as he'd intended to do only a minute before, drove him to fury. With anger and revulsion he looked at Smerdyakov's emasculate, sickly face, with the little curls combed forward on his forehead. His left eye winked and he grinned as if to say, “Where are you going? You're not going to walk past; you see that we two clever people have something to say to each other.”

37.7.oldText: Ivan shook. “Get away, miserable idiot. What have I got to do with you?” was on the tip of his tongue, but to his profound astonishment he heard himself say, “Is my father still asleep, or is he awake?”

37.8.oldText: He asked the question softly and meekly, to his own surprise, and at once, again to his own surprise, sat down on the bench. For an instant he felt almost frightened; he remembered it afterward. Smerdyakov stood facing him, his hands behind his back, looking at him with confidence and almost severity.

37.9.oldText: “His honor is still asleep,” he articulated deliberately (“You were the first to speak, not I,” he seemed to say). “I'm surprised at you, sir,” he added after a pause, lowering his eyes affectedly, setting his right foot forward, and playing with the tip of his polished boot.

37.10.oldText: “Why are you surprised at me?” Ivan asked abruptly and sullenly, doing his utmost to restrain himself, and realizing with disgust that he was feeling intense curiosity and wouldn't have gone away without satisfying it for anything.

37.11.oldText: “Why don't you go to Tchermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov suddenly raised his eyes and smiled familiarly. “You must understand why I'm smiling for yourself, if you're a clever man,” his screwed-up left eye seemed to say.

37.12.oldText: “Why should I go to Tchermashnya?” Ivan asked in surprise.

37.14.oldText: “Fyodor Pavlovitch himself has so begged you to,” he said at last, slowly and apparently attaching no significance to his answer. “I'm putting you off with a secondary reason,” he seemed to imply, “simply to say something.”

37.15.oldText: “Damn you! Speak out — what do you want!” Ivan cried angrily at last, passing from meekness to violence.

37.16.oldText: Smerdyakov drew his right foot up to his left, pulled himself up, but still looked at him with the same serenity and the same little smile.

37.17.oldText: “Nothing substantially — just by way of conversation.”

37.18.oldText: Another silence followed. They didn't speak for nearly a minute. Ivan knew he ought to get up and show anger, and Smerdyakov stood before him as if waiting to see whether he would be angry or not. So at least it seemed to Ivan. At last he moved to get up. Smerdyakov seemed to seize the moment.

37.19.oldText: “I'm in an awful position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don't know how to help myself,” he said resolutely and distinctly, and at his last word he sighed. Ivan Fyodorovitch sat back down.

37.20.oldText: “They are both utterly crazy — they're no better than little children,” Smerdyakov went on. “I'm speaking of your parent and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Any moment now, Fyodor Pavlovitch will get up and start worrying me every minute: ‘Has she come? Why hasn't she come?’ and so on until midnight and even after midnight. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn't come (and very likely she doesn't mean to come at all), then he'll be at me again tomorrow morning: ‘Why hasn't she come? When will she come?’ — as though I'm to blame. On the other side it's no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even before, your brother will appear with his gun in his hands: ‘Look out, you rogue, you soup-maker — if you miss her and don't let me know she's been here, I'll kill you before anyone.’ When the night's over, in the morning, he too, like Fyodor Pavlovitch, starts worrying me to death: ‘Why hasn't she come? Will she come soon?’ And he, too, thinks I'm to blame because his lady hasn't come. Every day and every hour they grow angrier and angrier, so that sometimes I think I'll kill myself out of fright. I can't rely on them, sir.”

37.21.oldText: “And why have you meddled? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?” Ivan said irritably.

37.22.oldText: “How could I help meddling? Though, indeed, I haven't meddled at all, if you want to know the truth of the matter. I kept quiet from the very beginning, not daring to answer; but he fixed on me to be his servant. He's had only one thing to say, over and over: ‘I'll kill you, you scoundrel, if you miss her.’ I feel certain, sir, that I'll have a long fit tomorrow.”

37.23.oldText: “What do you mean by ‘a long fit’?”

37.24.oldText: “A long fit, lasting a long time — several hours, or perhaps a day or two. Once it went on for three days. I fell from the garret that time. The struggling stopped and then began again, and for three days I couldn't come back to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried another remedy too.... I might have died.”

37.25.oldText: “But they say you can't tell with epilepsy when a fit is coming. What makes you say you'll have one tomorrow?” Ivan asked, with peculiar, irritable curiosity.

37.26.oldText: “That's just so. You can't tell beforehand.”

37.27.oldText: “Besides, you fell from the garret then.”

37.28.oldText: “I climb up to the garret every day. I might fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not, I might fall down the cellar steps. I have to go into the cellar every day, too.”

37.29.oldText: Ivan took a long look at him.

37.30.oldText: “You're talking nonsense, I see, and I don't quite follow you,” he said softly, but with a sort of menace. “Are you planning to pretend to be ill tomorrow for three days, eh?”

37.31.oldText: Smerdyakov, who had lowered his eyes again and was playing with the toe of his right foot, set that foot down, moved the left one forward, and, grinning, articulated:

37.32.oldText: “If I were able to pull off such a trick — that is, pretend to have a fit — and it wouldn't be difficult for a man accustomed to them — I'd have a perfect right to use such a means to save myself from death. For even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to see his father while I'm ill, his honor can't blame a sick man for not telling him. He'd be ashamed to.”

37.33.oldText: “Hang it all!” Ivan cried, his face working with anger, “why are you always in such a funk for your life? All my brother Dmitri's threats are only hasty words and mean nothing. He won't kill you — it's not you he'll kill!”

37.34.oldText: “He'd kill me first of all, like a fly. But even more than that, I'm afraid I'd be taken for an accomplice of his when he does something crazy to his father.”

37.35.oldText: “Why should you be taken for an accomplice?”

37.36.oldText: “They'll think I'm an accomplice because I told him the signals as a great secret.”

37.37.oldText: “What signals? Whom did you tell? Confound you, speak more plainly.”

37.38.oldText: “I'm bound to admit it,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, “that I have a secret with Fyodor Pavlovitch in this business. As you yourself know (if indeed you do know it), for several days past he's been locking himself in as soon as night, or even evening, comes on. Lately you've been going upstairs to your room early every evening, and yesterday you didn't come down at all, and so perhaps you don't know how carefully he's begun to lock himself in at night, and that even if Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door, he won't open to him until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn't come, because I wait on him alone in his room now. That's the arrangement he made himself, ever since this to-do with Agrafena Alexandrovna began. But at night, by his orders, I go out to the lodge, so that I don't get to sleep until midnight but am on watch, getting up and walking about the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to come. For the last few days he's been perfectly frantic expecting her. What he argues is, she's afraid of him — Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya, as he calls him) — ‘and so,’ says he, ‘she'll come the back way, late at night, to me. You keep watch for her,’ says he, ‘until midnight and later; and if she comes, you run up and knock at my door, or at the window from the garden. Knock first twice, rather gently, and then three times more quickly; then,’ says he, ‘I'll understand at once that she's come, and will open the door to you quietly.’ Another signal he gave me in case anything unexpected happens. At first, two knocks, and then, after an interval, another much louder. Then he'll understand that something has happened suddenly and that I have to see him, and he'll open to me so I can go in and speak to him. That's all in case Agrafena Alexandrovna can't come herself but sends a message. Besides, Dmitri Fyodorovitch might come too, so I have to let him know he's nearby. His honor is terribly afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, so that even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had come and were locked in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch were to turn up anywhere nearby at the time, I'd be bound to let him know at once, by knocking three times. So the first signal of five knocks means ‘Agrafena Alexandrovna has come,’ while the second signal of three knocks means ‘something important to tell you.’ His honor has shown me them several times and explained them. And since in the whole universe no one knows of these signals but myself and his honor, he'd open the door without the slightest hesitation and without calling out (he's terribly afraid of calling out aloud). Well, those signals are known to Dmitri Fyodorovitch too, now.”

37.39.oldText: “How are they known? Did you tell him? How dared you tell him?”

37.40.oldText: “It was out of fright I did it. How could I dare keep it back from him? Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept insisting every day, ‘You're deceiving me, you're hiding something from me! I'll break both your legs for you.’ So I told him those secret signals, so he might see my slavish devotion and be satisfied that I wasn't deceiving him, but was telling him everything I could.”

37.41.oldText: “If you think he'll make use of those signals and try to get in, don't let him in.”

37.42.oldText: “But if I'm laid up with a fit, how can I prevent him coming in, even if I dared prevent him, knowing how desperate he is?”

37.43.oldText: “Hang it! How can you be so sure you're going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”

37.44.oldText: “How would I dare laugh at you? I'm in no laughing mood, with this fear on me. I feel I'm going to have a fit. I have a presentiment. Fright alone will bring it on.”

37.45.oldText: “Confound it! If you're laid up, Grigory will be on watch. Tell Grigory beforehand; he'll be sure not to let him in.”

37.46.oldText: “I'd never dare tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals without orders from my master. And as for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and not admitting him — he's been ill since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna plans to give him medicine tomorrow. They've just arranged it. It's a very peculiar remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows of a preparation and always keeps some of it. It's a strong thing made from a certain herb. She has the secret of it, and she always gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year when his lumbago is so bad it almost paralyzes him. Then she takes a towel, wets it with the stuff, and rubs his whole back for half an hour until it's red and swollen, and what's left in the bottle she gives him to drink with a special prayer — but not quite all, for on such occasions she leaves some for herself, and drinks it herself. And since they never take strong drink, I assure you they both drop asleep at once and sleep soundly for a very long time. When Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes up he's perfectly well after it, but Marfa Ignatyevna always has a headache. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her intention tomorrow, they won't hear anything and won't hinder Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They'll be asleep.”

37.47.oldText: “What a rigmarole! And it all seems to happen at once, as though it were planned. You'll have a fit and they'll both be unconscious,” Ivan cried. “Aren't you trying to arrange it so?” suddenly broke from him, and he frowned menacingly.

37.48.oldText: “How could I?... And why should I, when it all depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and his plans?... If he means to do something, he'll do it; but if not, I'm not going to push him onto his father.”

37.49.oldText: “And why would he go to father — especially on the sly — if, as you say yourself, Agrafena Alexandrovna won't come at all?” Ivan went on, turning white with anger. “You say that yourself, and the whole time I've been here I've been sure it was all the old man's fantasy, and that the creature won't come to him. Why should Dmitri break in on him if she doesn't come? Speak — I want to know what you're thinking!”

37.50.oldText: “You know yourself why he'll come. What's the use of what I think? His honor will come simply because he's in a rage, or suspicious perhaps on account of my illness, and he'll dash in, as he did yesterday, through impatience to search the rooms to see whether she hasn't slipped in on the sly. He's perfectly well aware, too, that Fyodor Pavlovitch has a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied up with ribbon and sealed with three seals. On it is written in his own hand, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she'll come,’ to which he added three days later, ‘for my little chicken.’ There's no telling what that might do.”

37.51.oldText: “Nonsense!” Ivan cried, almost beside himself. “Dmitri won't come to steal money and kill my father to do it. He might have killed him yesterday on account of Grushenka, like the frantic, savage fool he is, but he won't steal.”

37.52.oldText: “He's in very great need of money now — the greatest need, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don't know how much need he's in,” Smerdyakov explained with perfect composure and remarkable distinctness. “He looks on that three thousand as his own, too. He said so to me himself. ‘My father still owes me three thousand,’ he said. And besides that, consider, Ivan Fyodorovitch — there's something else perfectly true. It's as good as certain, so to speak, that Agrafena Alexandrovna will force him, if she only wants to, to marry her — the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch — if she only wants to, and of course she may want to. All I've said is that she won't come, but maybe she's looking for more than that — I mean, to be mistress here. I know myself that Samsonov, her merchant, was laughing with her about it, telling her quite openly that it wouldn't be at all a stupid thing to do. And she's got plenty of sense. She wouldn't marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking that into consideration, Ivan Fyodorovitch, reflect that then neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch nor yourself, nor your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch, would have anything after the master's death — not a rouble — because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him simply to get hold of it all, all the money there is. But if your father were to die now, there'd be some forty thousand for sure, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so — because he's made no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that very well.”

37.53.oldText: A sort of shudder passed over Ivan's face. He suddenly flushed.

37.54.oldText: “Then why on earth,” he suddenly interrupted Smerdyakov, “do you advise me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by that? If I go away, you see what will happen here.” Ivan drew his breath with difficulty.

37.55.oldText: “Precisely so,” Smerdyakov said, softly and reasonably, watching Ivan intently all the while.

37.56.oldText: “What do you mean by ‘precisely so’?” Ivan questioned him, with a menacing light in his eyes, restraining himself with difficulty.

37.57.oldText: “I spoke because I felt sorry for you. If I were in your place, I'd simply throw it all up ... rather than stay on in such a position,” Smerdyakov answered, with the most candid air, looking at Ivan's flashing eyes. They were both silent.

37.58.oldText: “You seem to be a perfect idiot, and what's more ... an awful scoundrel, too.” Ivan rose abruptly from the bench. He was about to pass straight through the gate, but he stopped short and turned to Smerdyakov. Something strange followed. In a sudden paroxysm, Ivan bit his lip, clenched his fists, and in another moment would have flung himself on Smerdyakov. The latter, at any rate, noticed it at the same moment, started, and shrank back. But the moment passed without harm to Smerdyakov, and Ivan turned in silence, in what seemed like perplexity, to the gate.

37.59.oldText: “I'm going away to Moscow tomorrow, if you care to know — early tomorrow morning. That's all!” he suddenly said aloud, angrily, and wondered afterward what need there was to say that to Smerdyakov.

37.60.oldText: “That's the best thing you can do,” Smerdyakov answered, as though he'd expected to hear it; “except that you can always be telegraphed for from Moscow, if anything should happen here.”

37.61.oldText: Ivan stopped again, and again turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But a change had passed over him, too. All his familiarity and carelessness had completely vanished. His face expressed attention and expectation, intent but timid and cringing.

37.62.oldText: “Haven't you something more to say — something to add?” could be read in the intent gaze he fixed on Ivan.

37.63.oldText: “And couldn't I be sent for from Tchermashnya, too — in case anything happens?” Ivan shouted suddenly, for some unknown reason raising his voice.

37.64.oldText: “From Tchermashnya, too ... you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered, almost in a whisper, looking disconcerted, but gazing intently into Ivan's eyes.

37.65.oldText: “Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is nearer. Is it to save me spending money on the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way, that you insist on Tchermashnya?”

37.66.oldText: “Precisely so...” Smerdyakov muttered, with a breaking voice. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile, and again made ready to draw back. But to his astonishment Ivan broke into a laugh, and went through the gate still laughing. Anyone who had seen his face at that moment would have known that he wasn't laughing from lightness of heart, and he himself couldn't have explained what he was feeling at that instant. He moved and walked as though in a nervous frenzy.

38.0.oldText: And in that same nervous frenzy he spoke. Meeting Fyodor Pavlovitch in the drawing room the moment he went in, he shouted at him, waving his hands, “I'm going upstairs to my room, not in to you. Good-bye!” and passed by, trying not even to look at his father. Very possibly the old man was too hateful to him at that moment; but such an unceremonious display of hostility was a surprise even to Fyodor Pavlovitch. And the old man had evidently wanted to tell him something right away and had come out to meet him in the drawing room on purpose. Greeted like that, he stood still in silence, and with an ironical air watched his son going upstairs, until he passed out of sight.

38.1.oldText: “What's the matter with him?” he promptly asked Smerdyakov, who had followed Ivan.

38.2.oldText: “Angry about something. Who can tell?” the valet muttered evasively.

38.3.oldText: “Confound him! Let him be angry then. Bring in the samovar, and get along with you. Look sharp! No news?”

38.4.oldText: Then followed a series of questions such as Smerdyakov had just complained of to Ivan, all relating to his expected visitor, which we will leave out. Half an hour later the house was locked up, and the crazy old man was wandering through the rooms in excited expectation of hearing every minute the five knocks they had agreed on. Now and then he peered out into the darkness, seeing nothing.

38.5.oldText: It was very late, but Ivan was still awake and thinking. He sat up late that night, until two o'clock. But we won't give an account of his thoughts, and this isn't the place to look into that soul — its turn will come. And even if one tried, it would be very hard to give an account of them, for there weren't really thoughts in his brain, but something very vague — and, above all, intense excitement. He felt himself that he had lost his bearings. He was fretted, too, by all sorts of strange and almost surprising desires; for instance, after midnight he was suddenly gripped by an intense, irresistible urge to go downstairs, open the door, go to the lodge and beat Smerdyakov. But if he'd been asked why, he couldn't have given any exact reason, except perhaps that he loathed the valet as someone who had insulted him more grievously than anyone else in the world. On the other hand, he was more than once that night overcome by a sort of inexplicable, humiliating terror that he felt positively paralyzed his physical powers. His head ached and he was dizzy. A feeling of hatred rankled in his heart, as though he meant to take revenge on someone. He even hated Alyosha, remembering the conversation they'd just had. At moments he hated himself intensely. He almost forgot to think about Katerina Ivanovna, and wondered greatly at that afterward, especially as he remembered perfectly how, when he'd been so valiantly protesting to Katerina Ivanovna that he'd be leaving next day for Moscow, something had whispered in his heart, “That's nonsense, you're not going, and it won't be so easy to tear yourself away as you're boasting now.”

38.6.oldText: Remembering that night long afterward, Ivan recalled with peculiar revulsion how he had suddenly got up from the sofa and had stealthily, as though afraid of being watched, opened the door, gone out onto the staircase, and listened to Fyodor Pavlovitch stirring down below; he had listened a long while — some five minutes — with a sort of strange curiosity, holding his breath while his heart throbbed. And why he'd done all this, why he was listening, he couldn't have said. That “action” he forever afterward called “infamous,” and in the bottom of his heart he thought of it as the basest action of his life. For Fyodor Pavlovitch himself he felt no hatred at that moment, but was simply intensely curious to know how he was walking around down there, and what he must be doing now. He wondered and imagined how he must be peeping out of the dark windows and stopping in the middle of the room, listening, listening — for someone to knock. Ivan went out onto the stairs twice to listen like that.

38.7.oldText: Around two o'clock, when everything was quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan got into bed firmly resolved to fall asleep at once, as he felt fearfully exhausted. And he did fall asleep at once, and slept soundly without dreams, but woke early, at seven, when it was broad daylight. Opening his eyes, he was surprised to feel himself extraordinarily vigorous. He jumped up at once and dressed quickly; then dragged out his trunk and started packing straight away. His linen had come back from the laundress the previous morning. Ivan actually smiled at the thought that everything was helping his sudden departure. And his departure certainly was sudden. Though Ivan had said the day before (to Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha, and Smerdyakov) that he was leaving the next day, he remembered that he'd had no thought of leaving when he went to bed — or at any rate, had not dreamed that his first act in the morning would be to pack his trunk. At last his trunk and bag were ready. It was about nine o'clock when Marfa Ignatyevna came in with her usual inquiry: “Where will your honor take your tea — in your own room or downstairs?” He looked almost cheerful, but there was something about him, about his words and gestures, that was hurried and scattered. Greeting his father amiably, and even inquiring specially after his health — though he didn't wait to hear his answer to the end — he announced that he was setting off in an hour to return to Moscow for good, and asked him to send for the horses. His father heard this announcement with no sign of surprise, and forgot in an unmannerly way to show regret at losing him. Instead, he flew into a great flutter at the recollection of some important business of his own.

38.8.oldText: “What a fellow you are! Not to tell me yesterday! Never mind — we'll manage it all the same. Do me a great service, my dear boy. Stop by Tchermashnya on the way. It's just a left turn from the station at Volovya — only another twelve versts and you come to Tchermashnya.”

38.9.oldText: “I'm sorry, I can't. It's eighty versts to the railway, and the train leaves for Moscow at seven o'clock tonight. I can only just catch it.”

38.10.oldText: “You'll catch it tomorrow or the day after — but today turn off to Tchermashnya. It won't put you out much to humor your father! If I hadn't had something to keep me here, I'd have run over myself long ago, because I've some urgent business there. But here I ... this isn't the time for me to go.... You see, I have two plots of copse land there. The Maslovs, an old merchant and his son, will give eight thousand for the timber. But last year I just missed a buyer who would have given twelve. There's no finding anyone around here to buy it. The Maslovs have it all their own way. One has to take what they'll give, because no one around here dares bid against them. The priest at Ilyinskoe wrote to me last Thursday that a merchant called Gorstkin, a man I know, had turned up. What makes him valuable is that he's not from these parts, so he's not afraid of the Maslovs. He says he'll give me eleven thousand for the copse. Do you hear? But, the priest writes, he'll only be here for a week altogether, so you have to go at once and strike a bargain with him.”

38.11.oldText: “Well, write to the priest then; he'll make the bargain.”

38.12.oldText: “He can't do it. He has no eye for business. He's a perfect treasure, I'd give him twenty thousand to look after for me without a receipt — but he has no eye for business, he's a perfect child, a crow could deceive him. And yet he's a learned man, would you believe it? This Gorstkin looks like a peasant — he wears a blue kaftan — but he's a regular rogue. That's the common complaint. He's a liar. Sometimes he tells such lies that you wonder why he's doing it. He told me the year before last that his wife had died and that he'd married another, and would you believe it, there wasn't a word of truth in it? His wife has never died at all; she's alive to this day and gives him a beating twice a week. So what you have to find out is whether he's lying or telling the truth when he says he wants to buy it and would give eleven thousand.”

38.13.oldText: “I'd be no use in such a business. I have no eye for it either.”

38.14.oldText: “Wait, wait a bit! You'll be useful, because I'll tell you the signs by which you can judge Gorstkin. I've done business with him a long time. You see, you have to watch his beard; he has a nasty, thin, red beard. If his beard shakes when he talks, and he gets cross, then it's all right, he means what he says, he wants to do business. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins — he's trying to cheat you. Don't watch his eyes, you won't learn anything from his eyes, he's a deep one, a rogue — but watch his beard! I'll give you a note to show him. He's called Gorstkin, though his real name is Lyagavy;[4] but don't call him that, he'll be offended. If you come to an understanding with him and see it's all right, write here at once. You only have to write: ‘He's not lying.’ Hold out for eleven thousand; you can knock off one thousand, but no more. Just think! there's a difference between eight thousand and eleven thousand. It's as good as picking up three thousand; it's not so easy to find a purchaser, and I'm in desperate need of money. Just let me know it's serious, and I'll run over and fix it up. I'll snatch the time somehow. But what's the good of my galloping over if it's all some notion of the priest's? Come, will you go?”

38.15.oldText: “Oh, I can't spare the time. You'll have to excuse me.”

38.16.oldText: “Come, you might oblige your father. I won't forget it. You've got no heart, any of you — that's the truth! What's a day or two to you? Where are you off to now — Venice? Your Venice will still be there in two more days. I'd have sent Alyosha, but what use is Alyosha in a thing like this? I'm sending you precisely because you're a clever fellow. Do you think I don't see that? You know nothing about timber, but you've got an eye. All that's needed is to see whether the man's in earnest. I tell you, watch his beard — if his beard shakes, you know he's in earnest.”

38.17.oldText: “You're forcing me to go to that damned Tchermashnya yourself, then?” Ivan cried, with a malignant smile.

38.18.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't catch, or wouldn't catch, the malignancy, but he caught the smile.

38.19.oldText: “Then you'll go, you'll go? I'll scribble the note for you at once.”

38.20.oldText: “I don't know whether I'll go. I don't know. I'll decide on the way.”

38.21.oldText: “Nonsense! Decide at once. My dear fellow, decide! If you settle the matter, write me a line; give it to the priest and he'll send it on to me at once. And I won't delay you any longer than that. You can go to Venice. The priest will give you horses back to Volovya station.”

38.22.oldText: The old man was quite delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased he usually became expansive, but today he seemed to restrain himself. Of Dmitri, for instance, he didn't say a word. He was quite unmoved by the parting, and seemed, in fact, at a loss for something to say. Ivan noticed this particularly. “He must be bored with me,” he thought. Only when he was accompanying his son out onto the steps did the old man begin to fuss. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hastily held out his hand, obviously avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once, and instantly pulled himself up.

38.23.oldText: “Well, good luck to you, good luck to you!” he repeated from the steps. “You'll come back again some time or other? Mind you do come. I'll always be glad to see you. Well, Christ be with you!”

38.25.oldText: “Good-bye, Ivan! Don't be too hard on me!” his father called for the last time.

38.26.oldText: The whole household came out to take leave — Smerdyakov, Marfa, and Grigory. Ivan gave them ten roubles each. When he had seated himself in the carriage, Smerdyakov jumped up to arrange the rug.

38.27.oldText: “You see ... I'm going to Tchermashnya,” suddenly broke from Ivan. Again, as the day before, the words seemed to drop out of themselves, and he laughed, too, a peculiar, nervous laugh. He remembered it long after.

38.28.oldText: “It's a true saying, then, that ‘it's always worth while speaking to a clever man,’” Smerdyakov answered firmly, looking meaningfully at Ivan.

38.29.oldText: The carriage rolled away. Nothing was clear in Ivan's soul, but he looked eagerly around him at the fields, at the hills, at the trees, at a flock of geese flying high overhead in the bright sky. And all of a sudden he felt very happy. He tried to speak to the driver, and felt intensely interested in an answer the peasant gave him; but a minute later he realized he wasn't catching anything, and hadn't really even taken in the peasant's answer. He fell silent, and it was pleasant even so. The air was fresh, pure, and cool, the sky bright. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna floated into his mind. But he softly smiled, blew softly on the friendly phantoms, and they flew away. “There's plenty of time for them,” he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and galloped on to Volovya. “Why is it worth while speaking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?” The thought seemed to grip his breathing. “And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?” They reached Volovya station. Ivan got out of the carriage, and the drivers stood around him bargaining over the twelve-verst journey to Tchermashnya. He told them to harness the horses. He went into the station house, looked around, glanced at the overseer's wife, and suddenly went back out to the entrance.

38.30.oldText: “I won't go to Tchermashnya. Am I too late to reach the railway by seven, brothers?”

38.31.oldText: “We'll just make it. Shall we get the carriage out?”

38.32.oldText: “At once. Is any of you going to the town tomorrow?”

38.34.oldText: “Can you do me a service, Mitri? Go to my father's, to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, and tell him I haven't gone to Tchermashnya. Can you?”

38.35.oldText: “Of course I can. I've known Fyodor Pavlovitch a long time.”

38.36.oldText: “And here's something for you, for I dare say he won't give you anything,” Ivan said, laughing cheerfully.

38.37.oldText: “You may depend on it, he won't.” Mitya laughed too. “Thank you, sir. I'll be sure to do it.”

38.38.oldText: At seven o'clock Ivan got on the train and set off for Moscow. “Away with the past. I'm done with the old world forever, and may I have no news, no echo, from it. On to a new life, new places, and no looking back!” But instead of delight, his soul was filled with such gloom, and his heart ached with such anguish, as he had never known in his life before. He thought all night long. The train flew on, and only at daybreak, as he was approaching Moscow, did he suddenly rouse himself from his brooding.

38.40.oldText: Fyodor Pavlovitch was quite satisfied at having seen his son off. For two hours afterward he felt almost happy, and sat drinking brandy. But suddenly something happened which was very annoying and unpleasant for everyone in the house, and immediately upset Fyodor Pavlovitch's equanimity. Smerdyakov went to the cellar for something and fell down from the top of the steps. Fortunately, Marfa Ignatyevna was in the yard and heard him in time. She didn't see the fall, but heard his scream — the strange, peculiar scream, long familiar to her — the scream of an epileptic falling in a fit. They couldn't tell whether the fit had come on him at the moment he was descending the steps, so that he must have fallen unconscious, or whether it was the fall and the shock that had caused the fit in Smerdyakov, who was known to be liable to them. They found him at the bottom of the cellar steps, writhing in convulsions and foaming at the mouth. It was thought at first that he must have broken something — an arm or a leg — and injured himself, but “God had preserved him,” as Marfa Ignatyevna put it — nothing of the kind had happened. But it was difficult to get him out of the cellar. They asked the neighbors to help, and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovitch himself was present through the whole business. He helped, evidently alarmed and upset. The sick man didn't regain consciousness; the convulsions ceased for a time, but then started again, and everyone concluded that the same thing would happen as had happened a year before, when he accidentally fell from the garret. They remembered that ice had been put on his head then. There was still ice in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna had some brought up. In the evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who arrived at once. He was a most estimable old man, and the most careful and conscientious doctor in the province. After careful examination, he concluded that the fit was a very violent one and might have serious consequences; that in the meantime he, Herzenstube, didn't fully understand it, but that by tomorrow morning, if the present remedies were unavailing, he would venture to try something else. The sick man was taken to the lodge, to a room next to Grigory and Marfa Ignatyevna's.

38.41.oldText: Then Fyodor Pavlovitch had one misfortune after another to put up with that day. Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and the soup, compared with Smerdyakov's, was “no better than dish-water,” and the fowl was so dried up it was impossible to chew. To her master's bitter, though deserved, reproaches, Marfa Ignatyevna replied that the fowl had been a very old one to begin with, and that she had never been trained as a cook. In the evening there was more trouble in store for Fyodor Pavlovitch; he was informed that Grigory, who hadn't been well for the past three days, was completely laid up by his lumbago. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea as early as possible and locked himself in the house alone. He was in terrible excitement and suspense. That evening he counted on Grushenka's coming almost as a certainty. He had received an assurance from Smerdyakov that morning “that she had promised to come without fail.” The incorrigible old man's heart throbbed with excitement; he paced up and down his empty rooms listening. He had to be on the alert. Dmitri might be on the watch for her somewhere, and when she knocked on the window (Smerdyakov had told him two days before that he'd told her where and how to knock), the door had to be opened at once. She mustn't be a second in the passage, for fear — which God forbid! — that she should be frightened and run away. Fyodor Pavlovitch had much to think about, but never had his heart been steeped in such voluptuous hopes. This time he could say almost for certain that she'd come!

39.0.oldText: When Alyosha, with an anxious and aching heart, went into his elder's cell, he stood still almost astonished. Instead of finding a sick man at his last gasp, perhaps unconscious, as he'd feared, he saw him sitting up in his chair — and though weak and exhausted, his face was bright and cheerful; he was surrounded by visitors and engaged in a quiet, joyful conversation. But he had only got up from his bed a quarter of an hour before Alyosha's arrival; his visitors had gathered together in his cell earlier, waiting for him to wake, having received a most confident assurance from Father Païssy that “the teacher would get up, and, as he himself had promised in the morning, would converse once more with those dear to his heart.” This promise, and indeed every word of the dying elder, Father Païssy trusted implicitly. If he had seen him unconscious, if he had seen him breathe his last and yet had his promise that he would rise up and say good-bye to him, he would perhaps not have believed even in his death, but would still have expected the dead man to recover and fulfill his promise. In the morning as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him positively: “I shall not die without the delight of another conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I shall look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you once again.” The monks who had gathered for this probably last conversation with Father Zossima had all been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them: Father Iosif and Father Païssy; Father Mihaïl, the warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned — he was of humble origin, of strong will and steadfast faith, of austere appearance but of deep tenderness, though he obviously concealed it as though almost ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old and humble little monk of the poorest peasant class. He was almost illiterate, and very quiet, scarcely speaking to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and looked as though he had been frightened by something great and awful, something beyond the scope of his intelligence. Father Zossima had a great affection for this timorous man, and always treated him with marked respect, though perhaps there was no one he had known to whom he had said less, in spite of the fact that he had spent years wandering about holy Russia with him. That was very long ago, forty years earlier, when Father Zossima first began his life as a monk in a poor little monastery at Kostroma, and when, shortly afterward, he had accompanied Father Anfim on his pilgrimage to collect alms for their poor monastery.

39.1.oldText: The whole party was in the bedroom which, as we've mentioned before, was very small, so that there was scarcely room for the four of them (in addition to Porfiry, the novice, who stood) to sit around Father Zossima on chairs brought in from the sitting room. It was already beginning to get dark; the room was lit by the lamps and the candles before the icons.

39.3.oldText: “Welcome, my quiet one, welcome, my dear — here you are too. I knew you'd come.”

39.4.oldText: Alyosha went up to him, bowed down to the ground before him, and wept. Something surged up from his heart, his soul was quivering, he wanted to sob.

39.5.oldText: “Come, don't weep over me yet,” Father Zossima smiled, laying his right hand on his head. “You see I'm sitting up talking; maybe I'll live another twenty years yet, as that dear good woman from Vishegorye, with her little Lizaveta in her arms, wished me yesterday. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta,” he crossed himself. “Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you?”

39.6.oldText: He meant the sixty copecks brought to him the day before by the good-humored woman, to be given “to someone poorer than me.” Such offerings, always of money earned by personal toil, are made by way of penance voluntarily undertaken. The elder had sent Porfiry the evening before to a widow whose house had recently burned down and who, after the fire, had gone out with her children begging alms. Porfiry hastened to reply that he had given the money, as he had been instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

39.7.oldText: “Get up, my dear boy,” the elder went on to Alyosha. “Let me look at you. Have you been home, and have you seen your brother?” It seemed strange to Alyosha that he asked so confidently and precisely about only one of his brothers — but which one? Then perhaps he'd sent him out both yesterday and today for the sake of that brother.

39.8.oldText: “I've seen one of my brothers,” Alyosha answered.

39.9.oldText: “I mean the elder one, to whom I bowed down.”

39.10.oldText: “I only saw him yesterday and couldn't find him today,” said Alyosha.

39.11.oldText: “Hurry and find him; go again tomorrow and hurry; leave everything and hurry. Perhaps you may still have time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down before the great suffering that is in store for him.”

39.12.oldText: He suddenly fell silent and seemed to be pondering. His words were strange. Father Iosif, who had witnessed the scene the day before, exchanged glances with Father Païssy. Alyosha could not restrain himself from asking:

39.13.oldText: “Father and teacher,” he began with extreme emotion, “your words are too obscure.... What is this suffering in store for him?”

39.14.oldText: “Don't inquire. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as though his whole future were expressed in his eyes. A look came into his eyes — so that I was instantly horror-stricken at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I've seen such a look in a man's face ... reflecting, as it were, his future fate, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, is from the Lord. ‘Except a grain of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. You, Alexey, I have many times silently blessed for your face — know that,” the elder added with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you: you will go forth from these walls, but will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, but even your foes will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but you will find your happiness in them, and will bless life and will make others bless it — which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he addressed his friends with a tender smile, “up till today I have never told even him why the face of this youth is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been, as it were, a remembrance and a prophecy for me. At the dawn of my life, when I was a child, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at seventeen. And later, in the course of my life, I gradually became convinced that that brother had been a guidance and a sign from on high for me. If he had not come into my life, I should never perhaps — so I fancy at least — have become a monk and entered this precious path. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and here, at the end of my pilgrimage, he seems to have come to me again. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers, that Alexey, who bears some, though not a great, resemblance in face, seems to me so like him spiritually, that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, mysteriously come back to me at the end of my pilgrimage, as a reminder and an inspiration. So that I was positively amazed at such a strange dream in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” he turned to the novice who waited on him. “Many times I've seen, as it were, a look of mortification on your face that I love Alexey more than you. Now you know why that was so; but I love you too, know that, and many times I grieved at your mortification. I'd like to tell you, dear friends, of that youth, my brother, for there has been no presence in my life more precious, more significant, and more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though living through it again.”

39.15.oldText: Here I must observe that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the last day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov wrote it down from memory, some time after his elder's death. But whether this was only the conversation that took place then, or whether he added to it his notes of parts of previous conversations with his teacher, I cannot determine. In his account, Father Zossima's talk goes on without interruption, as though he told his life to his friends in the form of a story — though there is no doubt, from other accounts of it, that the conversation that evening was general. Though the guests didn't interrupt Father Zossima much, they too spoke, perhaps even told something themselves. Besides, Father Zossima couldn't have carried on an uninterrupted narrative, for he was sometimes gasping for breath, his voice failed him, and he even lay down to rest on his bed, though he didn't fall asleep, and his visitors didn't leave their seats. Once or twice the conversation was interrupted by Father Païssy reading the Gospel. It's worth noting, too, that none of them supposed that he would die that night, for on that evening of his life, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed suddenly to have found new strength, which kept him up through this long conversation. It was like a last effort of love which gave him marvelous energy; only for a little while, however, for his life was cut short immediately afterward.... But of that later. I'll only add now that I've preferred to confine myself to the account given by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and not so fatiguing, though of course, as I must repeat, Alyosha took a great deal from previous conversations and added it in.

39.16.oldText: Notes of the Life of the deceased Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, taken from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.

39.19.oldText: Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a distant province in the north, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but of no great consequence or position. He died when I was only two years old, and I don't remember him at all. He left my mother a small wooden house and a fortune — not large, but enough to keep her and her children in comfort. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was, of hasty, irritable temperament but kindhearted and never ironical. He was remarkably silent, especially at home with me, our mother, and the servants. He did well at school, but didn't get on with his schoolfellows, though he never quarreled — at least that's what my mother told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he made friends with a political exile who had been banished from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and who lived a solitary life there. He was a good scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something made him take a liking to Markel, and he used to invite him over. The young man would spend whole evenings with him that winter, until the exile was summoned back to Petersburg to resume his post at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

39.20.oldText: It was the beginning of Lent, and Markel refused to fast; he was rude and laughed at it. “That's all silly twaddle, and there is no God,” he said, horrifying my mother, the servants, and me too. For though I was only nine, I too was aghast at hearing such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of the four, the cook Afimya, who was lame and elderly, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant to take her place.

39.21.oldText: In the sixth week of Lent, my brother, who was never strong and had a tendency to consumption, fell ill. He was tall but thin and delicate-looking, and of very pleasing appearance. I suppose he caught a cold; at any rate the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption, and that he wouldn't live through the spring. My mother began weeping, and, careful not to alarm my brother, she entreated him to go to church, to confess and take the sacrament, while he was still able to move about. This made him angry, and he said something profane about the Church. He grew thoughtful, however; he guessed at once that he was seriously ill, and that that was why his mother was begging him to confess and take the sacrament. He had in fact been aware for a long time that he was far from well, and a year earlier had coolly remarked at dinner to our mother and me, “My life won't be long among you — I may not live another year,” which now seemed like a prophecy.

39.22.oldText: Three days passed and Holy Week had come. And on Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. “I'm doing this simply for your sake, mother, to please and comfort you,” he said. My mother wept with joy and grief. “His end must be near,” she thought, “if there's such a change in him.” But he wasn't able to go to church for long; he took to his bed, so he had to confess and take the sacrament at home.

39.23.oldText: It was a late Easter, and the days were bright, fine, and full of fragrance. I remember he used to cough all night and sleep badly, but in the morning he dressed and tried to sit up in an armchair. That's how I remember him sitting — sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyous, in spite of his illness. A marvelous change came over him; his spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp before the holy image, my dear.” And once he would not have allowed it, and would have blown it out.

39.24.oldText: “Light it, light it, dear; I was a wretch to have prevented you doing it. You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice seeing you. So we are praying to the same God.”

39.25.oldText: Those words seemed strange to us, and mother would go to her room and weep, but when she came in to him she wiped her eyes and looked cheerful. “Mother, don't weep, darling,” he would say, “I've long to live yet, long to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful.”

39.26.oldText: “Ah, dear boy, how can you talk of joy when you lie feverish at night, coughing as though you'd tear yourself to pieces.”

39.27.oldText: “Don't cry, mother,” he would answer. “Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we won't see it; if we would, we should have heaven on earth the next day.”

39.28.oldText: Everyone marveled at his words; he spoke so strangely and positively. We were all touched and wept. Friends came to see us. “Dear ones,” he would say to them, “what have I done that you should love me so? How can you love anyone like me — and how was it I didn't know, I didn't appreciate it before?”

39.29.oldText: When the servants came in to him he would say continually, “Dear, kind people, why are you doing so much for me — do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God's will for me to live, I would wait on you, for all men should wait on one another.”

39.30.oldText: Mother shook her head as she listened. “My darling, it's your illness that makes you talk like that.”

39.31.oldText: “Mother, darling,” he would say, “there have to be servants and masters, but if so I will be the servant of my servants, the same as they are to me. And another thing, mother: every one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than anyone.”

39.32.oldText: Mother positively smiled at that — smiled through her tears. “Why, how could you have sinned against all men, more than all? Robbers and murderers have done that, but what sin have you committed already, that you hold yourself more guilty than all?”

39.33.oldText: “Mother, little heart of mine,” he said (he had begun using such strange, endearing words at that time), “little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, every one is really responsible to all men for all men and for everything. I don't know how to explain it to you, but I feel it is so, painfully even. And how is it we went on then living, getting angry and not knowing?”

39.34.oldText: So he would get up every day, more and more sweet and joyous and full of love. When the doctor, an old German called Eisenschmidt, came in:

39.35.oldText: “Well, doctor, have I another day in this world?” he would ask jokingly.

39.36.oldText: “You'll live many days yet,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.”

39.37.oldText: “Months and years!” he would exclaim. “Why count the days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, try to outshine one another, and hold grudges against each other? Let's go straight into the garden, walk and play there, love, appreciate, and kiss one another, and glorify life.”

39.38.oldText: “Your son cannot last long,” the doctor told my mother as she accompanied him to the door. “The disease is affecting his brain.”
