He realized that what he wanted was to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch's and find out if anything had happened there. “On account of some stupid nonsense — as it's sure to turn out — am I going to wake up the household and make a scandal? Fooh! damn it, is it my business to look after them?”

50.187.oldText: In a very bad humor he went straight home, and suddenly remembered Fenya. “Damn it all! I ought to have questioned her just now,” he thought with vexation, “I should have heard everything.” And the desire to speak to her, and so find out, became so pressing and importunate that when he was halfway home he turned abruptly and went toward the house where Grushenka lodged. Going up to the gate he knocked. The sound of the knock in the silence of the night sobered him and made him feel annoyed. And no one answered him; everyone in the house was asleep.

50.188.oldText: “And I shall be making a fuss!” he thought, with a feeling of positive discomfort. But instead of going away altogether, he fell to knocking again with all his might, filling the street with clamor.

50.189.oldText: “Not coming? Well, I will knock them up, I will!” he muttered at each knock, fuming at himself, but at the same time he redoubled his knocks on the gate.

51.0.oldText: But Dmitri Fyodorovitch was speeding along the road. It was a little more than twenty versts to Mokroe, but Andrey's three horses galloped at such a pace that the distance might be covered in an hour and a quarter. The swift motion revived Mitya. The air was fresh and cool, there were big stars shining in the sky. It was the very night, and perhaps the very hour, in which Alyosha fell on the earth and rapturously swore to love it for ever and ever.

51.1.oldText: All was confusion, confusion, in Mitya's soul, but although many things were goading his heart, at that moment his whole being was yearning for her, his queen, to whom he was flying to look on her for the last time. One thing I can say for certain: his heart did not waver for one instant. I shall perhaps not be believed when I say that this jealous lover felt not the slightest jealousy of this new rival, who seemed to have sprung out of the earth. If any other had appeared on the scene, he would have been jealous at once, and would perhaps have stained his fierce hands with blood again. But as he flew through the night, he felt no envy, no hostility even, for the man who had been her first lover.... It is true he had not yet seen him.

51.2.oldText: “Here there was no room for dispute: it was her right and his; this was her first love which, after five years, she had not forgotten; so she had loved him only for those five years, and I, how do I come in? What right have I? Step aside, Mitya, and make way! What am I now? Now everything is over apart from the officer — even if he had not appeared, everything would be over ...”

51.3.oldText: These words would roughly have expressed his feelings, if he had been capable of reasoning. But he could not reason at that moment. His present plan of action had arisen without reasoning. At Fenya's first words, it had sprung from feeling, and been adopted in a flash, with all its consequences. And yet, in spite of his resolution, there was confusion in his soul, an agonizing confusion: his resolution did not give him peace. There was so much behind that tortured him. And it seemed strange to him, at moments, to think that he had written his own sentence of death with pen and paper: “I punish myself,” and the paper was lying there in his pocket, ready; the pistol was loaded; he had already resolved how, next morning, he would meet the first warm ray of “golden-haired Phœbus.”

51.4.oldText: And yet he could not be quit of the past, of all that he had left behind and that tortured him. He felt that miserably, and the thought of it sank into his heart with despair. There was one moment when he felt an impulse to stop Andrey, to jump out of the cart, to pull out his loaded pistol, and to make an end of everything without waiting for the dawn. But that moment flew by like a spark. The horses galloped on, “devouring space,” and as he drew near his goal, again the thought of her, of her alone, took more and more complete possession of his soul, chasing away the fearful images that had been haunting it. Oh, how he longed to look upon her, if only for a moment, if only from a distance!

51.5.oldText: “She's now with _him_,” he thought, “now I shall see what she looks like with him, her first love — and that's all I want.” Never had this woman, who was such a fateful influence in his life, aroused such love in his breast, such new and unknown feeling, surprising even to himself, a feeling tender to devoutness, to self-effacement before her! “I will efface myself!” he said, in a rush of almost hysterical ecstasy.

51.6.oldText: They had been galloping nearly an hour. Mitya was silent, and though Andrey was, as a rule, a talkative peasant, he did not utter a word either. He seemed afraid to talk; he only whipped up smartly his three lean but mettlesome bay horses. Suddenly Mitya cried out in horrible anxiety:

51.8.oldText: This thought fell upon him like a blow. It had not occurred to him before.

51.9.oldText: “It may well be that they're gone to bed by now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

51.10.oldText: Mitya frowned as though in pain. Yes, indeed ... he was rushing there ... with such feelings ... while they were asleep ... she was asleep, perhaps, there too.... An angry feeling surged up in his heart.

51.12.oldText: “But maybe they're not in bed!” Andrey went on after a pause. “Timofey said they were a lot of them there —”

51.14.oldText: “Not at the posting-station, but at Plastunov's, at the inn, where they let out horses, too.”

51.15.oldText: “I know. So you say there are a lot of them? How's that? Who are they?” cried Mitya, greatly dismayed at this unexpected news.

51.16.oldText: “Well, Timofey was saying they're all gentlefolk. Two from our town — who they are I can't say — and there are two others, strangers, maybe more besides. I didn't ask particularly. They've set to playing cards, so Timofey said.”

51.18.oldText: “So, maybe they're not in bed if they're at cards. It's most likely not more than eleven.”

51.19.oldText: “Quicker, Andrey! Quicker!” Mitya cried again, nervously.

51.20.oldText: “May I ask you something, sir?” said Andrey, after a pause. “Only I'm afraid of angering you, sir.”

51.22.oldText: “Why, Fenya threw herself at your feet just now, and begged you not to harm her mistress, and someone else, too ... so you see, sir — It's I am taking you there ... forgive me, sir, it's my conscience ... maybe it's stupid of me to speak of it —”

51.23.oldText: Mitya suddenly seized him by the shoulders from behind.

51.24.oldText: “Are you a driver?” he asked frantically.

51.26.oldText: “Then you know that one has to make way. What would you say to a driver who wouldn't make way for anyone, but would just drive on and crush people? No, a driver mustn't run over people. One can't run over a man. One can't spoil people's lives. And if you have spoilt a life — punish yourself.... If only you've spoilt, if only you've ruined anyone's life — punish yourself and go away.”

51.27.oldText: These phrases burst from Mitya almost hysterically. Though Andrey was surprised at him, he kept up the conversation.

51.28.oldText: “That's right, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you're quite right, one mustn't crush or torment a man, or any kind of creature, for every creature is created by God. Take a horse, for instance — for some folks, even among us drivers, drive anyhow. Nothing will restrain them, they just force it along.”

51.29.oldText: “To hell?” Mitya interrupted, and went off into his abrupt, short laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” he seized him by the shoulders again, “tell me, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell, or not — what do you think?”

51.30.oldText: “I don't know, darling, it depends on you, for you are ... you see, sir, when the Son of God was nailed on the Cross and died, He went straight down to hell from the Cross, and set free all sinners that were in agony. And the devil groaned, because he thought that he would get no more sinners in hell. And God said to him, then, ‘Don't groan, for you shall have all the mighty of the earth, the rulers, the chief judges, and the rich men, and shall be filled up as you have been in all the ages till I come again.’ Those were His very words ...”

51.31.oldText: “A peasant legend! Capital! Whip up the left, Andrey!”

51.32.oldText: “So you see, sir, who it is hell's for,” said Andrey, whipping up the left horse, “but you're like a little child ... that's how we look on you ... and though you're hasty-tempered, sir, yet God will forgive you for your kind heart.”

51.33.oldText: “And you, do you forgive me, Andrey?”

51.34.oldText: “What should I forgive you for, sir? You've never done me any harm.”

51.35.oldText: “No, for everyone, for everyone — you here alone, on the road, will you forgive me for everyone? Speak, simple peasant heart!”

51.36.oldText: “Oh, sir! I feel afraid of driving you, your talk is so strange.”

51.37.oldText: But Mitya did not hear. He was frantically praying and muttering to himself.

51.38.oldText: “Lord, receive me, with all my lawlessness, and do not condemn me. Let me pass by Thy judgment ... do not condemn me, for I have condemned myself, do not condemn me, for I love Thee, O Lord. I am a wretch, but I love Thee. If Thou sendest me to hell, I shall love Thee there, and from there I shall cry out that I love Thee for ever and ever.... But let me love to the end.... Here and now for just five hours ... till the first light of Thy day ... for I love the queen of my soul ... I love her and I cannot help loving her. Thou seest my whole heart.... I shall gallop up, I shall fall before her and say, ‘You are right to pass on and leave me. Farewell and forget your victim ... never fret yourself about me!’”

51.40.oldText: Through the pale darkness of the night loomed a solid black mass of buildings, flung down, as it were, in the vast plain. The village of Mokroe numbered two thousand inhabitants, but at that hour all were asleep, and only here and there a few lights still twinkled.

51.41.oldText: “Drive on, Andrey, I come!” Mitya exclaimed, feverishly.

51.42.oldText: “They're not asleep,” said Andrey again, pointing with his whip to the Plastunovs' inn, which was at the entrance to the village. The six windows, looking on the street, were all brightly lighted up.

51.43.oldText: “They're not asleep,” Mitya repeated joyously. “Quicker, Andrey! Gallop! Drive up with a dash! Set the bells ringing! Let all know that I have come. I'm coming! I'm coming, too!”

51.44.oldText: Andrey lashed his exhausted team into a gallop, drove with a dash, and pulled up his steaming, panting horses at the high flight of steps.

51.45.oldText: Mitya jumped out of the cart just as the innkeeper, on his way to bed, peeped out from the steps, curious to see who had arrived.

51.47.oldText: The innkeeper bent down, looked intently, ran down the steps, and rushed up to the guest with obsequious delight.

51.48.oldText: “Dmitri Fyodorovitch, your honor! Do I see you again?”

51.49.oldText: Trifon Borissovitch was a thickset, healthy peasant, of middle height, with a rather fat face. His expression was severe and uncompromising, especially with the peasants of Mokroe, but he had the power of assuming the most obsequious countenance, when he had an inkling that it was to his interest. He dressed in Russian style, with a shirt buttoning down on one side, and a full-skirted coat. He had saved a good sum of money, but was for ever dreaming of improving his position. More than half the peasants were in his clutches, everyone in the neighborhood was in debt to him. From the neighboring landowners he bought and rented lands which were worked by the peasants, in payment of debts they could never shake off. He was a widower, with four grown-up daughters. One of them was already a widow and lived in the inn with her two children, his grandchildren, and worked for him like a charwoman. Another of his daughters was married to a petty official, and in one of the rooms of the inn, on the wall could be seen, among the family photographs, a miniature photograph of this official in uniform and official epaulettes. The two younger daughters used to wear fashionable blue or green dresses, fitting tight at the back, and with trains a yard long, on Church holidays or when they went to pay visits. But next morning they would get up at dawn, as usual, sweep out the rooms with a birch broom, empty the slops, and clean up after lodgers.

51.50.oldText: In spite of the thousands of roubles he had saved, Trifon Borissovitch was very fond of emptying the pockets of a drunken guest, and remembering that not a month ago he had, in twenty-four hours, made two if not three hundred roubles out of Dmitri, when he had come on his escapade with Grushenka, he met him now with eager welcome, scenting his prey the moment Mitya drove up to the steps.

51.51.oldText: “Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear sir, we see you once more!”

51.52.oldText: “Stay, Trifon Borissovitch,” began Mitya, “first and foremost, where is she?”

51.53.oldText: “Agrafena Alexandrovna?” The innkeeper understood at once, looking sharply into Mitya's face. “She's here, too ...”

51.55.oldText: “Some strangers. One is an official gentleman, a Pole, to judge from his speech. He sent the horses for her from here; and there's another with him, a friend of his, or a fellow traveler — there's no telling. They're dressed like civilians.”

51.57.oldText: “Poor sort of a feast! Nothing to boast of, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

51.58.oldText: “Nothing to boast of? And who are the others?”

51.59.oldText: “They're two gentlemen from the town.... They've come back from Tcherny, and are putting up here. One's quite a young gentleman, a relative of Mr. Miüsov, he must be, but I've forgotten his name ... and I expect you know the other, too, a gentleman called Maximov. He's been on a pilgrimage, so he says, to the monastery in the town. He's traveling with this young relation of Mr. Miüsov.”

51.62.oldText: “Stay, listen, Trifon Borissovitch. Tell me the chief thing: What of her? How is she?”

51.63.oldText: “Oh, she's only just come. She's sitting with them.”

51.65.oldText: “No, I think she's not laughing much. She's sitting quite dull. She's combing the young gentleman's hair.”

51.67.oldText: “He's not young, and he's not an officer, either. Not him, sir. It's the young gentleman that's Mr. Miüsov's relation ... I've forgotten his name.”

51.70.oldText: “All right. I'll see for myself. Are they playing cards?”

51.71.oldText: “They have been playing, but they've left off. They've been drinking tea — the official gentleman asked for liqueurs.”

51.72.oldText: “Stay, Trifon Borissovitch, stay, my good soul, I'll see for myself. Now answer one more question: are the gypsies here?”

51.73.oldText: “You can't have the gypsies now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The authorities have sent them away. But we've Jews that play the cymbals and the fiddle in the village, so one might send for them. They'd come.”

51.74.oldText: “Send for them. Certainly send for them!” cried Mitya. “And you can get the girls together as you did then — Marya especially, Stepanida, too, and Arina. Two hundred roubles for a chorus!”

51.75.oldText: “Oh, for a sum like that I can get all the village together, though by now they're asleep. Are the peasants here worth such kindness, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or the girls either? To spend a sum like that on such coarseness and rudeness! What's the good of giving a peasant a cigar to smoke, the stinking ruffian! And the girls are all lousy. Besides, I'll get my daughters up for nothing, let alone a sum like that. They've only just gone to bed, I'll give them a kick and set them singing for you. You gave the peasants champagne to drink the other day, e—ech!”

51.76.oldText: For all his pretended compassion for Mitya, Trifon Borissovitch had hidden half a dozen bottles of champagne on that last occasion, and had picked up a hundred-rouble note under the table, and it had remained in his clutches.

51.77.oldText: “Trifon Borissovitch, I sent more than one thousand flying last time I was here. Do you remember?”

51.78.oldText: “You did send it flying. I may well remember. You must have left three thousand behind you.”

51.79.oldText: “Well, I've come to do the same again, do you see?”

51.80.oldText: And he pulled out his roll of notes, and held them up before the innkeeper's nose.

51.81.oldText: “Now, listen and remember. In an hour's time the wine will arrive, savories, pies, and sweets — bring them all up at once. That box Andrey has got is to be brought up at once, too. Open it, and hand champagne immediately. And the girls, we must have the girls, Marya especially.”

51.82.oldText: He turned to the cart and pulled out the box of pistols.

51.83.oldText: “Here, Andrey, let's settle. Here's fifteen roubles for the drive, and fifty for vodka ... for your readiness, for your love.... Remember Karamazov!”

51.84.oldText: “I'm afraid, sir,” faltered Andrey. “Give me five roubles extra, but more I won't take. Trifon Borissovitch, bear witness. Forgive my foolish words ...”

51.85.oldText: “What are you afraid of?” asked Mitya, scanning him. “Well, go to the devil, if that's it!” he cried, flinging him five roubles. “Now, Trifon Borissovitch, take me up quietly and let me first get a look at them, so that they don't see me. Where are they? In the blue room?”

51.86.oldText: Trifon Borissovitch looked apprehensively at Mitya, but at once obediently did his bidding. Leading him into the passage, he went himself into the first large room, adjoining that in which the visitors were sitting, and took the light away. Then he stealthily led Mitya in, and put him in a corner in the dark, whence he could freely watch the company without being seen. But Mitya did not look long, and, indeed, he could not see them — he saw her, his heart throbbed violently, and all was dark before his eyes.

51.87.oldText: She was sitting sideways to the table in a low chair, and beside her, on the sofa, was the pretty youth, Kalganov. She was holding his hand and seemed to be laughing, while he, seeming vexed and not looking at her, was saying something in a loud voice to Maximov, who sat the other side of the table, facing Grushenka. Maximov was laughing violently at something. On the sofa sat _he_, and on a chair by the sofa there was another stranger. The one on the sofa was lolling backward, smoking a pipe, and Mitya had an impression of a stoutish, broad-faced, short little man, who was apparently angry about something. His friend, the other stranger, struck Mitya as extraordinarily tall, but he could make out nothing more. He caught his breath. He could not bear it for a minute — he put the pistol-case on a chest, and with a throbbing heart he walked, feeling cold all over, straight into the blue room to face the company.

51.88.oldText: “Aie!” shrieked Grushenka, the first to notice him.

52.0.oldText: With his long, rapid strides, Mitya walked straight up to the table.

52.1.oldText: “Gentlemen,” he said loudly, almost shouting, yet stammering on every word, “I—I'm fine! Don't be afraid!” he exclaimed. “There's nothing the matter with me,” he said, turning suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand tightly. “I—I'm coming too. I'll stay until morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Just until morning, for the last time, in this same room?”

52.2.oldText: He finished by turning to the fat little man with the pipe, sitting on the sofa. The man removed his pipe from his lips with dignity and observed severely:

52.3.oldText: “_Panie_, we're here in private. There are other rooms.”

52.4.oldText: “Why, it's you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What are you doing?” Kalganov put in suddenly. “Sit down with us. How are you?”

52.5.oldText: “Delighted to see you, dear—precious fellow, I always thought a lot of you,” Mitya responded joyfully and eagerly, at once reaching his hand across the table.

52.6.oldText: “Ouch! You squeeze so hard! You've nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

52.7.oldText: “He always squeezes like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile, suddenly convinced from Mitya's face that he wasn't going to make a scene. She was watching him with intense curiosity and still some unease. Something about him impressed her, and the last thing she'd expected was that he would walk in and speak like this at such a moment.

52.8.oldText: “Good evening,” Maximov ventured blandly on the left. Mitya rushed up to him too.

52.9.oldText: “Good evening. You're here too! How glad I am to find you here as well! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned back to the Polish gentleman with the pipe, evidently taking him for the most important person present.) “I flew here. I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room—where I too adored—my queen. Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly. “I flew here and swore—Oh, don't be afraid, it's my last night! Let's drink to our good understanding. The wine will be here any minute. I brought this with me.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of banknotes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a celebration, the way we had before. But the worm, the unnecessary worm, will crawl away, and there'll be no more of him. I'll mark my day of joy on my last night.”

52.10.oldText: He was almost choking. There was so much, so much he wanted to say, but only strange exclamations kept coming out. The Pole stared fixedly at him, at the bundle of notes in his hand, then looked at Grushenka, clearly puzzled.

52.11.oldText: “If my suverin lady is permitting—” he began.

52.12.oldText: “What does ‘suverin' mean? ‘Sovereign,' I suppose?” Grushenka interrupted. “I can't help laughing at the way you talk. Sit down, Mitya, what are you talking about? Don't frighten us, please. You won't frighten us, will you? If you won't, I'm glad to see you—”

52.13.oldText: “Me, frighten you?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won't get in your way!”

52.14.oldText: And suddenly he surprised them all—and no doubt himself too—by throwing himself into a chair and bursting into tears, turning his head away toward the opposite wall while his arms clutched the back of the chair tight, as though embracing it.

52.15.oldText: “Come on, what a fellow you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That's exactly how he comes to see me—he starts talking, and I can't make out what he means. He cried like that once before, and now he's crying again! It's shameful! What are you crying for? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added enigmatically, emphasizing each word with a touch of irritation.

52.16.oldText: “I—I'm not crying. Well, good evening!” He turned back in his chair at once and suddenly laughed—not his abrupt wooden laugh, but a long, quivering, almost inaudible nervous laugh.

52.17.oldText: “There you go again. Come, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka said coaxingly. “I'm very glad you've come, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I'm very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she said firmly, addressing the whole company, though her words were obviously meant for the man on the sofa. “I want it, I want it! And if he leaves, I'll leave too!” she added, her eyes flashing.

52.18.oldText: “Whatever my queen commands is law!” pronounced the Pole, gallantly kissing Grushenka's hand. “I beg you, _panie_, to join our company,” he added politely, turning to Mitya.

52.19.oldText: Mitya was about to jump up with the obvious intention of delivering another tirade, but the words wouldn't come.

52.20.oldText: “Let's drink, _panie_,” he blurted out instead of making a speech. Everyone laughed.

52.21.oldText: “Good heavens! I thought he was going to start again!” Grushenka exclaimed nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on insistently, “don't prance around, but it's nice that you brought champagne. I want some myself, and I can't stand liqueurs. And best of all, you've come yourself. We were terribly dull here. You've come for a spree again, I suppose? But put your money in your pocket. Where did you get so much?”

52.22.oldText: Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand the whole time, and every eye—especially the Poles'—was fixed on it. Embarrassed, he hurriedly stuffed them into his pocket. He flushed. At that moment the innkeeper brought in an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya snatched up the bottle, but he was so flustered he didn't know what to do with it. Kalganov took it from him and poured.

52.23.oldText: “Another! Another bottle!” Mitya called to the innkeeper, and, forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly invited to drink to their good understanding, he tossed back his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face suddenly changed. The solemn, tragic expression with which he'd entered vanished completely, and something childlike came into his face. He seemed to have turned suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked shyly and happily at everyone, with a continual nervous little laugh and the blissful expression of a dog who has done wrong, been punished, and forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything and was gazing around with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing constantly, and moved his chair close to hers. Gradually he had formed some idea of the two Poles, though he hadn't settled on any definite impression of them yet.

52.24.oldText: The Pole on the sofa struck him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and above all with his pipe. “Well, what of it? It's a good thing he's smoking a pipe,” he thought. The Pole's puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and two very thin, pointed, dyed, and impudent mustaches, hadn't yet raised the faintest doubt in Mitya. He wasn't even particularly struck by the Pole's absurd wig, made in Siberia, with silly love-locks combed forward over the temples. “I suppose it's all right since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other, younger Pole, who was staring insolently and defiantly at the company and listening to the conversation with silent contempt, still only impressed Mitya by his great height, which was in striking contrast to the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he'd be six foot three,” the thought flickered through Mitya's mind. It also occurred to him that this Pole must be the other one's friend—a kind of “bodyguard”—and that the big Pole was no doubt at the disposal of the little Pole with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly right and not to be questioned. In his mood of dog-like submissiveness, every feeling of rivalry had died away.

52.25.oldText: Grushenka's mood and the enigmatic tone of some of her words he completely failed to grasp. All he understood, with a thrilling heart, was that she was kind to him, that she had forgiven him, and had made him sit beside her. He was beside himself with delight, watching her sip her glass of champagne. But the silence in the company seemed to strike him, and he glanced around at everyone with expectant eyes.

52.26.oldText: “Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don't you start doing something?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.

52.27.oldText: “He keeps talking nonsense, and we were all laughing at him,” Kalganov began suddenly, as though reading his thought, and pointed at Maximov.

52.28.oldText: Mitya immediately stared at Kalganov, then at Maximov.

52.29.oldText: “He's talking nonsense?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted at something. “Ha ha!”

52.30.oldText: “Yes. Would you believe it, he insists that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. That's absolute nonsense, isn't it?”

52.32.oldText: Kalganov was well aware of Mitya's feelings for Grushenka, and he had guessed about the Pole too, but that didn't interest him much—perhaps didn't interest him at all. What he was interested in was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he had met the Poles here at the inn for the first time in his life. He already knew Grushenka and had once come with someone to see her, but she hadn't taken to him. Here, though, she was looking at him very affectionately: before Mitya's arrival, she had been making a fuss over him, but he seemed somehow unmoved by it. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick, fair hair. From his pale face looked out beautiful pale-blue eyes, with an intelligent and sometimes even deep expression, beyond his years—though the young man sometimes looked and talked quite like a child, and wasn't at all ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Sometimes there was something fixed and obstinate in his expression. He would look at you and listen, seeming all the while to be persistently dreaming about something else. Often he was listless and lazy; at other times he would grow excited, sometimes, apparently, over the most trivial matters.

52.33.oldText: “Just imagine, I've been taking him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling his words indolently, yet quite naturally, without the slightest affectation. “Ever since your brother, remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That made me take an interest in him at the time, and I brought him out to the country, but he keeps talking such rubbish I'm ashamed to be seen with him. I'm taking him back.”

52.34.oldText: “The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is impossible,” the Pole with the pipe remarked to Maximov.

52.35.oldText: He spoke Russian fairly well—much better, in any case, than he pretended. When he did use Russian words, he always twisted them into a Polish form.

52.37.oldText: “But were you in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov put in at once.

52.38.oldText: “Was he a cavalry officer, indeed? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly and turning his inquiring eyes on each speaker in turn, as though there was no telling what he might hear.

52.39.oldText: “No, you see,” Maximov turned to him. “What I mean is that those pretty Polish ladies—when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans—when one of them dances a mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten, a little white one, and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother look on and allow it. They allow it—and the next day the Uhlan comes and offers her his hand. That's how it is—offers her his hand, heh heh!” Maximov ended, tittering.

52.40.oldText: “The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole in the chair suddenly growled, and crossed one leg over the other. Mitya's eye was caught by the Pole's huge greased boot, with its thick, dirty sole. The clothing of both Poles looked rather greasy.

52.41.oldText: “Well, now it's _lajdak_! What's he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly annoyed.

52.42.oldText: “_Pani_ Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies of good family,” the Pole with the pipe observed to Grushenka.

52.43.oldText: “You can count on that,” the tall Pole snapped contemptuously.

52.44.oldText: “What now! Let him talk! People talk—why stop them? It makes things cheerful,” Grushenka said crossly.

52.45.oldText: “I'm not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig, with a long look at Grushenka, and then, falling into dignified silence, he sucked on his pipe again.

52.46.oldText: “No, no. The Polish gentleman spoke the truth.” Kalganov got excited again, as though it were a matter of great importance. “He's never been in Poland, so how can he talk about it? You weren't married in Poland, were you?”

52.47.oldText: “No, in the Smolensk Province. But a Uhlan had brought her to Russia before that—my future wife, I mean—with her mamma, her aunt, and another female relative with a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. But he didn't marry her, because she turned out to be lame.”

52.49.oldText: “Yes. They both deceived me a little at the time and hid it. I thought she was just skipping; she kept hopping along. I thought it was for fun.”

52.50.oldText: “She was so pleased she was going to marry you!” yelped Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

52.51.oldText: “Yes, so pleased. But it turned out to be a very different cause. Afterwards, once we were married, that very evening, after the wedding, she confessed, and very touchingly begged my forgiveness. ‘I jumped over a puddle once when I was a child,' she said, ‘and hurt my leg.' Heh heh!”

52.52.oldText: Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter, almost falling onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

52.53.oldText: “Do you know, that's the truth, he's not lying this time,” Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya. “And do you know, he's been married twice—it's his first wife he's talking about. But his second wife, do you know, ran away and is still alive.”

52.54.oldText: “Is that possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov with an expression of utter astonishment.

52.55.oldText: “Yes. She ran away. I had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov modestly agreed, “with a _monsieur_. And what was worse, she'd had all my little property transferred to her beforehand. ‘You're an educated man,' she told me. ‘You can always make a living.' She settled my affairs like that. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.' Heh heh!”

52.56.oldText: “Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he's lying—and he often is—he's only doing it to entertain us all. There's no harm in that, is there? You know, I sometimes like him. He's terribly low, but it's natural to him, isn't it? Don't you think? Some people are low out of self-interest, but he's just like that by nature. Just imagine—he claims (he was arguing about it all day yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Remember, there's a landowner in it named Maximov, whom Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, remember, ‘for inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov while in a drunken state.' Would you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov, and that he was beaten! Now, can that be? Tchitchikov made his journey at the latest at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don't fit. He couldn't have been beaten then, could he?”

52.57.oldText: It was hard to imagine what Kalganov was so excited about, but his excitement was genuine. Mitya followed along without objecting.

52.58.oldText: “Well, but what if they did beat him!” he cried, laughing.

52.59.oldText: “It's not that they beat me exactly, but what I mean is—” Maximov put in.

52.60.oldText: “What do you mean? Either they beat you or they didn't.”

52.61.oldText: “What time is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, with a bored expression. The other shrugged his shoulders in reply. Neither of them had a watch.

52.62.oldText: “Why not talk? Let other people talk. Must other people be quiet just because you're bored?” Grushenka flew at him, clearly looking for a fight. Something seemed for the first time to flash across Mitya's mind. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.

52.63.oldText: “_Pani_, I didn't oppose it. I didn't say anything.”

52.64.oldText: “All right then. Come on, tell us your story,” Grushenka called to Maximov. “Why is everyone silent?”

52.65.oldText: “There's nothing to tell, it's all so silly,” Maximov answered at once, with evident satisfaction, affecting a mincing tone. “Besides, all of that's allegory in Gogol, since he gave all the names a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name—he was called Shkvornev. Fenardi really was named Fenardi, only he wasn't Italian but Russian, and Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl with pretty little legs in tights, and she had a short little skirt with spangles, and she kept spinning round and round—only not for four hours, but just four minutes—and she bewitched everyone—”

52.66.oldText: “But what were you beaten for?” cried Kalganov.

52.69.oldText: “The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking then, a big party of us, in a tavern at that very fair. They'd invited me, and first of all I began quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny get-up!' And Boileau answers that he's going to a masquerade—meaning to the baths, heh heh! And they took it personally, so I hurried to recite another one, very sarcastic and well known to all educated people:

52.70.oldText: Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don't know your way to the sea!

52.71.oldText: They were even more offended and began cursing me in the most unseemly way for it. And as bad luck would have it, to set things right, I started telling a very cultivated anecdote about Piron—how he wasn't accepted into the French Academy, and how, in revenge, he wrote his own epitaph:

52.75.oldText: “For my education. People can beat a man for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.

52.76.oldText: “Enough! That's all stupid, I don't want to listen. I thought it would be amusing,” Grushenka cut them off abruptly.

52.77.oldText: Mitya started, and at once stopped laughing. The tall Pole rose to his feet and, with the haughty air of a man bored and out of his element, began pacing from corner to corner of the room, his hands behind his back.

52.78.oldText: “Ah, he can't sit still,” Grushenka said, looking at him contemptuously. Mitya began to feel anxious. He noticed, too, that the Pole on the sofa was looking at him with an irritated expression.

52.79.oldText: “_Panie!_” cried Mitya. “Let's drink! And the other _pan_ too! Let's drink.”

52.80.oldText: In a flash he pulled three glasses toward him and filled them with champagne.

52.81.oldText: “To Poland, _panovie_, I drink to your Poland!” cried Mitya.

52.82.oldText: “I shall be delighted, _panie_,” said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and affable condescension, and he took his glass.

52.83.oldText: “And the other _pan_, what's his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!” Mitya urged.

52.85.oldText: Pan Vrublevsky came up to the table, swaying as he walked.

52.86.oldText: “To Poland, _panovie_!” cried Mitya, raising his glass. “Hurrah!”

52.87.oldText: All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and poured out three more glasses.

52.88.oldText: “Now to Russia, _panovie_, and let us be brothers!”

52.89.oldText: “Pour some for us,” said Grushenka. “I'll drink to Russia too!”

52.91.oldText: “And I would, too—to Russia, the old grandmother!” Maximov tittered.

52.92.oldText: “All! All!” cried Mitya. “Trifon Borissovitch, more bottles!”

52.94.oldText: “To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted again. All drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka tossed off her whole glass at once. The Poles didn't touch theirs.

52.95.oldText: “What's this, _panovie_?” cried Mitya. “You won't drink it?”

52.96.oldText: Pan Vrublevsky took up the glass, raised it, and said in a resonant voice:

52.98.oldText: “Now, that's better!” cried the other Pole, and they both emptied their glasses at once.

52.99.oldText: “You're fools, you _panovie_,” burst suddenly from Mitya.

52.100.oldText: “_Panie!_” shouted both Poles menacingly, turning on Mitya like a pair of roosters. Pan Vrublevsky was especially furious.

52.102.oldText: “Silence! No quarreling! I won't have any quarreling!” cried Grushenka imperiously, and she stamped her foot on the floor. Her face glowed, her eyes shone. The glass she had just drunk was taking effect. Mitya was terribly alarmed.

52.103.oldText: “_Panovie_, forgive me! It was my fault, I'm sorry. Vrublevsky, _panie_ Vrublevsky, I'm sorry.”

52.104.oldText: “Hold your tongue, you, anyway! Sit down, you stupid man!” Grushenka scolded with angry annoyance.

52.105.oldText: Everyone sat down, all fell silent, looking at one another.

52.106.oldText: “Gentlemen, I was the cause of it all,” Mitya began again, unable to make anything of Grushenka's words. “Come, why are we sitting here? What shall we do—to amuse ourselves again?”

52.107.oldText: “Ah, this is certainly anything but amusing!” Kalganov mumbled lazily.

52.108.oldText: “Let's play faro again, the way we just did,” Maximov tittered suddenly.

52.110.oldText: “It's lite, _panovie_,” the Pole on the sofa responded, reluctantly.

52.112.oldText: “Lite? What do you mean, ‘lite'?” Grushenka asked.

52.113.oldText: “Late, _pani_! ‘A late hour,' I mean,” the Pole on the sofa explained.

52.114.oldText: “It's always late with them. They can't do anything!” Grushenka almost shrieked in anger. “They're dull themselves, so they want others to be dull too. Before you came, Mitya, they were just as silent and kept turning up their noses at me.”

52.115.oldText: “My goddess!” cried the Pole on the sofa. “I see you're not well-disposed to me, and that's why I'm gloomy. I'm ready, _panie_,” he added, turning to Mitya.

52.116.oldText: “Begin, _panie_,” Mitya agreed, pulling his notes out of his pocket and laying two hundred-rouble notes on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take the cards. Make the bank.”

52.117.oldText: “We'll have cards from the landlord, _panie_,” said the little Pole gravely and emphatically.

52.118.oldText: “That's much the best way,” chimed in Pan Vrublevsky.

52.119.oldText: “From the landlord? Very well, I understand, let's get them from him. Cards!” Mitya shouted to the landlord.

52.120.oldText: The landlord brought in a new, unopened pack and informed Mitya that the girls were getting ready and that the Jews with the cymbals would likely be there soon, but the cart with the provisions hadn't yet arrived. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give orders, but only three girls had arrived, and Marya wasn't there yet. He didn't know himself what orders to give, or why he had run out. He only told them to take the presents for the girls out of the box—the sweets, the toffee, and the fondants. “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!” he cried hurriedly. “I was rude to Andrey!”

52.121.oldText: Suddenly Maximov, who had followed him out, touched him on the shoulder.

52.122.oldText: “Give me five roubles,” he whispered to Mitya. “I'll stake something at faro too, heh heh!”

52.124.oldText: Again he took all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. “And if you lose that, come again, come again.”

52.125.oldText: “Very good,” Maximov whispered joyfully, and he hurried back again. Mitya too returned, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had already sat down and opened the pack. They looked much more amiable now, almost cordial. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was preparing to deal. He wore an air of solemnity.

52.126.oldText: “To your places, gentlemen,” cried Pan Vrublevsky.

52.127.oldText: “No, I'm not going to play any more,” Kalganov remarked. “I lost fifty roubles to them just now.”

52.128.oldText: “The _pan_ had no luck—perhaps he'll be lucky this time,” the Pole on the sofa said in his direction.

52.129.oldText: “How much is in the bank? To match?” asked Mitya.

52.130.oldText: “That's as you like, _panie_—maybe a hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you want to stake.”

52.132.oldText: “The Pan Captain has perhaps heard of Pan Podvysotsky?”

52.134.oldText: “In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone who came could stake against it. Podvysotsky comes in, sees a thousand gold pieces, and stakes against the bank. The banker says, ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky, are you laying down the gold, or must we trust to your honor?' ‘To my honor, _panie_,' says Podvysotsky. ‘So much the better.' The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. ‘Take it, _panie_,' says the banker, and pulling out the drawer, he hands him a million. ‘Take it, _panie_, these are your winnings.' There was a million in the bank. ‘I didn't know that,' says Podvysotsky. ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky,' said the banker, ‘you pledged your honor, and we pledged ours.' Podvysotsky took the million.”

52.136.oldText: “_Panie_ Kalganov, in gentlemanly society one doesn't say such things.”

52.137.oldText: “As if a Polish gambler would give away a million!” cried Mitya, but he checked himself at once. “Forgive me, _panie_, it's my fault again—he would, he would give away a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I stake ten roubles—the knave leads.”

52.138.oldText: “And I'll put a rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little _panienotchka_, heh heh!” laughed Maximov, pulling out his queen and, as though trying to hide it from everyone, moved right up and crossed himself hurriedly under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won too.

52.140.oldText: “I'll bet another rouble, a ‘single' stake,” Maximov muttered gleefully, thrilled at having won a rouble.

52.144.oldText: “Double! Double!” Mitya kept doubling his stakes, and each time he doubled, the card he doubled was trumped by the Poles. The rouble stakes kept winning.

52.146.oldText: “You've lost two hundred, _panie_. Will you stake another hundred?” asked the Pole on the sofa.

52.147.oldText: “What? Lost two hundred already? Then another two hundred! All on doubles!”

52.148.oldText: And pulling his money out of his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.

52.149.oldText: “That's enough!” he shouted in his ringing voice.

52.150.oldText: “What's the matter?” Mitya stared at him.

52.151.oldText: “That's enough! I don't want you to play any more. Don't!”

52.153.oldText: “Because I don't. Damn it, come away. That's why. I won't let you go on playing.”

52.154.oldText: Mitya gazed at him in astonishment.

52.155.oldText: “Give it up, Mitya. He may be right. You've lost a lot already,” Grushenka said, with a strange note in her voice. Both Poles rose from their seats with a deeply offended air.

52.156.oldText: “Are you joking, _panie_?” said the short one, looking severely at Kalganov.

52.157.oldText: “How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov too.

52.158.oldText: “Don't you dare shout like that,” cried Grushenka. “Ah, you turkey-cocks!”

52.159.oldText: Mitya looked at each of them in turn. But something in Grushenka's face suddenly struck him, and at the same instant something new flashed into his mind—a strange new thought!

52.160.oldText: “_Pani_ Agrippina,” the little Pole was beginning, crimson with anger, when Mitya suddenly walked up to him and slapped him on the shoulder.

52.163.oldText: “In the next room—I've two words to say to you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You'll be glad to hear it.”

52.164.oldText: The little _pan_ was taken aback and looked apprehensively at Mitya. He agreed at once, however, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky went with them.

52.165.oldText: “The bodyguard? Let him come—I want him there too. I must have him!” cried Mitya. “March, _panovie_!”

52.166.oldText: “Where are you going?” Grushenka asked anxiously.

52.167.oldText: “We'll be back in a moment,” Mitya answered.

52.168.oldText: There was a sort of boldness, a sudden confidence shining in his eyes. His face had looked very different when he entered the room an hour before.

52.169.oldText: He led the Poles not into the large room where the chorus of girls was assembling and the table was being set, but into the bedroom on the right, where the trunks and packages were kept, and where there were two large beds with pyramids of cotton pillows on each. A lighted candle stood on a small deal table in the corner. The small man and Mitya sat down at this table, facing each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood beside them, his hands behind his back. The Poles looked severe but were obviously curious.

52.171.oldText: “Well, look here, _panie_, I won't keep you long. There's money for you,” he said, pulling out his notes. “Would you like three thousand? Take it and go on your way.”

52.172.oldText: The Pole stared wide-eyed at Mitya, with a searching look.

52.173.oldText: “Three thousand, _panie_?” He exchanged glances with Vrublevsky.

52.174.oldText: “Three, _panovie_, three! Listen, _panie_, I see you're a sensible man. Take three thousand and go to the devil, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear? But at once, this very minute, and for good. You understand, _panie_—for good. Here's the door, you go out of it. What do you have there, an overcoat, a fur coat? I'll bring it out to you. They'll get the horses ready right away, and then—goodbye, _panie_!”

52.175.oldText: Mitya awaited an answer with assurance. He had no doubts. An expression of extraordinary resolution passed over the Pole's face.

52.177.oldText: “The money, _panie_? Five hundred roubles I'll give you this instant for the journey, as a first installment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow, in the town—I swear on my honor, I'll get it, I'll get it at any cost!” cried Mitya.

52.178.oldText: The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man's face looked more forbidding.

52.179.oldText: “Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, at once, this minute, cash in hand!” Mitya added, feeling something was wrong. “What's the matter, _panie_? Don't you trust me? I can't give you the whole three thousand straight off. If I did, you might come back to her tomorrow. Besides, I don't have the three thousand here. It's at home in the town,” Mitya faltered, his spirits sinking with every word. “I swear, the money's there, hidden.”

52.180.oldText: In an instant an extraordinary sense of personal dignity rose in the little man's face.

52.181.oldText: “What next?” he asked ironically. “For shame!” and he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.

52.182.oldText: “You spit, _panie_,” said Mitya, recognizing in despair that it was all over, “because you hope to get more out of Grushenka? You're a pair of capons, that's what you are!”

52.183.oldText: “This is a mortal insult!” The little Pole turned as red as a crab and walked briskly out of the room, as though unwilling to hear another word. Vrublevsky stormed out after him, and Mitya followed, confused and crestfallen. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the _pan_ would at once raise an outcry. And that's exactly what he did. The Pole walked into the room and threw himself into a theatrical pose before Grushenka.

52.184.oldText: “_Pani_ Agrippina, I have received a mortal insult!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they had wounded her in the tenderest spot.

52.185.oldText: “Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she cried. “Not another word of Polish! You used to talk Russian. You can't have forgotten it in five years.”

52.188.oldText: “My name's Agrafena, Grushenka—speak Russian, or I won't listen!”

52.189.oldText: The Pole gasped with offended dignity and, quickly and pompously, delivered himself in broken Russian:

52.190.oldText: “_Pani_ Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget everything that has happened up to today—”

52.191.oldText: “Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him short, jumping up from her seat.

52.192.oldText: “Just so, _pani_, I'm not pusillanimous, I'm magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya, in the other room, offered me three thousand to depart. I spat in the _pan's_ face.”

52.193.oldText: “What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterically. “Is it true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”

52.194.oldText: “_Panie, panie!_” yelled Mitya. “She's pure and shining, and I have never been her lover! That's a lie—”

52.195.oldText: “How dare you defend me to him?” shrieked Grushenka. “It wasn't virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn't that I was afraid of Kuzma—I did it so I could hold my head up when I met him and tell him he's a scoundrel. And he actually refused the money?”

52.196.oldText: “He took it! He took it!” cried Mitya. “Only he wanted the whole three thousand at once, and I could only give him seven hundred straight off.”

52.198.oldText: “_Pani_ Agrippina!” cried the little Pole. “I'm a knight, I'm a nobleman, and not a _lajdak_. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman—perverse and shameless.”

52.199.oldText: “Oh, go back where you came from! I'll tell them to throw you out, and you'll be thrown out,” cried Grushenka, furious. “I've been a fool, a fool, to have been miserable these five years! And it wasn't for his sake—it was my anger that made me miserable. And this isn't him at all! Was he like this? This could be his father! Where did you get your wig from? He was a falcon, but this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing to me. And I've been crying for five years, damned fool, abject, shameless that I was!”

52.200.oldText: She sank back in her low chair and hid her face in her hands. At that instant the chorus of Mokroe began singing in the room on the left—a rollicking dance song.

52.201.oldText: “A regular Sodom!” Vrublevsky roared suddenly. “Landlord, send the shameless hussies away!”

52.202.oldText: The landlord, who had been curiously peeping in at the door for some time, heard the shouts and, guessing that his guests were quarreling, entered the room at once.

52.203.oldText: “What are you shouting for? You want to split your throat?” he said to Vrublevsky with surprising rudeness.

52.205.oldText: “Animal? And what sort of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You played with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, do you know that? It's the same as false banknotes—”

52.206.oldText: And going up to the sofa, he thrust his fingers between the back of the sofa and the cushion and pulled out an unopened pack of cards.

52.208.oldText: He held it up and showed it to everyone in the room. “From where I stood, I saw him slip my pack away and put his in place of it—you're a cheat, not a gentleman!”

52.209.oldText: “And I saw the _pan_ change a card twice!” cried Kalganov.

52.210.oldText: “How shameful! How shameful!” exclaimed Grushenka, clasping her hands and blushing with genuine shame. “Good Lord, he's come to that!”

52.211.oldText: “I thought so too!” said Mitya. But before he had finished the words, Vrublevsky, with a confused and infuriated face, shook his fist at Grushenka, shouting:

52.213.oldText: Mitya flew at him at once, seized him with both hands, lifted him into the air, and in an instant had carried him into the room on the right, from which they had just come.

52.214.oldText: “I've laid him on the floor in there,” he announced, returning at once, gasping with excitement. “He's struggling, the scoundrel! But he won't come back, no fear of that!”

52.215.oldText: He closed one half of the folding doors and, holding the other ajar, called out to the little Pole:

52.216.oldText: “Most illustrious, will you be pleased to retire as well?”

52.217.oldText: “My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch, “make them give you back the money you lost. It's as good as stolen from you.”

52.218.oldText: “I don't want my fifty roubles back,” Kalganov declared suddenly.

52.219.oldText: “I don't want my two hundred either,” cried Mitya. “I wouldn't take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation.”

52.220.oldText: “Bravo, Mitya! You're a trump, Mitya!” cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in her exclamation.

52.221.oldText: The little _pan_, crimson with fury but still mindful of his dignity, was making for the door, but he stopped short and said suddenly, addressing Grushenka:

52.222.oldText: “_Pani_, if you want to come with me, come. If not, goodbye.”

52.223.oldText: And swelling with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. This was a man of character: he had so high an opinion of himself that after all that had happened, he still expected her to marry him. Mitya slammed the door after him.

52.224.oldText: “Lock it,” said Kalganov. But the key clicked on the other side—they had locked it from within.

52.225.oldText: “That's capital!” exclaimed Grushenka relentlessly. “Serves them right!”

53.0.oldText: What followed was almost an orgy, a feast to which everyone was welcome. Grushenka was the first to call for wine.

53.1.oldText: “I want to drink. I want to be completely drunk, the way we were before. Do you remember, Mitya, do you remember how we made friends here last time!”

53.2.oldText: Mitya himself was almost delirious, feeling that his happiness was at hand. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her.

53.3.oldText: “Go and enjoy yourself. Tell them to dance, to have a good time, ‘let the stove and cottage dance,' the way we had it last time,” she kept exclaiming. She was tremendously excited. And Mitya hurried to obey her. The chorus was in the next room. The room where they had been sitting until that moment was too small and was divided in two by cotton curtains, behind which stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pyramid of cotton pillows. There were beds in each of the four rooms reserved for visitors. Grushenka settled herself right by the door. Mitya placed an easy chair for her. She had sat in the same spot to watch the dancing and singing “the time before,” when they had made merry there. All the girls who came had been there then; the Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come too, and at last the long-expected cart had arrived with the wines and provisions.

53.4.oldText: Mitya bustled about. All sorts of people began coming into the room to watch—peasants and their wives, who had been roused from sleep and drawn by the hope of another marvelous entertainment like the one they had enjoyed a month earlier. Mitya remembered their faces, greeting and embracing everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured out wine for everyone who stepped forward. Only the girls were really eager for the champagne. The men preferred rum, brandy, and, above all, hot punch. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls and ordered that three samovars be kept boiling all night so that anyone could help themselves to tea and punch.

53.5.oldText: An absurd, chaotic confusion followed, but Mitya was in his natural element, and the sillier it became, the higher his spirits rose. If the peasants had asked him for money at that moment, he would have pulled out his notes and given them away right and left. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering near Mitya to protect him. He seemed to have given up all idea of going to bed that night, though he drank little—only one glass of punch—and kept a sharp eye on Mitya's interests in his own way. He stepped in just in time, civilly and obsequiously persuading Mitya not to give away “cigars and Rhine wine,” and above all money, to the peasants as he had done before. He was also very indignant about the peasant girls drinking liqueur and eating sweets.

53.6.oldText: “They're a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said. “I'd give every one of them a kick, and they'd take it as an honor—that's all they're worth!”

53.7.oldText: Mitya remembered Andrey again and ordered punch to be sent out to him. “I was rude to him just now,” he repeated, his voice sinking, softened. Kalganov didn't want to drink, and at first didn't care for the girls' singing; but after he'd had a couple of glasses of champagne, he became extraordinarily lively, strolling around the room, laughing, praising the music and the songs, admiring everyone and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka, too, was starting to get drunk. Pointing to Kalganov, she said to Mitya:

53.9.oldText: And Mitya, delighted, ran to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, his hopes were immense! She had said nothing yet, and seemed, in fact, to be deliberately holding back. But she looked at him from time to time with caressing, passionate eyes. At last she suddenly gripped his hand and pulled him vigorously toward her. She was sitting just then in the low chair by the door.

53.10.oldText: “How was it you came in just now, hm? Did you walk in? I was frightened. So you meant to give me up to him, did you? Did you really mean it?”

53.11.oldText: “I didn't want to spoil your happiness!” Mitya faltered blissfully. But she didn't need his answer.

53.12.oldText: “Well, go and enjoy yourself—” she sent him away once more. “Don't cry, I'll call you back again.”

53.13.oldText: He would run off, and she listened to the singing and watched the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. But in another quarter of an hour she would call him back again, and again he would come running.

53.14.oldText: “Come, sit beside me, tell me, how did you hear about me, and that I was coming here yesterday? Who did you first hear it from?”

53.15.oldText: And Mitya began telling her all about it, disconnectedly, incoherently, feverishly. He spoke strangely, often frowning and breaking off abruptly.

53.16.oldText: “What are you frowning at?” she asked.

53.17.oldText: “Nothing. I left a man ill back there. I'd give ten years of my life for him to recover—just to know he was all right!”

53.18.oldText: “Well, never mind him if he's ill. So you meant to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! What for? I like reckless fellows like you,” she lisped, her tongue a little thick. “So you'd go to any lengths for me, would you? Did you really mean to shoot yourself tomorrow, you stupid? No, wait a little. Tomorrow I may have something to say to you. I won't say it today, but tomorrow. You'd like it to be today? No, I don't want to today. Come, go along now, go and amuse yourself.”

53.19.oldText: Once, though, she called him back with a puzzled, uneasy look.

53.20.oldText: “Why are you sad? I see you're sad. Yes, I see it,” she added, looking intently into his eyes. “Even though you keep kissing the peasants and shouting, I see something. No, be merry. I'm merry; you be merry too. I love somebody here. Guess who it is. Ah, look, my boy has fallen asleep, poor dear, he's drunk.”

53.21.oldText: She meant Kalganov. He was, in fact, drunk and had dropped asleep for a moment sitting on the sofa. But he wasn't just drowsy from drink; he had suddenly felt dejected, or, as he put it, “bored.” He was intensely depressed by the girls' songs, which, as the drinking went on, gradually grew coarser and more reckless. The dances were just as bad. Two girls dressed up as bears, and a lively girl called Stepanida, with a stick in her hand, played the part of keeper and began to “show them off.”

53.22.oldText: “Look alive, Marya, or you'll get the stick!”

53.23.oldText: The bears finally rolled on the ground in the most unseemly fashion, amid roars of laughter from the tightly packed crowd of men and women.

53.24.oldText: “Well, let them! Let them!” said Grushenka sententiously, with an ecstatic expression. “When they do get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn't folks be happy?”

53.25.oldText: Kalganov looked as though he had been splattered with dirt.

53.26.oldText: “It's swinish, all this peasant foolery,” he murmured, moving away. “It's the sort of thing they play when it's light all night in summer.”

53.27.oldText: He particularly disliked one “new” song set to a jaunty dance tune. It described a gentleman coming to try his luck with the girls, to see whether they would love him:

53.28.oldText: The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?

53.29.oldText: But the girls couldn't love the master:

53.30.oldText: He would beat me cruelly And such love won't do for me.

53.31.oldText: Then a gypsy comes along, and he too tries:

53.32.oldText: The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?

53.33.oldText: But they couldn't love the gypsy either:

53.34.oldText: He would be a thief, I fear, And would cause me many a tear.

53.35.oldText: And many more men come to try their luck, among them a soldier:

53.36.oldText: The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?

53.37.oldText: But the soldier is rejected with contempt, in two indecent lines sung with absolute frankness and producing a furore in the audience. The song ends with a merchant:

53.38.oldText: The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?

53.39.oldText: And it turns out that he wins their love because:

53.40.oldText: The merchant will make gold for me And his queen I'll gladly be.

53.42.oldText: “That's just a song from yesterday,” he said out loud. “Who writes such things for them? They might just as well have had a railwayman or a Jew come to try his luck with the girls—they'd have carried the day.”

53.43.oldText: And, almost as though it were a personal affront, he declared on the spot that he was bored, sat down on the sofa, and immediately fell asleep. His pretty little face looked rather pale as it fell back against the sofa cushion.

53.44.oldText: “Look how pretty he is,” said Grushenka, taking Mitya over to him. “I was combing his hair just now; his hair's like flax, and so thick—”

53.45.oldText: And, bending over him tenderly, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov instantly opened his eyes, looked at her, stood up, and with the most anxious air asked where Maximov was.

53.46.oldText: “So that's who you want.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov.”

53.47.oldText: Maximov, it turned out, couldn't tear himself away from the girls, only running off now and then to pour himself a glass of liqueur. He had drunk two cups of chocolate. His face was red, his nose was crimson, his eyes were moist and mawkishly sweet. He ran up and announced that he was going to dance the “sabotière.”

53.48.oldText: “They taught me all those well-bred, aristocratic dances when I was little—”

53.49.oldText: “Go on, go with him, Mitya, and I'll watch from here how he dances,” said Grushenka.

53.50.oldText: “No, no, I'm coming to watch too,” exclaimed Kalganov, brushing aside in the most naïve way Grushenka's offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But it roused no great admiration in anyone except Mitya. It consisted of nothing but skipping and hopping, kicking up his feet, and at every skip Maximov slapped the upturned sole of his foot. Kalganov didn't like it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.

53.51.oldText: “Thanks. Are you tired, perhaps? What are you looking for here? Would you like some sweets? A cigar, maybe?”

53.54.oldText: “I'll just have a liqueur. Do you have any chocolates?”

53.55.oldText: “Yes, there's a heap of them on the table over there. Choose one, my dear soul!”

53.56.oldText: “I like one with vanilla—for old people. Heh heh!”

53.57.oldText: “No, brother, we don't have any of that special kind.”

53.58.oldText: “Listen,” the old man bent down to whisper in Mitya's ear, “that girl over there, little Marya, heh heh! How would it be if you helped me make friends with her?”

53.59.oldText: “So that's what you're after! No, brother, that won't do!”

53.60.oldText: “I'd do no harm to anyone,” Maximov muttered disconsolately.

53.61.oldText: “Oh, all right, all right. They only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. But damn it all, wait a bit! Eat and drink and be merry in the meantime. Do you want money?”

53.64.oldText: Mitya's head was burning. He stepped out onto the wooden balcony that ran all around the inside of the building, overlooking the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner and suddenly clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts came together; his sensations fused into a whole and threw a sudden light into his mind. A fearful and terrible light! “If I'm going to shoot myself, why not now?” passed through his mind. “Why not go for the pistols, bring them here, and here, in this dark, dirty corner, put an end to it?” For almost a minute he stood undecided. A few hours earlier, when he had been racing here, he was pursued by disgrace, by the theft he had committed, and that blood, that blood! And yet it had been easier for him then. Then everything was over: he had lost her, given her up. She was gone, for him—oh, then his death sentence had been easier; at least it had seemed necessary, inevitable, for what did he have to stay on earth for?

53.65.oldText: But now? Was it the same as then? Now one phantom, one terror at least was finished: that first, rightful lover, that fateful figure had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had turned into something so small, so comic; it had been carried into the bedroom and locked in. It would never return. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could see now whom she loved. Now he had everything to make life happy—but he couldn't go on living, he couldn't; oh, damnation! “O God! Restore to life the man I knocked down at the fence! Let this fearful cup pass from me! Lord, You have worked miracles for sinners like me! But what, what if the old man's alive? Oh, then I would wipe away the shame of the other disgrace. I'd restore the stolen money. I'd give it back; I'd get it somehow. No trace of that shame will remain, except in my heart forever! But no, no; oh, impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!”

53.66.oldText: Yet there was a ray of light and hope in his darkness. He jumped up and ran back to the room—to her, to her, his queen forever! Wasn't one moment of her love worth all the rest of life, even in the agonies of disgrace? This wild question clutched at his heart. “To her, to her alone, to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for that night, for an hour, for a moment!” Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he ran into the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. He thought he looked gloomy and worried, and fancied he had come looking for him.

53.68.oldText: “No, sir.” The landlord seemed disconcerted. “Why should I be looking for you? Where have you been?”

53.69.oldText: “Why do you look so glum? You're not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you'll be in bed soon. What's the time?”

53.70.oldText: “It'll be three o'clock. Past three, it must be.”

53.72.oldText: “Don't mention it; it's nothing. Keep it up as long as you like—”

53.73.oldText: “What's the matter with him?” Mitya wondered for a moment, and he ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she wasn't there. She wasn't in the blue room either; there was no one but Kalganov, asleep on the sofa. Mitya peeked behind the curtain—she was there. She was sitting in the corner, on a trunk. Bent forward, with her head and arms on the bed next to it, she was crying bitterly, doing her utmost to stifle her sobs so she wouldn't be heard. Seeing Mitya, she beckoned to him, and when he hurried over she grasped his hand tightly.

53.74.oldText: “Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I loved him these five years, all that time! Did I love him, or just my own anger? No, him, him! It's a lie that it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then; he was so kind to me, so merry; he used to sing to me. Or so it seemed to a silly girl like me. And now, O Lord, it's not the same man. Even his face isn't the same; he's different altogether. I wouldn't have recognized him. I drove here with Timofey, and the whole way I was thinking how I'd meet him, what I'd say to him, how we'd look at one another. My soul was faint, and all at once it was as though he'd emptied a pail of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, all so grave and learned; he met me so solemnly I was struck dumb. I couldn't get a word in. At first I thought he was ashamed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat staring at him, wondering why I couldn't say a word to him now. It must have been his wife that ruined him; you know he threw me over to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it is! Oh, Mitya, I'm ashamed, I'm ashamed for my whole life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!”

53.75.oldText: And again she burst into tears, but clung tight to Mitya's hand and wouldn't let it go.

53.76.oldText: “Mitya, darling, stay, don't go away. I want to tell you one thing,” she whispered, and suddenly raised her face to him. “Listen, tell me who it is I love? I love one man here. Who is that man? That's what you have to tell me.”

53.77.oldText: A smile lit up her face that was swollen from weeping, and her eyes shone in the half darkness.

53.78.oldText: “A falcon flew in, and my heart sank. ‘Fool! that's the man you love!' That was what my heart whispered to me at once. You came in, and everything grew bright. What's he afraid of? I wondered. For you were frightened; you couldn't speak. It's not them he's afraid of—could you be frightened of anyone? It's me he's afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you little fool, how I called out to Alyosha from the window that I'd loved Mityenka for one hour, and was now going to love—another. Mitya, Mitya, how could I be such a fool as to think I could love anyone after you? Do you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or not? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She jumped up and held him with both hands on his shoulders. Mitya, dumb with rapture, gazed into her eyes, at her face, at her smile, and suddenly clasped her tightly in his arms and kissed her passionately.

53.79.oldText: “You will forgive me for having tormented you? It was out of spite that I tormented you all. It was out of spite I drove the old man out of his mind. Do you remember how you drank at my house one day and broke the wineglass? I remembered that, and I broke a glass today and drank ‘to my vile heart.' Mitya, my falcon, why don't you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he draws back and looks and listens. Why listen to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, that's right. If you love, well then, love! I'll be your slave now, your slave for the rest of my life. It's sweet to be a slave. Kiss me! Beat me, mistreat me, do whatever you want with me. And I deserve to suffer. Stop, wait, afterwards, I don't want that—” she suddenly pushed him away. “Go along, Mitya, I'll come and have some wine, I want to be drunk, I'm going to get drunk and dance; I must, I must!” She tore herself away from him and disappeared behind the curtain. Mitya followed like a drunken man.

53.80.oldText: “Yes, come what may—whatever happens now, I'd give the whole world for one minute,” he thought. Grushenka did, in fact, toss back a whole glass of champagne in one gulp, and she became very tipsy at once. She sat down in the same chair as before, with a blissful smile on her face. Her cheeks were glowing, her lips were burning, her flashing eyes were moist; there was a passionate appeal in her gaze. Even Kalganov felt a stir in his heart and went over to her.

53.81.oldText: “Did you feel how I kissed you just now while you were asleep?” she said thickly. “I'm drunk now, that's what it is. And aren't you drunk? And why isn't Mitya drinking? Why don't you drink, Mitya? I'm drunk, and you don't drink—”

53.82.oldText: “I am drunk! I'm drunk as it is—drunk on you—and now I'll be drunk on wine too.”

53.83.oldText: He drank off another glass, and—he thought it strange himself—that glass made him completely drunk. He was suddenly drunk, even though up until that moment he had been quite sober; he remembered that. From that moment everything whirled around him, as though he were delirious. He walked, laughed, talked to everybody, without knowing what he was doing. Only one persistent, burning sensation made itself felt continually, “like a red-hot coal in his heart,” he said afterwards. He went over to her, sat beside her, gazed at her, listened to her. She became very talkative, kept calling everyone over, and beckoned to different girls out of the chorus. When a girl came up, she either kissed her or made the sign of the cross over her. In another minute she might start crying. She was greatly amused by the “little old man,” as she called Maximov. He ran up every minute to kiss her hands, “each little finger,” and finally he danced another dance to an old song, which he sang himself. He danced with special vigor to the refrain:

53.84.oldText: The little pig says—umph! umph! umph! The little calf says—moo, moo, moo, The little duck says—quack, quack, quack, The little goose says—ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say!

53.85.oldText: “Give him something, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Give him a present, he's poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted! Do you know, Mitya, I'm going into a nunnery. No, I really will one day. Alyosha said something to me today that I'll remember all my life. Yes. But today, let's dance. Tomorrow to the nunnery, but today we'll dance. I want to play today, good people, and what of it? God will forgive us. If I were God, I'd forgive everyone: ‘My dear sinners, from this day forth I forgive you.' I'm going to beg forgiveness: ‘Forgive me, good people, a silly wench.' I'm a beast, that's what I am. But I want to pray. I gave a little onion. Wicked as I've been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don't stop them. Everyone in the world is good. Everyone—even the worst of them. The world's a nice place. Though we're bad, the world's all right. We're good and bad, good and bad. Come, tell me, I've something to ask you: come here everyone, and I'll ask: Why am I so good? You know I'm good. I'm very good. Come, why am I so good?”

53.86.oldText: So Grushenka rambled on, getting more and more drunk. At last she announced that she was going to dance too. She got up from her chair, staggering. “Mitya, don't give me any more wine—if I ask, don't give me any. Wine doesn't bring peace. Everything's spinning, the stove, everything. I want to dance. Let everyone see how I dance—let them see how beautifully I dance—”

53.87.oldText: She really meant it. She pulled a white cambric handkerchief out of her pocket and took it by one corner in her right hand, to wave it in the dance. Mitya ran back and forth, the girls were quiet and got ready to break into a dancing song at the first signal. Maximov, hearing that Grushenka wanted to dance, squealed with delight and ran skipping about in front of her, humming:

53.89.oldText: But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and drove him away.

53.90.oldText: “Shh! Mitya, why don't they come? Let everyone come—to watch. Call them in, too, the ones that were locked in. Why did you lock them in? Tell them I'm going to dance. Let them watch too—”

53.91.oldText: Mitya walked with a drunken swagger to the locked door and began knocking at the Poles with his fist.

53.92.oldText: “Hey, you Podvysotskys! Come on, she's going to dance. She's calling you.”

53.93.oldText: “_Lajdak!_” one of the Poles shouted back.

53.94.oldText: “You're a _lajdak_ yourself! You're a little scoundrel, that's what you are.”

53.95.oldText: “Stop making fun of Poland,” said Kalganov sententiously. He was drunk too.

53.96.oldText: “Be quiet, boy! Just because I call him a scoundrel doesn't mean I called all of Poland so. One _lajdak_ doesn't make a Poland. Be quiet, my pretty boy, eat a sweet.”
