53.97.oldText: “Ach, what fellows! As though they weren't men. Why won't they make friends?” said Grushenka, and she stepped forward to dance. The chorus broke into “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka flung back her head, half opened her lips, smiled, waved her handkerchief, and suddenly, with a violent lurch, stood still in the middle of the room, looking bewildered.

53.98.oldText: “I'm weak—” she said in an exhausted voice. “Forgive me. I'm weak, I can't. I'm sorry.”

53.99.oldText: She bowed to the chorus, then began bowing in every direction.

53.101.oldText: “The lady's been drinking. The pretty lady has been drinking,” voices were saying.

53.102.oldText: “The lady's drunk too much,” Maximov explained to the girls, giggling.

53.103.oldText: “Mitya, lead me away—take me,” said Grushenka helplessly. Mitya pounced on her, snatched her up in his arms, and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

53.104.oldText: “Well, now I'll go,” thought Kalganov, and walking out of the blue room, he closed the two halves of the door behind him. But the orgy in the larger room went on and grew louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

53.105.oldText: “Don't touch me—” she faltered, in a pleading voice. “Don't touch me, until I'm yours. I've told you I'm yours, but don't touch me—spare me. With them here, with them so close, you mustn't. He's here. It's nasty here—”

53.106.oldText: “I'll obey you! I won't think of it—I worship you!” muttered Mitya. “Yes, it's nasty here, it's abominable.”

53.107.oldText: And still holding her in his arms, he sank to his knees by the bedside.

53.108.oldText: “I know, though you're a brute, you're generous,” Grushenka said with difficulty. “It must be honorable—it shall be honorable for the future—and let us be honest, let us be good, not brutes, but good. Take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don't want it to be here, but far, far away—”

53.109.oldText: “Oh, yes, yes, it must be!” said Mitya, pressing her in his arms. “I'll take you and we'll fly away. Oh, I'd give my whole life for just one year of knowing about that blood!”

53.111.oldText: “Nothing,” muttered Mitya through his teeth. “Grusha, you wanted to be honest, but I'm a thief. I stole money from Katya. Disgrace, disgrace!”

53.112.oldText: “From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn't steal it. Give it back to her, take it from me. Why make a fuss? Everything of mine is yours now. What does money matter? We'll waste it anyway. People like us are bound to waste money. But we'd better go and work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We have to work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won't be your mistress, I'll be faithful to you, I'll be your slave, I'll work for you. We'll go to the young lady and bow down before her together, so that she may forgive us, and then we'll go away. And if she won't forgive us, we'll go anyway. Take her her money, and love me. Don't love her. Don't love her any more. If you love her, I'll strangle her. I'll put out both her eyes with a needle—”

53.113.oldText: “I love you. I love only you. I'll love you in Siberia—”

53.114.oldText: “Why Siberia? Never mind, Siberia, if you like. I don't care—we'll work. There's snow in Siberia. I love driving through the snow—and we must have bells. Do you hear, there's a bell ringing? Where is that bell ringing? There are people coming. Now it's stopped.”

53.115.oldText: She closed her eyes, exhausted, and suddenly fell asleep for an instant. There had definitely been the sound of a bell in the distance, but the ringing had ceased. Mitya let his head sink onto her breast. He didn't notice that the bell had stopped, nor did he notice that the songs had ceased and that instead of singing and drunken clamor there was absolute stillness in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

53.116.oldText: “What's the matter? Was I asleep? Yes—a bell—I was asleep and dreamed I was driving through the snow with bells, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved, with you. And far, far away. I was holding you and kissing you, nestling close. I was cold, and the snow glistened. You know how the snow glistens at night when the moon shines. It was as if I wasn't on earth. I woke up, and my dear one is close to me. How sweet that is!”

53.117.oldText: “Close to you,” murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her bosom, her hands. And suddenly he had a strange sensation: it seemed to him that she was looking straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but over his head, with an intent, almost uncanny fixity. An expression of wonder, almost of alarm, came suddenly into her face.

53.118.oldText: “Mitya, who is that looking at us?” she whispered.

53.119.oldText: Mitya turned and saw that someone had indeed parted the curtains and seemed to be watching them. And not just one person, it seemed.

53.120.oldText: He jumped up and walked quickly over to the intruder.

53.121.oldText: “Here, come over to us, come here,” said a voice, speaking not loudly, but firmly and with authority.

53.122.oldText: Mitya passed to the other side of the curtain and stood stock still. The room was filled with people, but not the ones who had been there before. An instantaneous shiver ran down his back, and he shuddered. He recognized everyone in an instant. That tall, stout old man in the overcoat and forage-cap with a cockade—was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And that “consumptive-looking” trim dandy, “who always has such polished boots”—that was the deputy prosecutor. “He has a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me.” And that small young man in spectacles—Mitya forgot his surname, though he knew him, had seen him: he was the “investigating lawyer,” from the “school of jurisprudence,” who had only recently come to town. And this man—the inspector of police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a man he knew well. And those fellows with the brass plates on—why are they here? And those other two—peasants. And there at the door stood Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch.

53.123.oldText: “Gentlemen! What is this for, gentlemen?” Mitya began, but suddenly, as though beside himself, not knowing what he was doing, he cried out at the top of his voice:

53.125.oldText: The young man in spectacles moved forward suddenly, and stepping up to Mitya, began with dignity, though hurriedly:

53.126.oldText: “We have to—in brief, I beg you to come this way, this way to the sofa. It's absolutely imperative that you give an explanation.”

53.127.oldText: “The old man!” cried Mitya frantically. “The old man and his blood! I understand.”

53.128.oldText: And he sank, almost fell, onto a chair close by, as though he had been mown down by a scythe.

53.129.oldText: “You understand? He understands it! Monster and parricide! Your father's blood cries out against you!” the old police captain suddenly roared, stepping up to Mitya.

53.130.oldText: He was beside himself, crimson in the face and trembling all over.

53.131.oldText: “This is impossible!” cried the small young man. “Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won't do! Please allow me to speak. I would never have expected such behavior from you—”

53.132.oldText: “This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium,” cried the police captain. “Look at him: drunk, at this time of night, in the company of a disreputable woman, with the blood of his father on his hands. It's delirium!”

53.133.oldText: “I beg you most earnestly, dear Mihail Makarovitch, to restrain your feelings,” the prosecutor said in a rapid whisper to the old police captain, “or I shall be forced to resort to—”

53.134.oldText: But the little lawyer wouldn't let him finish. He turned to Mitya and delivered himself in a loud, firm, dignified voice:

53.135.oldText: “Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, it is my duty to inform you that you are charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed this night—”

53.136.oldText: He said something more, and the prosecutor put in something too, but though Mitya heard them, he didn't understand them. He stared at them all with wild eyes.

54.0.oldText: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, whom we left knocking at the sturdy locked gates of the widow Morozov's house, of course ended up making himself heard. Fenya, who was still shaken by the fright she had had two hours before, and too “upset” to go to bed, was almost driven into hysterics by the furious knocking at the gate. Even though she had seen him drive away with her own eyes, she imagined it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again—no one else could pound so savagely. She ran to the house-porter, who had already woken and gone out to the gate, and began begging him not to open it. But once he'd questioned Pyotr Ilyitch and learned that he wanted to see Fenya on very “important business,” the man finally made up his mind to open up. Pyotr Ilyitch was admitted into Fenya's kitchen, but the girl asked him to let the house-porter stay, “because of her misgivings.” He began questioning her and at once learned the crucial fact: when Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run out to look for Grushenka, he had snatched up a pestle from the mortar, and when he returned, the pestle was gone and his hands were smeared with blood.

54.1.oldText: “And the blood was just flowing, dripping from him, dripping!” Fenya kept exclaiming. This horrible detail was really just the product of her disordered imagination. But although it hadn't been “dripping,” Pyotr Ilyitch had seen those blood-stained hands himself and had helped to wash them. Besides, the question he had to settle wasn't how soon the blood had dried, but where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run with the pestle—or rather, whether it really was to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, and how he could satisfactorily confirm it. Pyotr Ilyitch kept returning to this point, and though he found nothing conclusive, he came away with the conviction that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere except his father's house, and that therefore something must have happened there.

54.2.oldText: “And when he came back,” Fenya added excitedly, “I told him the whole story, and then I began asking him, ‘Why do you have blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?' and he answered that it was human blood, and that he had just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, and suddenly ran off like a madman. I sat down and began thinking, where's he running off to now like a madman? He'll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running to his lodgings, but I looked at Plotnikov's shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya had noticed this and remembered it.) Fenya's old grandmother confirmed her testimony as well as she could. After asking a few more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house even more upset and uneasy than when he'd entered.

54.3.oldText: The most direct and easiest thing for him to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, find out whether anything had happened there, and if so, what; and then to go to the police captain, as Pyotr Ilyitch firmly intended to do once he'd satisfied himself of the facts. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch's gates were strong, and he would have to knock again. His acquaintance with Fyodor Pavlovitch was slight, and what if, after he'd been knocking, they opened to him and nothing had happened? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, in his jeering way, would tell the story all over town—how a stranger called Perhotin had broken in on him at midnight to ask if anyone had killed him. It would make a scandal. And scandal was what Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded more than anything in the world.

54.4.oldText: Still, the feeling that had hold of him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and swore at himself, he set off again—not to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, but to Madame Hohlakov's. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he would go straight to the police captain; but if she admitted having given him the money, he would go home and let the matter rest until morning.

54.5.oldText: It is, of course, perfectly obvious that there was even more potential for scandal in going at eleven o'clock at night to a fashionable lady, a complete stranger, and perhaps rousing her from her bed to ask her an amazing question, than in going to Fyodor Pavlovitch's. But that's just how it sometimes goes, especially in cases like this one, with the decisions of the most precise and phlegmatic people. Pyotr Ilyitch was by no means phlegmatic at that moment. He remembered all his life how a nagging unease gradually took hold of him, growing more and more painful and driving him on against his will. Of course, he kept cursing himself the whole way for going to this lady, but “I'll get to the bottom of it, I will!” he repeated for the tenth time, grinding his teeth, and he carried out his intention.

54.6.oldText: It was exactly eleven o'clock when he entered Madame Hohlakov's house. He was admitted into the yard fairly quickly, but when he asked whether the lady was still up, the porter could give no answer, except that she was usually in bed by that hour.

54.7.oldText: “Ask at the top of the stairs. If the lady wants to receive you, she'll receive you. If she doesn't, she won't.”

54.8.oldText: Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but he didn't find things so easy there. The footman was unwilling to announce him, but eventually called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch politely but insistently begged her to tell her lady that an official living in town, named Perhotin, had called on particular business, and that if it hadn't been of the greatest importance, he wouldn't have ventured to come. “Tell her in those words, in those words exactly,” he urged the girl.

54.9.oldText: She went away. He stayed waiting in the entry. Madame Hohlakov was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She had felt upset ever since Mitya's visit and had a premonition that she wouldn't get through the night without the sick headache that always followed such excitement in her. She was surprised when the maid announced her visitor. She refused irritably to see him, though the unexpected arrival at such an hour of “an official living in town,” a total stranger, stirred her feminine curiosity intensely. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch was stubborn as a mule. He begged the maid most earnestly to deliver another message, in these very words:

54.10.oldText: “That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might have cause to regret it later if she refused to see him now.”

54.11.oldText: “I plunged headlong,” he described it afterwards.

54.12.oldText: The maid, gazing at him in amazement, went to deliver his message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought for a little, asked what he looked like, and learned that he was “very well dressed, young, and so polite.” We may note, parenthetically, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and well aware of the fact. Madame Hohlakov decided to see him. She was in her dressing gown and slippers, but she flung a black shawl over her shoulders. “The official” was asked to walk into the drawing room—the very room where Mitya had been received a short while before. The lady came out to meet her visitor with a sternly inquiring expression and, without inviting him to sit down, began at once with the question:

54.14.oldText: “I have ventured to disturb you, madam, on a matter concerning our common acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.

54.15.oldText: But he had scarcely uttered the name before the lady's face showed signs of acute irritation. She almost shrieked and interrupted him in a fury:

54.16.oldText: “How much longer am I to be tormented by that awful man?” she cried hysterically. “How dare you, sir, how could you venture to disturb a lady who is a stranger to you, in her own house at such an hour, and to force yourself upon her to talk of a man who came here, to this very drawing room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and went stamping out of the room, as no one would go out of a decent house. Let me tell you, sir, that I shall lodge a complaint against you—I will not let this pass. Kindly leave me at once. I am a mother. I—I—”

54.17.oldText: “Murder! Then he tried to murder you too?”

54.19.oldText: “If you would kindly listen, madam, for half a moment, I'll explain it all in a couple of words,” answered Perhotin, firmly. “At five o'clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact he had no money. Yet at nine o'clock, he came to see me with a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand—about two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were all covered in blood, and he looked like a madman. When I asked him where he'd got so much money, he answered that he had just received it from you—that you had given him a sum of three thousand to go to the gold mines—”

54.20.oldText: Madame Hohlakov's face took on an expression of intense, painful excitement.

54.21.oldText: “Good God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, clasping her hands. “I never gave him money, never! Oh, run, run! Don't say another word! Save the old man—run to his father—run!”

54.22.oldText: “Excuse me, madam, so you did not give him money? You remember for a fact that you did not give him any money?”

54.23.oldText: “No, I didn't, I didn't! I refused to give it to him, for he could not appreciate it. He ran out in a fury, stamping. He rushed at me, but I slipped away. And let me tell you, as I want to hide nothing from you now, he actually spat at me. Can you imagine that! But why are we standing? Ah, sit down.”

54.25.oldText: “Or better, run, run, you must run and save the poor old man from an awful death!”

54.26.oldText: “But what if he has killed him already?”

54.27.oldText: “Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do now? What do you think we ought to do now?”

54.28.oldText: Meanwhile she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down and sat down herself, facing him. Briefly but fairly clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her the history of the affair—at least the part he had witnessed himself. He described his visit to Fenya too, and told her about the pestle. All these details had an overwhelming effect on the distracted lady, who kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands.

54.29.oldText: “Would you believe it, I foresaw all of this! I have that special gift—whatever I imagine comes to pass. And how often I've looked at that awful man and always thought, that man will end by murdering me. And now it's happened—that is, if he hasn't murdered me, but only his own father, it's only because the finger of God preserved me, and what's more, he was ashamed to murder me because, in this very place, I put the holy ikon from the relics of the holy martyr, Saint Varvara, on his neck. And to think how close I was to death at that moment—I went right up to him, and he stretched out his neck toward me! Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch (I think you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch), I don't believe in miracles, but that ikon and this unmistakable miracle with me now—it shakes me, and I'm ready to believe in anything you like. Have you heard about Father Zossima? But I don't know what I'm saying—and just imagine, with the ikon on his neck he spat at me. He only spat, it's true, he didn't murder me, and—he dashed away! But what shall we do, what must we do now? What do you think?”

54.30.oldText: Pyotr Ilyitch stood up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain, to tell him everything, and leave him to do what he thought fit.

54.31.oldText: “Oh, he's an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he's the person to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you've thought of everything! I would never have thought of it in your place!”

54.32.oldText: “Especially as I know the police captain very well myself,” remarked Pyotr Ilyitch, who was still standing and was obviously anxious to escape as quickly as possible from the impulsive lady, who wouldn't let him say goodbye and go.

54.33.oldText: “And be sure, be sure,” she prattled on, “to come back and tell me what you see there, and what you find out—what comes to light—how they'll try him—and what he's sentenced to. Tell me, we don't have capital punishment, do we? But be sure to come, even if it's at three o'clock in the morning, at four, at half past four. Tell them to wake me, to wake me, to shake me, if I don't get up. But, good heavens, I shan't sleep! But wait, hadn't I better come with you?”

54.34.oldText: “N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, stating that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch money, it might perhaps be useful—in case it's needed—”

54.35.oldText: “To be sure!” Madame Hohlakov skipped delightedly to her bureau. “And you know, I'm simply struck, amazed by your resourcefulness, your good sense in these affairs. Are you in the service here? I'm delighted to think you're in the service here!”

54.36.oldText: And still talking, she scribbled on half a sheet of notepaper the following lines:

54.37.oldText: I have never in my life lent to that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, in spite of all, he is unhappy), three thousand roubles today. I have never given him money, never: That I swear by all that's holy!

54.39.oldText: “Here's the note!” she said, turning quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go, save him. It's a noble deed on your part!”

54.40.oldText: And she made the sign of the cross three times over him. She ran out to accompany him to the passage.

54.41.oldText: “How grateful I am to you! You can't imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it we haven't met before? I shall feel flattered to see you at my house in the future. How delightful that you're living here! Such precision! Such practical ability! They must appreciate you, they must understand you. If there's anything I can do, believe me—oh, I love young people! I'm in love with young people! The younger generation is the one prop of our suffering country. Her one hope. Oh, go, go!”

54.42.oldText: But Pyotr Ilyitch had already hurried away, or she wouldn't have let him go so soon. Yet Madame Hohlakov had made a rather agreeable impression on him, which somewhat softened his anxiety about being drawn into such an unpleasant affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. “She's by no means so elderly,” he thought, feeling pleased. “On the contrary, I'd have taken her for her own daughter.”

54.43.oldText: As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply enchanted by the young man. “Such sense! Such exactness! In so young a man! In our day! And all that with such manners and appearance! People say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here's an example!” and so on. So she simply forgot about this “dreadful affair,” and it was only as she was getting into bed that, suddenly recalling “how close she had been to death,” she exclaimed: “Ah, it is awful, awful!”

54.44.oldText: But she fell at once into a sound, sweet sleep.

54.45.oldText: I would not, however, have dwelt on such trivial and irrelevant details, had this eccentric meeting of the young official with the by no means elderly widow not later turned out to be the foundation of the whole career of that practical and precise young man. His story is remembered to this day with amazement in our town, and I shall perhaps have something to say about it once I have finished my long history of the Brothers Karamazov.

55.0.oldText: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, a retired lieutenant colonel, was a widower and an excellent man. He had only come to us three years before, but he had won general esteem, chiefly because he “knew how to keep society together.” He was never without visitors and couldn't have got along without them. Someone was always dining with him; he never sat down to table without guests. He gave regular dinners too, on all sorts of occasions, sometimes very surprising ones. Though the food wasn't _recherché_, it was abundant. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity for what it lacked in quality.

55.1.oldText: The first room his guests entered was a well-fitted billiard room, with pictures of English race-horses in black frames on the walls—an essential decoration, as we all know, for a bachelor's billiard room. There was card-playing every evening at his house, even if only at one table. But at frequent intervals, all the society of our town, with the mammas and young ladies, gathered at his house to dance. Though Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, he didn't live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, with her two unmarried daughters—grown-up girls who had finished their education. They had an agreeable appearance and a lively character, and though everyone knew they would have no dowry, they attracted all the fashionable young men to their grandfather's house.

55.2.oldText: Mihail Makarovitch was by no means very efficient in his work, though he performed his duties no worse than many others. To speak plainly, he was a man of rather narrow education. His understanding of the limits of his administrative power could not always be relied on. It wasn't so much that he failed to grasp certain reforms passed during the present reign, as that he made conspicuous blunders in interpreting them. This wasn't from any special lack of intelligence, but from carelessness—he was always in too great a hurry to really go into the subject.

55.3.oldText: “I have the heart of a soldier rather than of a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He hadn't even formed a definite idea of the fundamental principles of the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs, and only picked it up, so to speak, from year to year, involuntarily increasing his knowledge by practice. And yet he was himself a landowner. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would meet some of Mihail Makarovitch's visitors there that evening, but he didn't know which ones. As it happened, at that moment the prosecutor and Varvinsky, our district doctor—a young man who had only just come to us from Petersburg after taking a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine—were playing whist at the police captain's. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (he was really the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor), was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to be consumptive, and married to a fat, childless woman. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good intellect, and even a kind heart. It seemed the only thing wrong with him was that he had a higher opinion of himself than his ability warranted. And that made him seem constantly uneasy. He also had certain higher, even artistic, leanings—toward psychology, for instance, a special study of the human heart, a particular knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He nursed a grievance on this ground, feeling he had been passed over in the service, and firmly convinced that in higher spheres he had not been properly appreciated and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to give up his post and practice as a barrister in criminal cases. The unexpected Karamazov case agitated him profoundly: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am getting ahead of myself.

55.4.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer, who had come from Petersburg only two months earlier, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. People talked about it afterwards and wondered at how all the gentlemen, as if intentionally, on the evening of “the crime,” had been gathered together at the house of the executive authority. Yet it was perfectly simple and happened quite naturally.

55.5.oldText: Ippolit Kirillovitch's wife had had a toothache for the last two days, and he was obliged to go out to escape her groans. The doctor, by the very nature of his being, couldn't spend an evening anywhere but at cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days now to drop in that evening at Mihail Makarovitch's, so to speak casually, so as slyly to startle the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, by showing he knew her secret—that he knew it was her birthday, and that she was trying to conceal it on purpose, so as not to be obliged to give a dance. He anticipated a great deal of merriment, many playful jests about her age and her being afraid to reveal it, about his knowing her secret and telling everybody, and so on. The charming young man was a great adept at such teasing; the ladies had christened him “the naughty man,” and he seemed delighted with the name. He was extremely well-bred, however, of good family, education, and feelings, and though he led a life of pleasure, his sallies were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking. On his white, slender little fingers he always wore a number of big, glittering rings. When he was engaged in his official duties, he always became extraordinarily grave, as though he was conscious of his position and the sanctity of the obligations laid on him. He had a special gift for mystifying murderers and other criminals of the peasant class during interrogation, and if he didn't win their respect, he certainly succeeded in arousing their wonder.

55.6.oldText: Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain's. He saw instantly that everyone already knew. They had actually thrown down their cards; all were standing and talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and come running in, looking strenuous and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was met with the astounding news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening in his own house—murdered and robbed. The news had only just reached them, in the following way.

55.7.oldText: Marfa Ignatyevna, the wife of old Grigory, who had been knocked senseless near the fence, was sleeping soundly in her bed and might well have slept till morning after the draught she'd taken. But all at once she woke up, no doubt roused by a fearful epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, who was lying in the next room unconscious. That scream always came before his fits, and always terrified and upset Marfa Ignatyevna. She could never get used to it. She jumped up and ran half-awake to Smerdyakov's room. But it was dark there, and all she could hear was the invalid beginning to gasp and struggle. Then Marfa Ignatyevna herself screamed out and was about to call her husband, when she suddenly realized that when she had got up, he wasn't beside her in bed. She ran back to the bedstead and began groping with her hands, but the bed really was empty. Then he must have gone out—where? She ran to the steps and timidly called to him. She got no answer, of course, but she did catch the sound of groans far away in the garden in the darkness. She listened. The groans were repeated, and it was clear they came from the garden.

55.8.oldText: “Good Lord! Just as it was with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought distractedly. She went timidly down the steps and saw that the gate into the garden was open.

55.9.oldText: “He must be out there, poor dear,” she thought. She went up to the gate and all at once she distinctly heard Grigory calling her by name, “Marfa! Marfa!” in a weak, moaning, dreadful voice.

55.10.oldText: “Lord, preserve us from harm!” Marfa Ignatyevna murmured, and ran toward the voice, and that was how she found Grigory. But she found him not by the fence where he had been knocked down, but about twenty paces off. It turned out later that he had crawled away after coming to himself, and had probably been a long time getting that far, losing consciousness several times along the way. She noticed at once that he was covered in blood, and screamed at the top of her voice. Grigory was muttering incoherently:

55.11.oldText: “He has murdered—his father murdered. Why scream, silly—run—fetch someone—”

55.12.oldText: But Marfa kept on screaming, and seeing that her master's window was open and that there was a candle lit in it, she ran over and began calling for Fyodor Pavlovitch. But as she peered through the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master was lying on his back, motionless, on the floor. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked with blood. The candle on the table brightly lit up the blood and the motionless dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed away from the window, ran out of the garden, drew the bolt of the big gate, and ran headlong by the back way to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Both mother and daughter were asleep, but they woke at Marfa's desperate, persistent screaming and knocking at the shutter. Marfa, shrieking and screaming incoherently, managed to tell them the main fact and to beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was staying the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way, Marya Kondratyevna remembered that at about eight o'clock she had heard a dreadful scream from their garden, and this was no doubt Grigory's cry, “Parricide!”—uttered when he caught hold of Mitya's leg.

55.13.oldText: “One person screamed out and then was silent,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. When they reached the place where Grigory lay, the two women, with Foma's help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better, that he was writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, and that foam was flowing from his lips. They moistened Grigory's forehead with water mixed with vinegar, and the water revived him at once. He asked immediately:

55.15.oldText: Then Foma and both women ran to the house and saw this time that not only the window but also the door into the garden was wide open, though for the past week Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night and wouldn't let even Grigory come in on any pretext. Seeing that door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch “for fear anything should happen afterwards.” When they got back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and raised the alarm with the whole party at the police captain's. She arrived only five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch, so that his story came not as his own surmise and theory, but as the direct confirmation, by a witness, of the theory they all held about the identity of the criminal (a theory he had, in the bottom of his heart, refused to believe until that moment).

55.16.oldText: It was decided to act with energy. The deputy police inspector of the town was assigned to take four witnesses, enter Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, and open an inquiry on the spot according to the regular procedures, which I will not go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man, new to his work, practically insisted on accompanying the police captain, the prosecutor, and the investigating lawyer.

55.17.oldText: I will note briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found to be quite dead, with his skull battered in. But with what? Most likely the same weapon with which Grigory had been attacked. And as soon as that weapon was found, Grigory—who was now given every possible medical assistance—described in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They began searching with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. There were no signs of disturbance in the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch was lying. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope inscribed: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” And below, Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” There were three seals of red sealing-wax on the envelope, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been removed. They also found on the floor a piece of narrow pink ribbon with which the envelope had been tied.

55.18.oldText: One piece of Pyotr Ilyitch's evidence made a great impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate—namely, his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would shoot himself before daybreak, that he had resolved to do so, had spoken of it to Ilyitch, had taken the pistols, loaded them in front of him, written a letter, put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, though still unwilling to believe in it, had threatened to tell someone in order to prevent the suicide, Mitya had answered with a grin: “You'll be too late.” So they had to hurry to Mokroe to find the criminal before he really did shoot himself.

55.19.oldText: “That's clear, that's clear!” the prosecutor kept repeating in great excitement. “That's just the way with mad fellows like that: ‘I'll kill myself tomorrow, so I'll make merry till I die!'”

55.20.oldText: The story of how he had bought the wine and provisions excited the prosecutor more than ever.

55.21.oldText: “Do you remember the fellow who murdered a merchant called Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost in his hand in just the same way, he went off to the girls.”

55.22.oldText: They were all delayed, however, by the inquiry, the search, the formalities, and so on, at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. It all took time, and so, two hours before setting out, they sent on ahead to Mokroe the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had arrived in town the morning before to collect his pay. He was instructed to avoid raising the alarm when he reached Mokroe, but to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and also to secure witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told, preserving his incognito and giving no one but his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch the slightest hint of his secret business. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and Mitya had at once noticed a change in Trifon Borissovitch's face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew that he was being watched. The box with the pistols had been carried off by Trifon Borissovitch and put in a suitable place. Only after four o'clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials—the police captain, the prosecutor, the investigating lawyer—drive up in two carriages, each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch's to perform a post-mortem on the body the next day. But he was particularly interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

55.23.oldText: “Such violent and prolonged epileptic fits, recurring continually for twenty-four hours, are rarely met with and are of interest to science,” he declared enthusiastically to his companions, and as they left they laughingly congratulated him on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer distinctly remembered the doctor's saying that Smerdyakov could not outlive the night.

55.24.oldText: After these long but, I think, necessary explanations, we will return to the point in our tale where we left off.

56.0.oldText: And so Mitya sat looking wildly at the people around him, not understanding what was being said to him. Suddenly he got up, flung up his hands, and shouted aloud:

56.1.oldText: “I'm not guilty! I'm not guilty of that blood! I'm not guilty of my father's blood. I meant to kill him. But I'm not guilty. Not I.”

56.2.oldText: But he had hardly said this when Grushenka rushed from behind the curtain and flung herself at the police captain's feet.

56.3.oldText: “It was my fault! Mine! My wickedness!” she cried in a heartrending voice, bathed in tears, stretching her clasped hands toward them. “He did it because of me. I tortured him and drove him to it. I tortured that poor old man who's dead too, in my wickedness, and brought it all to this! It's my fault, mine first, mine most, my fault!”

56.4.oldText: “Yes, it's your fault! You're the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You're the most to blame!” shouted the police captain, threatening her with his hand. But he was quickly and firmly silenced. The prosecutor actually seized hold of him.

56.5.oldText: “This is absolutely irregular, Mihail Makarovitch!” he cried. “You are actually hindering the inquiry. You're ruining the case—” he almost gasped.

56.6.oldText: “Follow the regular course! Follow the regular course!” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, fearfully excited too. “Otherwise it's absolutely impossible!”

56.7.oldText: “Judge us together!” Grushenka cried frantically, still kneeling. “Punish us together. I'll go with him now, even to death!”

56.8.oldText: “Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!” Mitya fell to his knees beside her and held her tight in his arms. “Don't believe her,” he cried, “she's not guilty of anything, of any blood, of anything!”

56.9.oldText: He remembered afterwards that he was forcibly dragged away from her by several men, and that she was led out, and that when he came to himself he was sitting at the table. Beside him and behind him stood the men with metal plates. Facing him on the other side of the table sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer. He kept urging him to drink a little water from a glass on the table.

56.10.oldText: “That will refresh you, that will calm you. Be calm, don't be frightened,” he added, extremely politely. Mitya (he remembered it afterwards) became suddenly intensely interested in his big rings—one with an amethyst, and another with a transparent bright yellow stone of great brilliance. And long afterwards he remembered with wonder how those rings had riveted his attention throughout those terrible hours of interrogation, so that he was utterly unable to tear himself away from them and dismiss them, as things that had nothing to do with his situation. On Mitya's left, in the spot where Maximov had been sitting at the start of the evening, the prosecutor was now seated, and on Mitya's right, where Grushenka had been, sat a rosy-cheeked young man in a sort of shabby hunting jacket, with ink and paper in front of him. This was the secretary, whom the investigating lawyer had brought with him. The police captain was now standing by the window at the other end of the room, beside Kalganov, who was seated there.

56.11.oldText: “Drink some water,” said the investigating lawyer softly, for the tenth time.

56.12.oldText: “I have drunk it, gentlemen, I have—but—come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!” cried Mitya, staring with terribly fixed, wide-open eyes at the investigating lawyer.

56.13.oldText: “So you positively declare that you are not guilty of the death of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch?” asked the investigating lawyer, softly but insistently.

56.14.oldText: “I am not guilty. I'm guilty of the blood of another old man, but not of my father's. And I weep for it! I killed, I killed the old man and knocked him down. But it's hard to have to answer for that murder with another, a terrible murder of which I am not guilty. It's a terrible accusation, gentlemen, a knock-down blow. But who has killed my father, who has killed him? Who can have killed him if I didn't? It's marvelous, extraordinary, impossible.”

56.15.oldText: “Yes, who can have killed him?” the investigating lawyer was beginning, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glancing at him, addressed Mitya.

56.16.oldText: “You needn't worry yourself about the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He is alive, he has recovered, and in spite of the terrible blows inflicted—according to his own and your testimony—by you, there seems no doubt that he will live, so the doctor says, at least.”

56.17.oldText: “Alive? He's alive?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. His face beamed. “Lord, I thank Thee for the miracle Thou hast wrought for me, a sinner and evildoer. That's an answer to my prayer. I've been praying all night.” And he crossed himself three times. He was almost breathless.

56.18.oldText: “So from this Grigory we have received such important evidence concerning you, that—” The prosecutor was about to continue, but Mitya suddenly jumped up from his chair.

56.19.oldText: “One minute, gentlemen, for God's sake, one minute; I'll run to her—”

56.20.oldText: “Excuse me, at this moment it's quite impossible,” Nikolay Parfenovitch almost shrieked. He too leapt to his feet. Mitya was seized by the men with the metal plates, but he sat down of his own accord.

56.21.oldText: “Gentlemen, what a pity! I wanted to see her for just one minute; I wanted to tell her that it's been washed away, it's gone—that blood that was weighing on my heart all night—and that I'm not a murderer now! Gentlemen, she's my betrothed!” he said ecstatically and reverently, looking around at them all. “Oh, thank you, gentlemen! Oh, in one minute you've given me new life, new heart! That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He used to wash me in the tub when I was a baby of three years old, abandoned by everyone—he was like a father to me!”

56.23.oldText: “Allow me, gentlemen, allow me one minute more,” Mitya interrupted, putting his elbows on the table and covering his face with his hands. “Let me have a moment to think, let me breathe, gentlemen. All this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man is not a drum, gentlemen!”

56.24.oldText: “Drink a little more water,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.

56.25.oldText: Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were confident. He seemed completely transformed in a moment. His whole bearing had changed; he was once more the equal of these men, all of whom he was acquainted with, as though they had all met the day before, when nothing had happened, at some social gathering. We may note in passing that, on his first arrival, Mitya had been made very welcome at the police captain's, but later, and during the last month especially, Mitya had hardly called at all, and when the police captain ran into him—in the street, for instance—Mitya had noticed that he frowned and only bowed out of politeness. His acquaintance with the prosecutor was less intimate, though he sometimes paid the prosecutor's wife, a nervous and fanciful lady, visits of politeness, without quite knowing why, and she always received him graciously and had, for some reason, taken an interest in him up till the very last. He hadn't had time to get to know the investigating lawyer, though he had met him and talked to him twice, each time about the fair sex.

56.26.oldText: “You're a most skillful lawyer, I see, Nikolay Parfenovitch,” cried Mitya, laughing cheerfully, “but I can help you now. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don't be offended at my addressing you so simply and directly. I'm rather drunk too, I'll tell you that frankly. I believe I've had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov's. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don't pretend to be on equal terms with you. I understand, of course, in what capacity I'm sitting before you. Oh, of course, there's a horrible suspicion hanging over me—if Grigory has given evidence. A horrible suspicion! It's awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen, I'm ready, and we'll put an end to it in one moment; for, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I'm innocent, we can put an end to it in a minute. Can't we? Can't we?”

56.27.oldText: Mitya spoke much and quickly, nervously and effusively, as though he took his listeners to be his best friends.

56.28.oldText: “So, for the present, we'll write down that you absolutely deny the charge brought against you,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, impressively, and bending down to the secretary he dictated to him in an undertone what to write.

56.29.oldText: “Write it down? You want to write that down? Well, write it; I consent, I give my full consent, gentlemen, only—do you see? Stay, stay, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence against a poor old man I am guilty. And there's something else at the bottom of my heart I'm guilty of too—but that you don't need to write down” (he turned suddenly to the secretary); “that's my personal life, gentlemen, that doesn't concern you—the bottom of my heart, that is. But of the murder of my old father I'm not guilty. That's a wild idea. It's quite a wild idea! I'll prove it to you, and you'll be convinced right away. You'll laugh, gentlemen. You'll laugh at your own suspicions!”

56.30.oldText: “Be calm, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said the investigating lawyer, evidently trying to allay Mitya's excitement with his own composure. “Before we go on with our inquiry, I should like, if you'll consent to answer, to hear you confirm the statement that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, that you were involved in continual disputes with him. Here, at least, a quarter of an hour ago, you exclaimed that you wanted to kill him: ‘I didn't kill him,' you said, ‘but I wanted to kill him.'”

56.31.oldText: “Did I exclaim that? Ach, that may be so, gentlemen! Yes, unhappily, I did want to kill him. Many times I wanted to. Unhappily, unhappily!”

56.32.oldText: “You wanted to. Would you consent to explain what motives precisely led you to such a sentiment of hatred for your parent?”

56.33.oldText: “What is there to explain, gentlemen?” Mitya shrugged his shoulders sullenly, looking down. “I've never hidden my feelings. The whole town knows about it—everyone in the tavern knows. Only recently I declared them in Father Zossima's cell. And the very same day, in the evening, I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore in front of witnesses that I'd come back and kill him. Oh, a thousand witnesses! I've been shouting it out loud for the last month—anyone can tell you that! The fact stares you in the face, it speaks for itself, it cries aloud—but feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter. You see, gentlemen”—Mitya frowned—“it seems to me that you have no right to question me about feelings. I know you're bound by your office, I quite understand that, but that's my affair, my private, intimate affair, and yet—since I haven't hidden my feelings in the past—in the tavern, for instance, I've talked to everyone, so—so I won't make a secret of it now. You see, I understand, gentlemen, that there are terrible facts against me in this business. I told everyone I'd kill him, and now, all of a sudden, he's been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I can quite make allowances. I'm struck all of a heap myself, for who can have murdered him, if not I? That's what it comes down to, isn't it? If not I, who can it be, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!” he exclaimed suddenly. “Where was he murdered? How was he murdered? How, and with what? Tell me,” he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.

56.34.oldText: “We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, with his head battered in,” said the prosecutor.

56.35.oldText: “That's horrible!” Mitya shuddered and, putting his elbows on the table, hid his face in his right hand.

56.36.oldText: “We will continue,” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in. “So what was it that drove you to this sentiment of hatred? You've asserted in public, I believe, that it was based on jealousy?”

56.40.oldText: “There was a dispute about three thousand roubles, I think, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?”

56.41.oldText: “Three thousand! More, more,” cried Mitya hotly. “More than six thousand, more than ten, perhaps. I told everyone so, shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to let it go at three thousand. I was desperately in need of that three thousand—so the bundle of notes for three thousand that I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I considered simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I looked on it as mine, as my own property—”

56.42.oldText: The prosecutor looked meaningfully at the investigating lawyer, and had time to wink at him on the sly.

56.43.oldText: “We'll return to that subject later,” said the lawyer promptly. “You'll allow us to note that point and write it down—that you looked on that money as your own property?”

56.44.oldText: “Write it down, by all means. I know that's another fact that tells against me, but I'm not afraid of facts, and I say them against myself. Do you hear? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different sort of man than I am,” he added, suddenly gloomy and dejected. “You have to deal with a man of honor, a man of the highest honor; above all—don't lose sight of this—a man who's done many nasty things, but has always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, in his inner being. I don't know how to express it. That's just what's made me wretched all my life, that I yearned to be honorable, that I was, so to say, a martyr to a sense of honor, seeking it with a lantern, with the lantern of Diogenes, and yet all my life I've been doing filthy things like all of us, gentlemen—that is, like me alone. That was a mistake, like me alone, me alone! Gentlemen, my head aches—” His brows contracted with pain. “You see, gentlemen, I couldn't bear the look of him, there was something in him ignoble, impudent, trampling on everything sacred, something sneering and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he's dead, I feel differently.”

56.46.oldText: “I don't feel differently, but I wish I hadn't hated him so.”

56.48.oldText: “No, not remorseful, don't write that. I'm not much good myself, I'm not very beautiful, so I had no right to consider him repulsive. That's what I mean. Write that down, if you like.”

56.49.oldText: Saying this, Mitya became very mournful. He had grown more and more gloomy as the inquiry continued.

56.50.oldText: At that moment another unexpected scene played out. Though Grushenka had been taken away, she hadn't been taken far—only to the room next but one from the blue room in which the examination was proceeding. It was a little room with one window, just beyond the large room in which they had danced and feasted so lavishly. She was sitting there with no one beside her except Maximov, who was terribly depressed, terribly scared, and clung to her side as though for safety. At their door stood one of the peasants with a metal plate on his chest. Grushenka was crying, and suddenly her grief became too much for her; she jumped up, flung her arms in the air, and with a loud wail of sorrow rushed out of the room toward him, toward her Mitya—and so unexpectedly that they had no time to stop her. Mitya, hearing her cry, trembled, jumped up, and with a yell rushed impetuously to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they weren't allowed to come together, though they saw each other. He was seized by the arms. He struggled, and tried to tear himself free. It took three or four men to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her stretching out her arms to him, crying aloud as they carried her away. When the scene was over, he came to himself again, sitting in the same place as before, opposite the investigating lawyer, and crying out to them:

56.51.oldText: “What do you want with her? Why do you torment her? She's done nothing, nothing!”

56.52.oldText: The lawyers tried to soothe him. About ten minutes passed like this. At last Mihail Makarovitch, who had been absent, came hurriedly into the room and said in a loud, excited voice to the prosecutor:

56.53.oldText: “She's been removed, she's downstairs. Will you allow me to say one word to this unhappy man, gentlemen? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence.”

56.54.oldText: “By all means, Mihail Makarovitch,” answered the investigating lawyer. “In the present case we have nothing against it.”

56.55.oldText: “Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow,” began the police captain, and there was a look of warm, almost fatherly feeling for the luckless prisoner on his excited face. “I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and handed her over to the care of the landlord's daughters, and that old fellow Maximov is with her the whole time. And I soothed her, do you hear? I soothed her and calmed her. I impressed on her that you have to clear yourself, so she mustn't hinder you, must not depress you, or you may lose your head and say the wrong thing in your evidence. In short, I talked to her, and she understood. She's a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl, she would have kissed my old hands, begging help for you. She sent me here herself, to tell you not to worry about her. And I must go, my dear fellow, I must go and tell her that you're calm and comforted about her. And so you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her; she is a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, she's a gentle soul, and not to blame for anything. So what am I to tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly or not?”

56.56.oldText: The good-natured police captain said much that was irregular, but Grushenka's suffering, a fellow creature's suffering, touched his good-natured heart, and tears stood in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

56.57.oldText: “Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!” he cried. “You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch, I thank you for her. I will, I will be calm, cheerful, in fact. Tell her, in the kindness of your heart, that I am cheerful, quite cheerful, that I'll be laughing in a minute, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I'll be done with all this in a moment, and as soon as I'm free, I'll be with her, she'll see, let her wait. Gentlemen,” he said, turning to the two lawyers, “now I'll open my whole soul to you; I'll pour out everything. We'll finish this off in a flash, finish it off merrily. We shall laugh at it in the end, shan't we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That one thing I'll tell you now. I see I'm with honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, ‘I'll go to death with you'? And what have I, a penniless beggar, done for her? Why such love for me? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with my ugly face, deserve such love, that she's ready to go into exile with me? And how she fell down at your feet for my sake, just now! And yet she's proud and has done nothing! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her as I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I am comforted.”

56.58.oldText: And he sank back into his chair and, covering his face with his hands, burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He recovered himself instantly. The old police captain seemed much pleased, and so did the lawyers. They felt that the examination was passing into a new phase. When the police captain went out, Mitya was positively cheerful.

56.59.oldText: “Now, gentlemen, I'm at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren't for all these trivial details, we'd understand one another in a minute. I'm at those details again. I'm at your disposal, gentlemen, but I declare that we must have mutual confidence, you in me and I in you, or there'll be no end to it. I'm speaking in your interests. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don't rummage in my soul; don't tease me with trifles, but only ask me about facts and what matters, and I'll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!”

57.0.oldText: “You have no idea how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by your willingness to answer,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, with an animated air and obvious satisfaction beaming in his very prominent, short-sighted, light gray eyes, from which he had removed his spectacles a moment before. “And you made a very sound point about mutual trust — without it, in cases of this importance, it is sometimes simply impossible to make headway, if the suspect genuinely hopes and wishes to defend himself and is in a position to do so. For our part, we will do everything in our power, and you can see for yourself how we are conducting the case. Do you approve, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He turned to the prosecutor.

57.1.oldText: “Oh, certainly,” replied the prosecutor. His tone was somewhat cool compared with Nikolay Parfenovitch’s impulsiveness.

57.2.oldText: I will note once and for all that Nikolay Parfenovitch, who had only recently arrived in our town, had from the very first developed a marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, and had become almost his bosom friend. He was nearly the only person who placed complete faith in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and orator, and in the justice of his grievance. He had heard of him in Petersburg. On the other hand, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the only person in the whole world whom our “underappreciated” prosecutor genuinely liked. On their way to Mokroe they had found time to reach an understanding about the present case. And now, as they sat at the table, the sharp-witted junior caught and interpreted every indication on his senior colleague’s face — half a word, a glance, or a wink.

57.3.oldText: “Gentlemen, just let me tell my own story and don’t interrupt me with trivial questions, and I’ll tell you everything in a moment,” said Mitya excitedly.

57.4.oldText: “Excellent! Thank you. But before we proceed to hear what you have to say, will you allow me to inquire about another small fact of great interest to us? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday at around five o’clock, against the security of your pistols, from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin.”

57.5.oldText: “I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. What else? That is all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them.”

57.6.oldText: “You got back to town? Then you had been out of town?”

57.7.oldText: “Yes, I went forty versts into the country. Didn’t you know?”

57.8.oldText: The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged glances.

57.9.oldText: “Well, how would it be if you began your account with a systematic description of everything you did yesterday, starting from the morning? Allow us, for example, to inquire why you were absent from town, and exactly when you left and when you came back — all those facts.”

57.10.oldText: “You should have asked me like that from the start,” cried Mitya, laughing out loud. “And if you like, we won’t begin from yesterday, but from the morning of the day before; then you’ll understand how and why and where I went. The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a merchant of the town called Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on reliable security. It was an urgent matter, gentlemen, a sudden necessity.”

57.11.oldText: “Allow me to interrupt you,” the prosecutor put in politely. “Why were you in such urgent need of exactly that sum — three thousand?”

57.12.oldText: “Oh, gentlemen, you needn’t go into details — how, when, why, why just that much money and not some other amount, and all that rigmarole. It will run to three volumes, and then you’ll want an epilogue!”

57.13.oldText: Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who is determined to tell the whole truth and is full of the best intentions.

57.14.oldText: “Gentlemen!” — he corrected himself hurriedly — “don’t be annoyed with me for being restless, I beg you again. Believe me once more, I have the greatest respect for you and understand the true state of affairs. Don’t think I’m drunk. I’m quite sober now. And besides, even being drunk would be no obstacle. It’s with me, you know, like the saying: ‘When he’s sober, he’s a fool; when he’s drunk, he’s a wise man.’ Ha ha! But I see, gentlemen, it isn’t appropriate to crack jokes with you until we’ve had our explanation out. And I have my own dignity to preserve, too. I quite understand the difference between us at this moment. After all, I am in the position of a criminal, and so far from being on equal footing with you. And it’s your job to keep watch on me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory — you can’t go breaking old men’s skulls and get away with it. I suppose you’ll lock me up for him for six months, maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don’t know what the punishment is — but it will be without loss of the rights of my rank, without loss of my rank, won’t it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But you must admit that you could baffle God Himself with such questions. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ I’ll get myself tangled up if you go on like this, and you’ll write it all down against me. And what will that lead to? To nothing! And even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! I’ll finish by asking you, gentlemen, to abandon that conventional method of questioning. I mean, beginning with some miserable trifle — how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat, and where I spat — and so distracting the criminal’s attention, and then suddenly stunning him with an overwhelming question: ‘Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?’ Ha ha! That is your standard method, that’s where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I was in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not angry, gentlemen? You’ll forgive my impertinence?” he cried, looking at them with a good nature that was almost astonishing. “It’s only Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can let it pass. It would be inexcusable in a sensible man, but in Mitya it’s forgivable. Ha ha!”

57.15.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed as well. Although the prosecutor did not laugh, he kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as if anxious not to miss the slightest syllable, the slightest movement, the smallest twitch of any feature of his face.

57.16.oldText: “That is how we have treated you from the beginning,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. “We haven’t tried to throw you off by asking how you got up in the morning and what you had for breakfast. We actually began with questions of the greatest importance.”

57.17.oldText: “I understand. I saw it and appreciated it, and I appreciate still more your present kindness to me — an unprecedented kindness, worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, and let everything be on a footing of mutual confidence between educated, well-bred people, who share the common bond of noble birth and honor. In any case, allow me to regard you as my best friends at this moment of my life, at this moment when my honor is under attack. That’s no offense to you, gentlemen, is it?”

57.18.oldText: “On the contrary. You’ve expressed all that so well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered with dignified approval.

57.19.oldText: “And enough of those petty questions, gentlemen — all those tricky questions!” Mitya cried enthusiastically. “Otherwise there’s simply no knowing where we’ll end up! Isn’t that so?”

57.20.oldText: “I will follow your sensible advice entirely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “I don’t withdraw my question, however. It is now vitally important for us to know exactly why you needed that sum, precisely three thousand.”

57.21.oldText: “Why I needed it?... Oh, for one thing and another.... Well, it was to pay a debt.”

57.23.oldText: “That I absolutely refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I couldn’t, or because I wouldn’t dare, or because it would be damaging — for it is all a petty matter and completely trivial — but because it is a matter of principle: this is my private life, and I will not allow any intrusion into my private life. That’s my principle. Your question has no bearing on the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my private affair. I wanted to pay a debt. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but to whom, I will not say.”

57.24.oldText: “Allow me to make a note of that,” said the prosecutor.

57.25.oldText: “By all means. Write down that I won’t say, that I won’t. Write that I should consider it dishonorable to say. Ech! you can write it; you’ve nothing else to do with your time.”

57.26.oldText: “Allow me to caution you, sir, and to remind you once more, in case you are unaware of it,” the prosecutor began, with a peculiar and stern emphasis, “that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now, and we, for our part, have no right to force an answer from you, if you decline to give one for one reason or another. That is entirely a matter for your personal decision. But it is our duty, on the other hand, in cases such as this, to explain and make clear to you the degree of injury you will be doing yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of evidence. With that, I beg you to continue.”

57.27.oldText: “Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ...” Mitya muttered in a rather disconcerted tone. “Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to then ...”

57.28.oldText: We will, of course, not repeat his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was impatiently anxious not to omit the slightest detail. At the same time, he was in a hurry to get it over with. But as he gave his evidence, it was being written down, and so they had continually to stop him. Mitya disliked this, but submitted; he grew angry, though still good-humoredly. It’s true he did exclaim from time to time, “Gentlemen, that’s enough to make an angel lose his patience!” Or, “Gentlemen, it’s no good your irritating me.”

57.29.oldText: But even as he exclaimed, he still kept for a time his genially expansive mood. He told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days earlier. (By now he had fully realized that he had been fooled.) The sale of his watch for six roubles to get money for the journey was something new to the lawyers. They were at once keenly interested, and even, to Mitya’s intense indignation, thought it necessary to write down the fact as secondary confirmation that he had barely a kopeck in his pocket at the time. Little by little, Mitya began to grow sullen. Then, after describing his trip to see Lyagavy, the night spent in the stifling hut, and so on, he came to his return to town. Here he began, without particular prompting, to give a detailed account of the agonies of jealousy he suffered on Grushenka’s account.

57.30.oldText: He was heard in silent attention. They inquired especially into the fact that he had a place of ambush in Marya Kondratyevna’s house at the back of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, to keep watch on Grushenka, and that Smerdyakov had brought him information. They placed particular emphasis on this and wrote it down. Of his jealousy he spoke warmly and at length, and though inwardly ashamed at exposing his most intimate feelings to “public indignity,” so to speak, he evidently overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and still more the prosecutor, stared intently at him as he told his story, in the end thoroughly disconcerted him.

57.31.oldText: “That boy Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor, are not worth my telling this to,” he reflected mournfully. “It’s humiliating. ‘Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.’” He wound up his reflections with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he came to telling of his visit to Madame Hohlakov, he regained his spirits and even wanted to tell a little anecdote about that lady, one that had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him, and civilly suggested that he move on to “more essential matters.” At last, when he described his despair and told them how, on leaving Madame Hohlakov’s, he had thought that he would “get three thousand even if he had to murder somebody to do it,” they stopped him again and wrote down that he had “meant to murder someone.” Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point in his story when he learned that Grushenka had deceived him and had returned from Samsonov’s as soon as he had left her there, although she had said she would stay until midnight.

57.32.oldText: “If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I had no time,” he suddenly blurted out at that point in his story. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited gloomily, and was beginning to tell how he had run into his father’s garden, when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him, and opening the big portfolio that lay on the sofa beside him, he brought out the brass pestle.

57.33.oldText: “Do you recognize this object?” he asked, showing it to Mitya.

57.34.oldText: “Oh, yes,” he laughed gloomily. “Of course I recognize it. Let me have a look at it.... Damn it, never mind!”

57.36.oldText: “Hang it all, I wouldn’t have concealed it from you. Do you suppose I could have managed without it? It simply slipped my memory.”

57.37.oldText: “Be so good as to tell us precisely how you came to arm yourself with it.”

57.38.oldText: “Certainly I will be so good, gentlemen.”

57.39.oldText: And Mitya described how he had taken the pestle and run.

57.40.oldText: “But what purpose did you have in mind, arming yourself with such a weapon?”

57.41.oldText: “What purpose? No purpose. I just picked it up and ran off.”

57.42.oldText: “What for, if you had no purpose?”

57.43.oldText: Mitya’s anger flared up. He looked intently at “the boy” and smiled gloomily and spitefully. He was feeling more and more ashamed at having told “such people” the story of his jealousy so sincerely and spontaneously.

57.44.oldText: “To hell with the pestle!” he suddenly burst out.

57.46.oldText: “Oh, to fend off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something came up.”

57.47.oldText: “But have you ever before taken a weapon with you when you went out, since you’re so afraid of the dark?”

57.48.oldText: “Ugh! damn it all, gentlemen! There’s simply no talking to you!” cried Mitya, exasperated beyond endurance, and turning to the secretary, crimson with anger, he said quickly, with a note of fury in his voice:

57.49.oldText: “Write down at once ... at once ... ‘that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by hitting him on the head with it!’ Well, now are you satisfied, gentlemen? Are your minds at rest?” he said, glaring defiantly at the lawyers.

57.50.oldText: “We quite understand that you made that statement just now out of exasperation with us and the questions we put to you, which you consider trivial, though they are in fact essential,” the prosecutor remarked dryly in reply.

57.51.oldText: “Well, for heaven’s sake, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does one pick things up for at such moments? I don’t know what for. I snatched it up and ran — that’s all. For my part, gentlemen, passons, or I swear I won’t tell you another thing.”

57.52.oldText: He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand. He sat sideways to them and stared at the wall, struggling against a wave of nausea. He had, in fact, a terrible urge to get up and declare that he would not say another word, “not if you hang me for it.”

57.53.oldText: “You see, gentlemen,” he said at last, with difficulty getting hold of himself, “you see. I listen to you and am haunted by a dream.... It’s a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I often dream it — it’s always the same ... that somebody is hunting me, somebody I’m dreadfully afraid of ... that he’s hunting me in the dark, in the night ... tracking me, and I hide somewhere from him, behind a door or a cupboard, hide in some degrading way, and the worst of it is, he always knows where I am, but pretends not to know where I am on purpose, to prolong my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That is just what you’re doing now. It’s exactly like that!”

57.54.oldText: “Is that the sort of thing you dream about?” inquired the prosecutor.

57.56.oldText: “No; no need to write it down. But still you do have curious dreams.”

57.57.oldText: “It’s not a question of dreams now, gentlemen — this is realism, this is real life! I’m a wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, hunt him down!”

57.59.oldText: “No, I’m not wrong, not at all!” Mitya flared up again, though his outburst of anger had obviously eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. “You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial being tortured by your questions, but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of the heart (I say that boldly!) — no! That you must believe, you have no right not to ... but —

57.62.oldText: “If you would be so kind,” answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.

58.0.oldText: Though Mitya spoke sullenly, it was evident that he was now trying harder than ever not to forget or skip a single detail of his story. He told them how he had leapt over the fence into his father’s garden; how he had gone up to the window; told them everything that had happened under the window. Clearly, precisely, distinctly, he described the feelings that troubled him during those moments in the garden, when he longed so desperately to know whether Grushenka was with his father or not. But, strange to say, both the lawyers now listened with a kind of dreadful reserve, looked at him coldly, asked few questions. Mitya could read nothing from their faces.

58.1.oldText: “They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, to hell with them!”

58.2.oldText: When he described how he had finally made up his mind to give the “signal” to his father that Grushenka had come, so that he would open the window, the lawyers paid no attention to the word “signal,” as though they entirely failed to grasp the meaning of the word in this context — so much so that Mitya noticed it. Coming at last to the moment when, on seeing his father peering out of the window, his hatred flared up and he pulled the pestle out of his pocket, he suddenly, as though on purpose, stopped short. He sat staring at the wall and was aware that their eyes were fixed on him.

58.3.oldText: “Well?” said the investigating lawyer. “You pulled out the weapon and ... and what happened then?”

58.4.oldText: “Then? Why, then I murdered him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... I suppose that’s your version. That’s it!”

58.5.oldText: His eyes suddenly flashed. All his smothered anger suddenly flared up with extraordinary violence in his soul.

58.6.oldText: “Our version?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch. “Well — and yours?”

58.7.oldText: Mitya dropped his eyes and was silent for a long time.

58.8.oldText: “My version, gentlemen? Well, it was like this,” he began softly. “Whether it was somebody’s tears, or my mother praying to God, or a good angel kissing me at that instant, I don’t know. But the devil was defeated. I tore away from the window and ran to the fence. My father was startled and for the first time saw me then, cried out, and sprang back from the window. I remember that very well. I ran across the garden to the fence ... and there Grigory caught me, when I was sitting on the fence.”

58.9.oldText: At that point he at last raised his eyes and looked at his listeners. They seemed to be staring at him with perfectly unruffled attention. A sort of spasm of indignation seized Mitya’s soul.
