58.10.oldText: “Why, you’re laughing at me at this very moment, gentlemen!” he broke off suddenly.

58.11.oldText: “What makes you think that?” observed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

58.12.oldText: “You don’t believe a word — that’s why! I understand, of course, that I have come to the crucial point. The old man is lying there now with his skull broken, while I — after dramatically describing how I wanted to kill him, and how I grabbed the pestle — suddenly run away from the window. A romance! Poetry! As if anyone could take a man at his word. Ha ha! You are scoffers, gentlemen!”

58.13.oldText: And he spun around on his chair so hard that it creaked.

58.14.oldText: “And did you notice,” the prosecutor asked suddenly, as if ignoring Mitya’s excitement, “did you notice, when you ran away from the window, whether the door into the garden was open?”

58.17.oldText: “It was shut. And who could have opened it? Bah! the door. Wait a bit!” he seemed suddenly to catch himself, and almost with a start:

58.20.oldText: “Why, who could have opened it, if you didn’t open it yourselves?” cried Mitya, greatly astonished.

58.21.oldText: “The door stood open, and your father’s murderer undoubtedly went in through that door, and, having committed the crime, went out again by the same door,” the prosecutor pronounced deliberately, as though chiseling out each word separately. “That is perfectly clear. The murder was committed in the room and not through the window; that is absolutely certain from the investigation that has been made, from the position of the body and everything else. There can be no doubt about that fact.”

58.23.oldText: “But that is utterly impossible!” he cried, completely at a loss. “I ... I didn’t go in.... I tell you positively, definitely, the door was shut the whole time I was in the garden, and when I ran out of the garden. I only stood at the window and saw him through the window. That’s all, that’s all.... I remember everything to the last minute. And even if I didn’t remember, it would still be the same. I know it, because no one knew the signals except Smerdyakov, and me, and the dead man. And he wouldn’t have opened the door to anyone in the world without the signals.”

58.24.oldText: “Signals? What signals?” asked the prosecutor, with greedy, almost hysterical curiosity. Instantly he lost all trace of his reserve and dignity. He put the question with a kind of cringing timidity. He had caught the scent of an important fact of which he had known nothing, and was already filled with dread that Mitya might be unwilling to disclose it.

58.25.oldText: “So you didn’t know!” Mitya winked at him with a malicious, mocking smile. “What if I won’t tell you? From whom could you find out? No one knew about the signals except my father, Smerdyakov, and me: that was all. Heaven knew too, but it won’t tell you. But it’s an interesting fact. There’s no telling what you could build on it. Ha ha! Take comfort, gentlemen, I’ll reveal it. You have some foolish idea in your heads. You don’t know the man you are dealing with! You are dealing with a prisoner who gives evidence against himself, to his own cost! Yes, for I am a man of honor, and you — are not.”

58.26.oldText: The prosecutor swallowed this without a murmur. He was trembling with impatience to hear the new fact. In minute detail, Mitya told them everything about the signals that Fyodor Pavlovitch had invented for Smerdyakov. He told them exactly what each tap on the window meant, tapped the signals out on the table, and when Nikolay Parfenovitch said that he assumed Mitya had tapped out the signal “Grushenka has come” when he tapped to his father, he answered precisely that he had tapped that signal, that “Grushenka had come.”

58.27.oldText: “So now you can build up your tower,” Mitya broke off, and again turned away from them contemptuously.

58.28.oldText: “So no one knew of the signals but your late father, you, and the servant Smerdyakov? And no one else?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired once more.

58.29.oldText: “Yes. The servant Smerdyakov, and Heaven. Write that down about Heaven. That may come in useful. Besides, you’ll need God yourselves.”

58.30.oldText: And of course they had already begun writing it down. But while they wrote, the prosecutor said suddenly, as though seizing on a new idea:

58.31.oldText: “But if Smerdyakov also knew of these signals, and you absolutely deny all responsibility for the death of your father, wasn’t it perhaps he who knocked out the agreed signal, got your father to open the door for him, and then ... committed the crime?”

58.32.oldText: Mitya turned on him a look of profound irony and intense hatred. His silent stare lasted so long that it made the prosecutor blink.

58.33.oldText: “You’ve caught the fox again,” Mitya commented at last; “you’ve got the beast by the tail. Ha ha! I see through you, Mr. Prosecutor. You assumed, of course, that I would jump at that, seize on your suggestion, and shout at the top of my voice, ‘Aha! it’s Smerdyakov; he’s the murderer.’ Admit it — that’s what you thought. Admit it, and I’ll go on.”

58.34.oldText: But the prosecutor did not admit it. He held his tongue and waited.

58.35.oldText: “You’re mistaken. I’m not going to shout ‘It’s Smerdyakov,’” said Mitya.

58.39.oldText: Mitya fixed his eyes on the floor.

58.40.oldText: “Joking aside,” he brought out gloomily. “Listen. From the very beginning, almost from the moment when I ran out from behind the curtain to you, the thought of Smerdyakov has been in my mind. I’ve been sitting here shouting that I’m innocent, and thinking the whole time ‘Smerdyakov!’ I can’t get Smerdyakov out of my head. In fact, I, too, thought of Smerdyakov just now; but only for a second. Almost at once I thought, ‘No, it’s not Smerdyakov.’ It’s not his doing, gentlemen.”

58.41.oldText: “In that case, is there anyone else you suspect?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired cautiously.

58.42.oldText: “I don’t know who it could be, whether it’s the hand of Heaven or of Satan, but ... not Smerdyakov,” Mitya jerked out decisively.

58.43.oldText: “But what makes you claim so confidently and so emphatically that it isn’t him?”

58.44.oldText: “From my conviction — my impression. Because Smerdyakov is a man of the most abject character and a coward. He’s not just a coward, he’s the epitome of all the cowardice in the world walking on two legs. He has the heart of a chicken. When he talked to me, he was always trembling with fear that I might kill him, though I never raised a hand against him. He fell at my feet and blubbered; he has literally kissed these very boots, begging me ‘not to frighten him.’ Do you hear? ‘Not to frighten him.’ What a thing to say! Why, I offered him money. He’s a whimpering chicken — sickly, epileptic, weak-minded — a child of eight could thrash him. He has no character worth speaking of. It’s not Smerdyakov, gentlemen. He doesn’t care for money; he wouldn’t take my presents. Besides, what motive did he have to murder the old man? Why, he’s very likely his son, you know — his natural son. Did you know that?”

58.45.oldText: “We have heard that legend. But you are your father’s son, too, aren’t you; yet you yourself told everyone you meant to murder him.”

58.46.oldText: “That’s a jab! And a nasty, mean one, too! I’m not afraid! Oh, gentlemen, isn’t it base of you to say that to my face? It’s base, because I told you that myself. I not only wanted to murder him, but I might have done it. And what’s more, I went out of my way to tell you of my own accord that I nearly murdered him. But you see, I didn’t murder him; you see, my guardian angel saved me — that’s what you haven’t taken into account. And that’s why it’s so base of you. Because I didn’t kill him, I didn’t kill him! Do you hear? I did not kill him.”

58.47.oldText: He was almost choking. He had not been so moved before during the entire interrogation.

58.48.oldText: “And what has he told you, gentlemen — Smerdyakov, I mean?” he added suddenly, after a pause. “May I ask that question?”

58.49.oldText: “You may ask any question,” the prosecutor replied with frigid severity, “any question relating to the facts of the case, and we, I repeat, are bound to answer every inquiry you make. We found the servant Smerdyakov, about whom you are asking, lying unconscious in his bed, in an epileptic fit of extreme severity, which had returned, perhaps, ten times. The doctor who was with us told us, after examining him, that he may not outlive the night.”

58.50.oldText: “Well, if that’s so, the devil must have killed him,” broke suddenly from Mitya, as though until that moment he had been asking himself: “Was it Smerdyakov or not?”

58.51.oldText: “We will come back to this later,” Nikolay Parfenovitch decided. “Now, wouldn’t you like to continue your statement?”

58.52.oldText: Mitya asked for a rest. His request was politely granted. After resting, he continued his story. But he was clearly depressed. He was exhausted, humiliated, and morally shaken. To make things worse, the prosecutor kept irritating him, as though on purpose, with vexatious interruptions about “trifling points.” Mitya had barely described how, sitting on the wall, he had struck Grigory on the head with the pestle while the old man had hold of his left leg, and how he had then jumped down to look at him, when the prosecutor stopped him to ask him to describe exactly how he had been sitting on the wall. Mitya was surprised.

58.53.oldText: “Oh, I was sitting like this, astride, one leg on one side of the wall and one on the other.”

58.56.oldText: “Not in your pocket? Do you remember that precisely? Was it a violent blow you gave him?”

58.57.oldText: “It must have been a violent one. But why do you ask?”

58.58.oldText: “Would you mind sitting on the chair just the way you were sitting on the wall then, and showing us just how you moved your arm, and in what direction?”

58.59.oldText: “You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?” asked Mitya, looking haughtily at the speaker; but the other man did not flinch.

58.60.oldText: Mitya turned abruptly, sat astride his chair, and swung his arm.

58.61.oldText: “This is how I struck him! That’s how I knocked him down! What more do you want?”

58.62.oldText: “Thank you. May I trouble you now to explain why you jumped down, with what purpose, and what you had in mind?”

58.63.oldText: “Oh, hang it!... I jumped down to look at the man I’d hurt ... I don’t know what for!”

58.64.oldText: “Though you were so excited and were running away?”

58.65.oldText: “Yes, though I was excited and running away.”

58.67.oldText: “Help!... Yes, perhaps I did want to help him.... I don’t remember.”

58.68.oldText: “You don’t remember? Then you didn’t quite know what you were doing?”

58.69.oldText: “Not at all. I remember everything — every detail. I jumped down to look at him, and wiped his face with my handkerchief.”

58.70.oldText: “We have seen your handkerchief. Did you hope to restore him to consciousness?”

58.71.oldText: “I don’t know whether I hoped that. I just wanted to make sure whether he was alive or not.”

58.72.oldText: “Ah! You wanted to be sure? Well, what then?”

58.73.oldText: “I’m not a doctor. I couldn’t decide. I ran away thinking I’d killed him. And now he’s recovered.”

58.74.oldText: “Excellent,” commented the prosecutor. “Thank you. That’s all I wanted. Kindly proceed.”

58.75.oldText: Alas! it never entered Mitya’s head to tell them, though he remembered it, that he had jumped back out of pity, and that standing over the prostrate figure he had even uttered some words of regret: “You’ve come to grief, old man — there’s no help for it. Well, there you must lie.”

58.76.oldText: The prosecutor could only draw one conclusion: that the man had jumped back “at such a moment and in such a state of excitement, simply with the purpose of making sure whether the only witness of his crime was dead; that he must therefore have been a man of great strength, composure, resolve, and foresight, even at such a moment,” ... and so on. The prosecutor was satisfied: “I’ve provoked the high-strung fellow with ‘trifles’ and he has said more than he meant to.”

58.77.oldText: With painful effort Mitya went on. But this time he was pulled up immediately by Nikolay Parfenovitch.

58.78.oldText: “How did you come to run to the servant, Fedosya Markovna, with your hands so covered in blood, and, as it turns out, your face, too?”

58.79.oldText: “Why, I didn’t notice the blood at all at the time,” Mitya answered.

58.80.oldText: “That’s quite likely. It does happen sometimes.” The prosecutor exchanged glances with Nikolay Parfenovitch.

58.81.oldText: “I simply didn’t notice. You’re quite right there, prosecutor,” Mitya suddenly agreed.

58.82.oldText: Next came the account of Mitya’s sudden decision to “step aside” and make way for their happiness. But he could not bring himself to open his heart to them as he had before, and tell them about “the queen of his soul.” He disliked speaking of her in front of these chilly men, “who were fastening on him like bugs.” So in response to their repeated questions, he answered briefly and abruptly:

58.83.oldText: “Well, I made up my mind to kill myself. What had I left to live for? That question stared me in the face. Her first rightful lover had come back, the man who had wronged her, but who had hurried back to offer his love after five years and make amends for the wrong with marriage.... So I knew it was all over for me.... And behind me was disgrace, and that blood — Grigory’s.... What did I have to live for? So I went to redeem the pistols I had pawned, to load them and put a bullet in my brain tomorrow.”

58.85.oldText: “Yes, a grand feast the night before. Damn it all, gentlemen! Do hurry up and finish it. I meant to shoot myself not far from here, beyond the village, and I’d planned to do it at five o’clock in the morning. And I already had a note in my pocket. I wrote it at Perhotin’s when I loaded my pistols. Here’s the letter. Read it! It’s not for your sake that I’m telling you,” he added contemptuously. He took it from his waistcoat pocket and flung it on the table. The lawyers read it with curiosity, and, as is customary, added it to the papers connected with the case.

58.86.oldText: “And you didn’t even think of washing your hands at Perhotin’s? You weren’t afraid of arousing suspicion?”

58.87.oldText: “What suspicion? Suspicion or not, I would have galloped here just the same, and shot myself at five o’clock, and you wouldn’t have been in time to do anything. If it hadn’t been for what happened to my father, you would have known nothing about it, and wouldn’t have come here. Oh, it’s the devil’s doing. It was the devil who murdered father, it was through the devil that you found out about it so soon. How did you manage to get here so quick? It’s astonishing, a dream!”

58.88.oldText: “Mr. Perhotin informed us that when you came to him, you held in your hands ... your blood-stained hands ... your money ... a lot of money ... a bundle of hundred-rouble notes, and that his servant-boy saw it too.”

58.89.oldText: “That’s true, gentlemen. I remember it was so.”

58.90.oldText: “Now, there’s one small point that arises. Can you tell us,” Nikolay Parfenovitch began, with extreme gentleness, “where did you get so much money all of a sudden, when it appears from the facts, from the reckoning of time, that you had not been home?”

58.91.oldText: The prosecutor’s brows contracted at the question being put so plainly, but he did not interrupt Nikolay Parfenovitch.

58.92.oldText: “No, I didn’t go home,” Mitya answered, apparently perfectly composed, but looking at the floor.

58.93.oldText: “Allow me then to repeat my question,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, as though creeping up on the subject. “Where were you able to come by such a sum all at once, when by your own admission, at five o’clock the same day, you —”

58.94.oldText: “I was short ten roubles and pawned my pistols with Perhotin, and then went to Madame Hohlakov to borrow three thousand, which she wouldn’t give me, and so on and so on, and all the rest of it,” Mitya interrupted sharply. “Yes, gentlemen, I was short of it, and then suddenly thousands turned up, eh? Do you know, gentlemen, you are both afraid now ‘what if he won’t tell us where he got it?’ That’s exactly how it is. I am not going to tell you, gentlemen. You’ve guessed right. You’ll never know,” said Mitya, chipping out each word with extraordinary determination. The lawyers were silent for a moment.

58.95.oldText: “You must understand, Mr. Karamazov, that it is of vital importance for us to know,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, softly and smoothly.

58.96.oldText: “I understand; but still, I won’t tell you.”

58.97.oldText: The prosecutor, too, intervened, and again reminded the prisoner that he was at liberty to refuse to answer questions, if he thought it in his interest, and so on. But in view of the damage he might do himself by his silence, especially in a case of such importance as —

58.98.oldText: “And so on, gentlemen, and so on. Enough! I’ve heard that rigmarole before,” Mitya interrupted again. “I can see for myself how important it is, and that this is the vital point, and still I won’t say.”

58.99.oldText: “What is it to us? It’s not our business, but yours. You are doing yourself harm,” observed Nikolay Parfenovitch nervously.

58.100.oldText: “You see, gentlemen, joking aside” — Mitya lifted his eyes and looked firmly at both of them — “I had a feeling from the first that we’d come to loggerheads at this point. But at first, when I began to give my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all vague, and I was so naive that I began on the assumption that mutual confidence existed between us. Now I can see for myself that such confidence is out of the question, since in any case we were bound to come to this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve come to it! It’s impossible, and that’s an end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t simply take my word for it all. I understand that, of course.”

58.102.oldText: “Couldn’t you, without abandoning your resolution to stay silent about the main point, could you not at the same time give us some slight hint as to the nature of the motives that are strong enough to make you refuse to answer, at a moment so full of danger to yourself?”

58.104.oldText: “I’m much more good-natured than you think, gentlemen. I’ll tell you the reason, and I’ll give you that hint, though you don’t deserve it. I won’t speak of it, gentlemen, because it would be a stain on my honor. The answer to the question of where I got the money would expose me to far greater disgrace than the murder and robbery of my father, if I had murdered and robbed him. That’s why I can’t tell you. I can’t, for fear of disgrace. What, gentlemen, are you going to write that down?”

58.106.oldText: “You ought not to write that down about ‘disgrace.’ I only told you that out of the goodness of my heart. I didn’t have to tell you. I made you a present of it, so to speak, and you pounce on it at once. Oh, well — write, write what you like,” he concluded, with scornful disgust. “I’m not afraid of you, and I can still hold my head high in front of you.”

58.107.oldText: “And can’t you tell us the nature of that disgrace?” Nikolay Parfenovitch ventured.

58.109.oldText: “No, no, c’est fini, don’t trouble yourselves. It’s not worth soiling one’s hands. I’ve soiled myself enough because of you already. You’re not worth it — no one is ... Enough, gentlemen. I’m not going on.”

58.110.oldText: This was said too peremptorily. Nikolay Parfenovitch did not press further, but he could see from Ippolit Kirillovitch’s eyes that he had not given up hope.

58.111.oldText: “Can you not, at least, tell us what sum you had in your hands when you went into Mr. Perhotin’s — how many roubles exactly?”

58.113.oldText: “You mentioned to Mr. Perhotin, I believe, that you had received three thousand from Madame Hohlakov.”

58.114.oldText: “Perhaps I did. Enough, gentlemen. I won’t say how much I had.”

58.115.oldText: “Will you be so kind, then, as to tell us how you came here, and what you have done since you arrived?”

58.116.oldText: “Oh! you could ask the people here about that. But I’ll tell you if you like.”

58.117.oldText: He proceeded to do so, but we won’t repeat his story. He told it dryly and briefly. Of the raptures of his love, he said nothing, but told them that he had abandoned his determination to shoot himself, owing to “new factors in the case.” He told the story without going into motives or details. And this time the lawyers did not trouble him much. It was obvious that there was no essential point of interest to them here.

58.118.oldText: “We shall verify all that. We will come back to it during the examination of the witnesses, which will, of course, take place in your presence,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch in conclusion. “And now allow me to ask you to lay on the table everything in your possession, especially all the money you still have on you.”

58.119.oldText: “My money, gentlemen? Certainly. I understand that that is necessary. I’m actually surprised you haven’t asked about it sooner. It’s true I couldn’t get away anywhere. I’m sitting here where I can be seen. But here’s my money — count it, take it. That’s all, I think.”

58.120.oldText: He turned it all out of his pockets; even the small change — two twenty-kopeck pieces — he pulled out of his waistcoat pocket. They counted the money, which amounted to eight hundred and thirty-six roubles, and forty kopecks.

58.121.oldText: “And is that all?” asked the investigating lawyer.

58.123.oldText: “You stated just now in your evidence that you spent three hundred roubles at Plotnikovs’. You gave Perhotin ten, your driver twenty, you lost two hundred here, then....”

58.124.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch reckoned it all up. Mitya helped him readily. They recalled every kopeck and included it in the reckoning. Nikolay Parfenovitch hurriedly added up the total.

58.125.oldText: “With this eight hundred you must have had around fifteen hundred at the start?”

58.127.oldText: “How is it that everybody claims there was much more?”

58.131.oldText: “We will compare all this with the evidence of other witnesses not yet examined. Don’t be anxious about your money. It will be properly taken care of, and will be at your disposal at the conclusion of ... what is beginning ... if it appears, or, so to speak, is proved, that you have undisputed right to it. Well, and now....”

58.132.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly got up and informed Mitya firmly that it was his duty and obligation to conduct a thorough and detailed search “of your clothes and everything else....”

58.133.oldText: “By all means, gentlemen. I’ll turn out all my pockets, if you like.”

58.134.oldText: And he did, in fact, begin turning out his pockets.

58.135.oldText: “It will be necessary to take off your clothes, too.”

58.137.oldText: “It’s utterly impossible, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You must take off your clothes.”

58.138.oldText: “As you like,” Mitya submitted gloomily; “only, please, not here, but behind the curtains. Who’s going to search them?”

58.140.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch bent his head in assent. His small face wore an expression of peculiar solemnity.

59.0.oldText: Something utterly unexpected and astonishing to Mitya followed. He could never, even a minute earlier, have imagined that anyone could treat him, Mitya Karamazov, like that. Worst of all, there was something humiliating about it, and on their side something “supercilious and scornful.” It was nothing to take off his coat, but he was asked to undress further — or rather, not asked, but “commanded,” and he understood that perfectly. Out of pride and contempt he submitted without a word. Several peasants accompanied the lawyers and stayed on the same side of the curtain. “To be ready if force is required,” Mitya thought, “and perhaps for some other reason, too.”

59.1.oldText: “Well, must I take off my shirt, too?” he asked sharply, but Nikolay Parfenovitch did not answer. He was busy with the prosecutor, examining the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat, and the cap; and it was clear that they were both very interested in what they were inspecting. “They make no bones about it,” Mitya thought, “they don’t bother with even the most basic courtesy.”

59.2.oldText: “I’m asking you for the second time — do I need to take off my shirt or not?” he said, still more sharply and irritably.

59.3.oldText: “Don’t worry yourself. We’ll tell you what to do,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, and his voice was positively peremptory — or so it seemed to Mitya.

59.4.oldText: Meanwhile a consultation was going on in low voices between the lawyers. There turned out to be on the coat, especially on the left side at the back, a huge patch of blood, dry and still stiff. There were bloodstains on the trousers, too. What’s more, in the presence of the peasant witnesses, Nikolay Parfenovitch ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs, and every seam of the coat and trousers, obviously looking for something — money, of course. He didn’t even hide from Mitya his suspicion that he might be capable of sewing money into his clothes.

59.5.oldText: “He treats me not like an officer but like a thief,” Mitya muttered to himself. They shared their thoughts with one another with astonishing frankness. The secretary, for instance, who was also behind the curtain, fussing about and listening, called Nikolay Parfenovitch’s attention to the cap, which they were also fingering.

59.6.oldText: “You remember Gridyenko, the copying-clerk,” the secretary observed. “Last summer he received the wages of the whole office, and pretended to have lost the money when he was drunk. And where was it found? Why, in just such pipings in his cap. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up in little tubes and sewn into the piping.”

59.7.oldText: Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s case perfectly, and so they set Mitya’s cap aside and decided that all his clothes would have to be more thoroughly examined later.

59.8.oldText: “Excuse me,” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly, noticing that the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was turned in and covered with blood, “excuse me, what’s that — blood?”

59.10.oldText: “That is — what blood?... And why is the cuff turned in?”

59.11.oldText: Mitya told him how he had gotten the sleeve stained with blood looking after Grigory, and had turned it inside when he was washing his hands at Perhotin’s.

59.12.oldText: “You must take off your shirt, too. That’s very important as material evidence.”

59.13.oldText: Mitya flushed red and flew into a rage.

59.15.oldText: “Don’t worry yourself. We’ll arrange something. And meanwhile, take off your socks.”

59.16.oldText: “You’re not joking? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes flashed.

59.17.oldText: “We are in no mood for joking,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered sternly.

59.18.oldText: “Well, if I must —” muttered Mitya, and sitting down on the bed, he took off his socks. He felt unbearably awkward. All the others were clothed, while he was naked, and strange to say, when he was undressed he somehow felt guilty in their presence, and was almost ready to believe himself that he was inferior to them, and that they now had a perfect right to despise him.

59.19.oldText: “When everyone’s undressed, somehow there’s no shame in it, but when you’re the only one undressed and everyone’s looking, it’s degrading,” he kept saying to himself, over and over. “It’s like a dream, I’ve sometimes dreamed of being in such degrading positions.” It was agony for him to take off his socks. They were very dirty, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see it. And what was worse, he disliked his own feet. All his life he had thought both his big toes hideous. He particularly loathed the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they would all see it. Feeling unbearably ashamed made him, at once and deliberately, rougher. He pulled off his shirt himself.

59.20.oldText: “Would you like to look anywhere else, if you aren’t ashamed to?”

59.21.oldText: “No, there’s no need to, at present.”

59.22.oldText: “Well, am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.

59.23.oldText: “Yes, that can’t be helped for the time being.... Kindly sit down here for a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I’ll take care of all this.”

59.24.oldText: All the items were shown to the witnesses. The report of the search was drawn up, and at last Nikolay Parfenovitch went out, and the clothes were carried out after him. Ippolit Kirillovitch went out, too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who stood in silence, never taking their eyes off him. Mitya wrapped himself in the quilt. He felt cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t pull the quilt over to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, “an unbearable time.” “He thinks of me as a puppy,” Mitya thought, gnashing his teeth. “That rotten prosecutor has gone, too — out of contempt, no doubt; it disgusts him to see me naked!”

59.25.oldText: Mitya assumed, however, that his clothes would be examined and returned to him. But imagine his indignation when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back with completely different clothes, carried in behind him by a peasant.

59.26.oldText: “Here are some clothes for you,” he remarked airily, seeming quite pleased with the success of his errand. “Mr. Kalganov has kindly provided these for this unusual emergency, as well as a clean shirt. Luckily he had them all in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underclothes.”

59.28.oldText: “I won’t have other people’s clothes!” he shouted menacingly. “Give me my own!”

59.30.oldText: “Give me my own. To hell with Kalganov and his clothes, too!”

59.31.oldText: It took a long time to persuade him. But somehow they managed to calm him down. They impressed upon him that his clothes, being stained with blood, had to be “included with the other material evidence,” and that they “had no right to let him have them now ... taking into consideration the possible outcome of the case.” Mitya at last understood this. He sank into gloomy silence and hurriedly dressed himself. He only remarked, as he put them on, that the clothes were much better than his old ones, and that he disliked “gaining by the change.” Besides, the coat was “ridiculously tight. Am I to be dressed up like a fool ... for your amusement?”

59.32.oldText: They urged him again that he was exaggerating, that Kalganov was only a little taller, so that only the trousers might be a bit too long. But the coat really did turn out to be tight in the shoulders.

59.33.oldText: “Damn it all! I can hardly button it,” Mitya grumbled. “Be so good as to tell Mr. Kalganov from me that I didn’t ask for his clothes, and it’s not my doing that they’ve dressed me up like a clown.”

59.34.oldText: “He understands that, and is sorry ... I mean, not sorry to lend you his clothes, but sorry about all this business,” mumbled Nikolay Parfenovitch.

59.35.oldText: “Damn his sorrow! Well, where now? Am I to go on sitting here?”

59.36.oldText: He was asked to go back to the “other room.” Mitya went in, scowling with anger, and trying to avoid looking at anyone. Dressed in another man’s clothes, he felt disgraced, even in the eyes of the peasants, and of Trifon Borissovitch, whose face appeared, for some reason, in the doorway, and vanished at once. “He’s come to look at me dressed up,” Mitya thought. He sat down on the same chair as before. He had an absurd, nightmarish feeling, as though he were out of his mind.

59.37.oldText: “Well, what now? Are you going to flog me? That’s all that’s left for you,” he said, clenching his teeth and addressing the prosecutor. He would not turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though he disdained to speak to him.

59.38.oldText: “He looked too closely at my socks, and turned them inside out on purpose, to show everyone how dirty they were — the scoundrel!”

59.39.oldText: “Well, now we must proceed to the examination of witnesses,” Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, as though answering Mitya’s question.

59.40.oldText: “Yes,” said the prosecutor thoughtfully, as though reflecting on something.

59.41.oldText: “We’ve done what we could in your interest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, “but having received from you such an uncompromising refusal to explain to us the source from which you obtained the money found upon you, we are, at the present moment —”

59.42.oldText: “What is the stone in your ring?” Mitya interrupted suddenly, as though coming out of a daze. He pointed to one of the three large rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.

59.44.oldText: “Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins in it — what stone is that?” Mitya persisted, like a peevish child.

59.45.oldText: “That’s a smoky topaz,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, smiling. “Would you like to look at it? I’ll take it off ...”

59.46.oldText: “No, don’t take it off,” cried Mitya furiously, suddenly coming to himself and angry with himself. “Don’t take it off ... there’s no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you’ve sullied my heart! Do you really suppose I would conceal it from you, if I had actually killed my father — that I would shuffle, lie, and hide myself? No, that’s not like Dmitri Karamazov, he couldn’t do that, and if I were guilty, I swear, I wouldn’t have waited for your arrival, or for sunrise as I first intended — I would have killed myself before this, without waiting for the dawn! I know that about myself now. I couldn’t have learned so much in twenty years as I’ve found out in this accursed night!... And would I be like this on this night, at this moment, sitting with you, could I have talked like this, could I have moved like this, could I have looked at you and at the world like this, if I had really been the murderer of my father — when the very thought of having accidentally killed Grigory gave me no peace all night? Not from fear — oh, not simply from fear of your punishment! From the disgrace of it! And you expect me to be open with scoffers like you, who see nothing and believe in nothing — blind moles and scoffers — and to tell you another filthy thing I’ve done, another disgrace, even if it would save me from your charge? No, better Siberia! The man who opened the door to my father and went in at that door, he killed him, he robbed him. Who was he? I’m racking my brain and can’t figure it out. But I can tell you it was not Dmitri Karamazov, and that’s all I can tell you, and that’s enough — enough, leave me alone.... Exile me, punish me, but don’t bother me any more. I’ll say no more. Call your witnesses!”

59.47.oldText: Mitya uttered his sudden monologue as though he had made up his mind to be completely silent from then on. The prosecutor watched him the entire time, and only when he had stopped speaking did he observe, as though it were the most ordinary thing, with the most frigid and composed air:

59.48.oldText: “Oh, about the open door you just spoke of, we may as well inform you, in passing, of a very interesting piece of evidence of the greatest importance both to you and to us, given to us by Grigory, the old man you wounded. Upon his recovery, in answer to our questions, he clearly and emphatically stated that when, on coming out to the steps and hearing a noise in the garden, he decided to enter it through the little gate that stood open, before he noticed you running — as you have already told us — in the dark from the open window where you had seen your father, he, Grigory, glanced to the left, and, while noticing the open window, also observed at the same time, much closer to him, the door, standing wide open — that very door which you have stated to have been shut the whole time you were in the garden. I will not conceal from you that Grigory himself confidently affirms and bears witness that you must have run out through that door, though of course he did not see you do so with his own eyes, since he only noticed you first some distance away in the garden, running toward the fence.”

59.49.oldText: Mitya had leapt up from his chair halfway through this speech.

59.50.oldText: “Nonsense!” he yelled in a sudden frenzy. “It’s a barefaced lie. He couldn’t have seen the door open, because it was shut. He’s lying!”

59.51.oldText: “I consider it my duty to repeat that he is firm in his statement. He does not waver. He sticks to it. We’ve cross-examined him several times.”

59.52.oldText: “Precisely. I have cross-examined him several times,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed warmly.

59.53.oldText: “It’s false, false! It’s either an attempt to slander me, or the hallucination of a madman,” Mitya still shouted. “He’s simply raving, from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it when he came to.... He’s raving.”

59.54.oldText: “Yes, but he noticed the open door, not when he came to after his injuries, but before that, as soon as he went into the garden from the lodge.”

59.55.oldText: “But it’s false, it’s false! It can’t be! He’s slandering me out of spite.... He couldn’t have seen it ... I didn’t come from the door,” Mitya gasped.

59.56.oldText: The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said to him impressively:

59.59.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch laid on the table a large, thick official envelope, on which three seals still remained intact. The envelope was empty, and slit open at one end. Mitya stared at it wide-eyed.

59.60.oldText: “It ... it must be that envelope of my father’s, the envelope that contained the three thousand roubles ... and if there’s inscribed on it — allow me — ‘For my little chicken’ ... yes — three thousand!” he shouted. “Do you see, three thousand, do you see?”

59.61.oldText: “Of course, we see. But we didn’t find the money in it. It was empty, and lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen.”

59.62.oldText: For several seconds Mitya stood as though thunderstruck.

59.63.oldText: “Gentlemen, it’s Smerdyakov!” he suddenly shouted at the top of his voice. “It’s he who murdered him! He robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It’s Smerdyakov, that’s clear now!”

59.64.oldText: “But you, too, knew about the envelope, and that it was under the pillow.”

59.65.oldText: “I never knew it. I’ve never seen it. This is the first time I’ve looked at it. I only heard of it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden — I didn’t know ...” Mitya was completely breathless.

59.66.oldText: “But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known it.”

59.67.oldText: “We’ve got it written down,” confirmed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

59.68.oldText: “Nonsense! It’s absurd! I’d no idea it was under the pillow. And maybe it wasn’t under the pillow at all.... It was just a lucky guess that it was under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Have you asked him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say? that’s the main point.... And I went out of my way to tell lies on myself.... I told you without thinking that it was under the pillow, and now you — Oh, you know how one says the wrong thing without meaning to. No one knew but Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, and no one else.... He didn’t even tell me where it was! But it’s his doing, his doing; there’s no doubt about it, he murdered him, that’s as clear as daylight now,” Mitya exclaimed, more and more frantic, repeating himself incoherently, growing more and more exasperated and excited. “You must understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and while Grigory was unconscious, that’s clear now.... He gave the signal and father opened to him ... because no one but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened the door....”

59.69.oldText: “But you are again forgetting the fact,” the prosecutor observed, still with the same restraint, though with a note of triumph, “that there was no need to give the signal if the door already stood open when you were there, while you were in the garden....”

59.70.oldText: “The door, the door,” muttered Mitya, and he stared speechless at the prosecutor. He sank back helpless in his chair. All were silent.

59.71.oldText: “Yes, the door!... It’s a nightmare! God is against me!” he exclaimed, staring before him in complete stupefaction.

59.72.oldText: “There, you see,” the prosecutor went on with dignity, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On the one hand, we have the evidence of the open door from which you ran out — a fact that overwhelms both you and us. On the other hand, your incomprehensible, persistent, and, so to speak, obdurate silence about the source from which you obtained the money that was so suddenly seen in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own admission, you pledged your pistols for ten roubles! In the face of all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don’t accuse us of being ‘frigid, cynical, scoffing people,’ incapable of believing in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to put yourself in our position ...”

59.73.oldText: Mitya was indescribably agitated. He turned pale.

59.74.oldText: “Very well!” he exclaimed suddenly. “I will tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money!... I’ll reveal my shame, so that I won’t have to blame myself or you afterwards.”

59.75.oldText: “And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a voice of almost pathetic delight, “that every sincere and complete confession on your part at this moment may, later on, have an immense influence in your favor, and may, indeed, moreover —”

59.76.oldText: But the prosecutor gave him a slight shove under the table, and he checked himself in time. Mitya, in fact, had not heard him.

60.0.oldText: “Gentlemen,” he began, still in the same agitation, “I want to make a full confession: that money was my own.” The lawyers’ faces lengthened. That was not at all what they had expected.

60.1.oldText: “How do you mean?” faltered Nikolay Parfenovitch. “When at five o’clock that same day, from your own confession —”

60.2.oldText: “Damn five o’clock on the same day and my own confession! That’s nothing to do with it now! That money was my own, my own — that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, and it was fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me all the time, all the time ...”

60.4.oldText: “I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was here, round my neck, sewn up in a rag, and I’d had it round my neck a long time — it’s a month since I put it round my neck ... to my shame and disgrace!”

60.5.oldText: “And from whom did you ... obtain it?”

60.6.oldText: “You mean, ‘steal it’? Say it plainly now. Yes, I consider that I practically stole it, but if you prefer, I ‘obtained it.’ I consider I stole it. And last night I stole it finally.”

60.7.oldText: “Last night? But you said that it’s been a month since you ... obtained it?...”

60.8.oldText: “Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father — don’t be alarmed. I didn’t steal it from my father, but from her. Let me tell you without interrupting. It’s hard to do, you know. You see, a month ago, I was sent for by Katerina Ivanovna, formerly my betrothed. Do you know her?”

60.10.oldText: “I know you know her. She’s a noble creature, noblest of the noble. But she has hated me for ages, oh, for ages ... and hated me with good reason, good reason!”

60.11.oldText: “Katerina Ivanovna!” Nikolay Parfenovitch exclaimed in wonder. The prosecutor, too, stared.

60.12.oldText: “Oh, don’t take her name in vain! I’m a scoundrel to bring her into this. Yes, I saw that she hated me ... a long while.... From the very first, even that evening at my lodging ... but enough, enough. You’re unworthy even to know of that. No need for any of that.... I need only tell you that she sent for me a month ago, gave me three thousand roubles to send off to her sister and another relation in Moscow (as though she couldn’t have sent it off herself!) and I ... it was just at that fatal moment in my life when I ... well, in fact, when I had just come to love another — her, she’s sitting downstairs now, Grushenka. I carried her off here to Mokroe then, and wasted here in two days half of that damned three thousand, but the other half I kept on me. Well, I kept that other half, that fifteen hundred, like a locket round my neck, but yesterday I undid it, and spent it. What’s left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That’s the change out of the fifteen hundred I had yesterday.”

60.13.oldText: “Excuse me. How’s that? Why, when you were here a month ago, you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred — everybody knows that.”

60.14.oldText: “Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anyone count it?”

60.15.oldText: “Why, you told everyone yourself that you’d spent exactly three thousand.”

60.16.oldText: “It’s true, I did. I told the whole town so, and the whole town said so. And here, at Mokroe, too, everyone reckoned it was three thousand. Yet I didn’t spend three thousand, but fifteen hundred. And the other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little bag. That’s how it was, gentlemen. That’s where I got that money yesterday....”

60.17.oldText: “This is almost miraculous,” murmured Nikolay Parfenovitch.

60.18.oldText: “Allow me to inquire,” the prosecutor observed at last, “have you informed anyone whatsoever of this fact before — I mean, that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?”

60.20.oldText: “That’s strange. Do you mean absolutely no one?”

60.21.oldText: “Absolutely no one. No one and nobody.”

60.22.oldText: “What was your reason for this reticence? What was your motive for making such a secret of it? To be more precise: you have at last told us your secret, in your words, so ‘disgraceful,’ though in reality — that is, of course, comparatively speaking — this action, that is, the appropriation of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and, of course, only temporarily, is, in my view at least, only an act of the greatest recklessness and not so disgraceful, when one takes your character into consideration.... Even granting that it was an action in the highest degree discreditable, still, discreditable is not ‘disgraceful.’... Many people have already guessed, over this past month, about Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand that you spent, and I heard the story myself, apart from your confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for instance, had heard it, too, so that indeed, it was hardly a rumor any more, but the gossip of the whole town. There are indications, too, if I’m not mistaken, that you confessed this yourself to somebody — I mean, that the money was Katerina Ivanovna’s — and so, it’s extremely surprising to me that hitherto, that is, up to this moment, you have made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you say you set aside, connecting a feeling of positive horror, apparently, with that secret.... It’s hard to believe it could cost you such distress to confess such a secret.... You cried out, just now, that Siberia would be better than confessing it ...”

60.23.oldText: The prosecutor stopped speaking. He was provoked. He did not hide his annoyance, which was almost anger, and gave vent to all his pent-up spleen, disjointedly and incoherently, without choosing his words.

60.24.oldText: “It isn’t the fifteen hundred that’s the disgrace, but that I set it aside from the rest of the three thousand,” Mitya said firmly.

60.25.oldText: “Why?” smiled the prosecutor irritably. “What is there disgraceful, in your view, in your having set aside half of the three thousand you had discreditably — or if you prefer, ‘disgracefully’ — appropriated? Your taking the three thousand is more important than what you did with it. And by the way, why did you do that — why did you set apart that half, for what purpose, for what object did you do it? Can you explain that to us?”

60.26.oldText: “Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!” cried Mitya. “I set it aside because I was vile — that is, because I was calculating, and to be calculating in such a case is vile ... and that vileness went on a whole month.”

60.28.oldText: “I wonder at you. But I’ll make it clearer. Perhaps it really is hard to grasp. You see, pay attention to what I say. I appropriate three thousand entrusted to my honor, I spend it on a binge, let’s say I spend it all, and the next morning I go to her and say, ‘Katya, I’ve done wrong, I’ve squandered your three thousand,’ well, is that right? No, it’s not right — it’s dishonest and cowardly; I’m a beast, with no more self-control than a beast, that’s so, isn’t it? But still I’m not a thief? Not an outright thief, you’ll admit! I squandered it, but I didn’t steal it. Now a second, rather more favorable alternative: follow me closely, or I may get confused again — my head’s spinning — and so, for the second alternative: I spend here only fifteen hundred out of the three thousand, that is, only half. Next day I go and take that half to her: ‘Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me, I’m a low beast, and an untrustworthy scoundrel, because I’ve wasted half the money, and I shall waste this, too, so keep me from temptation!’ Well, what about that alternative? I’d be a beast and a scoundrel, and whatever you like; but not a thief, not outright a thief, or I wouldn’t have brought back what was left, but would have kept that, too. She would see at once that since I brought back half, I’d pay back what I’d spent, that I’d never give up trying, that I’d work to get it and pay it back. So in that case I’d be a scoundrel, but not a thief — you may say what you like, not a thief!”

60.29.oldText: “I admit there is a certain distinction,” said the prosecutor with a cold smile. “But it’s strange that you see such a vital difference.”

60.30.oldText: “Yes, I see a vital difference! Every man may be a scoundrel, and perhaps every man is a scoundrel, but not everyone can be a thief — it takes an arch-scoundrel to be that. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to make these fine distinctions ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s my conviction. Listen: I carry the money on me for a whole month, I may decide tomorrow to give it back, and I’m a scoundrel no longer, but I can’t bring myself to it, you see, though I make up my mind every day, and every day spur myself on to do it, and yet for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it, you see. Is that right, in your view, is that right?”

60.31.oldText: “Certainly, that’s not right — I can quite understand that, and I don’t dispute it,” the prosecutor answered with reserve. “And let us give up all discussion of these subtleties and distinctions, and, if you will be so kind, get back to the point. And the point is this: you still haven’t told us — we’ve asked you altogether — why, in the first place, you halved the money, squandering one half and hiding the other? For what purpose exactly did you hide it? What did you mean to do with that fifteen hundred? I insist on that question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

60.32.oldText: “Yes, of course!” cried Mitya, striking himself on the forehead. “Forgive me, I’m troubling you, and am not explaining the chief point, or you’d understand in a minute, because it’s the motive of it that’s the disgrace! You see, it was all to do with the old man, my late father. He was always pestering Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous; I thought then that she was hesitating between me and him. So I kept thinking every day, suppose she suddenly made up her mind, suppose she stopped tormenting me and suddenly said to me, ‘I love you, not him; take me to the ends of the earth.’ And I’d only forty kopecks; how could I take her away, what could I do? Why, I’d be lost. You see, I didn’t know her then, I didn’t understand her, I thought she wanted money, and that she wouldn’t forgive my poverty. And so I diabolically counted out half of that three thousand, sewed it up, calculatingly, sewed it up before I got drunk, and after I had sewn it up, I went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was base. Do you understand now?”

60.34.oldText: “I would have called it sensible and moral on your part not to have squandered it all,” chuckled Nikolay Parfenovitch. “For after all, what does it amount to?”

60.35.oldText: “Why, that I stole it, that’s what it amounts to! Oh, God, you horrify me by not understanding! Every day that I had that fifteen hundred sewn up round my neck, every day and every hour I said to myself, ‘You’re a thief! you’re a thief!’ Yes, that’s why I’ve been so savage all this month, that’s why I fought in the tavern, that’s why I attacked my father — because I felt I was a thief. I couldn’t bring myself to it; I didn’t even dare to tell Alyosha, my brother, about that fifteen hundred: I felt I was such a scoundrel and such a pickpocket. But, do you know, while I carried it I said to myself at the same time every hour: ‘No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you may yet not be a thief.’ Why? Because I could go the next day and pay back that fifteen hundred to Katya. And it was only yesterday that I made up my mind to tear my amulet off my neck, on my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin. I hadn’t been able, until that moment, to bring myself to it. And it was only when I tore it off that I became an outright thief, a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that I also destroyed my dream of going to Katya and saying, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief!’ Do you understand now? Do you understand?”

60.36.oldText: “What made you decide to do it yesterday?” Nikolay Parfenovitch interrupted.

60.37.oldText: “Why? It’s absurd to ask. Because I had condemned myself to die at five o’clock this morning, here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or a man of honor. But I see now that’s not so — it turns out that it does make a difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what has tortured me most during this night has not been the thought that I’d killed the old servant, and that I was in danger of Siberia just when my love was being rewarded, and Heaven was open to me again. Oh, that did torture me, but not in the same way: not as much as the damned awareness that I had finally torn that damned money off my breast and spent it, and had become an outright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I’ve learnt a great deal this night. I’ve learnt that it is not only impossible to live a scoundrel, but impossible to die a scoundrel.... No, gentlemen, one must die honest....”

60.38.oldText: Mitya was pale. His face had a haggard and exhausted look, in spite of his being intensely worked up.

60.39.oldText: “I am beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft and almost compassionate tone. “But all this, if you’ll forgive my saying so, is in my opinion a matter of nerves ... your overwrought nerves, that’s what it is. And why, for instance, should you not have spared yourself such misery for almost a month, by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who had entrusted it to you? And why could you not have explained things to her, and in view of your position, which you describe as so awful, why could you not have had recourse to the plan that would so naturally have occurred to one’s mind — that is, after honorably confessing your errors to her, why could you not have asked her to lend you the sum needed for your expenses, which, with her generous heart, she would certainly not have refused you in your distress, especially if it had been with some guarantee, or even on the security you offered to the merchant Samsonov, and to Madame Hohlakov? I suppose you still regard that security as of value?”

60.41.oldText: “Surely you don’t think me such a complete scoundrel as that? You can’t be serious?” he said with indignation, looking the prosecutor straight in the face, and seeming unable to believe his ears.

60.42.oldText: “I assure you I am serious.... Why do you imagine I’m not serious?” It was the prosecutor’s turn to be surprised.

60.43.oldText: “Oh, how base that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you are torturing me! Let me tell you everything, so be it. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but just to put you to shame, and you will be astonished yourselves at the depth of ignominy to which a tangle of human passions can sink. You should know that I had that very plan myself, that plan you spoke of just now, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, I, too, have had that thought in my mind all this past month, so that I was on the verge of deciding to go to Katya — I was low enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her of my treachery, and for that very treachery, to carry it out, for the expenses of that treachery, to beg for money from her, Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and go straight from her to run away with the other, the rival, who hated and insulted her — to think of it! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

60.44.oldText: “Mad I am not, but I did speak in haste, without thinking ... of that feminine jealousy ... if there could be jealousy in this case, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there is something of the kind,” said the prosecutor, smiling.

60.45.oldText: “But that would have been so infamous!” Mitya brought his fist down on the table fiercely. “That would have been filthy beyond anything! Yes, do you know that she might have given me that money — yes, and she would have given it, too; she’d certainly have given it, to be revenged on me, she’d have given it to satisfy her vengeance, to show her contempt for me, because hers is an infernal nature, too, and she’s a woman of great wrath. I’d have taken the money, too, oh, I would have taken it; I would have taken it, and then, for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m making such an outcry because I have had that thought in my mind so recently — only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that bother with Lyagavy, and afterwards yesterday, all day yesterday, I remember, until what happened ...”

60.46.oldText: “Until what happened?” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in inquisitively, but Mitya did not hear it.

60.47.oldText: “I have made you an awful confession,” Mitya said gloomily in conclusion. “You must appreciate it, and what’s more, you must respect it, because if not — if that leaves your souls untouched — then you simply have no respect for me, gentlemen, I tell you that, and I shall die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I shall shoot myself! Yes, I see, I see already that you don’t believe me. What, you want to write that down, too?” he cried in dismay.

60.48.oldText: “Yes, what you said just now,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking at him in surprise, “that is, that up to the last hour you were still contemplating going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, that’s a very important piece of evidence for us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — I mean for the whole case ... and particularly important for you.”

60.49.oldText: “Have mercy, gentlemen!” Mitya flung up his hands. “Don’t write that, at least; have some shame. Here I’ve torn my heart asunder before you, and you seize the opportunity and are fingering the wounds in both halves.... Oh, my God!”

60.50.oldText: In despair he hid his face in his hands.

60.51.oldText: “Don’t worry yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” observed the prosecutor. “Everything that is written down will be read over to you afterwards, and what you don’t agree to we’ll alter as you like. But now I’ll ask you one small question for the second time. Has no one, absolutely no one, heard from you about that money you sewed up? That, I must tell you, is almost impossible to believe.”

60.52.oldText: “No one, no one, I told you so before — or you’ve understood nothing! Let me alone!”

60.53.oldText: “Very well, this matter is bound to be cleared up, and there’s plenty of time for it, but in the meantime, consider: we have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you yourself spread it around, and even shouted almost everywhere, about the three thousand you’d spent here; three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And now, too, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you gave many people to understand that you had brought three thousand with you.”

60.54.oldText: “You’ve got not dozens but hundreds of witnesses, two hundred witnesses, two hundred have heard it, thousands have heard it!” cried Mitya.

60.55.oldText: “Well, you see, all bear witness to it. And the word all means something.”

60.56.oldText: “It means nothing. I talked rot, and everyone began repeating it.”

60.57.oldText: “But what need had you to ‘talk rot,’ as you call it?”

60.58.oldText: “The devil knows. From bravado, perhaps ... at having wasted so much money.... To try to forget that money I had sewn up, perhaps ... yes, that was why ... damn it ... how many more times will you ask me that question? Well, I told a fib, and that was the end of it; once I’d said it, I didn’t care to correct it. What does a man tell lies for sometimes?”

60.59.oldText: “That’s very difficult to decide, Dmitri Fyodorovitch — what makes a man tell lies,” the prosecutor observed impressively. “Tell me, though, was that ‘amulet,’ as you call it, on your neck, a big thing?”

60.62.oldText: “If you folded a hundred-rouble note in half, that would be the size.”

60.63.oldText: “You’d better show us the remains of it. You must have them somewhere.”

60.64.oldText: “Damnation, what nonsense! I don’t know where they are.”

60.65.oldText: “But excuse me: where and when did you take it off your neck? According to your own evidence you didn’t go home.”

60.66.oldText: “When I was going from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s, on the way I tore it off my neck and took out the money.”

60.68.oldText: “What would I want a light for? I did it with my fingers in one minute.”

60.70.oldText: “In the market-square, I think it was. Why scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute.”

60.74.oldText: “In the market-square, in the market-square! The devil knows whereabouts. What do you want to know for?”

60.75.oldText: “That’s extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you don’t understand that? Who helped you sew it up a month ago?”

60.78.oldText: “A soldier has to know how to sew. No special knowledge was needed for that.”

60.79.oldText: “Where did you get the material — that is, the rag in which you sewed the money?”

60.81.oldText: “Not at all. And we are in no mood for laughing, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

60.82.oldText: “I don’t know where I got the rag from — from somewhere, I suppose.”

60.83.oldText: “I should have thought you couldn’t have forgotten that.”

60.84.oldText: “Upon my word, I don’t remember. I might have torn a bit off my linen.”

60.85.oldText: “That’s very interesting. We might find, in your lodgings tomorrow, the shirt or whatever it is from which you tore the rag. What sort of rag was it — cloth or linen?”

60.86.oldText: “Goodness only knows what it was. Wait a bit.... I don’t think I tore it off anything. It was a bit of calico.... I believe I sewed it up in a cap of my landlady’s.”

60.90.oldText: “You see, I remember once taking a cap for a rag, perhaps to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, because it was a worthless rag. I tore it up, and I took the notes and sewed them up in it. I think it was in that very rag I sewed them. An old piece of calico, washed a thousand times.”

60.92.oldText: “I don’t know whether for certain. I think it was in the cap. But, hang it, what does it matter?”

60.93.oldText: “In that case your landlady will remember that the thing was lost?”

60.94.oldText: “No, she won’t, she didn’t miss it. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a kopeck.”

60.96.oldText: “I’ll stop now. I won’t say any more. Enough of it!” said Mitya, losing his temper at last.

60.97.oldText: “It’s strange that you should have so completely forgotten where you threw the pieces in the market-square.”

60.98.oldText: “Give orders for the market-square to be swept tomorrow, and maybe you’ll find it,” said Mitya, sneering. “Enough, gentlemen, enough!” he decided, in an exhausted voice. “I see you don’t believe me! Not for a moment! It’s my fault, not yours. I shouldn’t have been so ready. Why, why did I degrade myself by confessing my secret to you? It’s a joke to you. I see that from your eyes. You led me to it, prosecutor! Sing a hymn of triumph if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!”

60.99.oldText: He bent his head, and hid his face in his hands. The lawyers were silent. A minute later he raised his head and looked at them almost blankly. His face now expressed complete, hopeless despair, and he sat mute and passive, as though hardly conscious of what was happening. Meanwhile they had to finish what they were about. They had immediately to begin examining the witnesses. By now it was eight o’clock in the morning. The lights had been extinguished long ago. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who had been continually in and out of the room all the while the interrogation had been going on, had now both gone out again. The lawyers, too, looked very tired. It was a wretched morning, the whole sky was overcast, and the rain streamed down in bucketfuls. Mitya gazed blankly out the window.

60.100.oldText: “May I look out the window?” he asked Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly.

60.101.oldText: “Oh, as much as you like,” the other replied.

60.102.oldText: Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed against its little greenish panes. He could see the muddy road just below the house, and further off, in the rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts, looking even blacker and poorer in the rain. Mitya thought of “Phoebus the golden-haired,” and how he had meant to shoot himself at his first ray. “Perhaps it would be even better on a morning like this,” he thought with a smile, and suddenly, flinging his hand downwards, he turned to his “torturers.”

60.103.oldText: “Gentlemen,” he cried, “I see that I am lost! But what about her? Tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she need not be ruined with me? She’s innocent, you know, she was out of her mind when she cried last night, ‘It’s all my fault!’ She’s done nothing, nothing! I’ve been grieving over her all night as I sat with you.... Can’t you, won’t you tell me what you are going to do with her now?”

60.104.oldText: “You can set your mind quite at rest on that score, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor answered at once, with evident alacrity. “We have, so far, no grounds for interfering with the lady in whom you are so interested. I trust that it may be the same in the later stages of the case.... On the contrary, we’ll do everything in our power in that matter. Set your mind completely at rest.”

60.105.oldText: “Gentlemen, I thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward people in spite of everything. You’ve taken a weight off my heart.... Well, what are we to do now? I’m ready.”

60.106.oldText: “Well, we ought to get on. We must move to examining the witnesses without delay. That must be done in your presence, and therefore —”

60.107.oldText: “Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” interposed Nikolay Parfenovitch. “I think we’ve earned it!”

60.108.oldText: They decided that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to get some), they would have a glass and then “go on and on,” putting off their proper breakfast until a more favorable opportunity. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. Mitya at first refused the glass that Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but afterwards he asked for it himself and drank it greedily. He looked astonishingly exhausted. It might have been supposed, given his Herculean strength, that one night of carousing, even accompanied by the most violent emotions, could have had little effect on him. But he felt that he could hardly hold his head up, and from time to time all the objects around him seemed to heave and dance before his eyes. “A little more, and I shall begin raving,” he said to himself.

61.0.oldText: The examination of the witnesses began. But I won't continue the story in the same level of detail as before. So I'll skip over how Nikolay Parfenovitch impressed on every witness called that he had to give his evidence according to truth and conscience, and that he would later have to repeat his testimony under oath; how every witness was required to sign the protocol of his evidence, and so on. I'll only note that the central point pressed in the examination was the question of the three thousand roubles—that is, was the sum Mitya spent here at Mokroe on the first occasion, a month earlier, three thousand or fifteen hundred? And again, had he spent three thousand or fifteen hundred the night before? Sadly, all the evidence given by every witness turned out to be against Mitya. Not one piece supported him, and some witnesses introduced new, almost crushing facts that contradicted Mitya's own account.

61.1.oldText: The first witness examined was Trifon Borissovitch. He wasn't the least bit flustered as he stood before the lawyers. On the contrary, he had an air of stern and severe indignation toward the accused, which gave him an appearance of truthfulness and personal dignity. He spoke little, and with restraint, waited to be questioned, and answered precisely and deliberately. Firmly and without hesitation, he testified that the sum spent a month before couldn't have been less than three thousand, that every peasant around here would confirm they had heard Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself mention the sum of three thousand. “The amount he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! He must have wasted a thousand on them by himself.”

61.2.oldText: “I don't believe I gave them five hundred,” was Mitya's gloomy comment on this. “It's a shame I didn't count the money at the time, but I was drunk…”

61.3.oldText: Mitya was sitting sideways with his back to the curtains. He listened grimly, with a melancholy and exhausted air, as though he were saying:

61.4.oldText: “Oh, say whatever you like. It makes no difference now.”

61.5.oldText: “More than a thousand went to them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Trifon Borissovitch shot back firmly. “You flung it around at random and they snatched it up. They were a thieving, roguish lot, horse-stealers—they've been driven out of here, or maybe they'd testify themselves how much they got from you. I saw the sum in your hands myself—count it I didn't, you wouldn't let me, that's true enough—but by the look of it I'd say it was far more than fifteen hundred… fifteen hundred, indeed! We've seen money too. We can judge amounts…”

61.6.oldText: As for the sum spent yesterday, he insisted that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him, the moment he arrived, that he had brought three thousand with him.

61.7.oldText: “Come on now, is that really so, Trifon Borissovitch?” Mitya replied. “Surely I didn't declare so plainly that I'd brought three thousand?”

61.8.oldText: “You did say so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey himself is still here. Send for him. And in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted straight out that you would leave your sixth thousand behind here—meaning along with what you'd spent before, that's how we're to understand it. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing right beside you at the time. Maybe he'd remember it…”

61.9.oldText: The evidence about the “sixth” thousand made an extraordinary impression on the two lawyers. They were delighted with this new mode of reckoning: three and three made six, three thousand then and three now made six—that was perfectly clear.

61.10.oldText: They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named—Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver confirmed Trifon Borissovitch's testimony without hesitation. They took particular care to note down Andrey's account of the conversation he'd had with Mitya on the road: “‘Where,' says he, ‘am I going, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell, and will I be forgiven in the next world or not?'”

61.11.oldText: The psychologically minded Ippolit Kirillovitch listened to this with a subtle smile, and ended by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch would end up be “included in the case.”

61.12.oldText: Kalganov, when called, came in reluctantly, frowning and ill-humored, and he spoke to the lawyers as though he'd never met them before in his life, though they were acquaintances he'd been meeting every day for a long time. He began by saying that “he knew nothing about it and didn't want to.” But it turned out he had heard of the “sixth” thousand, and he admitted he'd been standing close by at that moment. As far as he could tell, he “didn't know” how much money Mitya had in his hands. He confirmed that the Poles had cheated at cards. In response to repeated questions, he stated that after the Poles had been turned out, Mitya's standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had certainly improved, and that she had said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as though she were a lady of the highest society, and he never once let himself call her Grushenka. Despite the young man's obvious reluctance to give evidence, Ippolit Kirillovitch examined him at length, and only from him learned all the details of what had made up Mitya's “romance,” so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he left the room with undisguised indignation.

61.13.oldText: The Poles were examined too. Though they had gone to bed in their room, they hadn't slept all night, and when the police officers arrived they hurriedly dressed and got ready, knowing they would certainly be sent for. They gave their evidence with dignity, though not without some uneasiness. The little Pole turned out to be a retired twelfth-class official who had served in Siberia as a veterinary surgeon. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be an uncertified dentist. Although Nikolay Parfenovitch asked them the questions on their arrival, both of them directed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who was standing to one side, mistaking him in their ignorance for the most important person and the one in command, and addressed him with every word as “Pan Colonel.” Only after several reprimands from Mihail Makarovitch himself did they grasp that they had to address their answers only to Nikolay Parfenovitch. It turned out they could speak Russian quite correctly, except for their accent on certain words. Of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, Pan Mussyalovitch spoke proudly and warmly, so that Mitya was roused at once and declared he would not permit the “scoundrel” to speak that way in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch immediately called attention to the word “scoundrel” and requested that it be entered in the protocol. Mitya burned with rage.

61.14.oldText: “He's a scoundrel! A scoundrel! You can put that down. And put down, too, that in spite of the protocol I still declare that he's a scoundrel!” he shouted.

61.15.oldText: Though Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the protocol, he showed the most admirable tact and composure. After sternly reprimanding Mitya, he cut short any further inquiry into the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what was essential. One piece of testimony from the Poles aroused particular interest in the lawyers: how, in this very room, Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch, and had offered him three thousand roubles to surrender his claims—seven hundred roubles down, and the remaining two thousand three hundred “to be paid the next day in the town.” Mitya had sworn at the time that he didn't have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in town. Mitya heatedly observed that he had not said he would definitely pay him the remainder the next day in town. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed the statement, and after a moment's thought Mitya, frowning, admitted that it must have been as the Poles said—that he had been excited at the time and might well have said so.

61.16.oldText: The prosecutor pounced on this piece of evidence. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they did base this deduction on it) that half, or some part, of the three thousand that had come into Mitya's hands might actually have been left hidden somewhere in town, or even perhaps somewhere here in Mokroe. This would explain the circumstance, so puzzling to the prosecution, that only eight hundred roubles were found on Mitya. Small as it was, this had been the one piece of evidence that had so far told, to some extent, in Mitya's favor. Now this single piece of evidence in his favor had collapsed. When the prosecutor asked where he would have gotten the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, since he himself had denied having more than fifteen hundred, Mitya confidently replied that he had intended to offer the “little chap” not money, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya—those same rights he had already offered to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor actually smiled at the “naivety of this subterfuge.”

61.17.oldText: “And you imagine he would have accepted such a deed in place of two thousand three hundred roubles in cash?”

61.18.oldText: “He certainly would have accepted it,” Mitya declared warmly. “Why, look—he could have grabbed not two thousand but four or even six out of it. He would have set his lawyers on the job, Poles and Jews, and might have gotten not three thousand but the whole property out of the old man.”

61.19.oldText: Pan Mussyalovitch's evidence was, of course, entered in the protocol in the fullest detail. Then they let the Poles go. The incident of the cheating at cards was barely touched upon. Nikolay Parfenovitch was already too pleased with them, as it was, and didn't want to trouble them over trifles—besides, it was nothing but a foolish, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night… So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles' pockets.

61.20.oldText: Then old Maximov was called in. He came in timidly, approached with little steps, looking very disheveled and depressed. All this time he had taken refuge downstairs with Grushenka, sitting mutely beside her and “now and then breaking into tears over her and wiping his eyes with a blue checked handkerchief,” as Mihail Makarovitch described it afterwards. So she herself had to try to soothe and comfort him. The old man immediately confessed that he had done wrong, that he had borrowed “ten roubles in my poverty” from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that he was ready to pay it back. When Nikolay Parfenovitch asked him directly whether he had noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch was holding—since he must have seen the sum better than anyone when he took the note from him—Maximov, in the most positive manner, declared that there had been twenty thousand.

61.21.oldText: “Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired with a smile.
