61.22.oldText: “To be sure I have—not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She'd only let me look at it from a distance, boasting about it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch's were all rainbow-colored too…”

61.23.oldText: He wasn't kept long. At last it was Grushenka's turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch was clearly apprehensive about the effect her appearance might have on Mitya, and he murmured a few words of warning to him, but Mitya bowed his head in silence, giving him to understand “that he wouldn't make a scene.” Mihail Makarovitch himself led Grushenka in. She came in with a stern and gloomy face, looking almost composed, and sat down quietly on the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale, she seemed to be cold, and she wrapped herself tightly in her magnificent black shawl. She was suffering from a slight feverish chill—the first sign of the long illness that followed that night. Her grave bearing, her direct earnest look, and her quiet manner made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little “fascinated.” He admitted himself afterwards, when talking about it, that only then had he seen “how beautiful the woman was,” for though he had seen her several times before, he had always regarded her as something of a “provincial hetaira.” “She has the manners of the best society,” he said enthusiastically, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But this was received with downright indignation by the ladies, who immediately called him a “naughty man”—to his great satisfaction.

61.24.oldText: As she entered the room, Grushenka only glanced for an instant at Mitya, who looked at her uneasily. But her face reassured him at once. After the first unavoidable questions and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, hesitating slightly but maintaining the most courteous manner, what her relationship was with the retired lieutenant, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. To this Grushenka answered firmly and quietly:

61.25.oldText: “He was an acquaintance. He came to see me as an acquaintance over the last month.” To further inquisitive questions she answered plainly and with complete frankness: that though “at times” she had thought him attractive, she had not loved him, but had won his heart as well as his old father's “in my nasty spite”; that she had seen Mitya was intensely jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and everyone else, but that had only amused her. She had never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch, she had simply been laughing at him. “I had no thoughts for either of them this last month. I was expecting another man, one who had wronged me. But I think,” she said in conclusion, “there's no need for you to question me about that, nor for me to answer you, for that's my own affair.”

61.26.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch immediately took the hint. He once again set aside the “romantic” aspect of the case and moved on to the serious one—that is, to the most important question, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed the statement that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent on the first carousal at Mokroe, and although she had not counted the money herself, she had heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own lips.

61.27.oldText: “Did he tell you that when you were alone, or in front of someone else, or did you only hear him speak of it to others in your presence?” the prosecutor asked at once.

61.28.oldText: To which Grushenka replied that she had heard him say so in front of other people, and had heard him say so when they were alone.

61.29.oldText: “Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?” the prosecutor inquired, and learned that he had told Grushenka so several times.

61.30.oldText: Ippolit Kirillovitch was very well pleased with this piece of evidence. Further questioning brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from—that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had gotten it from Katerina Ivanovna.

61.31.oldText: “And did you never, even once, hear that the money spent a month ago was not three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had kept half of that sum for himself?”

61.32.oldText: “No, I never heard that,” answered Grushenka.

61.33.oldText: It came out further that on the contrary Mitya had often told her he didn't have a penny.

61.34.oldText: “He was always expecting to get some from his father,” Grushenka said in conclusion.

61.35.oldText: “Did he never say in your presence… casually, or in a moment of irritation,” Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly put in, “that he intended to make an attempt on his father's life?”

61.36.oldText: “Ach, he did say so,” Grushenka sighed.

61.38.oldText: “He mentioned it several times, always in anger.”

61.40.oldText: “No, I never believed it,” she answered firmly. “I had faith in his noble heart.”

61.41.oldText: “Gentlemen, allow me,” Mitya cried suddenly, “allow me to say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna in your presence.”

61.43.oldText: “Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya rose from his chair. “Have faith in God and in me. I am not guilty of my father's murder!”

61.44.oldText: Having said these words, Mitya sat down again on his chair. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. “Thanks be to Thee, O Lord,” she said, in a voice thrilled with emotion, and still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

61.45.oldText: “As he has spoken now, believe it! I know him. He'll say anything as a joke or out of stubbornness, but he'll never deceive you against his conscience. He's telling the whole truth, you can believe it.”

61.46.oldText: “Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you've given me fresh courage,” Mitya responded in a quivering voice.

61.47.oldText: As for the money spent the previous day, she declared that she didn't know what sum it was, but had heard him tell several people that he had three thousand with him. And when asked where he'd gotten the money, she said he had told her that he had “stolen” it from Katerina Ivanovna, and that she had replied that he hadn't stolen it and that he must pay the money back the next day. When the prosecutor pressed her emphatically to clarify whether the money he said he had stolen from Katerina Ivanovna was what he had spent yesterday or what he had squandered here a month ago, she declared that he meant the money spent a month ago, and that was how she understood him.

61.48.oldText: Grushenka was at last released, and Nikolay Parfenovitch impulsively informed her that she could return to the town at once, and that if he could be of any assistance to her—with horses, for example, or if she'd like an escort, he… would be—

61.49.oldText: “I thank you sincerely,” said Grushenka, bowing to him. “I'm going with this old gentleman, I am driving him back to town with me, and in the meantime, if you'll allow me, I'll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

61.50.oldText: She went out. Mitya was calm, and even looked more cheerful, but only for a moment. He felt increasingly oppressed by a strange physical weakness. His eyes were closing with exhaustion. The examination of the witnesses was finally over. They moved on to a final revision of the protocol. Mitya got up, moved from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a large chest covered with a rug, and instantly fell asleep.

61.51.oldText: He had a strange dream, utterly out of keeping with the place and the moment.

61.52.oldText: He was driving somewhere in the steppes, where he had been stationed long ago, and a peasant was driving him in a cart with a pair of horses through snow and sleet. He was cold, it was early November, and the snow was falling in big wet flakes, melting the moment it touched the earth. And the peasant drove him briskly; he had a fair, long beard. He wasn't an old man, somewhere around fifty, and he was wearing a gray peasant's smock. Not far off was a village; he could see the black huts, and half the huts were burned down—only the charred beams were sticking up. And as they drove in, there were peasant women lined up along the road—a lot of women, a whole row, all thin and wan, their faces a kind of brownish color, especially one at the edge, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but might have been only twenty, with a long thin face. And in her arms was a little baby crying. And her breasts seemed so dried up that there wasn't a drop of milk in them. And the child cried and cried, and held out its little bare arms, its little fists blue from the cold.

61.53.oldText: “Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked as they dashed cheerfully by.

61.54.oldText: “It's the babe,” answered the driver, “the babe weeping.”

61.55.oldText: And Mitya was struck by his saying, in his peasant way, “the babe,” and he liked the peasant's calling it a “babe.” There seemed more pity in it.

61.56.oldText: “But why is it weeping?” Mitya persisted stupidly. “Why are its little arms bare? Why don't they wrap it up?”

61.57.oldText: “The babe's cold, its little clothes are frozen and don't warm it.”

61.58.oldText: “But why is it? Why?” foolish Mitya kept insisting.

61.59.oldText: “Why, they're poor people, burned out. They've no bread. They're begging because they've been burned out.”

61.60.oldText: “No, no,” Mitya, still somehow not understanding. “Tell me why it is those poor mothers stand there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe barren? Why don't they hug each other and kiss? Why don't they sing songs of joy? Why are they so dark from black misery? Why don't they feed the babe?”

61.61.oldText: And he felt that, though his questions were unreasonable and made no sense, still he wanted to ask just that, and he had to ask it in just that way. And he felt that a surge of pity, such as he had never known before, was rising in his heart—that he wanted to cry, that he wanted to do something for them all, so that the babe should weep no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother should not weep, that no one should shed tears again from that moment on. And he wanted to do it at once, at once, regardless of all obstacles, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.

61.62.oldText: “And I'm coming with you. I won't leave you now for the rest of my life, I'm coming with you,” he heard close beside him Grushenka's tender voice, trembling with emotion. And his heart glowed, and he struggled forward toward the light, and he longed to live, to live, to go on and on, toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

61.63.oldText: “What! Where?” he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, as though he had revived from a faint, smiling brightly. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, suggesting he hear the protocol read aloud and sign it. Mitya guessed he had been asleep an hour or more, but he didn't hear Nikolay Parfenovitch. He was suddenly struck by the fact that there was a pillow under his head, which hadn't been there when he had leaned back, exhausted, on the chest.

61.64.oldText: “Who put that pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried, with a kind of ecstatic gratitude and tears in his voice, as though some great kindness had been shown him.

61.65.oldText: He never found out who this kind man was—perhaps one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch's little secretary, had compassionately thought to put a pillow under his head—but his whole soul was quivering with tears. He went to the table and said he would sign whatever they wanted.

61.66.oldText: “I've had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in a strange voice, with a new light, like joy, in his face.

62.0.oldText: When the protocol had been signed, Nikolay Parfenovitch turned solemnly to the prisoner and read him the “Committal,” stating that on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a place, the investigating lawyer of such-and-such a district court, having examined so-and-so (namely, Mitya) accused of this and that (all the charges were carefully written out) and having considered that the accused, not pleading guilty to the charges brought against him, had presented nothing in his defense, while the witnesses, so-and-so and so-and-so, and the circumstances such-and-such testified against him, acting in accordance with such-and-such articles of the Statute Book, and so on, had ruled that, in order to prevent so-and-so (Mitya) from any means of evading pursuit and judgment, he be detained in such-and-such a prison, which he hereby notified to the accused and communicated a copy of this same “Committal” to the deputy prosecutor, and so on, and so on.

62.1.oldText: In short, Mitya was informed that from that moment he was a prisoner, and that he would be driven at once to the town and there locked up in a very unpleasant place. Mitya listened attentively and only shrugged his shoulders.

62.2.oldText: “Well, gentlemen, I don't blame you. I'm ready… I understand that there's nothing else for you to do.”

62.3.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch gently informed him that he would be escorted at once by the rural police officer, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, who happened to be on the spot…

62.4.oldText: “Stay,” Mitya suddenly interrupted, and driven by an uncontrollable feeling, he declared, addressing everyone in the room:

62.5.oldText: “Gentlemen, we're all cruel, we're all monsters, we all make men weep, and mothers, and babes at the breast—but of all, let it be settled here and now, of all I am the lowest reptile! I've sworn to reform, and every day I've done the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow, a blow of destiny to catch them as with a noose and bind them by a force from outside. Never, never would I have risen on my own! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torture of accusation and my public shame, I want to suffer and by suffering be purified. Perhaps I shall be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time, I am not guilty of my father's blood. I accept my punishment—not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and perhaps I really might have killed him. Still, I mean to fight it out with you. I warn you of that. I'll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Good-by, gentlemen, don't be angry with me for having shouted at you during the examination. Oh, I was still such a fool then… In another minute I shall be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. Saying good-by to you, I say it to all men.”

62.6.oldText: His voice quivered and he stretched out his hand, but Nikolay Parfenovitch, who happened to be standing nearest, with a sudden, almost nervous movement, hid his hands behind his back. Mitya noticed this at once and started. He let his outstretched hand fall immediately.

62.7.oldText: “The preliminary inquiry is not yet over,” Nikolay Parfenovitch faltered, somewhat embarrassed. “We will continue it in town, and I, for my part, of course, am ready to wish you every success… in your defense… As a matter of fact, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I've always been inclined to regard you as, so to speak, more unfortunate than guilty. All of us here, if I may be so bold as to speak for all, are ready to recognize that you are, at heart, a young man of honor, but, alas, one who has been carried away by certain passions to a somewhat excessive degree…”

62.8.oldText: Nikolay Parfenovitch's little figure looked positively majestic by the time he had finished speaking. It struck Mitya that in another minute this “boy” would take his arm, lead him off to another corner, and pick up their conversation about “girls.” But many quite irrelevant and inappropriate thoughts sometimes occur even to a prisoner being led out to execution.

62.9.oldText: “Gentlemen, you are good, you are humane—may I see her to say ‘good-by' for the last time?” Mitya asked.

62.10.oldText: “Certainly, but considering… in fact, now it's impossible except in the presence of—”

62.11.oldText: “Oh well, if it must be so, it must!”

62.12.oldText: Grushenka was brought in, but the farewell was brief, of few words, and did not satisfy Nikolay Parfenovitch at all. Grushenka made a deep bow to Mitya.

62.13.oldText: “I have told you I am yours, and I will be yours. I will follow you forever, wherever they may send you. Farewell; you are guiltless, though you've been your own undoing.”

62.14.oldText: Her lips quivered, tears flowed from her eyes.

62.15.oldText: “Forgive me, Grusha, for my love, for ruining you too with my love.”

62.16.oldText: Mitya would have said something more, but he broke off and went out. He was at once surrounded by men who kept constant watch over him. At the bottom of the steps, where he had driven up with such a dash the day before with Andrey's three horses, two carts stood ready. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a sturdy, thick-set man with a wrinkled face, was annoyed about something—some sudden irregularity. He was shouting angrily. He asked Mitya to get into the cart with somewhat excessive surliness.

62.17.oldText: “When I stood him drinks in the tavern, the man had quite a different face,” Mitya thought as he climbed in. At the gates was a crowd of people—peasants, women, and drivers. Trifon Borissovitch came down the steps as well. Everyone stared at Mitya.

62.19.oldText: “Forgive us too!” he heard two or three voices respond.

62.21.oldText: But Trifon Borissovitch didn't even turn around. Perhaps he was too busy. He, too, was shouting and fussing about something. It appeared that everything was not yet ready in the second cart, in which two constables were to accompany Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. The peasant who had been ordered to drive the second cart was pulling on his smock, stoutly maintaining that it wasn't his turn but Akim's. But Akim was nowhere to be seen. They ran to look for him. The peasant kept insisting and begged them to wait.

62.22.oldText: “You see what our peasants are, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. They've no shame!” exclaimed Trifon Borissovitch. “Akim gave you twenty-five kopecks the day before yesterday. You've drunk it all and now you're complaining. I'm simply amazed at your good nature with our low peasants, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, that's all I can say.”

62.23.oldText: “But what do we need a second cart for?” Mitya put in. “Let's start off with the one, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch. I won't be unruly, I won't run away from you, old fellow. What do we need an escort for?”

62.24.oldText: “I'll trouble you, sir, to learn how to speak to me if you've never been taught. I'm not ‘old fellow' to you, and you can save your advice for another time!” Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped savagely, as though glad for a chance to vent his anger.

62.25.oldText: Mitya was reduced to silence. He flushed all over. A moment later he suddenly felt very cold. The rain had stopped, but the dull sky was still overcast with clouds, and a sharp wind was blowing straight in his face.

62.26.oldText: “I've caught a chill,” Mitya thought, twitching his shoulders.

62.27.oldText: At last Mavriky Mavrikyevitch climbed into the cart too, sat down heavily, and, as though without noticing, squeezed Mitya into the corner. It's true that he was out of humor and strongly disliked the task laid upon him.

62.28.oldText: “Good-by, Trifon Borissovitch!” Mitya shouted again, and felt himself that this time he had called out not from good nature but involuntarily, out of resentment.

62.29.oldText: But Trifon Borissovitch stood proudly, both hands behind his back, staring straight at Mitya with a stern and angry face, and made no reply.

62.30.oldText: “Good-by, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, good-by!” he suddenly heard the voice of Kalganov, who had darted out of nowhere. Running up to the cart, he held out his hand to Mitya. He had no cap on.

62.31.oldText: Mitya managed to seize and press his hand.

62.32.oldText: “Good-by, dear fellow! I shan't forget your generosity,” he cried warmly.

62.33.oldText: But the cart moved and their hands parted. The bell began ringing and Mitya was driven away.

62.34.oldText: Kalganov ran back, sat down in a corner, bent his head, hid his face in his hands, and burst into tears. For a long while he sat like that, crying as though he were a little boy instead of a young man of twenty. Oh, he believed almost without a doubt in Mitya's guilt.

62.35.oldText: “What are these people? What can men be after this?” he exclaimed incoherently, in bitter despondency, almost despair. At that moment he had no desire to live.

62.36.oldText: “Is it worth it? Is it worth it?” the boy exclaimed in his grief.

63.0.oldText: It was the beginning of November. A hard frost had set in—eleven degrees Réaumur, without snow—but a little dry snow had fallen on the frozen ground during the night, and a sharp, dry wind was lifting and blowing it along the dreary streets of our town, especially around the market-place. It was a dull morning, but the snow had stopped.

63.1.oldText: Not far from the market-place, close to Plotnikov's shop, there stood a small house, very clean both outside and in. It belonged to Madame Krassotkin, the widow of a former provincial secretary who had been dead for fourteen years. His widow, still a pleasant-looking woman of thirty-two, was living in her neat little house on her private means. She lived in respectable seclusion; she was of a soft but fairly cheerful disposition. She had been about eighteen at the time of her husband's death; she had been married only a year and had just borne him a son. From the day of his death she had devoted herself heart and soul to bringing up her precious treasure, her boy Kolya. Though she had loved him passionately those fourteen years, he had caused her far more suffering than happiness. She had been trembling and fainting with terror almost every day, afraid he would fall ill, catch cold, get up to some mischief, climb on a chair and fall off it, and so on and so on. When Kolya started going to school, the mother devoted herself to studying all the subjects with him so she could help him and go through his lessons at his side. She hurried to make the acquaintance of his teachers and their wives; she even sucked up to Kolya's schoolmates and flattered them in hopes of sparing Kolya from being teased, laughed at, or beaten by them. She went so far that the boys actually began mocking him because of her, taunting him with being a “mother's darling.”

63.2.oldText: But the boy could stand up for himself. He was a resolute boy, “tremendously strong,” as the rumor went in his class, and that soon proved to be true; he was agile, strong-willed, and of an audacious and enterprising temperament. He was good at his lessons, and there was a rumor at the school that he could beat the teacher, Dardanelov, at arithmetic and universal history. Though he looked down on everyone, he was a good comrade and not supercilious. He accepted his schoolmates' respect as his due, but he was friendly with them. Above all, he knew where to draw the line. He could restrain himself when necessary, and in his dealings with the teachers he never crossed that final, mysterious limit beyond which a prank becomes an unpardonable breach of discipline. But he was as fond of mischief at every opportunity as the smallest boy in the school—not so much for the mischief itself, but for the sake of creating a sensation, inventing something striking and conspicuous. He was extremely vain. He knew how to make even his mother give way to him; he was almost despotic in his control over her. She gave way to him—oh, she had been giving way to him for years. The one thing she could not bear was the thought that her boy didn't really love her. She was always imagining that Kolya was “unfeeling” toward her, and at times, dissolving into hysterical tears, she would reproach him for his coldness. The boy disliked this, and the more demonstrations of feeling were demanded of him, the more he seemed deliberately to avoid them. Yet it wasn't deliberate on his part but instinctive—it was his character. His mother was mistaken; he was very fond of her. He only disliked “sheepish sentimentality,” as he put it in his schoolboy language.

63.3.oldText: There was a bookcase in the house containing a few books that had belonged to his father. Kolya liked to read and had worked his way through several of them on his own. His mother didn't mind and was only occasionally surprised to see the boy stand for hours by the bookcase, poring over a book instead of going out to play. And in this way Kolya read some things unsuitable for his age.

63.4.oldText: Though the boy, as a rule, knew where to draw the line in his mischief, he had lately begun to play pranks that seriously alarmed his mother. It's true there was nothing vicious in what he did, but there was a wild, mad recklessness.

63.5.oldText: It happened that July, during the summer holidays, that the mother and son went to another district, forty-five miles away, to spend a week with a distant relation whose husband was an official at the railway station (the very station, the one nearest our town, from which a month later Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov set off for Moscow). There Kolya began by carefully investigating every detail connected with the railways, knowing he could impress his schoolmates back home with his newly acquired knowledge. But there happened to be some other boys in the area with whom he soon made friends. Some of them were living at the station, others nearby; there were six or seven of them, all between twelve and fifteen, and two of them came from our town. The boys played together, and on the fourth or fifth day of Kolya's stay at the station, a mad bet was struck between these foolish boys. Kolya, who was almost the youngest of the group and consequently rather looked down on by the others, was moved by vanity or reckless bravado to bet them two roubles that he would lie down between the rails at night when the eleven o'clock train was due, and would lie there without moving while the train rolled over him at full speed. True, they conducted a preliminary investigation, which showed that it was possible to lie flat enough between the rails for the train to pass over without touching you—but to actually lie there was no joke! Kolya insisted stoutly that he would. At first they laughed at him, called him a little liar, a braggart—but that only egged him on. What galled him most was that these fifteen-year-old boys turned up their noses at him with too much superiority, and were at first inclined to treat him as “a small boy,” not fit to associate with them—and that was an unendurable insult.

63.6.oldText: So it was resolved that they would go out in the evening, half a mile from the station, so the train would have time to pick up full speed after leaving the station. The boys gathered. It was a pitch-dark night without a moon. At the appointed time, Kolya lay down between the rails. The five others who had taken the bet waited in the bushes below the embankment, their hearts pounding with suspense, which turned into alarm and remorse. At last they heard in the distance the rumble of the train leaving the station. Two red lights gleamed out of the darkness; the monster roared as it approached.

63.7.oldText: “Run, run away from the rails,” the boys cried to Kolya from the bushes, breathless with terror. But it was too late: the train darted up and flew past. The boys rushed to Kolya. He lay without moving. They began pulling at him, lifting him up. He suddenly got to his feet and walked away without a word. Then he explained that he had lain there as though unconscious in order to frighten them, but the truth was that he really had lost consciousness, as he confessed long afterwards to his mother. In this way his reputation as “a desperate character” was established forever. He returned to the house at the station as white as a sheet. The next day he had a slight attack of nervous fever, but he was in high spirits and very pleased with himself. The incident didn't become known at once, but once they got back to town it penetrated the school and even reached the ears of the masters. Then Kolya's mother hurried to plead with the masters on her boy's behalf, and in the end Dardanelov, a respected and influential teacher, intervened on his side, and the affair was dropped.

63.8.oldText: Dardanelov was a middle-aged bachelor who had been passionately in love with Madame Krassotkin for many years, and once already, about a year earlier, he had ventured—trembling with fear and the delicacy of his feelings—to offer her, most respectfully, his hand in marriage. But she had refused him flatly, feeling that to accept him would be an act of betrayal toward her son—though Dardanelov had, judging by certain mysterious symptoms, some reason to believe he was not an object of aversion to the charming but too chaste and tender-hearted widow. Kolya's mad prank seemed to have broken the ice, and Dardanelov was rewarded for his intercession with a suggestion of hope. The suggestion, it's true, was a faint one, but then Dardanelov was such a paragon of purity and delicacy that for the moment it was enough to make him perfectly happy. He was fond of the boy, though he would have thought it beneath him to try to win him over, and he was severe and strict with him in class. Kolya, too, kept him at a respectful distance. He learned his lessons perfectly; he was second in his class, was reserved with Dardanelov, and the whole class firmly believed that Kolya was so good at universal history that he could “beat” even Dardanelov. Kolya had indeed once asked him the question, “Who founded Troy?” to which Dardanelov had given a very vague reply, referring to the movements and migrations of races, the remoteness of the period, the mythical legends. But the question of who had founded Troy—that is, what individuals—he could not answer, and for some reason even regarded the question as idle and frivolous. But the boys remained convinced that Dardanelov did not know who founded Troy. Kolya had read of the founders of Troy in Smaragdov, whose history was among the books in his father's bookcase. In the end all the boys became interested in the question of who had founded Troy, but Krassotkin wouldn't give up his secret, and his reputation for knowledge remained intact.

63.9.oldText: After the incident on the railway a certain change came over Kolya's attitude toward his mother. When Anna Fyodorovna (Madame Krassotkin) heard of her son's exploit, she almost went out of her mind with horror. She had such terrible attacks of hysterics, lasting on and off for several days, that Kolya, seriously alarmed at last, promised on his honor that such pranks would never be repeated. He swore on his knees before the holy image, and swore by the memory of his father, at Madame Krassotkin's urging—and the “manly” Kolya burst into tears like a boy of six. And all that day mother and son kept rushing into each other's arms, sobbing. The next day Kolya woke up as “unfeeling” as before, but he had become more silent, more modest, sterner, more thoughtful.

63.10.oldText: Six weeks later, it's true, he got into another scrape, one that even brought his name to the ears of our Justice of the Peace—but it was a scrape of quite a different sort, amusing, silly, and as it turned out he had not played the leading part in it, but was only implicated in it. But more on that later. His mother still fretted and trembled, but the more uneasy she became, the greater grew Dardanelov's hopes. It should be noted that Kolya understood and guessed what was in Dardanelov's heart, and of course despised him profoundly for his “feelings.” In the past he had been so tactless as to show this contempt in front of his mother, hinting vaguely that he knew what Dardanelov was after. But after the railway incident his behavior on this score changed too; he never allowed himself the slightest allusion to the subject and began to speak more respectfully of Dardanelov in front of his mother—which the sensitive woman at once appreciated with boundless gratitude. But at the faintest mention of Dardanelov by a visitor in Kolya's presence, she would flush as pink as a rose. At such moments Kolya would either stare out of the window scowling, or study the state of his boots, or shout angrily for “Perezvon”—the big, shaggy, mangy dog he had picked up a month before, brought home, and for some reason kept secretly indoors, not showing him to any of his schoolmates. He bullied him frightfully, teaching him all sorts of tricks, so that the poor dog howled for him whenever he was off at school, and when he came in, would whine with delight, rush about like a crazy thing, beg, lie down on the ground pretending to be dead, and so on—in fact, go through all the tricks Kolya had taught him, not at the word of command but simply out of the zeal of his excited and grateful heart.

63.11.oldText: I have forgotten, by the way, to mention that Kolya Krassotkin was the boy stabbed with a penknife by the boy already known to the reader as the son of Captain Snegiryov. Ilusha had been defending his father when the schoolboys jeered at him, shouting the nickname “wisp of tow.”

64.0.oldText: And so on that frosty, snowy, and windy day in November, Kolya Krassotkin was sitting at home. It was Sunday and there was no school. It had just struck eleven, and he particularly wanted to go out “on very urgent business,” but he was left alone in charge of the house, since it so happened that all its elder inmates were absent due to a sudden and singular event. Madame Krassotkin had rented two little rooms, separated from the rest of the house by a passage, to a doctor's wife and her two small children. This lady was the same age as Anna Fyodorovna, and a great friend of hers. Her husband, the doctor, had taken his leave twelve months earlier, going first to Orenburg and then to Tashkend, and for the last six months she hadn't heard a word from him. Had it not been for her friendship with Madame Krassotkin, which was some consolation to the forsaken lady, she would certainly have dissolved away in tears entirely. And now, to add to her misfortunes, Katerina, her only servant, had been suddenly moved the previous evening to announce, to her mistress's amazement, that she proposed to bring a child into the world before morning. It seemed almost miraculous to everyone that no one had noticed the probability of it earlier. The astounded doctor's wife decided to move Katerina, while there was still time, to an establishment in town kept by a midwife for such emergencies. As she valued her servant highly, she promptly carried out this plan and stayed there to look after her. By morning, all of Madame Krassotkin's friendly sympathy and energy had been called on to render assistance and to appeal to someone for help in the case.

64.1.oldText: So both ladies were away from home, the Krassotkins' servant, Agafya, had gone out to the market, and Kolya was thus left for a while to protect and look after “the kids”—that is, the son and daughter of the doctor's wife, who were left on their own. Kolya wasn't afraid of taking care of the house; besides, he had Perezvon, who had been told to lie flat, without moving, under the bench in the hall. Every time Kolya, walking to and fro through the rooms, came into the hall, the dog shook his head and gave two loud, insinuating taps on the floor with his tail—but alas, the whistle did not sound to release him. Kolya would look sternly at the luckless dog, who relapsed once again into obedient rigidity. The one thing that troubled Kolya was “the kids.” He looked, of course, with the utmost scorn on Katerina's unexpected adventure, but he was very fond of the bereaved “kiddies” and had already taken them a picture-book. Nastya, the elder, a girl of eight, could read, and Kostya, the boy, aged seven, loved being read to by her. Krassotkin could, of course, have provided more diverting entertainment for them. He could have made them stand side by side and played soldiers with them, or sent them hiding all over the house. He had done so more than once before and wasn't above doing it, so much so that a report had once spread at school that Krassotkin played horses with the little lodgers at home, prancing with his head tilted to one side like a trace-horse. But Krassotkin haughtily parried this thrust, pointing out that to play horses with boys his own age, boys of thirteen, would certainly be disgraceful “at this date,” but that he did it for the sake of “the kids” because he liked them, and no one had any right to call him to account for his feelings. The two “kids” adored him.

64.2.oldText: But on this occasion he was in no mood for games. He had very important business of his own ahead of him, something almost mysterious. Meanwhile time was passing, and Agafya, with whom he could have left the children, still had not come back from the market. He had already crossed the passage several times, opened the door to the lodgers' room, and looked anxiously at “the kids,” who were sitting over the book as he had instructed them. Every time he opened the door they grinned at him, hoping he would come in and do something delightful and amusing. But Kolya was preoccupied and did not go in.

64.3.oldText: At last it struck eleven and he made up his mind once and for all that if that “damned” Agafya didn't come back within ten minutes, he would go out without waiting for her, making “the kids” promise, of course, to be brave while he was gone, not to be naughty, not to cry from fright. With this in mind he put on his padded winter overcoat with its catskin fur collar, slung his satchel over his shoulder, and, ignoring his mother's constantly repeated pleas that he always wear galoshes in such cold weather, he looked at them contemptuously as he crossed the hall and went out wearing only his boots. Perezvon, seeing him in his outdoor clothes, began tapping nervously but vigorously on the floor with his tail. Twitching all over, he even let out a plaintive whine. But Kolya, seeing the dog's passionate excitement, decided it was a breach of discipline, kept him another minute under the bench, and only when he had opened the door into the passage did he whistle for him. The dog leapt up like a mad creature and came rushing and bounding before him in rapture.

64.4.oldText: Kolya opened the door to peek at “the kids.” They were both sitting as before at the table, not reading but warmly arguing about something. The children often argued with each other about various exciting problems of life, and Nastya, being the elder, always got the best of it. If Kostya didn't agree with her, he almost always appealed to Kolya Krassotkin, and his verdict was regarded as infallible by both of them. This time the “kids'” discussion rather interested Krassotkin, and he stood still in the passage to listen. The children saw he was listening, and that made them argue with even greater energy.

64.5.oldText: “I shall never, never believe,” Nastya prattled, “that the old women find babies among the cabbages in the kitchen garden. It's winter now and there are no cabbages, and so the old woman couldn't have brought Katerina a daughter.”

64.7.oldText: “Or perhaps they do bring babies from somewhere, but only to those who are married.”

64.8.oldText: Kostya stared at Nastya and listened, pondering deeply.

64.9.oldText: “Nastya, how silly you are!” he said at last, firmly and calmly. “How can Katerina have a baby when she isn't married?”

64.11.oldText: “You know nothing about it,” she snapped irritably. “Perhaps she has a husband, only he's in prison, so now she's got a baby.”

64.12.oldText: “But is her husband in prison?” the matter-of-fact Kostya inquired gravely.

64.13.oldText: “Or, I tell you what,” Nastya interrupted impulsively, completely rejecting and forgetting her first hypothesis, “she hasn't a husband, you're right there, but she wants to be married, so she's been thinking of getting married, and thinking and thinking of it until now she's got it—that is, not a husband but a baby.”

64.14.oldText: “Well, perhaps so,” Kostya agreed, entirely defeated. “But you didn't say so before. So how could I tell?”

64.15.oldText: “Come, kiddies,” said Kolya, stepping into the room, “you're terrible people, I see.”

64.16.oldText: “And Perezvon with you!” Kostya grinned, and began snapping his fingers and calling Perezvon.

64.17.oldText: “I'm in a difficulty, kids,” Krassotkin began solemnly, “and you must help me. Agafya must have broken her leg, since she still hasn't turned up—that's certain. I have to go out. Will you let me go?”

64.18.oldText: The children looked anxiously at one another. Their smiling faces showed signs of uneasiness, but they didn't yet fully grasp what was being asked of them.

64.19.oldText: “You won't be naughty while I'm gone? You won't climb on the cupboard and break your legs? You won't be frightened alone and cry?”

64.20.oldText: A look of profound despondency came over the children's faces.

64.21.oldText: “And I could show you something as a reward—a little copper cannon that can be fired with real gunpowder.”

64.22.oldText: The children's faces instantly brightened. “Show us the cannon,” said Kostya, beaming all over.

64.23.oldText: Krassotkin put his hand in his satchel and, pulling out a little bronze cannon, stood it on the table.

64.24.oldText: “Ah, you are bound to ask that! Look, it's on wheels.” He rolled the toy along the table. “And it can be fired off, too. It can be loaded with shot and fired off.”

64.26.oldText: “It can kill anyone; you've only got to aim at somebody,” and Krassotkin explained where the powder had to go, where the shot should be rolled in, showing a tiny hole like a touch-hole, and told them that it kicked when it was fired.

64.27.oldText: The children listened with intense interest. What particularly struck their imagination was that the cannon kicked.

64.28.oldText: “And do you have any powder?” Nastya inquired.

64.30.oldText: “Show us the powder, too,” she drawled with a pleading smile.

64.31.oldText: Krassotkin dived back into his satchel and pulled out a small flask containing a little real gunpowder. He had some shot, too, in a twist of paper. He even uncorked the flask and shook a little powder into the palm of his hand.

64.32.oldText: “One has to be careful there's no fire about, or it would blow up and kill us all,” Krassotkin warned them sensationally.

64.33.oldText: The children gazed at the powder with an awe-stricken alarm that only intensified their enjoyment. But Kostya liked the shot better.

64.34.oldText: “And does the shot burn?” he inquired.

64.36.oldText: “Give me a little shot,” he asked in an imploring voice.

64.37.oldText: “I'll give you a little shot; here, take it, but don't show it to your mother till I come back, or she's sure to think it's gunpowder and will die of fright and give you a thrashing.”

64.38.oldText: “Mother never does whip us,” Nastya observed at once.

64.39.oldText: “I know, I only said it to finish the sentence. And don't you ever deceive your mother except just this once, until I come back. And so, kiddies, can I go out? You won't be frightened and cry when I'm gone?”

64.40.oldText: “We sha—all cry,” drawled Kostya, on the verge of tears already.

64.41.oldText: “We shall cry, we shall be sure to cry,” Nastya chimed in with timid haste.

64.42.oldText: “Oh, children, children, how fraught with peril are your years! There's no help for it, chickens, I shall have to stay with you I don't know how long. And time is passing, time is passing, oogh!”

64.43.oldText: “Tell Perezvon to pretend to be dead!” Kostya begged.

64.44.oldText: “There's no help for it, we must have recourse to Perezvon. Ici, Perezvon.” And Kolya began giving orders to the dog, who performed all his tricks.

64.45.oldText: He was a rough-haired dog of medium size, with a coat of a sort of lilac-gray color. He was blind in his right eye, and his left ear was torn. He whined and jumped, stood and walked on his hind legs, lay on his back with his paws in the air, rigid as though he were dead. While this last performance was going on, the door opened and Agafya, Madame Krassotkin's servant, a stout woman of forty, pockmarked with smallpox, appeared in the doorway. She had come back from the market and had a bag full of provisions in her hand. Holding up the bag in her left hand, she stood still to watch the dog. Though Kolya had been so anxious for her return, he did not cut the performance short, and after keeping Perezvon dead for the usual time, at last he whistled to him. The dog jumped up and began bounding about in joy at having done his duty.

64.46.oldText: “Only think, a dog!” Agafya observed sententiously.

64.50.oldText: “Yes, a brat. What is it to you if I'm late? If I'm late, you may be sure I had good reason,” muttered Agafya, busying herself about the stove, without a trace of anger or displeasure in her voice. She seemed quite pleased, in fact, to enjoy a skirmish with her merry young master.

64.51.oldText: “Listen, you frivolous young woman,” Krassotkin began, getting up from the sofa, “can you swear by all you hold sacred in the world, and something else besides, that you will watch vigilantly over the kids in my absence? I am going out.”

64.52.oldText: “And what am I going to swear for?” laughed Agafya. “I shall look after them without that.”

64.53.oldText: “No, you must swear on your eternal salvation. Otherwise I shan't go.”

64.54.oldText: “Well, don't then. What does it matter to me? It's cold out; stay at home.”

64.55.oldText: “Kids,” Kolya turned to the children, “this woman will stay with you till I come back, or till your mother comes—she should have been back long ago. She'll give you some lunch, too. You'll give them something, Agafya, won't you?”

64.57.oldText: “Good-by, chickens, I go with my heart at rest. And you, granny,” he added gravely, in an undertone, as he passed Agafya, “I hope you'll spare their tender years and not tell them any of your old woman's nonsense about Katerina. Ici, Perezvon!”

64.58.oldText: “Get along with you!” retorted Agafya, really angry this time. “Ridiculous boy! You want a whipping for saying such things, that's what you want!”

65.0.oldText: But Kolya didn't hear her. At last he could leave. As he stepped through the gate he looked around, shrugged his shoulders, muttered “It's freezing,” and walked straight down the street, turning right toward the marketplace. At the last house before the market he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle from his pocket, and blew on it with all his strength as though sending a signal. He didn't have to wait more than a minute before a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, in a warm, neat, even stylish coat, came darting out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin), the son of a well-to-do official. Apparently his parents had forbidden him to keep company with Krassotkin, who was known around town as a desperately naughty boy, so Smurov was clearly sneaking out. He was — in case the reader has forgotten — one of the group of boys who two months earlier had thrown stones at Ilusha. He was also the one who had told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.

65.1.oldText: “I've been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin,” Smurov said stolidly, and the two boys set off toward the marketplace.

65.2.oldText: “I'm late,” Krassotkin answered. “I was held up by circumstances. You won't get thrashed for coming with me, will you?”

65.3.oldText: “Come on, I never get thrashed! And you've brought Perezvon?”

65.8.oldText: “Impossible. Zhutchka doesn't exist. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of oblivion.”

65.9.oldText: “Ah — couldn't we try this?” Smurov stopped suddenly. “Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog like Perezvon. Couldn't you tell him this is Zhutchka? Maybe he'd believe you.”

65.10.oldText: “My boy, steer clear of lying, that's one thing; and steer clear of it even for a good cause, that's another. Above all, I hope you haven't told them anything about my coming.”

65.11.oldText: “Heaven forbid! I know what I'm doing. But Perezvon won't comfort him,” Smurov said with a sigh. “You know his father, the captain — the one they call ‘the wisp of tow’ — told us today he's bringing Ilusha a real mastiff puppy, black-nosed, the works. He thinks it will comfort Ilusha, but I doubt it.”

65.13.oldText: “Bad, very bad. I think he has consumption. He's quite conscious, but his breathing — his breathing is all wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots put on so he could be led around the room. He tried to walk but couldn't stand up. ‘Ah, I told you before, father,’ he said, ‘that those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.’ He thought it was the boots making him stagger, but it was just weakness. He won't last another week. Herzenstube is looking after him. They've got money again now — heaps of it.”

65.16.oldText: “Doctors, and the whole tribe of quacks — collectively, and individually, of course. I don't believe in medicine. It's a useless institution. I intend to look into all of that. But what's this sentimental business going on at your place? The whole class seems to be dropping by every day.”

65.17.oldText: “Not the whole class: only about ten of our fellows go to see him every day. That's nothing.”

65.18.oldText: “What I don't understand in all this is Alexey Karamazov's part in it. His brother is going to be tried tomorrow or the day after for such a crime, and he still has so much time to spend on sentimental visits with boys.”

65.19.oldText: “There's nothing sentimental about it. You're going yourself, right now, to patch things up with Ilusha.”

65.20.oldText: “Patch things up with him? What a ridiculous expression. But I don't let anyone analyze my actions.”

65.21.oldText: “And how thrilled Ilusha will be to see you! He has no idea you're coming. Why, why wouldn't you come all this time?” Smurov cried with sudden feeling.

65.22.oldText: “My dear boy, that's my business, not yours. I'm going on my own because I choose to, but the rest of you have been dragged there by Alexey Karamazov — there's a difference. And how do you know? Maybe I'm not going to patch anything up at all. It's a stupid expression.”

65.23.oldText: “It has nothing to do with Karamazov — it wasn't his doing. Our fellows started going on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. But there's been none of that kind of nonsense. One went, then another. His father was overjoyed to see us. You know he'll simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He sees that Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we've made up with Ilusha. Ilusha asked after you, that was all. He just asks and says nothing more. His father will go out of his mind — or hang himself. He was behaving like a madman before. He's a decent man, really. We made a mistake then. It was all the fault of that murderer who beat him.”

65.24.oldText: “Karamazov is still a riddle to me. I could have made his acquaintance long ago, but I prefer to keep a certain pride in some cases. Besides, I have a theory about him I need to work out and verify.”

65.25.oldText: Kolya lapsed into dignified silence. Smurov kept quiet too. He worshipped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on the same footing. He was intensely curious now about Kolya's saying that he was going “on his own” to see Ilusha. He sensed some mystery in Kolya's sudden decision to come today. They crossed the marketplace, which at that hour was crowded with loaded wagons from the countryside and great numbers of live fowls. Market women sat in their booths selling rolls, cotton, thread, and the like. These Sunday markets were naively called “fairs” in town, and there were many such fairs in the course of the year.

65.26.oldText: Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing first one side, then the other. When he met other dogs they eagerly sniffed each other over according to the rules of canine etiquette.

65.27.oldText: “I like watching scenes like this, Smurov,” Kolya said suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”

65.29.oldText: “No, it's not funny — you're wrong there. There's nothing funny in nature, however funny it may look to man with all his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they'd certainly find just as much — if not far more — to laugh at in the social relations between humans, their masters. Far more, in fact. I'll say it again, because I'm convinced there's far more foolishness among us. That's Rakitin's idea — a remarkable one. I'm a Socialist, Smurov.”

65.31.oldText: “It's when everyone is equal and everyone shares property in common, there are no marriages, and everyone follows any religion and laws he likes, and so on. You're not old enough to understand all that yet. It's cold, though.”

65.32.oldText: “Yes — twelve degrees of frost. Father just checked the thermometer.”

65.33.oldText: “Have you noticed, Smurov, how in the middle of winter we don't feel the cold even at fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost as much as we do now, at the start of winter, when there's a sudden twelve-degree freeze — especially when there isn't much snow yet? It's because people aren't used to it. Everything is habit with human beings — even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great motive power. What a funny-looking peasant!”

65.34.oldText: Kolya pointed at a tall peasant with a good-natured face in a long sheepskin coat, standing beside his wagon, clapping his hands in shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was all white with frost.

65.35.oldText: “That peasant's beard is frozen,” Kolya shouted in a loud, provocative voice as he passed him.

65.36.oldText: “Lots of people's beards are frozen,” the peasant replied calmly and sententiously.

65.38.oldText: “It's all right — he won't get angry. He's a decent fellow. Good-bye, Matvey.”

65.42.oldText: “No, I didn't. It was a guess.”

65.43.oldText: “You don't say! You're a schoolboy, I take it?”

65.49.oldText: “Ech, what a life!” the peasant sighed from the bottom of his heart.

65.51.oldText: “Good-bye. You're a nice lad, that you are.”

65.53.oldText: “That was a nice peasant,” Kolya observed to Smurov. “I enjoy talking with peasants, and I'm always happy to give them their due.”

65.54.oldText: “Why did you lie and tell him we get thrashed?” Smurov asked.

65.55.oldText: “I had to say it to please him.”

65.57.oldText: “Smurov, I don't like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on the first time. Some things can't be explained. In a peasant's mind, schoolboys are whipped — and ought to be. What sort of schoolboy would one be if he weren't whipped? And if I had told him we aren't, he'd have been disappointed. But you don't understand that. You have to know how to talk to peasants.”

65.58.oldText: “Just don't tease them, please, or you'll land in another scrape, like that business with the goose.”

65.60.oldText: “Don't laugh, Kolya. Of course I'm scared. My father would be furious. I'm strictly forbidden to go out with you.”

65.61.oldText: “Don't worry — nothing will happen this time. Hey there, Natasha!” he shouted to a market woman in one of the booths.

65.62.oldText: “Calling me Natasha! Really! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged market woman shouted back at him.

65.64.oldText: “Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on so!”

65.65.oldText: “I'm in a hurry. I can't stop. You can tell me next Sunday.” Kolya waved her off as though she had attacked him and not the other way around.

65.66.oldText: “I've nothing to tell you next Sunday. You jumped on me, you impudent little monkey. I said nothing,” Marya bellowed. “You need a whipping, that's what you need, you saucy jackanapes!”

65.67.oldText: There was a roar of laughter from the other market women around her. Suddenly a man in a fit of rage burst out from the arcade of shops nearby. He was a young man, not a native of the town, with dark, curly hair and a long, pale face pitted with smallpox scars. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap and looked like a merchant's clerk. He was in a state of stupid excitement and was brandishing his fist at Kolya.

65.69.oldText: Kolya stared at him. He couldn't recall ever having a row with this man. But he'd been in so many street rows he could hardly keep track of them all.

65.72.oldText: “All the better for you. Well, it's time I was off. Good-bye!”

65.73.oldText: “At your saucy pranks again?” the man cried. “At your saucy pranks again? I know it, you're at it again!”

65.74.oldText: “It's not your business, brother, whether I'm at my saucy pranks or not,” Kolya said, standing his ground and sizing him up.

65.79.oldText: “What Trifon Nikititch?” the young man asked, staring at Kolya with loutish amazement, though still just as angry.

65.81.oldText: “Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he asked suddenly, with stern emphasis.

65.82.oldText: “What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven't,” the young man said, thrown off a little.

65.83.oldText: “Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya went on, even more emphatically, even more severely.

65.84.oldText: “What Sabaneyev? No, I don't know him.”

65.85.oldText: “Then you can go to the devil,” Kolya said, cutting the exchange short; and turning sharply to the right he strode quickly on his way as though he disdained any further conversation with a dolt who didn't even know Sabaneyev.

65.86.oldText: “Stop — hey! What Sabaneyev?” the young man cried, jolted out of his stupor and as worked up as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women with a foolish stare.

65.88.oldText: “There's no telling what he's up to,” said one.

65.89.oldText: “What Sabaneyev is it he's talking about?” the young man kept repeating, still furious and shaking his right arm.

65.90.oldText: “It must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs — that must be who it is,” one of the women suggested.

65.91.oldText: The young man gave her a wild stare.

65.92.oldText: “For the Kuzmitchovs?” another woman repeated. “But his name wasn't Trifon. His name's Kuzma, not Trifon; and the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can't be the same man.”

65.93.oldText: “His name isn't Trifon, and it isn't Sabaneyev — it's Tchizhov,” a third woman put in suddenly. She had been silent until then, listening gravely. “Alexey Ivanitch is his first name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”

65.94.oldText: “Of course — it's Tchizhov,” a fourth woman confirmed emphatically.

65.95.oldText: The bewildered youth looked from one to another.

65.96.oldText: “But what did he want with me? What did he want with me, good people?” he cried almost in desperation. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ he says. And who the devil can know who Sabaneyev is?”

65.97.oldText: “You're a fool. I'm telling you it's not Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov — Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that's who it is!” one of the women shouted at him impressively.

65.98.oldText: “What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”

65.99.oldText: “That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer.”

65.100.oldText: “And what's your Tchizhov got to do with me, good people, eh?”

65.101.oldText: “How should I know what he's got to do with you?” another put in. “You ought to know for yourself what you want with him, if you're going to raise such a racket about him. He was talking to you, not to us, you fool. Don't you really know him?”

65.104.oldText: “To the devil with Tchizhov and you along with him. I'll give him a hiding, that I will. He was making fun of me!”

65.105.oldText: “Give Tchizhov a hiding? More likely he'll give you one. You're a fool, that's what you are!”

65.106.oldText: “Not Tchizhov — not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischievous woman. I'll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

65.107.oldText: The woman guffawed. But Kolya was already far off by now, marching along with a triumphant air. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group behind them. He too was in high spirits, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya's company.

65.108.oldText: “What Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, guessing what the answer would be.

65.109.oldText: “How should I know? Now there'll be a commotion among them all day. I like stirring up fools in every class of society. There's another blockhead, that peasant over there. They say ‘there's no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,' but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just as much. Can't you see all over his face that peasant's a fool, eh?”

65.110.oldText: “Leave him alone, Kolya. Let's keep going.”

65.111.oldText: “Nothing can stop me now that I've got started. Hey, good morning, peasant!”

65.112.oldText: A sturdy peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard, walking past, raised his head and looked at the boy. He didn't seem quite sober.

65.113.oldText: “Good morning, if you aren't laughing at me,” he said deliberately in reply.

65.114.oldText: “And what if I am?” Kolya laughed.

65.115.oldText: “Well, a joke's a joke. Laugh away. I don't mind. There's no harm in a joke.”

65.116.oldText: “I beg your pardon, brother, it was a joke.”

65.119.oldText: “I forgive you entirely. Be on your way.”

65.120.oldText: “I say, you seem to be a clever peasant.”

65.122.oldText: “I doubt it,” Kolya said, somewhat taken aback.

65.128.oldText: “There are all sorts of peasants,” Kolya observed to Smurov after a short silence. “How was I to know I'd landed on a clever one? I'm always ready to recognize intelligence in the peasantry.”

65.129.oldText: In the distance the cathedral clock struck half past eleven. The boys hurried and walked the considerable distance to Captain Snegiryov's lodgings quickly and almost without speaking. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go on ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.

65.130.oldText: “One needs to sniff around a little first,” he remarked to Smurov.

65.131.oldText: “Why ask him to come out?” Smurov protested. “Just go in — they'll be overjoyed to see you. What's the sense of making friends in the frost out here?”

65.132.oldText: “I know why I want to see him out here in the frost,” Kolya cut him short in the despotic tone he liked to adopt with “small boys,” and Smurov ran off to do his bidding.

66.0.oldText: Kolya leaned against the fence with an air of dignity, waiting for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he had wanted to meet him for a long time. He had heard a great deal about him from the boys, but until now he had always put on a look of disdainful indifference whenever Alyosha's name came up, and had even “criticized” what he heard about him. Secretly, though, he longed to make his acquaintance; everything he'd been told about Alyosha struck him as sympathetic and attractive. So this moment mattered: to begin with, he had to show himself at his best, to show his independence. “Otherwise he'll think of me as thirteen and take me for a boy, like the rest of them. And what are these little boys to him? I'll ask him once I know him. It's a pity I'm so short, though. Tuzikov is younger than I am, yet he's half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I'm not good-looking. I know I'm ugly, but I've got a clever face. I mustn't talk too freely; if I fall into his arms all at once, he may think — pah, how horrible if he should think — !”

66.1.oldText: Such were the thoughts that kept Kolya on edge while he did everything he could to look as independent as possible. What distressed him most was being so short; his “ugly” face bothered him less than his height. A year earlier he had made a pencil mark on the wall at home in one corner to show his height, and every two months since then he had anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he had gained. But alas — he was growing very slowly, and this sometimes reduced him almost to despair. His face was in fact by no means “ugly”; on the contrary, it was rather attractive, with fair, pale skin dusted with freckles. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often lit up with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones, small, very red but not very full lips, and a small, unmistakably turned-up nose. “I've got a regular pug nose, a regular pug nose,” Kolya used to mutter when he caught sight of himself in the mirror, always turning away indignantly. “Or maybe I don't even have a clever face?” he sometimes wondered, doubting even that. But it should not be supposed that his mind was preoccupied with his face and height. On the contrary, however bitter the moments in front of the mirror were, he quickly forgot them, and forgot them for a long time, “giving himself up entirely to ideas and to real life,” as he put it to himself.

66.2.oldText: Alyosha came out quickly and hurried up to Kolya. Before he reached him, Kolya could see that he looked delighted. “Can he really be so glad to see me?” Kolya wondered, pleased. Let us note in passing that Alyosha's appearance had changed completely since we last saw him. He had given up the cassock and was now wearing a well-cut coat and a soft, round hat, and his hair had been cropped short. It all suited him; he looked quite handsome. His charming face always carried a good-humored expression, but there was a gentleness and serenity in that good humor. To Kolya's surprise, Alyosha came out just as he was, without an overcoat. He had obviously come in a hurry. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.

66.3.oldText: “So here you are at last! How anxious we've been to see you!”

66.4.oldText: “There were reasons you'll know about in a moment. In any case, I'm glad to meet you. I've long hoped for the chance, and I've heard a great deal about you,” Kolya muttered, a little breathless.

66.5.oldText: “We were bound to meet anyway. I've heard a lot about you too; but you've taken a long time coming here.”

66.7.oldText: “Ilusha is very ill. He's certainly dying.”

66.8.oldText: “How awful! You must admit medicine is a fraud, Karamazov,” Kolya cried warmly.

66.9.oldText: “Ilusha has spoken of you often — very often, even in his sleep, in his delirium, you know. One can see you used to be very, very dear to him ... before that incident ... with the knife. Then there's another reason ... Tell me, is that your dog?”

66.11.oldText: “Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. “Is she lost forever?”

66.12.oldText: “I know you'd all like it to be Zhutchka. I've heard all about it.” Kolya smiled mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I'll tell you everything. That's what I came for; that's why I asked you to come out here — to explain the whole business to you before we go in,” he began eagerly. “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha started in the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is like — a pack of small boys. They began teasing Ilusha at once. I'm two classes higher up, of course, so I only watched them from a distance. I could see the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn't give in; he fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was that he was dressed horribly at the time — his breeches were too small for him, and there were holes in his boots. They tormented him about it; they jeered at him. I can't stand that. I stood up for him at once and gave them a real hiding. I beat them up, and yet they adore me, do you know that, Karamazov?” Kolya boasted impulsively. “I'm always fond of children. I've got two little chicks in my hands at home right now — that's what held me up today. So they stopped beating Ilusha, and I took him under my protection. I could see the boy was proud. I'm telling you, the boy was proud. But in the end he became slavishly devoted to me; he'd do the smallest thing I asked, obeyed me as though I were God, tried to imitate me. In the breaks between classes he'd run to me at once, and I'd spend time with him. On Sundays too. People always laugh when an older boy takes up with a younger one like that, but that's a prejudice. If it's my fancy, that's enough. I'm teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn't I develop him if I like him? Here you are, Karamazov, you've taken up with all these little nestlings — I see you want to influence the younger generation, to develop them, to be of use to them, and I'll admit, this trait in your character, which I knew by hearsay, attracted me more than anything. But let's get to the point. I noticed a certain softness and sentimentality coming over the boy, and you know I have a positive hatred of this sheepish sentimentality — I've hated it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him, too: he was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he'd refuse to agree with me; he'd argue, fly into a rage. I sometimes put forward certain ideas just to see, and I could tell it wasn't that he disagreed with the ideas so much as that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in response to his affection. And so, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he became, the colder I became. I did it on purpose — that was my plan. My aim was to form his character, to knock him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you understand me at a word. All of a sudden I noticed he was downcast and dejected for three days in a row — not because of my coldness, but for some other reason, something more serious. I wondered what the tragedy was. I dug it out of him and found out he'd somehow gotten to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father — this was before his death, of course — and Smerdyakov had taught the little fool a stupid trick — that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry street dogs that snap up anything without chewing it, and then watch what happened. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there's been all this fuss about. The people of the house that owned her never fed her, though she barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can't stand it.) So she lunged at the bread, swallowed it, and began to yelp; she spun around and ran off, yelping as she went, until she was out of sight. That was Ilusha's own account. He confessed it to me and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, ‘She ran away yelping, she ran away yelping' — the sight of it haunted him. He was tormented by remorse; I could see it. I took it seriously. I decided to give him a lesson, for other things as well. So I must confess I wasn't altogether straightforward — I pretended to be more indignant than I really was. ‘You've done a nasty thing,' I said. ‘You're a scoundrel. I won't tell on you, of course, but I'll have nothing more to do with you for a while. I'll think it over and let you know through Smurov' — that's the boy who's come with me just now; he's always ready to do anything for me — ‘whether I will have anything to do with you in the future or whether I give you up for good as a scoundrel.' He was tremendously upset. I'll admit I felt as I was speaking that I'd gone too far, but there was no helping it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two later I sent Smurov to tell him I'd stopped speaking to him. That's what we call it at school when two boys refuse to have anything more to do with each other. Secretly, I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you suppose happened? He heard Smurov's message, his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,' he cried, ‘that I'll throw bread with pins in it to all the dogs — all of them, all of them!' ‘So he's going in for a little temper,' I thought. ‘We must smoke it out of him.' And I started treating him with contempt; whenever we crossed paths I'd turn away or smile sarcastically. And just then that business with his father happened. Do you remember? You have to realize he was already horribly worked up by everything that had happened. The boys, seeing I'd given him up, turned on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!' He was soon in regular fights with them, which I'm very sorry for. Apparently they gave him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they were coming out of school. I stood a few yards off, watching. And I swear, I don't remember laughing; quite the opposite — I felt terribly sorry for him, and in another minute I'd have run up to take his side. But then he suddenly met my eyes. I don't know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and jabbed at my thigh — right here, on my right leg. I didn't move. I don't mind admitting I'm brave sometimes, Karamazov. I just looked at him contemptuously, as if to say, ‘So this is how you repay all my kindness? Do it again, if you like — I'm at your service.' But he didn't stab me again; he broke down, frightened at what he'd done, threw the knife away, burst into tears, and ran off. Of course I didn't snitch on him, and I made all the other boys keep quiet so it wouldn't reach the masters' ears. I didn't even tell my mother until the wound had healed up. And the wound was nothing — a scratch. Then I heard that the same day he'd been throwing stones and had bitten your finger — but you understand now the state he was in! Well, it can't be helped: it was stupid of me not to go and forgive him — that is, make it up with him — when he was taken ill. I'm sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I've told you the whole thing ... though I'm afraid it was stupid of me.”

66.13.oldText: “Oh, what a pity,” Alyosha exclaimed with feeling, “that I didn't know sooner what terms you two were on — I'd have come to you long ago to beg you to go to him with me. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I had no idea how much you meant to him! And you really haven't managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting for it all over town. Would you believe it, since he's been ill, I've three times heard him repeat with tears, ‘It's because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I'm ill now. God is punishing me for it.' He can't get that idea out of his head. And if the dog could be found and shown to be alive, you might almost think the joy would cure him. We've all been pinning our hopes on you.”

66.14.oldText: “Tell me, what made you hope I'd be the one to find her?” Kolya asked with great curiosity. “Why count on me rather than anyone else?”

66.15.oldText: “There was a rumor that you were looking for the dog and that you'd bring her once you found her. Smurov said something of the kind. We've all been trying to persuade Ilusha that the dog is alive, that she's been spotted. The boys brought him a live hare; he just glanced at it with a faint smile and asked them to set it free in the fields. So we did. His father has only just come back with a mastiff puppy, hoping to comfort him that way; but I think it only makes things worse.”

66.16.oldText: “Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but how do you see him — as a mountebank, a buffoon?”

66.17.oldText: “Oh no. There are people of deep feeling who have somehow been crushed. In them, buffoonery becomes a kind of resentful irony against people they don't dare tell the truth to, from years of being humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is wrapped up in Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he'll either go mad with grief or kill himself. I'm almost certain of it when I look at him now.”

66.18.oldText: “I understand you, Karamazov. I see you understand human nature,” Kolya added with feeling.

66.20.oldText: “Wait a bit, Karamazov — perhaps we'll find her yet; but this is Perezvon. I'll let him go in now, and maybe he'll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff puppy. Hang on, Karamazov, in a minute you'll see something. But — I say — I'm keeping you standing out here!” Kolya cried suddenly. “You don't even have an overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we're all egoists, Karamazov!”

66.21.oldText: “Don't worry about that. It is cold, but I don't catch cold easily. Let's go in, though. And, by the way, what's your name? I know you're called Kolya, but what else?”

66.22.oldText: “Nikolay — Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, ‘Krassotkin, son of.'” Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, “Of course I hate the name Nikolay.”

66.26.oldText: “No, fourteen — or rather, I'll be fourteen very soon, in a fortnight. I'll confess one weakness of mine, Karamazov, to you alone, since this is our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age, more than hate it ... and on top of that ... there's a libelous story going around about me — that last week I played robbers with the preparatory boys. It's true that I did play with them, but it's a complete libel to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reason to believe you've heard the story; but I wasn't playing for my own amusement, I was doing it for the children, because they couldn't think up anything to do by themselves. But there's always some silly tale going around. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you.”

66.27.oldText: “But what if you had been playing for your own amusement — what's wrong with that?”

66.28.oldText: “Come on — for my own amusement? You don't play horses, do you?”

66.29.oldText: “You should look at it this way,” Alyosha said, smiling. “Grown-up people go to the theater, and there they watch the adventures of all sorts of heroes — sometimes robbers and battles too — and isn't that just the same thing, in another form? And young people's games of soldiers or robbers in their play time are also art in its first stage. You know, they spring from the growing artistic instincts of the young. And sometimes these games are much better than theater performances; the only difference is that in the theater people go to watch the actors, while in these games young people are the actors themselves. But that's only natural.”

66.30.oldText: “You think so? Is that your view?” Kolya looked at him intently. “You know, that's a rather interesting idea. When I go home I'll think it over. I'll admit, I thought I might learn something from you. I've come to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya concluded, his voice full of spontaneous feeling.

66.31.oldText: “And I from you,” Alyosha said, smiling and pressing his hand.

66.32.oldText: Kolya was thoroughly pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly like an equal and talked to him as if he were “quite grown up.”

66.33.oldText: “I'll show you something in a moment, Karamazov — a theatrical performance too,” he said, laughing nervously. “That's why I've come.”

66.34.oldText: “Let's go first to the people of the house on the left. All the boys leave their coats there, because the room is small and hot.”
