66.35.oldText: “Oh, I'm only coming in for a minute. I'll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the passage and be dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how he's dead. I'll go in first and scout it out, then I'll whistle to him when I think it's the right moment, and you'll see — he'll come charging in like mad. Only Smurov mustn't forget to open the door at the right moment. I'll arrange it all, and you'll see something.”

67.0.oldText: The room occupied by the family of the retired captain Snegiryov is already familiar to the reader. At that moment it was close and crowded with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha, and though they were all ready, like Smurov, to deny that Alyosha had brought them and reconciled them with Ilusha, the fact was that he had. All the artistry he had used was to lead each of them to Ilusha one by one, without any “sheepish sentimentality,” appearing to do so casually and without any plan. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply moved by the almost tender affection and sympathy shown him by these boys who had once been his enemies. Krassotkin was the only one still missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha's heart. Of all his bitter memories, perhaps the most bitter was having stabbed Krassotkin, who had been his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, the first to make it up with Ilusha, thought so too. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come and see him about something, the latter cut him off, telling Smurov to inform “Karamazov” right then that he knew best what to do, that he didn't need anyone's advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha, he'd choose his own time — he had “his own reasons.”

67.1.oldText: That was a fortnight before this Sunday. That's why Alyosha hadn't come himself, as he had intended. But even as he waited, he sent Smurov to him twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal, sending Alyosha the message to stop bothering him, and that if Alyosha came in person, Krassotkin would refuse to go to Ilusha at all. Right up to the last day, Smurov didn't know that Kolya meant to visit Ilusha that morning — only on the evening before, as he parted from Smurov, did Kolya abruptly tell him to wait at home for him next morning, because they'd go to the Snegiryovs' together; but he warned him on no account to say he was coming, as he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov's notion that Kolya would bring back the lost dog was based on words Kolya had dropped — that “they must be asses not to find the dog, if it was alive.” When Smurov, watching for an opportunity, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. “I'm not such an ass as to go hunting around town for other people's dogs when I've got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could still be alive after swallowing a pin? Sheepish sentimentality, that's what it is!”

67.2.oldText: For the last fortnight Ilusha had not left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He had not been at school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He had fallen ill the same day, though for a month afterward he was sometimes able to get up and walk about the room and the passage. But lately he had grown so weak that he couldn't move without his father's help. His father was terribly worried about him. He even gave up drinking and was nearly out of his mind with terror that his boy might die. Often, especially after leading him around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he would run to a dark corner of the passage and, pressing his head against the wall, break into fits of violent weeping, stifling his sobs so Ilusha wouldn't hear.

67.3.oldText: Coming back into the room, he would usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy — telling him stories, funny anecdotes, or mimicking comic people he happened to have met, even imitating the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha couldn't bear to see his father fooling and playing the buffoon. Though the boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, he saw with an aching heart that his father was an object of contempt, and he was constantly haunted by the memory of the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day.”

67.4.oldText: Nina, Ilusha's gentle, crippled sister, did not like her father's buffoonery either (Varvara had been gone some time now to Petersburg to study at the university). But the half-witted mother was greatly entertained and laughed heartily when her husband began capering about or performing some routine. It was the only way she could be amused; the rest of the time she was grumbling and complaining that everyone had forgotten her, that no one treated her with respect, that she was being slighted, and so on. Lately, though, she had changed completely. She had begun gazing constantly at Ilusha's bed in the corner and seemed lost in thought. She had grown more silent, quieter, and, if she cried, she cried quietly so as not to be heard. The captain noticed the change in her with mournful perplexity. The boys' visits had at first only angered her, but later on their cheerful shouts and stories began to divert her, and at last she grew so fond of them that, if the boys had stopped coming, she would have felt miserable without them. When the children told some story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She would call some of them over and kiss them. She was especially fond of Smurov.

67.5.oldText: As for the captain, the presence in his room of the children who came to cheer up Ilusha filled his heart from the first with ecstatic joy. He even hoped that Ilusha would now shake off his low spirits, and that this would speed his recovery. Despite his alarm about Ilusha, he had not, until very recently, felt even a moment's doubt that the boy would ultimately recover.

67.6.oldText: He welcomed his little visitors with deference, waited on them hand and foot; he was ready to be their horse and even started letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha didn't like the game and it was given up. He began buying them little things — gingerbread and nuts — gave them tea, and made them sandwiches. It must be noted that he had plenty of money all this time. He had taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, exactly as Alyosha had predicted. And afterward Katerina Ivanovna, learning more about their circumstances and Ilusha's illness, had visited them herself, gotten to know the family, and succeeded in charming the half-witted mother. Since then she had been lavish in helping them, and the captain, terrified that his boy might be dying, forgot his pride and humbly accepted her assistance.

67.7.oldText: All this time Doctor Herzenstube, sent for by Katerina Ivanovna, had been coming punctually every other day, but little was gained from his visits, and he dosed the invalid mercilessly. But that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, who had come from Moscow where he had a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at great expense, not specifically for Ilusha, but for another purpose which will be explained in its proper place. Since he had come, she had asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had no idea that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, even though he had long hoped for a visit from the boy Ilusha was fretting over.

67.8.oldText: At the moment Krassotkin opened the door and stepped into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha's bed, looking at a tiny mastiff puppy that had been born only the day before. The captain had spoken for it a week ago, hoping to comfort and amuse Ilusha, who was still grieving over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha, who had heard three days earlier that he was to be presented with a puppy — not just any puppy, but a pedigreed mastiff (a very important detail, of course) — had tried, out of delicacy of feeling, to pretend to be pleased. But his father and the boys could see plainly that the puppy only recalled to his little heart the unhappy dog he had killed. The puppy lay next to him, moving feebly, and he, smiling sadly, stroked it with his thin, pale, wasted hand. He clearly liked the puppy, but ... it wasn't Zhutchka. If he could have had Zhutchka and the puppy, then he would have been completely happy.

67.9.oldText: “Krassotkin!” one of the boys cried out suddenly. He was the first to notice him come in.

67.10.oldText: Krassotkin's entrance caused a general stir; the boys stepped back and stood on either side of the bed so that he could get a full view of Ilusha. The captain rushed eagerly to meet Kolya.

67.11.oldText: “Please come in ... you are most welcome!” he said hurriedly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!”

67.12.oldText: But Krassotkin, shaking hands with him hurriedly, immediately demonstrated his complete grasp of polite society's manners. He turned first to the captain's wife, sitting in her armchair — who was in an ill humor just then, grumbling that the boys were standing between her and Ilusha's bed, keeping her from seeing the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he made her a bow, scraping his foot, and then turning to Nina, he made her, as the only other lady present, an identical bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.

67.13.oldText: “There, you can see at once he's a young man who's been well brought up,” she commented aloud, throwing up her hands. “But as for our other visitors, they come piling in one on top of another.”

67.14.oldText: “How do you mean, mamma, one on top of another — how is that?” the captain muttered affectionately, though a little anxious on her account.

67.15.oldText: “That's how they ride in. They climb up on each other's shoulders in the passage and come prancing in on a respectable family. Strange sort of visitors!”

67.16.oldText: “But who's come in that way, mamma?”

67.17.oldText: “Why, that boy came in riding on that one's back, and this one was on that one's.”

67.18.oldText: Kolya was already at Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy turned visibly paler. He raised himself up in bed and gazed intently at Kolya. Kolya had not seen his little friend for two months, and he was struck at the sight of him. He had never imagined he would see such a wasted, yellow face, such enormous, feverishly burning eyes, such thin little hands. With grieved surprise he saw Ilusha's rapid, labored breathing and dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand, and, almost overcome, said:

67.19.oldText: “Well, old man ... how are you?” But his voice failed him; he couldn't quite carry off an easy manner; his face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth quivered. Ilusha gave him a pitiful little smile, still unable to utter a word. Something moved Kolya to raise his hand and run it over Ilusha's hair.

67.20.oldText: “Never mind!” he murmured softly to him, to cheer him up, or perhaps not knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.

67.21.oldText: “Hello — so you've got a new puppy?” Kolya said suddenly, in his most unfeeling voice.

67.23.oldText: “Black nose — that means he'll be fierce, a good house dog,” Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as if the puppy and its black nose were the only thing on his mind. In reality, he was still doing his utmost to control his feelings and not burst out crying like a child, and try as he might he couldn't quite master them. “When he grows up, you'll have to keep him on a chain, I'm sure.”

67.24.oldText: “He'll be a huge dog!” one of the boys cried.

67.26.oldText: “As big as a calf, as a real calf,” the captain chimed in. “I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breeds; his parents are huge and very fierce, they stand this high from the floor. Sit down here, on Ilusha's bed, or here on the bench. You are most welcome; we've been hoping to see you for a long time. You were kind enough to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?”

67.27.oldText: Krassotkin sat down on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha's feet. Though on the way he had perhaps prepared a free and easy opening for the conversation, he now completely lost his thread.

67.28.oldText: “No ... I came with Perezvon. I've got a dog now, called Perezvon. A Slavonic name. He's out there ... if I whistle, he'll come running in. I've brought a dog too,” he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he suddenly fired the question at him.

67.29.oldText: Ilusha's little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an agonized expression. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and signaled to Kolya not to speak of Zhutchka, but Kolya didn't see it, or pretended not to.

67.30.oldText: “Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked in a broken voice.

67.31.oldText: “Oh, well, my boy, your Zhutchka is lost and done for!”

67.32.oldText: Ilusha didn't speak, but he fixed an intent gaze on Kolya once more. Alyosha caught Kolya's eye and signaled to him vigorously again, but Kolya turned his eyes away, pretending not to have noticed.

67.33.oldText: “She must have run off and died somewhere. She was bound to die after a meal like that,” Kolya pronounced pitilessly, though he seemed a little breathless. “But I've got a dog, Perezvon ... A Slavonic name. I've brought him to show you.”

67.34.oldText: “I don't want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.

67.35.oldText: “No, no, you really must see him ... he'll amuse you. I brought him on purpose. He's the same sort of shaggy dog. Will you allow me to call in my dog, madam?” He suddenly turned to Madame Snegiryov, with inexplicable excitement in his manner.

67.36.oldText: “I don't want him, I don't want him!” cried Ilusha, with a mournful break in his voice. There was a reproachful light in his eyes.

67.37.oldText: “You'd better,” said the captain, starting up from the chest by the wall where he had just sat down, “you'd better ... another time,” he muttered, but Kolya could not be held back. He hurriedly shouted to Smurov, “Open the door,” and as soon as it was open, he blew his whistle. Perezvon came rushing headlong into the room.

67.38.oldText: “Jump, Perezvon, beg! Beg!” Kolya shouted, springing up, and the dog rose on his hind legs by Ilusha's bedside. What happened next took everyone by surprise: Ilusha started, lurched violently forward, bent over Perezvon, and gazed at him, faint with suspense.

67.39.oldText: “It's ... Zhutchka!” he cried suddenly, in a voice breaking with joy and suffering.

67.40.oldText: “And who did you think it was?” Krassotkin shouted at the top of his voice, in a ringing, joyful tone, and bending down he seized the dog and lifted him up to Ilusha.

67.41.oldText: “Look, old man — you see, blind in one eye and the left ear torn, just the marks you described to me. That's how I found him. I found him right away. He didn't belong to anyone!” he explained, turning quickly to the captain, to his wife, to Alyosha, and back to Ilusha. “He used to hang around the Fedotovs' back yard. Though he made his home there, they never fed him. He was a stray that had wandered in from the village. I found him. You see, old man, he couldn't have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he would have died — he'd have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he's alive. You didn't see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue — that's why he yelped. He ran off yelping, and you thought he'd swallowed it. He would have yelped, of course, because the skin of a dog's mouth is so tender ... tenderer than in a person, much tenderer!” Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight. Ilusha couldn't speak. White as a sheet, he gazed open-mouthed at Kolya, his great eyes almost bulging out of his head. And if Krassotkin, who had no suspicion of it, had known what a disastrous and fatal effect such a moment might have on the sick child's health, nothing would have induced him to pull such a stunt on him. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who grasped it. As for the captain, he was behaving like a little child.

67.42.oldText: “Zhutchka! It's Zhutchka!” he cried in a blissful voice. “Ilusha, this is Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, this is Zhutchka!” He was almost weeping.

67.43.oldText: “And I never guessed!” Smurov cried regretfully. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I said he'd find the dog, and here he's found him.”

67.44.oldText: “Here he's found him!” another boy repeated joyfully.

67.45.oldText: “Krassotkin's a champion!” a third voice cried.

67.46.oldText: “He's a champion, he's a champion!” the other boys cried, and began clapping.

67.47.oldText: “Hold on, hold on,” Krassotkin did his best to shout over them all. “I'll tell you how it happened, that's the whole point. I found him, I took him home and hid him right away. I kept him locked up at home and didn't show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov has known for the last fortnight, but I assured him the dog was called Perezvon and he didn't guess. Meanwhile I've been teaching the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog in fine shape, old man, so I could say to you, ‘See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!' Haven't you got a bit of meat? He'll show you a trick that'll make you die laughing. A piece of meat — have you got any?”

67.48.oldText: The captain ran across the passage to the landlady, where their cooking was done. So as not to waste precious time, Kolya, in desperate haste, shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” And the dog immediately turned over and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the person most delighted by the dog's performance was “mamma.” She laughed at the dog and began snapping her fingers and calling it, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

67.49.oldText: “Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. “He won't move for any shouting in the world, but if I call him, he'll jump up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog sprang up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain came running back with a piece of cooked beef.

67.50.oldText: “Is it hot?” Kolya asked hurriedly, with a businesslike air, taking the meat. “Dogs don't like hot things. No, it's fine. Look, everyone, look, Ilusha, look, old man — why aren't you looking? He does not look at him, now that I've brought him.”

67.51.oldText: The new trick consisted in making the dog stand motionless with his nose out, while a tempting morsel of meat was balanced on the tip of his nose. The luckless dog had to stand without moving, the meat on his nose, as long as his master chose to keep him there — without a movement, perhaps for half an hour. But he held Perezvon only a brief moment.

67.52.oldText: “Paid for!” Kolya cried, and the meat flashed from the dog's nose to his mouth. The audience, of course, expressed enthusiasm and surprise.

67.53.oldText: “Can you really have put off coming all this time just to train the dog?” Alyosha exclaimed, with an involuntary note of reproach in his voice.

67.54.oldText: “Just for that!” Kolya answered, with perfect simplicity. “I wanted to show him off in all his glory.”

67.55.oldText: “Perezvon! Perezvon!” called Ilusha suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

67.56.oldText: “What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed and Perezvon darted up next to Ilusha. The boy threw both arms around his head and Perezvon instantly licked his cheek. Ilusha pressed close against him, stretched himself out in bed, and buried his face in the dog's shaggy coat.

67.57.oldText: “Dear, dear!” the captain kept exclaiming. Kolya sat down again on the edge of the bed.

67.58.oldText: “Ilusha, I can show you another trick. I've brought you a little cannon. Remember, I told you about it before and you said how much you'd like to see it. Well — here, I've brought it to you.”

67.59.oldText: And Kolya hurriedly pulled out of his satchel the little bronze cannon. He hurried because he was happy himself. Another time he would have waited until the sensation made by Perezvon had worn off; now he hurried on without a thought for any of that. “You're all happy now,” he felt, “so here's something to make you happier!” He was himself utterly enchanted.

67.60.oldText: “I've been coveting this thing for a long time. It's for you, old man, it's for you. It belonged to Morozov; it was no use to him, he had it from his brother. I traded a book from father's bookcase for it — _A Kinsman of Mahomet, or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book printed in Moscow a hundred years ago, before they had any censorship. And Morozov has a taste for such things. He was grateful to me, too.”

67.61.oldText: Kolya held the cannon in his hand so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha raised himself up, and, with his right arm still around the dog, he gazed at the toy in enchantment. The sensation was even greater when Kolya announced that he had gunpowder, too, and that it could be fired off right then “if it won't alarm the ladies.” “Mamma” immediately asked to see the toy up close and her request was granted. She was much pleased with the little bronze cannon on wheels and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She readily gave permission for the cannon to be fired, without any idea what she had been asked. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, as an old military man, undertook to load it, putting in a tiny bit of powder. He asked that the shot be put off for another time. The cannon was set on the floor, aimed at an empty part of the room; three grains of powder were thrust into the touchhole and a match was put to it. A magnificent explosion followed. Mamma was startled, but at once laughed with delight. The boys gazed in speechless triumph. But the captain, looking at Ilusha, was more enchanted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and immediately presented it to Ilusha, along with the powder and the shot.

67.62.oldText: “I got it for you, for you! I've been keeping it for you a long time,” he repeated once more, in his delight.

67.63.oldText: “Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn't get it. Kolya was disconcerted. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

67.64.oldText: “Mamma, mamma,” he ran to her, “the cannon is yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, because it's a present to him, but it's just as good as yours. Ilusha will always let you play with it; it shall belong to both of you, both of you.”

67.65.oldText: “No, I don't want it to belong to both of us, I want it to be mine alone, not Ilusha's,” mamma persisted, on the verge of tears.

67.66.oldText: “Take it, mother, here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?” He turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as though afraid he might be offended at his giving his present to someone else.

67.67.oldText: “Of course you may,” Krassotkin agreed heartily, and, taking the cannon from Ilusha, he handed it to mamma himself with a polite bow. She was so moved she began to cry.

67.68.oldText: “Ilusha, darling — he's the one who loves his mamma!” she said tenderly, and at once began wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.

67.70.oldText: “And I've never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy,” said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

67.71.oldText: “And I'll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make the powder ourselves now. Borovikov found out how it's done — twenty-four parts of saltpeter, ten of sulfur, and six of birchwood charcoal. It's all pounded together, mixed into a paste with water, and rubbed through a tammy sieve — that's how it's done.”

67.72.oldText: “Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it's not real gunpowder,” Ilusha answered.

67.73.oldText: “Not real?” Kolya flushed. “It burns. I don't know, of course.”

67.74.oldText: “No, I didn't mean that,” the captain put in with a guilty face. “I only said that real powder isn't made like that, but that's nothing — it can be made that way.”

67.75.oldText: “I don't know, you know best. We lit some of it in a pomatum pot; it burned splendidly, all of it burned away leaving only a tiny bit of ash. But that was just the paste, and if you rub it through a sieve ... well, of course you know best, I don't know. And Bulkin's father thrashed him on account of our powder — did you hear?” he said, turning to Ilusha.

67.76.oldText: “Yes,” Ilusha answered. He listened to Kolya with enormous interest and enjoyment.

67.77.oldText: “We had prepared a whole bottle of it, and he used to keep it under his bed. His father saw it. He said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to lodge a complaint against me with the masters. He's not allowed to hang around with me now; no one is allowed to hang around with me now. Smurov isn't allowed to either. I've got a bad name with everyone. They say I'm a ‘desperate character,'” Kolya smiled scornfully. “It all started with what happened on the railway.”

67.78.oldText: “Ah, we've heard of that exploit of yours too,” the captain cried. “How could you lie still on the rails? Were you really not the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren't you frightened?”

67.79.oldText: The captain was positively abject in his flattery of Kolya.

67.80.oldText: “N-not particularly,” Kolya answered casually. “What's blasted my reputation more than anything here was that cursed goose,” he said, turning again to Ilusha. But though he assumed an unconcerned air as he talked, he still couldn't quite control himself and kept missing the note he tried to hit.

67.81.oldText: “Ah, I heard about the goose!” Ilusha laughed, beaming all over. “They told me, but I didn't understand. Did they really take you to the court?”

67.82.oldText: “The most stupid, trivial affair — they made a mountain of a molehill, as they always do,” Kolya began casually. “I was walking through the marketplace here one day, just when they'd driven the geese in. I stopped and looked at them. All at once a fellow, who works as an errand boy at Plotnikov's now, looked at me and said, ‘What are you looking at the geese for?' I looked at him: a stupid, moon-faced fellow of twenty. I'm always on the side of the peasantry, you know. I like talking to peasants. We've fallen behind the peasants — that's an axiom. I believe you're laughing, Karamazov?”

67.83.oldText: “No, Heaven forbid — I'm listening,” Alyosha said with a most good-natured air, and the sensitive Kolya was immediately reassured.

67.84.oldText: “My theory, Karamazov, is clear and simple,” he hurried on again, looking pleased. “I believe in the people and am always happy to give them their due, but I'm not for spoiling them — that's a _sine qua non_ ... But I was telling you about the goose. So I turned to the fool and answered, ‘I'm wondering what the goose is thinking about.' He looked at me quite stupidly. ‘And what's the goose thinking about?' he asked. ‘Do you see that cart full of oats?' I said. ‘The oats are spilling out of the sack, and the goose has stuck its neck right under the wheel to gobble them up — do you see?' ‘I see that quite clearly,' he said. ‘Well,' said I, ‘if that cart were to move forward just a little, would it break the goose's neck or not?' ‘It'd be sure to break it' — and he grinned all over his face, highly delighted. ‘Come on, then,' said I, ‘let's try.' ‘Let's,' he said. And it didn't take us long to arrange: he stood at the bridle without being noticed, and I stood on the other side to direct the goose. The owner wasn't looking, he was talking to someone, so I had nothing to do — the goose thrust its head in after the oats on its own, under the cart, right under the wheel. I winked at the lad, he tugged at the bridle, and crack! The goose's neck was broken in half. And, as luck would have it, all the peasants saw us at that moment, and they kicked up a row on the spot. ‘You did that on purpose!' ‘No, not on purpose.' ‘Yes, you did, on purpose!' Well, they shouted, ‘Take him to the justice of the peace!' They took me along too. ‘You were there,' they said, ‘you helped, you're known all over the market!' And, for some reason, I really am known all over the market,” Kolya added conceitedly. “We all went off to the justice's; they brought the goose along as well. The fellow was crying, in a dreadful funk, simply blubbering like a woman. And the farmer kept shouting that you could kill any number of geese that way. Well, of course, there were witnesses. The justice of the peace settled it in a minute: the farmer was to be paid a rouble for the goose, and the fellow was to have the goose. And he was warned not to pull pranks like that again. And the fellow kept blubbering like a woman. ‘It wasn't me,' he said, ‘it was he who egged me on,' and he pointed to me. I answered with the utmost composure that I hadn't egged him on, that I had simply stated the general proposition, had spoken hypothetically. The justice of the peace smiled, and was vexed with himself for it at once. ‘I'll complain to your masters,' he said, ‘so that in future you won't waste your time on such general propositions instead of sitting with your books and learning your lessons.' He didn't complain to the masters — that was a joke — but the matter was noised about and came to the masters' ears. Their ears are long, you know! The classics master, Kolbasnikov, was particularly shocked about it, but Dardanelov got me off again. But Kolbasnikov is savage with everyone now like a raw ass. Did you know, Ilusha, he's just been married — got a dowry of a thousand roubles — and his bride is a regular fright of the first rank and the last degree. The third-class fellows wrote an epigram about it:

67.86.oldText: And so on — awfully funny, I'll bring it to you later. I don't say anything against Dardanelov; he's a learned man, no doubt about it. I respect men like that, and it's not because he stood up for me.”

67.87.oldText: “But you took him down a peg about the founders of Troy!” Smurov suddenly put in, unmistakably proud of Krassotkin at that moment. He was especially pleased with the story of the goose.

67.88.oldText: “Did you really take him down?” the captain inquired in a flattering tone. “On the question of who founded Troy? We heard about that — Ilusha told me at the time.”

67.89.oldText: “He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” Ilusha put in. “He only pretends to be like that, but really he's top of the class in every subject.”

67.90.oldText: Ilusha looked at Kolya with infinite happiness.

67.91.oldText: “Oh, that's all nonsense about Troy, a trivial matter. I consider it an unimportant question,” Kolya said with haughty humility. By now he had completely recovered his dignity, though he was still a little uneasy. He felt he had been greatly excited and had talked about the goose, for instance, with too little reserve, while Alyosha had looked serious and hadn't said a word the whole time. And the vain boy began gradually to feel a nagging fear that Alyosha was silent because he despised him, thought he was showing off for him. If he dared to think anything like that, Kolya would —

67.92.oldText: “I regard the question as quite a trivial one,” he rapped out again, proudly.

67.93.oldText: “And I know who founded Troy,” said a boy who had not yet spoken, to everyone's surprise. He was quiet and seemed shy. He was a pretty boy of about eleven, called Kartashov. He was sitting near the door. Kolya looked at him with dignified amazement.

67.94.oldText: The fact was that the identity of the founders of Troy had become a secret for the whole school — a secret that could only be discovered by reading Smaragdov, and no one had Smaragdov except Kolya. One day, when Kolya's back was turned, Kartashov had hurriedly opened Smaragdov, which was lying among Kolya's books, and had immediately hit on the passage about the founding of Troy. That was some time ago, but he had felt uneasy and couldn't bring himself to announce publicly that he too knew who had founded Troy, afraid of what might happen — afraid Krassotkin would somehow put him to shame for it. But now he couldn't resist saying it. For weeks he had been longing to.

67.95.oldText: “Well, who did found it?” Kolya asked, turning to him with haughty condescension. He could see from his face that Kartashov really did know, and immediately made up his mind how to handle it. There was, so to speak, a discordant note in the general harmony.

67.96.oldText: “Troy was founded by Teucer, Dardanus, Ilius, and Tros,” the boy rapped out at once, and in the same instant he blushed, blushed so deeply it was painful to look at him. But the boys stared at him, stared at him for a whole minute, and then all the staring eyes turned at once and fastened on Kolya, who was still scanning the audacious boy with disdainful composure.

67.97.oldText: “In what sense did they found it?” he deigned to comment at last. “And what do we mean by founding a city or a state? What is it they do? Did they each go and lay a brick, do you suppose?”

67.98.oldText: There was laughter. The offending boy turned from pink to crimson. He was silent and on the verge of tears. Kolya held him like that for a minute.

67.99.oldText: “Before you talk about a historical event like the founding of a nationality, you first have to understand what you mean by it,” he admonished him in stern, cutting tones. “But I don't attach any consequence to these old wives' tales, and I don't think much of universal history in general,” he added carelessly, addressing the company as a whole.

67.100.oldText: “Universal history?” the captain asked, looking almost alarmed.

67.101.oldText: “Yes, universal history. It's the study of the successive follies of mankind and nothing more. The only subjects I respect are mathematics and natural science,” Kolya said. He was showing off, and he stole a glance at Alyosha — his was the only opinion he was afraid of there. But Alyosha was still silent and serious as before. If Alyosha had said a word, it would have stopped him — but Alyosha was silent and “it might be the silence of contempt,” and that finally irritated Kolya.

67.102.oldText: “The classical languages, too ... they're simply madness, nothing more. You seem to disagree with me again, Karamazov?”

67.103.oldText: “I don't agree,” Alyosha said, with a faint smile.

67.104.oldText: “The study of the classics, if you want my opinion, is simply a police measure — that's the sole reason it was introduced into our schools.” By degrees Kolya was starting to get breathless again. “Latin and Greek were introduced because they're a bore and because they dull the intellect. It was dull before, so what could they do to make things duller? It was senseless enough before, so what could they do to make it more senseless? So they thought of Greek and Latin. That's my opinion; I hope I never change it,” Kolya finished abruptly. His cheeks were flushed.

67.105.oldText: “That's true,” Smurov agreed suddenly, in a ringing tone of conviction. He had been listening attentively.

67.106.oldText: “And yet he's first in Latin himself,” one of the group of boys suddenly cried.

67.107.oldText: “Yes, father — he says that, and yet he's first in Latin,” Ilusha echoed.

67.108.oldText: “What of it?” Kolya thought fit to defend himself, though the praise was very sweet to him. “I am slaving away at Latin because I have to, because I promised my mother I'd pass my examination, and I think whatever you do, it's worth doing well. But in my soul I have a profound contempt for the classics and all that fraud ... You don't agree, Karamazov?”

67.110.oldText: “Well, all the classical authors have been translated into every language, so it wasn't for the sake of studying the classics that they introduced Latin, but solely as a police measure, to dull the intellect. So what can you call it but a fraud?”

67.111.oldText: “Why — who taught you all this?” Alyosha cried, surprised at last.

67.112.oldText: “In the first place, I'm capable of thinking for myself without being taught. Besides, what I just said about the classics being translated — our teacher Kolbasnikov has said the same thing to the whole of the third class.”

67.113.oldText: “The doctor has come!” cried Nina, who had been silent until then.

67.114.oldText: A carriage belonging to Madame Hohlakov drove up to the gate. The captain, who had been expecting the doctor all morning, rushed headlong outside to meet him. “Mamma” pulled herself together and assumed a dignified air. Alyosha went over to Ilusha and began straightening his pillows. From her invalid chair Nina anxiously watched him tidy the bed. The boys hurriedly took their leave. Some of them promised to come again in the evening. Kolya called Perezvon, and the dog jumped off the bed.

67.115.oldText: “I won't go away, I won't go away,” Kolya said hastily to Ilusha. “I'll wait in the passage and come back once the doctor has gone — I'll come back with Perezvon.”

67.116.oldText: But the doctor had already entered — an important-looking person with long, dark whiskers and a shiny, shaven chin, wearing a bearskin coat. As he crossed the threshold he stopped, taken aback; he probably thought he had come to the wrong place. “What's this? Where am I?” he muttered, not removing his coat or his peaked sealskin cap. The crowd, the poverty of the room, the washing hanging on a line in the corner — all of it puzzled him. The captain, bent double, was bowing low before him.

67.117.oldText: “It's here, sir, here, sir,” he muttered cringingly. “It's here — you've come to the right place, you were coming to us...”

67.118.oldText: “Sne-gi-ryov?” the doctor said loudly and pompously. “Mr. Snegiryov — is that you?”

67.121.oldText: The doctor looked around the room with a squeamish air once more and threw off his coat, revealing to everyone the grand decoration on his neck. The captain caught the fur coat as it fell, and the doctor took off his cap.

68.0.oldText: “What do you think the doctor will tell him?” Kolya asked quickly. “What a repulsive mug he has, though, doesn't he? I can't stand medicine!”

68.1.oldText: “Ilusha is dying. I think that's certain,” Alyosha answered mournfully.

68.2.oldText: “They're crooks! Medicine is a fraud! Still, I'm glad to have made your acquaintance, Karamazov. I've wanted to know you for a long time. I'm only sorry we're meeting in such sad circumstances.”

68.3.oldText: Kolya had a great urge to say something even warmer and more demonstrative, but he felt ill at ease. Alyosha noticed it, smiled, and squeezed his hand.

68.4.oldText: “I've long learned to respect you as a rare person,” Kolya muttered again, faltering and uncertain. “I've heard you're a mystic, and have been in the monastery. I know you're a mystic, but ... that hasn't put me off. Contact with real life will cure you. It's always that way with characters like yours.”

68.8.oldText: “Oh, I've nothing against God. Of course, God is only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He's necessary ... for the order of the universe and so on ... and that if there were no God He would have to be invented,” Kolya added, beginning to blush. He suddenly imagined that Alyosha might think he was showing off his knowledge and trying to prove he was “grown up.” “I haven't the slightest desire to show off my knowledge to him,” Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt horribly annoyed.

68.9.oldText: “I must admit I can't stand getting into such discussions,” he said with a final air. “It's possible for someone who doesn't believe in God to love humanity, don't you think? Voltaire didn't believe in God, and he loved humanity, didn't he?” (“I'm at it again,” he thought to himself.)

68.10.oldText: “Voltaire believed in God, though not very much, I think, and I don't think he loved humanity very much either,” Alyosha said quietly, gently, and quite naturally, as though he were talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck by Alyosha's apparent diffidence about his opinion of Voltaire. He seemed to be leaving the question open, for him — little Kolya — to settle.

68.12.oldText: “No, not really ... But I've read _Candide_ in Russian translation ... in an absurd, grotesque old translation. (At it again! Again!)”

68.14.oldText: “Oh, yes, all of it. That is ... why do you suppose I wouldn't understand it? There's a lot of nastiness in it, of course. Of course I can understand that it's a philosophical novel, written to advance an idea.” Kolya was getting tangled up by now. “I am a Socialist, Karamazov — I'm an incurable Socialist,” he announced suddenly, out of nowhere.

68.15.oldText: “A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when have you had time to become one? Why, I thought you were only thirteen?”

68.17.oldText: “First of all, I am not thirteen, but fourteen — fourteen in a fortnight,” he flushed angrily, “and secondly, I am at a complete loss to understand what my age has to do with it. The question is, what are my convictions — not what is my age, isn't it?”

68.18.oldText: “When you're older, you'll understand for yourself the influence of age on one's convictions. I also had the impression you weren't expressing your own ideas,” Alyosha answered serenely and modestly, but Kolya cut him off hotly:

68.19.oldText: “Come, you want obedience and mysticism. You must admit, for instance, that the Christian religion has only been of use to the rich and the powerful to keep the lower classes in slavery. That's so, isn't it?”

68.20.oldText: “Ah, I know where you read that, and I'm sure someone told you so!” Alyosha cried.

68.21.oldText: “Come now, what makes you think I read it? And certainly no one told me so. I can think for myself. I'm not opposed to Christ, if you like. He was a most humane person, and if He were alive today, He'd be in the ranks of the revolutionists, and might well play a prominent part. There's no doubt about that.”

68.22.oldText: “Oh, where, where did you get this from? What fool have you made friends with?” Alyosha exclaimed.

68.23.oldText: “Come, the truth will out! It just so happens that I've often talked to Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said that too, so they say.”

68.24.oldText: “Byelinsky? I don't remember. He hasn't written that anywhere.”

68.25.oldText: “If he didn't write it, they say he said it. I heard it from a ... never mind.”

68.27.oldText: “Well, no ... I haven't read all of him, but ... I read the passage about Tatyana, about why she didn't run off with Onyegin.”

68.28.oldText: “Didn't run off with Onyegin? Surely you don't ... understand that already?”

68.29.oldText: “Why, you seem to take me for little Smurov,” Kolya said, with an irritated grin. “But please don't imagine I'm such a revolutionist. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Even though I bring up Tatyana, I'm not at all for the emancipation of women. I admit that women are a subject race and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said.” Kolya smiled for some reason. “On that question at least, I'm quite in agreement with that pseudo-great man. I also think that leaving one's own country and fleeing to America is mean — worse than mean, silly. Why go to America when one can be of great service to humanity right here? Now, especially. There's a huge amount of fruitful work open to us. That's what I answered.”

68.31.oldText: “I must admit, they've been at me to go, but I refused. That's between ourselves, of course, Karamazov — do you hear, not a word to anyone. I'm telling you this only. I'm not at all eager to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain bridge.

68.33.oldText: Do you remember? It's splendid. Why are you laughing? You don't suppose I'm lying, do you?” (“What if he finds out I've only got the one number of _The Bell_ in father's bookcase, and haven't read any more of it?” Kolya thought with a shudder.)

68.34.oldText: “Oh no, I'm not laughing, and I don't suppose for a moment that you're lying. No, indeed, I can't think that — because all this, alas, is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin — _Onyegin_, for example?... You were speaking about Tatyana just now.”

68.35.oldText: “No, I haven't read it yet, but I want to. I have no prejudices, Karamazov; I want to hear both sides. What makes you ask?”

68.37.oldText: “Tell me, Karamazov, do you have an awful contempt for me?” Kolya rapped out suddenly, drawing himself up in front of Alyosha as though on drill. “Be so kind as to tell me without beating around the bush.”

68.38.oldText: “Contempt for you?” Alyosha looked at him in wonder. “What for? I'm only sad that a charming nature such as yours should be perverted by all this crude nonsense before you've even begun to live.”

68.39.oldText: “Don't worry about my nature,” Kolya interrupted, not without complacency. “But it's true I'm stupidly sensitive, crudely sensitive. You just smiled, and I imagined you seemed to —”

68.40.oldText: “Oh, my smile meant something quite different. I'll tell you why I smiled. Not long ago I read the criticism a German who had lived in Russia made about our students and schoolboys of today. ‘Show a Russian schoolboy,' he writes, ‘a map of the stars, which he knows nothing about, and he'll bring you back the map the next day with corrections on it.' No knowledge and unbounded conceit — that's what the German was saying about the Russian schoolboy.”

68.41.oldText: “Yes, that's absolutely right,” Kolya suddenly laughed. “Exactly so! Bravo, German! But he didn't see the good side — what do you think? Conceit, yes — that comes from youth, and it will be corrected if need be; but on the other hand, there's an independent spirit almost from childhood, boldness of thought and conviction, not the spirit of these sausage makers, groveling before authority. Still, the German was right all the same. Bravo, German! But the Germans should be strangled all the same. Though they're so good at science and learning, they must be strangled.”

68.43.oldText: “Well, perhaps I'm talking nonsense, I admit. I'm awfully childish sometimes, and when I'm pleased about anything I can't restrain myself and am ready to talk all kinds of rubbish. But look here, we're chattering away here about nothing, and that doctor's been in there a long time. But perhaps he's examining mamma and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. As I was leaving she whispered to me suddenly, ‘Why didn't you come before?' And in such a voice, so reproachfully! I think she's awfully nice and touching.”

68.44.oldText: “Yes, yes! Well, you'll be coming often; you'll see what she's like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like her — to learn to value a great deal that you'll only find out by knowing these people,” Alyosha observed warmly. “That would have more effect on you than anything.”

68.45.oldText: “Oh, how I regret and blame myself for not having come sooner!” Kolya exclaimed, with bitter feeling.

68.46.oldText: “Yes, it's a great pity. You saw for yourself how delighted the poor child was to see you. And how he fretted for you to come!”

68.47.oldText: “Don't tell me! You're making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me from coming was my conceit, my egoistic vanity, and the beastly willfulness I can never seem to shake, though I've struggled with it all my life. I see that now. I am a beast in many ways, Karamazov!”

68.48.oldText: “No, you have a charming nature, though it's been distorted, and I quite understand why you have had such an influence on this generous, morbidly sensitive boy,” Alyosha answered warmly.

68.49.oldText: “And you say that to me!” Kolya cried. “And would you believe it, I thought — I've thought several times since I've been here — that you despised me! If you only knew how I prize your opinion!”

68.50.oldText: “But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it, just now, as you were telling your story, I thought, watching you, that you must be very sensitive!”

68.51.oldText: “You thought so? What an eye you have, I say! I bet that was when I was talking about the goose. That was exactly when I was imagining you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I actually hated you for it, and began talking like a fool. Then I imagined — just now, here — when I said that if there were no God He would have to be invented, that I was in too great a hurry to parade my knowledge, especially since I got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn't showing off out of vanity, though I really don't know why. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I think it was because I was so pleased ... though it's perfectly disgraceful for anyone to start gushing the moment he's pleased, I know that. But I'm convinced now that you don't despise me — it was all in my imagination. Oh, Karamazov, I'm profoundly unhappy. I sometimes imagine all sorts of things — that everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things.”

68.52.oldText: “And you worry everyone around you,” Alyosha smiled.

68.53.oldText: “Yes, I worry everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me — am I very ridiculous now?”

68.54.oldText: “Don't think about that, don't think about it at all!” Alyosha cried. “And what does ridiculous mean? Isn't everyone constantly being or seeming ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people now are terribly afraid of being ridiculous, and that makes them unhappy. The only thing that surprises me is that you should be feeling it so early, though I've noticed it for some time, and not only in you. Nowadays even the children have begun to suffer from it. It's almost a kind of insanity. The devil has taken the form of that vanity and entered into the whole generation; it's simply the devil,” Alyosha added, without a trace of the smile Kolya, staring at him, had expected to see. “You are like everyone else,” Alyosha said in conclusion, “that is, like a great many others. Only you must not be like everyone else — that's all.”

68.56.oldText: “Yes, even if everyone is like that. Be the one who is not. You really are not like everyone else — here you're not ashamed to confess to something bad, and even ridiculous. And who will admit that much these days? No one. People have even stopped feeling the impulse to self-criticism. Don't be like everyone else, even if you're the only one.”

68.57.oldText: “Splendid! I wasn't mistaken in you. You know how to console a person. Oh, how I've longed to know you, Karamazov! I've long been eager for this meeting. Can you really have thought about me, too? You said just now that you had thought of me?”

68.58.oldText: “Yes, I'd heard about you and thought about you, too ... and if it's partly vanity that makes you ask — well, it doesn't matter.”

68.59.oldText: “You know, Karamazov, our talk has been like a declaration of love,” said Kolya, in a bashful, melting voice. “That's not ridiculous, is it?”

68.60.oldText: “Not at all ridiculous, and even if it were, it wouldn't matter, because it's been a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.

68.61.oldText: “But you know, Karamazov, you must admit that you're a little ashamed yourself, right now ... I can see it in your eyes.” Kolya smiled with a kind of sly happiness.

68.64.oldText: “It was you who made me blush,” Alyosha laughed, and he really did blush. “Oh, well, I am a little, goodness knows why — I don't know...” he muttered, almost embarrassed.

68.65.oldText: “Oh, how I love you and admire you at this moment, precisely because you're a little ashamed yourself! Because you are just like me!” Kolya cried, in positive ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes beamed.

68.66.oldText: “You know, Kolya, you're going to be very unhappy in life,” something made Alyosha say suddenly.

68.67.oldText: “I know, I know. How you know it all in advance!” Kolya agreed at once.

68.68.oldText: “But you'll bless life on the whole, all the same.”

68.69.oldText: “Exactly — hurrah! You're a prophet. Oh, we'll get on together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me entirely like an equal. But we are not equals, no, we are not — you are better. But we'll get on. Do you know, all this last month I've been saying to myself, ‘Either we'll be friends at once, forever, or we'll part as enemies to the grave!'”

68.71.oldText: “I did. I loved you awfully. I've been loving you and dreaming of you. And how is it you know everything in advance? Ah, here's the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!”

69.0.oldText: The doctor came out of the room again, bundled up in his fur coat and with his cap on his head. His face looked almost angry and disgusted, as though he were afraid of getting dirty. He cast a cursory glance around the passage, looking sternly at Alyosha and Kolya as he did so. Alyosha waved from the doorway to the coachman, and the carriage that had brought the doctor drove up. The captain darted out after the doctor and, bowing apologetically, stopped him to get one last word. The poor fellow looked utterly crushed; there was a scared look in his eyes.

69.1.oldText: “Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it possible?” he began, but couldn't go on, and clasped his hands in despair. Still he kept gazing imploringly at the doctor, as though a word from him might yet change the poor boy's fate.

69.2.oldText: “I can't help it — I am not God!” the doctor answered offhand, though with his customary air of importance.

69.3.oldText: “Doctor ... your Excellency ... and will it be soon, soon?”

69.4.oldText: “You must be prepared for anything,” the doctor said in emphatic, cutting tones, and, dropping his eyes, he was about to step out to the carriage.

69.5.oldText: “Your Excellency, for Christ's sake!” the terror-stricken captain stopped him again. “Your Excellency, can nothing, absolutely nothing save him now?”

69.6.oldText: “It's no longer in my hands,” the doctor said impatiently, “but h'mm ...” he stopped suddenly. “If you could, for instance ... send ... your patient ... at once, without delay” (the words “at once, without delay” the doctor uttered with an almost wrathful sternness that made the captain start) “to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-fi-cial climatic conditions might possibly —”

69.7.oldText: “To Syracuse!” the captain cried, unable to grasp what had been said.

69.8.oldText: “Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya jerked out suddenly by way of explanation. The doctor looked at him.

69.9.oldText: “Sicily! Your Excellency,” faltered the captain, “but you've seen” — he spread out his hands, taking in his surroundings — “mamma, and my family?”

69.10.oldText: “N-no, Sicily is not the place for the family — the family should go to the Caucasus in the early spring ... your daughter to the Caucasus, and your wife ... after a course of the waters in the Caucasus for her rheumatism ... must be sent straight to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier; I could give you a note to him, and then ... there might be a change —”

69.11.oldText: “Doctor, doctor! But you see!” The captain flung his hands wide again in despair, gesturing at the bare wooden walls of the passage.

69.12.oldText: “Well, that's not my business,” the doctor grinned. “I've only told you the answer of medical science to your question about possible treatment. As for the rest, to my regret —”

69.13.oldText: “Don't be afraid, apothecary — my dog won't bite you,” Kolya rapped out loudly, noticing the doctor's rather uneasy glance at Perezvon, who was standing in the doorway. There was a note of wrath in Kolya's voice. He used the word “apothecary” instead of “doctor” on purpose — and, as he explained later, used it “to insult him.”

69.14.oldText: “What's that?” The doctor flung up his head, staring with surprise at Kolya. “Who's this?” He turned to Alyosha, as if asking him to explain.

69.15.oldText: “It's Perezvon's master — don't worry about me,” Kolya said incisively, again.

69.17.oldText: “He hears the bell, but where it is he cannot tell. Good-bye, we'll meet again in Syracuse.”

69.18.oldText: “Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor flew into a terrible rage.

69.19.oldText: “He's a schoolboy, doctor, he's a mischievous boy — take no notice of him,” Alyosha said quickly, frowning. “Kolya, hold your tongue!” he cried to Krassotkin. “Take no notice of him, doctor,” he repeated, rather impatiently.

69.20.oldText: “He needs a thrashing, a good thrashing!” The doctor stamped his foot in a perfect fury.

69.21.oldText: “And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might bite!” said Kolya, turning pale, his voice quivering and his eyes flashing. “_Ici_, Perezvon!”

69.22.oldText: “Kolya, if you say another word I'll have nothing more to do with you,” Alyosha cried peremptorily.

69.23.oldText: “There's only one man in the world who can give an order to Nikolay Krassotkin — this is the man,” Kolya said, pointing at Alyosha. “I obey him. Good-bye!”

69.24.oldText: He stepped forward, opened the door, and went quickly into the inner room. Perezvon flew in after him. The doctor stood still for five seconds in amazement, looking at Alyosha; then, with a curse, he went out quickly to the carriage, muttering aloud, “This is ... this is ... I don't know what this is!” The captain darted ahead to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya into the room. He was already by Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back too.

69.25.oldText: “Father, father, come ... we ...” Ilusha faltered in violent excitement, but apparently unable to go on, he flung his wasted arms around his father and Kolya, uniting them in one embrace and hugging them as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly began to shake with silent sobs, and Kolya's lips and chin twitched.

69.26.oldText: “Father, father! How sorry I am for you!” Ilusha moaned bitterly.

69.27.oldText: “Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you'll be all right ... we'll be happy ... the doctor ...” the captain began.

69.28.oldText: “Ah, father! I know what the new doctor said to you about me. I saw!” Ilusha cried, and hugged them both again with all his strength, hiding his face on his father's shoulder.

69.29.oldText: “Father, don't cry. And when I die, take another good boy, another one ... choose one of them all, a good one, call him Ilusha and love him instead of me ...”

69.30.oldText: “Hush, old man, you'll get well,” Krassotkin cried suddenly, in a voice that sounded angry.

69.31.oldText: “But don't ever forget me, father,” Ilusha went on. “Come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go for our walk, and come to me there with Krassotkin in the evening ... and Perezvon ... I'll be waiting for you. Father, father!”

69.32.oldText: His voice broke. The three of them were silent, still embracing. Nina was crying quietly in her chair, and at last, seeing them all weep, “mamma” too burst into tears.

69.34.oldText: Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha's embrace.

69.35.oldText: “Good-bye, old man — mother's expecting me home for dinner,” he said quickly. “What a pity I didn't tell her! She'll be terribly anxious. But after dinner I'll come back to you for the whole day, for the whole evening, and I'll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I'll bring Perezvon — but now I'll take him with me, because he'll start howling when I'm gone and bother you. Good-bye!”

69.36.oldText: And he ran out into the passage. He didn't want to cry, but in the passage he burst into tears. Alyosha found him crying.

69.37.oldText: “Kolya, you must be sure to keep your word and come, or he'll be terribly disappointed,” Alyosha said emphatically.

69.38.oldText: “I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not having come sooner!” muttered Kolya, crying, and no longer ashamed of it.

69.39.oldText: At that moment the captain flew out of the room and at once closed the door behind him. His face looked frenzied; his lips were trembling. He stood in front of the two and flung up his arms.

69.40.oldText: “I don't want a good boy! I don't want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, clenching his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue —” He broke off with a sob and sank to his knees in front of the wooden bench. Pressing his fists against his head, he began sobbing with absurd whimpering cries, doing his utmost that his cries not be heard inside the room.

69.42.oldText: “Good-bye, Karamazov. Will you come yourself?” he cried sharply and angrily to Alyosha.

69.44.oldText: “What was that he said about Jerusalem? What did he mean by that?”

69.45.oldText: “It's from the Bible. ‘If I forget thee, Jerusalem,' that is, if I forget what is most precious to me, if I let anything take its place, may —”

69.46.oldText: “I understand, that's enough! Mind you come. _Ici_, Perezvon!” he cried with positive ferocity to the dog, and with rapid strides he set off for home.

70.0.oldText: Alyosha made his way to the cathedral square, to the widow Morozov's house, to see Grushenka, who had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message begging him to come. Questioning Fenya, Alyosha learned that her mistress had been particularly distressed since the day before. In the two months that had passed since Mitya's arrest, Alyosha had called frequently at the widow Morozov's house, both from his own inclination and to bring messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya's arrest, Grushenka had fallen very ill, and had been ill for nearly five weeks. For one whole week she had been unconscious. She was much changed — thinner and a little sallow — though she had been well enough to go out for the past fortnight. But to Alyosha her face was even more attractive than before, and he liked to meet her eyes when he went in to her. A look of firmness and intelligent purpose had developed in her face. There were signs of a spiritual transformation in her, and a steadfast, fine, humble resolve that nothing could shake could be seen in her. There was a small vertical line between her brows that gave her charming face a look of concentrated thought, almost austere at first glance. There was scarcely a trace left of her former frivolity.

70.1.oldText: It seemed strange to Alyosha, too, that in spite of the calamity that had overtaken the poor girl — betrothed to a man arrested for a terrible crime almost at the moment of their betrothal — in spite of her illness and the almost inevitable sentence hanging over Mitya, Grushenka had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. There was a soft light in the once proud eyes, though at times they flashed with the old vindictive fire when she was visited by one disturbing thought that had grown stronger than ever in her heart. The object of that uneasiness was still the same — Katerina Ivanovna, about whom Grushenka had even raved while lying delirious. Alyosha knew she was fearfully jealous of her. Yet Katerina Ivanovna had not once visited Mitya in prison, though she might have done so any time she liked. All this created a difficult problem for Alyosha, for he was the only person to whom Grushenka opened her heart, and from whom she was constantly asking advice. Sometimes he was unable to say anything.

70.2.oldText: Full of anxiety he entered her lodging. She was at home. She had come back from seeing Mitya half an hour earlier, and from the quick movement with which she sprang up from her chair to meet him he could see she had been expecting him with great impatience. A pack of cards dealt for a game of “fools” lay on the table. A bed had been made up on the leather sofa across from it, and Maximov lay on it, half-reclining. He was wearing a dressing gown and a cotton nightcap, and was clearly ill and weak, though he was smiling blissfully. When the homeless old man had come back with Grushenka from Mokroe two months before, he had simply stayed on, and was still staying with her. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa, drenched and scared, and gazed at her mutely with a timid, pleading smile. Grushenka, who was in terrible grief and in the first stage of fever, had almost forgotten his existence amid everything she had to do in the first half-hour after arriving. Then she happened to look at him closely: he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to bring him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same place, almost without stirring. When it got dark and the shutters were closed, Fenya asked her mistress:

70.3.oldText: “Is the gentleman going to stay the night, mistress?”

70.4.oldText: “Yes — make him a bed on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.

70.5.oldText: Questioning him more carefully, Grushenka learned from him that he literally had nowhere to go, and that “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me straight out that he wouldn't receive me again, and gave me five roubles.”

70.6.oldText: “Well, God bless you, you'd better stay, then,” Grushenka decided in her grief, smiling at him compassionately. Her smile wrung the old man's heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. And so the destitute wanderer had stayed with her ever since. He did not leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother the cook did not turn him out, but went on serving him meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had grown used to him, and coming back from seeing Mitya (whom she had started visiting in prison before she was really well) she would sit down and start chatting with “Maximushka” about trivial matters, to keep herself from dwelling on her sorrow. The old man turned out to be a good storyteller on occasion, so that in the end she found him a necessity. Apart from Alyosha — who didn't come every day and never stayed long — Grushenka saw scarcely anyone. Her old merchant lay gravely ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as they said around town, and he did indeed die a week after Mitya's trial. Three weeks before his death, sensing the end drawing near, he had at last summoned his sons, their wives, and their children upstairs and told them not to leave him again. From that moment he gave strict orders to his servants not to admit Grushenka, and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness, and tells you to forget him.” But Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

70.7.oldText: “You've come at last!” she cried, tossing aside the cards and greeting Alyosha joyfully. “Maximushka has been scaring me that perhaps you wouldn't come. Ah, how I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have — coffee?”

70.8.oldText: “Yes, please,” Alyosha said, sitting down at the table. “I'm very hungry.”

70.9.oldText: “That's good. Fenya, Fenya, coffee,” Grushenka cried. “It's been ready for you for ages. And bring some little pies, and mind they're hot. Do you know, we've had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and would you believe, he threw them back at me: he wouldn't eat them. He flung one of them on the floor and stamped on it. So I said to him, ‘I'll leave them with the warder; if you don't eat them by evening, then your venomous spite is enough to feed you!' With that, I left. We had another quarrel, would you believe it? Every time I go, we quarrel.”

70.10.oldText: Grushenka said all this in one breath in her agitation. Maximov, feeling nervous, smiled at once and stared at the floor.

70.11.oldText: “What did you quarrel about this time?” Alyosha asked.

70.12.oldText: “I didn't expect it in the least. Just imagine — he's jealous of the Pole. ‘Why are you keeping him?' he said. ‘So you've started keeping him.' He's jealous, jealous of me all the time — jealous over my eating and sleeping! Last week he even took it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”

70.13.oldText: “But he knew about the Pole before?”

70.14.oldText: “Yes, exactly. He has known about him from the very beginning, but today he suddenly got going and began scolding me about him. I'm ashamed to repeat what he said. Silly fool! Rakitin went in as I was leaving. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added carelessly.

70.15.oldText: “He loves you — that's what it is. He loves you so much. And right now he's especially worried.”

70.16.oldText: “I should think so, with the trial tomorrow. I went to him to say something about tomorrow, because I dread to think what's going to happen then. You say he's worried — but how worried am I! And he talks about the Pole! He's too silly! At least he's not jealous of Maximushka yet.”

70.17.oldText: “My wife was dreadfully jealous over me too,” Maximov put in.

70.18.oldText: “Jealous of you?” Grushenka laughed in spite of herself. “Of whom could she have been jealous?”

70.20.oldText: “Hush, Maximushka, I'm in no mood for laughing now; I'm angry. Don't stare at the pies. I won't give you any — they're no good for you, and I won't give you any vodka either. I have to look after him, too, as though I ran an almshouse,” she laughed.

70.21.oldText: “I don't deserve your kindness. I'm a worthless creature,” said Maximov, with tears in his voice. “You'd do better spending your kindness on people more useful than me.”

70.22.oldText: “Ech, everyone has some use, Maximushka — how can anyone say who's the most useful? If only that Pole didn't exist, Alyosha. He's taken it into his head to fall ill today too. I went to see him as well. And I'll send him some pies — on purpose. I hadn't been sending him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I'll send some! Ah, here's Fenya with a letter! Yes, it's from the Poles — begging again!”

70.23.oldText: Pan Mussyalovitch had in fact sent an extremely long and, in his characteristic fashion, eloquent letter, begging her to lend him three roubles. Enclosed with the letter was a receipt for the sum, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Grushenka had received many such letters, accompanied by such receipts, from her former lover during the fortnight of her convalescence. But she knew the two Poles had come to ask after her health during her illness. The first letter Grushenka got from them was a long one, written on large notepaper with a big family crest on the seal. It was so obscure and rhetorical that Grushenka put it down before she'd read half of it, unable to make head or tail of it. She couldn't be bothered with letters then. The first letter was followed next day by another, in which Pan Mussyalovitch begged her for a loan of two thousand roubles for a very short period. Grushenka left that letter unanswered too. A whole series of letters followed — one a day — all as pompous and rhetorical, but the sum asked for gradually shrank, down to a hundred roubles, then to twenty-five, to ten, and finally Grushenka received a letter in which both Poles begged her for a single rouble, enclosing a receipt signed by both.

70.24.oldText: At that point Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went over to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost destitute, without food or fuel, without cigarettes, in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon disappeared. But Grushenka was surprised to find them receiving her with arrogant dignity and self-assertion, with the greatest punctilio and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed, and gave her former admirer ten roubles. Then, laughing, she told Mitya about it, and he was not in the least jealous. But ever since, the Poles had attached themselves to Grushenka and bombarded her daily with requests for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, that day, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

70.25.oldText: “Like a fool, I went round to him just for a minute on the way to see Mitya, because he's ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again in nervous haste. “I was laughing, telling Mitya about it. ‘Imagine,' I said, ‘my Pole had the happy idea of singing his old songs to me on the guitar. He thought I'd be touched and marry him!' Mitya leapt up swearing. So, there — I'll send them the pies! Fenya, is that the little girl they've sent? Here, give her three roubles, and pack up a dozen pies in paper for her and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”

70.26.oldText: “I wouldn't tell him for anything,” Alyosha said, smiling.

70.27.oldText: “Ech, you think he's unhappy about it. Why, he's jealous on purpose. He doesn't care,” Grushenka said bitterly.

70.29.oldText: “I'm telling you, you're silly, Alyosha. You know nothing about it, for all your cleverness. I'm not offended that he's jealous of a girl like me. I'd be offended if he weren't jealous. That's who I am. I'm not offended by jealousy. I have a fierce heart too. I can be jealous myself. What offends me is that he doesn't love me at all. I'm telling you he's jealous now _on purpose_. Am I blind? Don't I see? Just now he started talking to me about that woman, about Katerina — saying she's this and that, how she has ordered a doctor from Moscow for him, to try to save him, and hired the best legal counsel, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he'll praise her to my face — all the more shame to him! He's treated me badly himself, so he's turned on me, to make out that I'm the one at fault first, and shift it all onto me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can't be blamed for Katerina,' — that's what it amounts to. He wants to pin the whole blame on me. He went at me on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I'll —”

70.30.oldText: Grushenka couldn't finish saying what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and sobbed violently.

70.31.oldText: “He doesn't love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.

70.32.oldText: “Well, whether he loves her or not, I'll soon find out for myself,” Grushenka said, with a menacing note in her voice, taking the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was distorted. Alyosha saw sadly that from being mild and serene, it had become sullen and spiteful.

70.33.oldText: “Enough of this foolishness,” she said suddenly. “That's not why I sent for you. Alyosha, darling — tomorrow — what will happen tomorrow? That's what's eating at me! And I'm the only one it's eating at! I look at everyone, and no one is thinking about it. No one cares. Are you even thinking about it? Tomorrow they'll try him, you know. Tell me, how will he be tried? It was the valet — the valet killed him! Good heavens! Can they convict him in place of the valet, and will no one stand up for him? They haven't bothered the valet at all, have they?”

70.34.oldText: “He's been severely cross-examined,” Alyosha observed thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion it wasn't him. Now he's lying very ill. He's been ill ever since that attack. Really ill,” Alyosha added.

70.35.oldText: “Oh, dear! Couldn't you go to that counsel yourself and tell him the whole thing in person? They say he's been brought from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

70.36.oldText: “We put up the three thousand together — Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna, and I — but she paid two thousand for the doctor from Moscow herself. The counsel, Fetyukovitch, would have charged more, but the case has become known all over Russia; it's being talked of in every newspaper and journal. Fetyukovitch agreed to come more for the glory of the thing, because the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”

70.37.oldText: “Well? Did you talk to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.

70.38.oldText: “He listened and said nothing. He told me he's already formed his opinion. But he promised to give my words consideration.”

70.39.oldText: “Consideration! Ah, they're swindlers! They'll ruin him. And why did she send for the doctor?”

70.40.oldText: “As an expert. They want to prove Mitya's mad, and that he committed the murder when he didn't know what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won't agree to that.”

70.41.oldText: “Yes — and that would be the truth if he had killed him!” Grushenka cried. “He was mad then, perfectly mad, and it was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn't do it, he didn't do it! And they're all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya's testimony went to prove he did it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern too — before, people had heard him say so! They are all, all against him, all crying out against him.”

70.42.oldText: “Yes, there's a fearful accumulation of evidence,” Alyosha observed grimly.

70.43.oldText: “And Grigory — Grigory Vassilyevitch — sticks to his story that the door was open, insists he saw it — there's no shaking him. I went and talked to him myself. He's rude about it too.”

70.44.oldText: “Yes, that's perhaps the strongest evidence against him,” Alyosha said.

70.45.oldText: “And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems like it now,” Grushenka began with a peculiarly anxious and mysterious air. “Do you know, Alyosha, I've been wanting to talk to you about this for a long time. I go to him every day and simply wonder at him. Tell me, now — what do you suppose he's always talking about? He talks and talks, and I can't make anything of it. I imagined he was talking about something intellectual that I was too foolish to understand. Then he suddenly started talking to me about a babe — about some child. ‘Why is the babe poor?' he said. ‘It's for that babe that I'm going to Siberia now. I am not a murderer, but I must go to Siberia!' What that meant, what babe, I couldn't tell for the life of me. Only I cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried himself, and I cried too. He suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha, tell me? What is this babe?”

70.46.oldText: “It must be Rakitin, who's been going to see him lately,” Alyosha said, smiling, “though ... that's not Rakitin's doing. I didn't see Mitya yesterday. I'll see him today.”

70.47.oldText: “No, it's not Rakitin — it's his brother Ivan Fyodorovitch upsetting him. It's his visits — that's what it is,” Grushenka began, and suddenly broke off. Alyosha stared at her in amazement.

70.48.oldText: “Ivan's visits? Has he been to see him? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn't been once.”

70.49.oldText: “There ... there! What a girl I am! Blurting it out!” Grushenka exclaimed, confused, and suddenly blushing. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I've said this much, I'll tell you the whole truth — he's been to see him twice, the first time right after he arrived. He galloped here from Moscow at once, of course, before I was taken ill; and the second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it under any circumstances — not to tell anyone, in fact. He came secretly.”

70.50.oldText: Alyosha sat plunged in thought, considering something. The news clearly struck him.

70.51.oldText: “Ivan doesn't talk to me about Mitya's case,” he said slowly. “He's said very little to me these last two months. And whenever I go to see him, he seems vexed that I've come, so I haven't been to see him for the last three weeks. Hm ... if he was there a week ago ... there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”
