70.52.oldText: “There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They have a secret, they have a secret! Mitya told me himself there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can't rest. Before this he was cheerful — and indeed he is cheerful now — but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and strides around the room and keeps tugging at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, I know there's something weighing on his mind. I know! He was cheerful before — and indeed, he is cheerful today.”

70.54.oldText: “Yes, he's worried, and yet cheerful. He keeps being irritable for a minute, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I'm constantly amazed at him — with this awful thing hanging over him, he sometimes laughs at such trifles, as though he were a child himself.”

70.55.oldText: “And did he really tell you not to tell me about Ivan? Did he say, ‘Don't tell him'?”

70.56.oldText: “Yes, he said, ‘Don't tell him.' It's you Mitya's most afraid of. Because it's a secret — he said himself it was a secret. Alyosha, darling, go to him and find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged him with sudden eagerness. “Set my mind at rest so I know the worst that's in store for me. That's why I sent for you.”

70.57.oldText: “You think it's something to do with you? If it were, he wouldn't have told you there was a secret.”

70.58.oldText: “I don't know. Perhaps he wants to tell me, but doesn't dare. He's warning me. There is a secret, he tells me — but he won't tell me what it is.”

70.60.oldText: “What do I think? It's the end for me, that's what I think. The three of them have been plotting my end — because Katerina's in it. It's all Katerina, it all comes from her. She's this and that — meaning that I'm not. He's telling me that in advance — warning me. He's planning to throw me over, that's the whole secret. They've planned it together, the three of them — Mitya, Katerina, and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I've been wanting to ask you for a long time. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he often goes to see her. Did he tell me the truth, or not? Tell me on your conscience — tell me the worst.”

70.61.oldText: “I won't tell you a lie. Ivan is not in love with Katerina Ivanovna — I think.”

70.62.oldText: “Oh, that's what I thought! He's lying to me, shameless deceiver, that's what it is! And he was jealous of me just now, so he could throw the blame on me afterwards. He's stupid — he can't disguise what he's up to; he's so transparent, you know. But I'll give it to him, I'll give it to him! ‘You believe I did it,' he said. He said that to me, to me. He reproached me with that! God forgive him! You wait, I'll make it hot for Katerina at the trial! I'll just say one word then ... I'll tell everything then!”

70.64.oldText: “This much I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” Alyosha said, getting up. “First, that he loves you — loves you more than anyone in the world, and you alone. Believe me. I know. I do know. The second thing is that I don't want to worm his secret out of him, but if he tells me of his own accord today, I'll tell him straight out that I've promised to tell you. Then I'll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I have a feeling ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. I'm sure of it. It hardly seems likely to be about Katerina Ivanovna — at least, that's how it seems to me. Good-bye for now.”

70.65.oldText: Alyosha shook her hand. Grushenka was still crying. He could see she put little faith in his consolation, but she was better for having cried herself out, for having spoken of it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state of mind, but he was in a hurry. He had a great many things still to do.

71.0.oldText: The first of these errands was at Madame Hohlakov's house, and he hurried there to get it over as quickly as possible and not be too late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been slightly unwell for the last three weeks: her foot had for some reason swollen up, and although she wasn't bedridden, she lay all day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir in a fascinating but decorous _déshabillé_. Alyosha had once noted with innocent amusement that in spite of her illness Madame Hohlakov had begun to be rather dressy — top-knots, ribbons, loose wrappers had appeared, and he had an inkling of the reason, though he dismissed such thoughts as frivolous. Over the last two months the young official Perhotin had become a regular visitor at the house.

71.1.oldText: Alyosha hadn't called for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight to Lise, since it was with her that he needed to speak; Lise had sent a maid to him the day before, specifically asking him to come to her “about something very important” — a request which, for certain reasons, was of interest to Alyosha. But while the maid went to take his name in to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived, and immediately sent word begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was better to accede to mamma's request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise's room every other minute while he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on a couch. She was particularly smartly dressed and was clearly in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

71.2.oldText: “It's ages, ages, absolute ages since I've seen you! A whole week — think of it! Ah, but you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You've come to see Lise. I'm sure you meant to slip into her room on tiptoe without my hearing. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But that later — though it is the most important thing, that later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust you with my Lise utterly. Since the death of Father Zossima — God rest his soul!” (she crossed herself) “— I look on you as a monk, though you look charming in your new suit. Where did you find such a tailor in these parts? No, no, that isn't the main thing — that later. Forgive me for sometimes calling you Alyosha; an old woman like me may take liberties,” she smiled coquettishly. “But that later too. The important thing is that I mustn't forget what's important. Please remind me of it yourself. As soon as my tongue runs away with me, you just say, ‘the important thing?' Ach — how do I know now what is most important? Ever since Lise took back her promise — her childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch — to marry you, of course you've realized it was only the playful fancy of a sick child who had been so long confined to her chair — thank God, she can walk now! — that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow for your unhappy brother, who tomorrow — But why speak of tomorrow? I'm ready to die at the very thought of tomorrow. Ready to die of curiosity. That doctor was with us yesterday and saw Lise. I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that's not the point, that's not the point again. You see, I'm mixing everything up. I'm in such a hurry. Why am I in a hurry? I don't know. It's dreadful how I seem to be losing my grip on everything. Everything seems mixed up in a sort of tangle. I'm afraid you're so bored you'll jump up and run away, and that will be all I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here and no coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”

71.3.oldText: Alyosha hurried to thank her and said he had only just had coffee.

71.6.oldText: “At ... that woman's? Ah, she's the one who has brought ruin on everyone. Though I know nothing about it. They say she has turned into a saint — though rather late in the day. She ought to have done it before. What use is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, for I have so much to say to you that I'm afraid I won't say any of it. This awful trial ... I'll certainly go, I'm making arrangements. I'll be carried there in my chair; besides, I can sit up. I'll have people with me. And, you know, I'm a witness. How am I to speak, how am I to speak? I don't know what I'll say. One has to take an oath, doesn't one?”

71.7.oldText: “Yes; but I don't think you'll be able to go.”

71.8.oldText: “I can sit up. Ah, you put me out! Ah — this trial, this savage business, and then they're all going off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all this so quickly, so quickly, everything changing, and in the end — nothing. Everyone grows old and has nothing to look forward to but death. Well, so be it! I'm weary. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has disappointed all my hopes. Now she's going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her, and live in the nearest town, and they'll all torment each other. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all — the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Ah, yes — would you believe it, there's a paragraph saying I was ‘a dear friend' of your brother's ——, I can't repeat the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!”

71.9.oldText: “Impossible! Where was the paragraph? What did it say?”

71.10.oldText: “I'll show you right away. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here — in the Petersburg paper _Gossip_. The paper began publishing this year. I'm awfully fond of gossip, and I subscribe, and now it pays me back — this is what gossip comes to! Here it is, here, this passage. Read it.”

71.11.oldText: And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that had been tucked under her pillow.

71.12.oldText: It wasn't exactly that she was upset — she seemed overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really was mixed up in a tangle in her head. The paragraph was very typical, and must have been a great shock to her, but, fortunately perhaps, she was unable at that moment to keep her mind fixed on any one subject, and so might race off a minute later to something else and forget the newspaper altogether.

71.13.oldText: Alyosha was well aware that the story of the terrible case had spread all over Russia. And, good heavens — what wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs, and about himself he had read in the course of those two months, among other equally credible items! One paper had even reported that he had entered a monastery and taken the cowl in horror at his brother's crime. Another contradicted this and said that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken into the monastery strongbox and “made tracks from the monastery.” The present paragraph in the paper _Gossip_ appeared under the heading “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk.” (That, alas, was the name of our little town. I had so far kept it concealed.) It was brief, and Madame Hohlakov was not directly mentioned in it. No names appeared at all, in fact. It merely stated that the criminal, whose forthcoming trial was causing such a sensation — retired army captain, idle swaggerer, and reactionary bully — was constantly involved in amorous intrigues and particularly popular with certain ladies “who were pining in solitude.” One such lady, a pining widow who tried to look young though she had a grown daughter, was so fascinated by him that only two hours before the crime she had offered him three thousand roubles on condition that he elope with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had preferred to murder his father for the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia with the middle-aged charms of his pining lady. This playful paragraph concluded, of course, with an outburst of generous indignation at the wickedness of parricide and at the recently abolished institution of serfdom. Reading it with curiosity, Alyosha folded up the paper and handed it back to Madame Hohlakov.

71.14.oldText: “Well, that must be me,” she hurried on again. “Of course I'm the one meant. Scarcely more than an hour before, I'd suggested gold mines to him, and here they talk of ‘middle-aged charms' as if that were my motive! He writes that out of spite! God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, as I forgive him! You know it's — Do you know who it is? It's your friend Rakitin.”

71.15.oldText: “Perhaps,” said Alyosha, “though I've heard nothing about it.”

71.16.oldText: “It's him, it's him! No ‘perhaps' about it. You know I turned him out of the house. You know the whole story, don't you?”

71.17.oldText: “I know you asked him not to visit you in the future, but why, exactly, I haven't heard ... at least, not from you.”

71.18.oldText: “Ah, then you've heard it from him! He abuses me, I suppose? Abuses me dreadfully?”

71.19.oldText: “Yes, he does; but then he abuses everyone. But why you've given him up, I haven't heard from him either. I see him very seldom these days, in fact. We're not friends.”

71.20.oldText: “Well, then, I'll tell you all about it. There's no help for it — I'll confess, because there's one point in which I was perhaps to blame. Only a little, little point, so small it may not even count. You see, my dear boy” — Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked arch, and a charming though enigmatic smile played over her lips — “you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I'm like a mother to you. No, no — quite the contrary. I speak to you now as though you were my father — mother is quite out of place. Well, it's as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that's just it. I called you a monk just now. Well, that poor young man, your friend, Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can't be angry with him. I feel cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have taken it into his head to fall in love with me. I only noticed it later. At first — a month ago — he just started dropping in more often, almost every day, though, of course, we'd been acquainted before. I knew nothing about it ... and then suddenly it dawned on me, and I began noticing things with surprise. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who works here in the service, began coming regularly. You've met him here any number of times yourself. And he's an excellent, earnest young man, isn't he? He comes once every three days, not every day (though I'd be glad to see him every day), and always so well dressed. Altogether, Alyosha, I love young people — talented, modest, like you — and he has almost the mind of a statesman, he speaks so charmingly, and I'll most certainly, certainly try to get him promotion. He's a future diplomat. On that dreadful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin comes in such boots, and always stretches them out across the carpet. Anyway, he began hinting at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell directly after he pressed my hand like that. He had met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he's always gibing at him, growling at him for some reason. I just watched the way they went on together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone — no, I was laid up by then. Well, I was lying here alone, and suddenly in comes Rakitin, and — imagine! — he brought me some verses of his own composition, a short poem, on my bad foot; that is, he had described my foot in a poem. Wait a minute — how did it go?

71.22.oldText: It began something like that. I can never remember poetry. I've got it here. I'll show it to you later. But it's a charming thing — charming — and, you know, it's not only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I've forgotten it; in fact, it was just the thing for an album. So, of course, I thanked him, and he was clearly flattered. I'd hardly finished thanking him when in comes Pyotr Ilyitch, and Rakitin suddenly looked as black as night. I could see that Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, because Rakitin had certainly wanted to say something after giving me the verses. I had a presentiment of it; but Pyotr Ilyitch came in. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses without saying who was the author. But I'm convinced he guessed, though he won't own it to this day and insists he had no idea. He only says that on purpose. Pyotr Ilyitch immediately began to laugh and set to criticizing it. ‘Wretched doggerel,' he said they were, ‘some divinity student must have written them,' and with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. ‘Good gracious,' I thought, ‘they'll fly at each other.' ‘I wrote them,' he said. ‘I wrote them as a joke,' he said, ‘for I think it degrading to write verses. But they are good poetry. They want to put up a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women's feet, while I wrote with a moral purpose, and you,' he said, ‘are an advocate of serfdom. You've no humane ideas,' he said. ‘You have no modern enlightened feelings, you're untouched by progress, you're a mere pen-pusher,' he said, ‘and you take bribes.' Then I began screaming and imploring them. And Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward, you know. He at once took up the most gentlemanly tone, looked at him sarcastically, listened, and apologized. ‘I'd no idea,' he said. ‘I wouldn't have said it if I had known. I'd have praised it. Poets are all so irritable,' he said. In short, he laughed at him under cover of the most gentlemanly tone. He explained to me afterwards that it had all been sarcastic. I'd thought he was in earnest. But as I lay there, just as before you now, I was thinking, ‘Would it, or would it not, be the proper thing for me to turn Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a visitor in my house?' And, would you believe it, I lay here, shut my eyes, and wondered, would it be the proper thing or not. I fretted and fretted, and my heart began to beat, and I couldn't make up my mind whether to make a scene or not. One voice seemed to be telling me, ‘Speak,' and the other, ‘No, don't speak.' And no sooner had the second voice said that than I cried out, and fainted. Of course, there was a fuss. I got up suddenly and said to Rakitin, ‘It's painful for me to say it, but I don't wish to see you in my house again.' So I turned him out. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch — I know myself that I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn't really angry with him at all; but I suddenly imagined — that was what did it — that it would be such a fine scene. And yet, believe me, it turned out quite natural, because I actually did shed tears and cried for several days afterwards, and then suddenly one afternoon I forgot all about it. So it's been a fortnight since he's been here, and I kept wondering whether he'd come again. I was even wondering yesterday, and then last night this _Gossip_ appeared. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have written it. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it off, and they printed it. It was a fortnight ago, you see. But Alyosha, it's awful how I keep talking and don't say what I want to say. Ah — the words come of themselves!”

71.23.oldText: “It's very important to me to get to my brother on time today,” Alyosha faltered.

71.24.oldText: “To be sure, to be sure! You bring it all back to me. Listen — what is an aberration?”

71.26.oldText: “In the legal sense. An aberration in which everything is pardonable. Whatever you do, you'll be acquitted right away.”

71.28.oldText: “I'll tell you. This Katya ... Ah, she's a charming, charming creature, only I can never make out who it is she's in love with. She was here with me some time ago and I couldn't get anything out of her. Especially since she won't talk to me about anything but surface matters now. She's always talking about my health, and nothing else, and she takes up such a tone with me, too. I simply said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don't care.' Oh yes — I was talking about aberration. This doctor has come. You know the doctor has come? Of course, you know — the one who diagnoses madmen. You sent for him. No, it wasn't you, it was Katya. It's all Katya's doing. Well, you see — a man may be sitting there perfectly sane and suddenly have an aberration. He may be conscious and know what he's doing, and yet be in a state of aberration. And there's no doubt Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. They discovered aberration as soon as the courts were reformed. It's all thanks to the reformed courts. The doctor was here and questioned me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?' he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He came in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!' and then went away and immediately did the murder. ‘I don't want to murder him,' he said, and he suddenly went and murdered him. That's why they'll acquit him — because he struggled against it, and yet he murdered him.”

71.29.oldText: “But he didn't murder him,” Alyosha interrupted rather sharply. He was growing more and more sick with anxiety and impatience.

71.30.oldText: “Yes, I know — it was that old man Grigory who murdered him.”

71.32.oldText: “Yes, yes — it was Grigory. He was lying there where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had struck him down, and then he got up, saw the door open, went in, and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”

71.34.oldText: “Suffering from aberration. When he recovered from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch had given him on the head, he was suffering from aberration; he went and committed the murder. As for his saying he didn't, he very likely doesn't remember. Only, you know, it'll be better, ever so much better, if Dmitri Fyodorovitch murdered him. That's how it must have been, though I'm saying it was Grigory. It certainly was Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that's better, ever so much better! Oh, not that a son should have killed his father — I don't defend that. Children ought to honor their parents — yet it would be better if it were he, because then you'd have nothing to cry about, since he did it while he was unconscious, or rather while he was conscious but didn't know what he was doing. Let them acquit him — that's so humane, and would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about it, but they say this has been going on for a long time. And when I heard it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he's acquitted, make him come straight from the courthouse to dinner with me, and I'll have a party of friends, and we'll drink to the reformed courts. I don't believe he'd be dangerous; besides, I'll invite a great many people, so he could always be led out if he did anything. Then he might be made a justice of the peace or something in another town, because people who've been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And besides, who isn't suffering from aberration nowadays? — you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are ever so many examples of it: a man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he comes across, and no one blames him for it. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are always confirming; they confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before too, and today I suddenly realized it's all down to aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I believe she's quite mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come on your own?”

71.35.oldText: “Yes, she sent for me, and I'm just going to her now.” Alyosha got up resolutely.

71.36.oldText: “Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, perhaps this is the most important thing,” Madame Hohlakov cried, suddenly bursting into tears. “God knows I trust Lise to you with all my heart, and never mind her sending for you on the sly, without telling her mother. But forgive me, I can't trust my daughter so easily to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still consider him the most chivalrous young man. But just imagine — he's been to see Lise, and I knew nothing about it!”

71.37.oldText: “How? What? When?” Alyosha was exceedingly surprised. He had not sat down again and was listening on his feet.

71.38.oldText: “I'll tell you; that's perhaps why I asked you to come — actually, I no longer know why I asked you to come. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has been to see me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend to call on me, and the second time Katya was here and he came because he heard she was here. Of course, I didn't expect him to come often, knowing what a lot he has to do as it is, _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But I suddenly heard he'd been here again — not to see me, but to see Lise. That's six days ago now. He came, stayed five minutes, and went away. And I didn't hear of it till three days afterwards, from Glafira, so it was a great shock to me. I sent for Lise directly. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,' she said, ‘and came in to me to ask after your health.' Of course, that's how it happened. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she distresses me! Would you believe it, one night, four days ago, right after you saw her last time and had gone away, she suddenly had a fit, screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why is it I never have hysterics? Then the next day another fit, and the same thing on the third, and yesterday too, and then yesterday — that aberration. She suddenly screamed out, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I insist you never let him come to the house again.' I was struck dumb at these amazing words, and answered, ‘On what grounds could I refuse to see such an excellent young man, a young man of such learning too, and so unfortunate?' — because all this business is a misfortune, isn't it? She suddenly burst out laughing at my words, and so rudely, you know. Well, I was pleased; I thought I'd amused her and the fits would pass off, especially since I wanted to refuse to see Ivan Fyodorovitch anyway, on account of his strange visits without my knowledge, and I meant to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a rage with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her in the face. That's monstrous; I'm always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was hugging Yulia's feet and kissing them. She sent a message to me that she wasn't coming to me at all, and would never come and see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, crying, and as she kissed me, she pushed me out of the room without saying a word, so I couldn't find out what was the matter. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I rest all my hopes on you — my whole life is in your hands, in fact. I simply beg you to go to Lise and find out everything from her, as you alone can, and come back and tell me — me, her mother — because you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I shall run away. I can stand no more. I have patience; but I may lose patience, and then ... then something awful will happen. Ah, dear me! At last — Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, beaming all over as she saw Perhotin enter the room. “You are late, you are late! Well, sit down, speak, put us out of our suspense. What does the counsel say? Where are you off to, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”

71.40.oldText: “Oh, yes. You won't forget, you won't forget what I asked you? It's a question of life and death!”

71.41.oldText: “Of course I won't forget, if I can ... but I'm so late,” Alyosha muttered, beating a hasty retreat.

71.42.oldText: “No, be sure, be sure to come back in; don't say ‘if I can.' I'll die if you don't,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.

72.0.oldText: Going in to Lise, he found her half reclining in the invalid chair in which she was wheeled about when she couldn't walk. She didn't move to meet him, but her sharp, keen eyes were riveted on his face. There was a feverish look in her eyes; her face was pale and yellow. Alyosha was astonished at the change that had come over her in three days. She was actually thinner. She didn't hold out her hand to him. He touched the thin, long fingers that lay motionless on her dress, then sat down facing her, without a word.

72.1.oldText: “I know you're in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said curtly, “and mamma's kept you for hours in there; she's just been telling you about me and Yulia.”

72.3.oldText: “I've been listening. Why do you stare at me? I wanted to listen, and I listened — there's no harm in that. I'm not going to apologize.”

72.5.oldText: “On the contrary, I'm very happy. Just now I was reflecting, for the thirtieth time, what a good thing it is I refused you and am not going to be your wife. You aren't fit to be a husband. If I were to marry you and give you a note to take to the man I loved after you, you'd take it and be sure to deliver it, and bring an answer back too. Even at forty, you'd still be carrying my love letters for me.”

72.7.oldText: “There's something spiteful about you and yet open-hearted,” Alyosha smiled at her.

72.8.oldText: “The open-heartedness is that I'm not ashamed of myself in front of you. What's more, I don't want to feel ashamed in front of you — in front of you above all. Alyosha, why is it I don't respect you? I'm very fond of you, but I don't respect you. If I respected you, I wouldn't talk to you without shame, would I?”

72.10.oldText: “But do you believe that I'm not ashamed in front of you?”

72.12.oldText: Lise laughed nervously again; she spoke rapidly.

72.13.oldText: “I sent your brother, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, some sweets in prison. Alyosha, you know, you are rather pretty! I'll love you awfully for so quickly letting me off loving you.”

72.15.oldText: “I wanted to tell you a longing I have. I'd like someone to torment me — marry me and then torment me, deceive me and leave. I don't want to be happy.”

72.17.oldText: “Yes, I want disorder. I keep wanting to set the house on fire. I keep picturing how I'll creep up and set fire to the house on the sly — it must be on the sly. They'll try to put it out, but it'll go on burning. And I'll know and say nothing. Ah, what silliness! And how bored I am!”

72.18.oldText: She waved her hand with a look of disgust.

72.19.oldText: “It's your luxurious life,” Alyosha said softly.

72.20.oldText: “Is it better, then, to be poor?”

72.22.oldText: “That's what your monk taught you. That's not true. Let me be rich and everyone else poor — I'll eat sweets and drink cream and not give any to anyone else. Ach, don't speak, don't say anything,” she waved her hand at him, though Alyosha hadn't opened his mouth. “You've told me all that before, I know it all by heart. It bores me. If I'm ever poor, I'll murder somebody, and even if I'm rich I may murder someone perhaps — why do nothing! But you know, I'd like to reap the harvest, to cut the rye? I'll marry you, and you'll become a peasant, a real peasant; we'll keep a colt — shall we? Do you know Kalganov?”

72.24.oldText: “He's always wandering about, dreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? It's better to dream. You can dream the most delightful things, but real life is a bore.' But he'll be married soon for all that; he's already been making love to me. Can you spin tops?”

72.26.oldText: “Well, he's just like a top: he wants to be wound up and set spinning, and then to be lashed, lashed, lashed with a whip. If I marry him, I'll keep him spinning all his life. You aren't ashamed to be with me?”

72.28.oldText: “You're awfully cross because I don't talk about holy things. I don't want to be holy. What will they do to a person in the next world for the greatest sin? You must know all about that.”

72.29.oldText: “God will judge you,” Alyosha said, watching her steadily.

72.30.oldText: “That's just what I'd like. I'd go up and they'd judge me, and I'd burst out laughing in their faces. I'd dreadfully like to set fire to the house, Alyosha — to our house. You still don't believe me?”

72.31.oldText: “Why not? There are children of twelve who long to set fire to something, and do set things on fire too. It's a sort of disease.”

72.32.oldText: “That's not true, that's not true; there may be children, but that's not what I mean.”

72.33.oldText: “You take evil for good; it's a passing crisis, perhaps the result of your illness.”

72.34.oldText: “You do despise me, though! It's simply that I don't want to do good, I want to do evil, and illness has nothing to do with it.”

72.36.oldText: “So that everything might be destroyed. Ah, how nice it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, I sometimes think of doing a fearful lot of harm, every bad thing I can, and I'd do it for a long time on the sly, and then suddenly everyone would find out. Everyone would stand around and point their fingers at me, and I'd look at them all. That would be awfully nice. Why would it be so nice, Alyosha?”

72.37.oldText: “I don't know. It's a craving to destroy something good — or, as you put it, to set fire to something. It happens sometimes.”

72.38.oldText: “I don't only say it, I will do it.”

72.40.oldText: “Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you are not lying one little bit. But perhaps you think I'm saying all this on purpose to annoy you?”

72.41.oldText: “No, I don't think that ... though perhaps there's a little wish to do that in it too.”

72.42.oldText: “There is a little. I can never lie to you,” she declared, with a strange fire in her eyes.

72.43.oldText: What struck Alyosha above everything was her earnestness. There was not a trace of humor or jesting in her face now, though in the old days fun and gaiety had never deserted her, even at her most “earnest” moments.

72.44.oldText: “There are moments when people love crime,” said Alyosha thoughtfully.

72.45.oldText: “Yes, yes! You've uttered my own thought. They love crime — everyone loves crime — they love it always, not just at some ‘moments.' You know, it's as if people made an agreement to lie about it and have lied about it ever since. They all declare that they hate evil, but secretly they all love it.”

72.46.oldText: “And are you still reading nasty books?”

72.47.oldText: “Yes, I am. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow and I steal them.”

72.49.oldText: “I want to destroy myself. There's a boy here who lay down between the rails while the train was passing. Lucky fellow! Listen — your brother is being tried now for murdering his father, and everyone loves that he's killed his father.”

72.51.oldText: “Yes, loves it — everyone loves it! Everyone says it's so awful, but secretly they simply love it. I for one love it.”

72.52.oldText: “There's some truth in what you say about everyone,” Alyosha said softly.

72.53.oldText: “Oh, what ideas you have!” Lise shrieked in delight. “And you a monk, too! You wouldn't believe how I respect you, Alyosha, for never telling lies. Oh, I must tell you a funny dream of mine. I sometimes dream of devils. It's night; I'm in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils all over the place, in all the corners, under the table, and they open the doors — there's a crowd of them behind the doors, and they want to come in and seize me. And they're just coming in, just about to seize me. But I suddenly cross myself and they all draw back, though they don't go away altogether — they stand at the doors and in the corners, waiting. Then suddenly I have a frightful longing to revile God aloud, and so I begin, and then they come crowding back toward me, delighted, and seize me again — and I cross myself again and they all draw back. It's awful fun. It takes one's breath away.”

72.54.oldText: “I've had the same dream too,” Alyosha said suddenly.

72.55.oldText: “Really?” Lise cried, surprised. “I say, Alyosha, don't laugh, that's awfully important. Can two different people have the same dream?”

72.57.oldText: “Alyosha, I tell you, it's awfully important,” Lise went on, with really excessive amazement. “It's not the dream that's important — it's your having had the same dream as me. You never lie to me — don't lie now: is it true? You're not laughing?”

72.59.oldText: Lise seemed extraordinarily impressed, and for half a minute she was silent.

72.60.oldText: “Alyosha, come and see me, come and see me more often,” she said suddenly, in a pleading voice.

72.61.oldText: “I'll always come to see you, all my life,” Alyosha answered firmly.

72.62.oldText: “You're the only person I can talk to, you know,” Lise began again. “I talk to no one but myself and you. Only you in the whole world. And to you more readily than to myself. And I'm not a bit ashamed with you, not a bit. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not a bit? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”

72.64.oldText: “There's a book here in which I read about the trial of a Jew who took a child of four years old and cut off the fingers from both hands, and then crucified him on the wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him, and afterwards, when he was tried, he said the child died soon, within four hours. That was ‘soon'! He said the child moaned, kept on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That's nice!”

72.66.oldText: “Nice. I sometimes imagine it was I who crucified him. He'd hang there moaning and I'd sit opposite him eating pineapple _compote_. I'm awfully fond of pineapple _compote_. Do you like it?”

72.67.oldText: Alyosha looked at her in silence. Her pale, sallow face was suddenly contorted, her eyes burned.

72.68.oldText: “You know, when I read about that Jew I shook with sobs all night. I kept picturing how the little thing cried and moaned (a child of four understands, you know), and all the while the thought of pineapple _compote_ haunted me. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him _particularly_ to come and see me. He came, and I suddenly told him all about the child and the pineapple _compote_. _All_ about it, _all_, and said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and left. He was only here five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up on the couch, her eyes flashing.

72.69.oldText: “Tell me,” Alyosha asked anxiously, “did you send for that person?”

72.73.oldText: “Simply to ask about that, about that child?”

72.74.oldText: “No, not about that at all. But when he came, I asked him about that at once. He answered, laughed, got up, and went away.”

72.77.oldText: “No, because perhaps he believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He's very ill now, too, Lise.”

72.78.oldText: “Yes, he does believe in it,” Lise said, with flashing eyes.

72.79.oldText: “He doesn't despise anyone,” Alyosha went on. “It's just that he doesn't believe anyone. And if he doesn't believe in people, of course he despises them.”

72.82.oldText: “Good,” Lise seemed to grind her teeth. “When he left laughing, I felt that it was nice to be despised. The child with its fingers cut off is nice, and to be despised is nice ...”

72.83.oldText: And she laughed in Alyosha's face, a feverish, malicious laugh.

72.84.oldText: “Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I'd like — Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly jumped up from the couch, rushed to him, and seized him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost groaned. “Is there anyone in the world I could tell what I've told you? I've told you the truth, the truth. I'll kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don't want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don't you love me in the least?” she finished in a frenzy.

72.86.oldText: “And will you weep over me — will you?”

72.88.oldText: “Not because I won't be your wife, but simply weep for me?”

72.90.oldText: “Thank you! It's only your tears I want. Everyone else can punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, not excepting _any one_. Because I don't love anyone. Do you hear, not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha — it's time you went to your brother.” She tore herself away from him suddenly.

72.91.oldText: “How can I leave you like this?” Alyosha said, almost in alarm.

72.92.oldText: “Go to your brother, the prison will be closing; go, here's your hat. Give my love to Mitya, go, go!”

72.93.oldText: And she almost forcibly pushed Alyosha out of the door. He looked at her in pained surprise, when he was suddenly aware of a letter in his right hand, a tiny letter folded up tight and sealed. He glanced at it and instantly read the address, “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had become almost menacing.

72.94.oldText: “Give it to him, you must give it to him!” she ordered him, trembling and beside herself. “Today, at once, or I'll poison myself! That's why I sent for you.”

72.95.oldText: And she slammed the door quickly. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs without going back to Madame Hohlakov — forgetting her, in fact. As soon as Alyosha had gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a little, slid her finger into the crack, and slammed the door with all her might, crushing her finger. Ten seconds later, freeing her finger, she walked softly, slowly, to her chair, sat up straight in it, and looked intently at her blackened finger and at the blood oozing from under the nail. Her lips were quivering and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:

73.0.oldText: It was quite late (days are short in November) when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. It was beginning to get dusk. But Alyosha knew he would be admitted without difficulty. Things were managed in our little town as they are everywhere else. At first, of course, once the preliminary inquiry concluded, relatives and a few other people could only obtain interviews with Mitya by going through certain inevitable formalities. But later, though the formalities weren't relaxed, exceptions were made for at least some of Mitya's visitors. So much so that sometimes the meetings with the prisoner in the room set aside for that purpose were practically _tête-à-tête_.

73.1.oldText: These exceptions, however, were few; only Grushenka, Alyosha, and Rakitin were treated this way. But the captain of police, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably disposed toward Grushenka. His abuse of her at Mokroe weighed on the old man's conscience, and when he learned the whole story, he completely changed his view of her. And, strangely, though he was firmly persuaded of Mitya's guilt, after Mitya was once in prison, the old man came to take a more and more lenient view of him. “He was a man of good heart, perhaps,” he thought, “who had come to grief through drinking and dissipation.” His first horror had given way to pity. As for Alyosha, the police captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin, who had lately taken to coming very often to see the prisoner, was one of the most intimate acquaintances of the “police captain's young ladies,” as he called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent, a scrupulous man in the performance of his duties but kind-hearted. Alyosha, again, had a close long-standing acquaintance with the superintendent, who was fond of talking with him, generally on sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch, and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a great philosopher himself — “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha had an irresistible attraction for him. In the last year the old man had taken to studying the Apocryphal Gospels and was constantly discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit him at the monastery and would spend hours talking with him and with the monks. So even if Alyosha were late at the prison, he had only to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the humblest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. The sentry, of course, didn't trouble him, so long as the authorities were satisfied.

73.2.oldText: When Mitya was summoned from his cell, he always came downstairs to the room set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered the room, he came upon Rakitin just taking his leave of Mitya. They were both talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw him out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin didn't like running into Alyosha, especially of late. He scarcely spoke to him and bowed to him stiffly. Seeing Alyosha enter now, he frowned and looked away as though entirely absorbed in buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began casting around for his umbrella.

73.3.oldText: “I mustn't forget my things,” he muttered, just to say something.

73.4.oldText: “Mind you don't forget other people's things either,” Mitya said as a joke, and laughed at once at his own wit. Rakitin flared up in an instant.

73.5.oldText: “You'd better offer that advice to your own family, who've always been a slave-driving lot, and not to Rakitin,” he cried, suddenly trembling with anger.

73.6.oldText: “What's the matter? I was joking,” Mitya cried. “Damn it all — they're all like that!” he turned to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin's hurriedly retreating figure. “He was sitting here laughing and cheerful, and all at once he boils over like that. He didn't even nod to you. Have you broken with him completely? Why are you so late? I haven't just been waiting for you, I've been thirsting for you all morning. But never mind. We'll make up for it now.”

73.7.oldText: “Why does he come here so often? Surely you two aren't such great friends?” Alyosha asked. He nodded toward the door Rakitin had disappeared through.

73.8.oldText: “Great friends with Rakitin? No, not that much. Is it likely — a pig like that? He considers me ... a scoundrel. They can't take a joke either, that's the worst of such people. They never get a joke, and their souls are dry, dry and flat; they remind me of the prison walls when I was first brought here. But he's a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it's all over with me now.”

73.9.oldText: He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit down next to him.

73.10.oldText: “Yes, the trial's tomorrow. Are you really so hopeless, brother?” Alyosha said, with an apprehensive feeling.

73.11.oldText: “What are you talking about?” Mitya said, looking at him rather uncertainly. “Oh, you mean the trial! Damn it all — until now we've been talking of things that don't matter, about this trial, but I haven't said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial's tomorrow; but it wasn't the trial I meant when I said it was all over with me. Why are you looking at me so critically?”

73.13.oldText: “Ideas, ideas, that's all! Ethics! What is ethics?”

73.16.oldText: “Yes, there is such a science ... but ... I admit I can't explain to you what sort of science it is.”

73.17.oldText: “Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows a lot, damn him! He's not going to be a monk. He means to go to Petersburg. There he'll go in for criticism with an uplifting tendency. Who knows, he may prove useful and make a career for himself too. Ough — they're first-rate, these people, at making careers! Damn ethics. I'm done for, Alexey, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. It makes my heart ache to look at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”

73.19.oldText: “No, not Karl. Wait, I made a mistake. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist or something?”

73.20.oldText: “He must be a savant,” Alyosha answered, “but I admit I can't tell you much about him either. I've heard of him as a savant, but what kind I don't know.”

73.21.oldText: “Well, damn him, then! I don't know either,” Mitya swore. “A scoundrel of some sort, most likely. They're all scoundrels. And Rakitin will make his way. Rakitin will get on anywhere; he's another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They're all over the place.”

73.22.oldText: “But what's the matter?” Alyosha asked insistently.

73.23.oldText: “He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and so launch his literary career. That's what he's coming for; he told me so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to say ‘he couldn't help murdering his father, he was corrupted by his environment,' and so on. He explained it all to me. He's going to give it a tinge of Socialism, he says. But damn the fellow, he can put in a tinge if he likes, I don't care. He can't stand Ivan, he hates him. He's not fond of you either. But I don't turn him out, because he's a clever fellow. Awfully conceited, though. I said to him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren't scoundrels, they're philosophers; all true Russians are philosophers, and though you've studied, you're not a philosopher — you're a vulgar fellow.' He laughed, so maliciously. And I said to him, ‘_De ideabus non est disputandum_.' Isn't that rather good? I can set up for a classicist, you see!” Mitya laughed suddenly.

73.24.oldText: “Why is it all over with you? You just said so,” Alyosha put in.

73.25.oldText: “Why is it all over with me? H'm ... The fact is ... taking it as a whole, I'm sorry to lose God — that's why.”

73.26.oldText: “What do you mean by ‘sorry to lose God'?”

73.27.oldText: “Imagine: inside, in the nerves, in the head — that is, these nerves are in the brain ... (damn them!) there are kinds of little tails, the little tails of those nerves, and as soon as they start quivering ... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes, and then they start quivering, those little tails ... and when they quiver, an image appears ... it doesn't appear at once, but an instant, a second, passes ... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment — devil take the moment! — but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That's why I see, and then think, because of those tails, not at all because I've got a soul, and because I am some sort of image and likeness. All that's nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply bowled me over. It's magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is arising — that much I understand. And yet I'm sorry to lose God!”

73.28.oldText: “Well, that's a good thing, anyway,” Alyosha said.

73.29.oldText: “That I'm sorry to lose God? It's chemistry, brother, chemistry! There's no help for it, your reverence, you'll have to make way for chemistry. And Rakitin does dislike God. Ough — doesn't he dislike Him! That's the sore point with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you preach this in your reviews?' I asked him. ‘Well, if I did it openly, they wouldn't let it through,' he said. He laughed. ‘But what will become of men then?' I asked him. ‘Without God and immortal life? Everything is lawful, they can do whatever they like?' ‘Didn't you know?' he said, laughing. ‘A clever man can do whatever he likes. A clever man knows his way around, but you've put your foot in it, committing a murder, and now you're rotting in prison.' He says that to my face! A regular pig! I used to kick such people out, but now I listen to them. He talks a lot of sense, too. Writes well. He began reading me an article last week. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a minute. Here it is.”

73.30.oldText: Mitya hurriedly pulled a piece of paper from his pocket and read:

73.31.oldText: “‘In order to determine this question, it is above all essential to put one's personality in contradiction to one's reality.' Do you understand that?”

73.32.oldText: “No, I don't,” Alyosha said. He looked at Mitya and listened to him with curiosity.

73.33.oldText: “I don't understand it either. It's dark and obscure, but intellectual. ‘Everyone writes like that now,' he says, ‘it's the effect of their environment.' They're afraid of the environment. He writes poetry too, the rascal. He's written in honor of Madame Hohlakov's foot. Ha ha ha!”

73.35.oldText: “Have you? And have you heard the poem?”

73.37.oldText: “I've got it. Here it is. I'll read it to you. You don't know — I haven't told you — there's quite a story about it. He's a rascal! Three weeks ago he started teasing me. ‘You've landed yourself in a mess, like a fool, for the sake of three thousand, but I'm going to collar a hundred and fifty thousand. I'm going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.' And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She hadn't much brains in her youth, and now at forty she's lost what she had. ‘But she's awfully sentimental,' he says. ‘That's how I'll get hold of her. Once I marry her, I'll take her to Petersburg and there I'll start a newspaper.' And his mouth was simply watering, the beast — not for the widow, but for the hundred and fifty thousand. And he had me believing it. He came to see me every day. ‘She's coming round,' he declared. He was beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he was turned out of the house. Perhotin's carrying everything before him, bravo! I could kiss the silly old noodle for turning him out of the house. And he had written this doggerel. ‘It's the first time I've soiled my hands with poetry,' he said. ‘It's to win her heart, so it's in a good cause. Once I get hold of the silly woman's fortune, I can be of great social utility.' They have this social justification for every nasty thing they do! ‘Anyway, it's better than your Pushkin's poetry,' he said, ‘because I've managed to advocate enlightenment even in that.' I understand what he means about Pushkin — I can quite see his point, if he really was a man of talent and only wrote about women's feet. But wasn't Rakitin stuck up about his doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! ‘On the convalescence of the swollen foot of the object of my affections' — he came up with that for a title. He's a waggish fellow.

73.39.oldText: Yet, 'tis not for her foot I dread — A theme for Pushkin's muse more fit — It's not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!

73.40.oldText: For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane — Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!

73.41.oldText: He's a pig, a regular pig, but he's very arch, the rascal! And he really did work a progressive idea into it. And wasn't he angry when she kicked him out! He was gnashing his teeth!”

73.42.oldText: “He's already taken his revenge,” Alyosha said. “He's written a paragraph about Madame Hohlakov.”

73.44.oldText: “That's his doing, that's his doing!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That's him! These paragraphs ... I know ... the insulting things that have been written about Grushenka, for instance. And about Katya, too. H'm!”

73.45.oldText: He paced across the room with a harassed look.

73.46.oldText: “Brother, I can't stay long,” Alyosha said, after a pause. “Tomorrow will be a great and awful day for you — the judgment of God will be accomplished ... I'm amazed at you — you're walking about here, talking of I don't know what ...”

73.47.oldText: “No, don't be amazed at me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Am I to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We've talked enough about him. I don't want to say any more about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you'll see. Hush!”

73.48.oldText: He went up to Alyosha excitedly and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

73.49.oldText: “Rakitin wouldn't understand it,” he began in a sort of exaltation, “but you, you'll understand it all. That's why I was thirsting for you. You see, there's so much I've been wanting to tell you for ever so long, here, within these peeling walls, but I haven't said a word about what matters most; the moment never seemed to come. Now I can wait no longer. I must pour out my heart to you. Brother, these last two months I've found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden in me, but he'd never have come to the surface if it hadn't been for this blow from heaven. I'm afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I'm not a bit afraid of that — it's something else I'm afraid of now: that that new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer beside me, and I may become friends with him, because even there one may live and love and suffer. One may thaw out and revive a frozen heart in that convict, one may wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature; one may bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we are all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe' at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?' That was a sign to me at that moment. It's for the babe that I'm going. Because we are all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,' because there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.' I go for all, because someone must go for all. I didn't kill father, but I've got to go. I accept it. It's all come to me here, here, within these peeling walls. There are crowds of them there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we'll be in chains and there'll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we'll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it's His privilege — a grand one. Ah, man ought to be dissolved in prayer! What would I be down there without God? Rakitin laughs! If they drive God from the earth, we'll shelter Him underground. One can't exist in prison without God; it's even more impossible than outside prison. And then we men underground will sing from the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”

73.50.oldText: Mitya was almost gasping for breath as he delivered his wild speech. He turned pale, his lips quivered, and tears rolled down his cheeks.

73.51.oldText: “Yes, life is full, there is life even underground,” he began again. “You wouldn't believe, Alexey, how I want to live now, what a thirst for existence and consciousness has sprung up in me within these peeling walls. Rakitin doesn't understand that; all he cares about is building a house and renting out flats. But I've been longing for you. And what is suffering? I'm not afraid of it, even if it were beyond reckoning. I'm not afraid of it now. I was afraid of it before. Do you know, perhaps I won't answer at the trial at all. And I feel such strength in me now that I think I could stand anything, any suffering, just so I can say and repeat to myself every moment, ‘I exist.' Through a thousand agonies — I exist. I'm tormented on the rack — but I exist! Though I sit alone atop a pillar — I exist! I see the sun, and even if I don't see the sun, I know it's there. And there's a whole life in that, in knowing that the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan —”

73.52.oldText: “What of brother Ivan?” Alyosha interrupted, but Mitya didn't hear.

73.53.oldText: “You see, I never had any of these doubts before, but it was all hidden away in me. It was perhaps just because ideas I didn't understand were surging up in me that I used to drink and fight and rage. It was to stifle them in myself, to still them, to smother them. Ivan is not Rakitin; there is an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx and is silent; he's always silent. It's God that's worrying me. That's the only thing worrying me. What if He doesn't exist? What if Rakitin's right — that it's an idea made up by men? Then if He doesn't exist, man is the chief of the earth, of the universe. Magnificent! Only how is he going to be good without God? That's the question. I always come back to that. For whom is man going to love, then? To whom will he be thankful? To whom will he sing the hymn? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says one can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot can maintain that. I can't understand it. Life's easy for Rakitin. ‘You'd better think about the extension of civic rights,' he tells me, ‘or even about keeping the price of meat down. You'll show your love for humanity more simply and directly that way than by philosophy.' I answered him, ‘Well, but you, without a God, are more likely to raise the price of meat, if it suits you, and make a rouble on every copeck.' He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing with me and another with a Chinaman, so it's a relative thing. Or isn't it? Is it not relative? A treacherous question! You won't laugh if I tell you it's kept me awake two nights. I only wonder now how people can live and think nothing about it. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It's beyond me. But he is silent. I think he's a freemason. I asked him, but he's silent. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul — he was silent. But once he did drop a word.”

73.54.oldText: “What did he say?” Alyosha took it up quickly.

73.55.oldText: “I said to him, ‘Then everything is lawful, if it's so?' He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,' he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were right enough.' That's what he let drop. That was all he said. That was going one better than Rakitin.”

73.56.oldText: “Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he with you?”

73.57.oldText: “That later; now I have to speak of something else. I haven't said anything about Ivan to you before. I put it off to the last. Once my business here is over and the verdict has been given, then I'll tell you something. I'll tell you everything. We've got something tremendous on our hands. And you shall be my judge in it. But don't start on that now; be silent. You talk of tomorrow, of the trial; but, would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”

73.59.oldText: “What's the use of the counsel? I told him all about it. He's a soft, city-bred rogue — a Bernard! But he doesn't believe me — not a bit of it. Just imagine — he thinks I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,' I asked him, ‘why have you come to defend me?' Hang the lot of them! They've got a doctor down, too, want to prove I'm mad. I won't have that! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do her ‘duty' to the end, whatever the strain!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “The cat! Hard-hearted creature! She knows what I said of her at Mokroe — that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.' They repeated it. Yes, the facts against me have grown as numerous as the sands of the sea. Grigory sticks to his point. Grigory's honest, but a fool. Many people are honest because they're fools: that's Rakitin's idea. Grigory's my enemy. And there are some people who are better as foes than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I'm afraid, oh, I'm afraid she'll tell how she bowed to the ground after that four thousand. She'll pay it back to the last farthing. I don't want her sacrifice; they'll put me to shame at the trial. I wonder how I can stand it. Go to her, Alyosha, ask her not to speak of that in court — can't you? But damn it all, it doesn't matter! I'll get through somehow. I don't pity her. It's her own doing. She deserves what she gets. I'll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why should she have to bear such suffering?” he exclaimed suddenly, with tears. “Grusha's killing me; the thought of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me just now.”

73.60.oldText: “She told me she was very much grieved by you today.”

73.61.oldText: “I know. Confound my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry, I kissed her as she was leaving. I didn't ask her forgiveness.”

73.64.oldText: “God preserve you, my dear boy, from ever asking forgiveness for a fault from a woman you love. From one you love, especially, however greatly you may have been at fault. Because a woman — the devil only knows what to make of a woman! I know something about them, anyway. But try admitting you're at fault to a woman. Say, ‘I'm sorry, forgive me,' and a shower of reproaches will follow! Nothing will make her forgive you simply and directly; she'll humble you to the dust, bring up things that never happened, recall everything, forget nothing, add things of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best, the best of them do it. She'll scrape up all the scrapings and heap them on your head. They're ready to flay you alive, I tell you, every one of them, all these angels without whom we can't live! I tell you plainly and openly, dear boy, every decent man ought to be under some woman's thumb. That's my conviction — not conviction, but feeling. A man ought to be magnanimous, and it's no disgrace to a man! No disgrace to a hero, not even a Caesar! But don't ever beg her pardon, all the same, for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who's come to ruin through women. No, I'd better make it up to Grusha somehow without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, worship her. Only she doesn't see it. No, she still thinks I don't love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! In the past it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me, but now I've taken all of her soul into my soul, and through her I've become a man myself. Will they marry us? If they don't, I'll die of jealousy. I imagine something every day. What did she say to you about me?”

73.65.oldText: Alyosha repeated all that Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him repeat things, and seemed pleased.

73.66.oldText: “Then she's not angry at my being jealous?” he exclaimed. “She's a regular woman! ‘I've a fierce heart myself!' Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can't bear anyone's being jealous of me. I can't stand it. We'll fight. But I'll love her, I'll love her infinitely. Will they marry us? Do they let convicts marry? That's the question. And without her I can't exist ...”

73.67.oldText: Mitya walked frowning across the room. It was almost dark. He suddenly seemed terribly worried.

73.68.oldText: “So there's a secret, she says, a secret? We've cooked up a plot against her, and Katya is mixed up in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that's not it. You're very wide of the mark, in your foolish feminine way. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I'll tell you our secret!”

73.69.oldText: He glanced around, went close up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered to him with an air of mystery, though in reality no one could hear them: the old warder was dozing in the corner, and not a word could reach the ears of the soldiers on guard.

73.70.oldText: “I'll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered hurriedly. “I meant to tell you later, because how could I decide anything without you? You're everything to me. Though I say Ivan is superior to us, you are my angel. It's your decision that will decide it. Perhaps it's you who are superior and not Ivan. You see, it's a question of conscience, a question of the higher conscience — the secret is so important that I can't settle it myself, and I've put it off until I could speak to you. But even so, it's too early to decide now, because we must wait for the verdict. As soon as the verdict is given, you'll decide my fate. Don't decide it now. I'll tell you now. You listen, but don't decide. Stand there and keep quiet. I won't tell you everything. I'll only tell you the idea, without the details, and you keep quiet. Not a question, not a movement. You agree? But, goodness, what shall I do with your eyes? I'm afraid your eyes will tell me your decision, even if you don't speak. Oo — I'm afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan is suggesting that I _escape_. I won't tell you the details: it's all been thought through, it can all be arranged. Hush, don't decide. I'd go to America with Grusha. You know I can't live without Grusha! What if they won't let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha what would I be doing there underground with a hammer? I'd only smash my own skull with the hammer! But on the other hand — my conscience? I'd have run away from suffering. A sign has come, I reject the sign. I have a way of salvation and I turn my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the goodwill,' I can be of more use than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What's America? America is vanity again! And there's plenty of swindling in America too, I expect. I'd have run away from crucifixion! I tell you, you know, Alexey, because you're the only person who can understand this. There's no one else. It's folly, madness to others, all that I've told you about the hymn. They'll say I'm out of my mind or a fool. I'm not out of my mind and I'm not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he doesn't answer — he doesn't speak. He doesn't believe in the hymn. Don't speak, don't speak. I see how you look! You've already decided. Don't decide, spare me! I can't live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”

73.71.oldText: Mitya finished beside himself. He held Alyosha with both hands on his shoulders, his yearning, feverish eyes fixed on his brother's.

73.72.oldText: “They don't let convicts marry, do they?” he repeated for the third time in a pleading voice.

73.73.oldText: Alyosha listened with extreme surprise and was deeply moved.

73.74.oldText: “Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very keen on it, and whose idea was it?”

73.75.oldText: “His, his, and he's very keen on it. He didn't come to see me at first, then he suddenly came a week ago and launched straight into it. He's awfully keen. He doesn't ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I'll obey him, even though I laid open my whole heart to him the way I have to you, and told him about the hymn, too. He told me he'd arrange it; he's found out about everything. But of that later. He's simply set on it. It's all a matter of money: he'll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says we can arrange a magnificent escape for ten thousand.”

73.76.oldText: “And he told you on no account to tell me?” Alyosha asked again.

73.77.oldText: “To tell no one, and especially not you; on no account to tell you. He's afraid, no doubt, that you'd stand before me as my conscience. Don't tell him I told you. Don't tell him, for anything.”

73.78.oldText: “You're right,” Alyosha pronounced. “It's impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you'll decide for yourself. Then you'll find that new man in yourself and he will decide.”

73.79.oldText: “A new man, or a Bernard who'll decide _à la_ Bernard — because I think I'm a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.

73.80.oldText: “But, brother, have you no hope, then, of being acquitted?”

73.81.oldText: Mitya shrugged his shoulders nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it's time you were going,” he said, with sudden haste. “There's the superintendent shouting in the yard. He'll be here in a moment. We're late; it's irregular. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Sign me with the cross, darling, for the cross I have to bear tomorrow.”

73.83.oldText: “Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “suggests my escaping; but, of course, he believes I did it.”

73.84.oldText: A mournful smile came to his lips.

73.85.oldText: “Have you asked him whether he believes it?” Alyosha asked.

73.86.oldText: “No, I haven't. I wanted to, but I couldn't. I hadn't the courage. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-bye!”

73.87.oldText: Once more they kissed hurriedly, and Alyosha was just on his way out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

73.88.oldText: “Stand facing me! That's right!” And again he seized Alyosha, putting both hands on his shoulders. His face suddenly went quite pale, so that it was dreadfully visible even in the gathering darkness. His lips twitched, his eyes locked on Alyosha.

73.89.oldText: “Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as you would before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you in yourself, believe it? The whole truth — don't lie!” he cried desperately.

73.90.oldText: Everything seemed to heave in front of Alyosha, and he felt something like a stab at his heart.

73.91.oldText: “Hush! What do you mean?” he faltered helplessly.

73.92.oldText: “The whole truth, the whole, don't lie!” Mitya repeated.

73.93.oldText: “I've never for one instant believed that you were the murderer!” broke in a shaking voice from Alyosha's chest, and he raised his right hand in the air, as though calling God to witness his words.

73.94.oldText: Mitya's whole face lit up with bliss.

73.95.oldText: “Thank you!” he said slowly, as though letting out a sigh after a faint. “Now you've given me new life. Would you believe it, till this moment I've been afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well — go! You've given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Go on — go! Love Ivan!” was Mitya's last word.

73.96.oldText: Alyosha went out in tears. Such distrust in Mitya, such a lack of confidence even toward him, toward Alyosha — all of it suddenly opened up before Alyosha an unsuspected depth of hopeless grief and despair in the soul of his unhappy brother. Intense, infinite compassion overwhelmed him in an instant. There was a poignant ache in his torn heart. “Love Ivan!” — he suddenly recalled Mitya's words. And he was going to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He was as worried about Ivan as about Mitya, and more so than ever now.

74.0.oldText: On the way to Ivan he had to pass the house where Katerina Ivanovna was living. There was light in the windows. He suddenly stopped and resolved to go in. He hadn't seen Katerina Ivanovna for more than a week. But now it struck him that Ivan might be with her, especially on the eve of the terrible day. Ringing the bell, and climbing the staircase, which was dimly lit by a Chinese lantern, he saw a man coming down, and as they met, he recognized him as his brother. So Ivan was just coming from Katerina Ivanovna.

74.1.oldText: “Ah, it's only you,” Ivan said dryly. “Well, good-bye. You're going to see her?”

74.3.oldText: “I don't advise it; she's upset and you'll upset her more.”

74.4.oldText: A door was instantly flung open above, and a voice cried suddenly:

74.5.oldText: “No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, have you come from him?”

74.7.oldText: “Has he sent me any message? Come up, Alyosha — and you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you must come back, you must. Do you hear?”

74.8.oldText: There was such a peremptory note in Katya's voice that Ivan, after a moment's hesitation, made up his mind to go back with Alyosha.

74.9.oldText: “She was listening,” he muttered angrily to himself, but Alyosha heard him.

74.10.oldText: “Excuse my keeping my greatcoat on,” Ivan said, going into the drawing room. “I won't sit down. I won't stay more than a minute.”

74.11.oldText: “Sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Katerina Ivanovna said, though she remained standing. She had changed very little in this time, but there was an ominous gleam in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered afterwards that she had struck him as particularly handsome at that moment.

74.13.oldText: “Only one thing,” Alyosha said, looking her straight in the face. “That you would spare yourself and say nothing at the trial about what” (he was a little flustered) “... passed between you ... at the time of your first acquaintance ... in that town.”

74.14.oldText: “Ah — that I bowed down to the ground for that money!” She broke into a bitter laugh. “Well — is he afraid for me, or for himself? He asks me to spare — whom? Him, or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!”

74.15.oldText: Alyosha watched her intently, trying to understand her.

74.16.oldText: “Both yourself and him,” he answered softly.

74.17.oldText: “I'm glad to hear it,” she snapped out maliciously, and she suddenly blushed.

74.18.oldText: “You don't know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said menacingly. “And I don't know myself yet. Perhaps you'll want to trample me underfoot after my examination tomorrow.”

74.19.oldText: “You will give your evidence honorably,” Alyosha said. “That's all that's needed.”

74.20.oldText: “Women are often dishonorable,” she snarled. “Only an hour ago I was thinking I was afraid to touch that monster ... as though he were a reptile ... but no, he's still a human being to me! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?” she suddenly cried, hysterically, turning quickly to Ivan. Alyosha saw at once that she had asked Ivan that question before, perhaps only a moment before he came in, and not for the first time but for the hundredth, and that they had ended by quarreling.

74.21.oldText: “I've been to see Smerdyakov. It was you, you who persuaded me that he murdered his father. It's only you I believed!” she went on, still addressing Ivan. He gave her a sort of strained smile. Alyosha started at her tone. He hadn't suspected such close intimacy between them.

74.22.oldText: “Well, that's enough, anyway,” Ivan cut the conversation short. “I'm going. I'll come tomorrow.” And turning at once, he walked out of the room and went straight down the stairs.

74.23.oldText: With an imperious gesture, Katerina Ivanovna seized Alyosha by both hands.

74.24.oldText: “Follow him! Catch up with him! Don't leave him alone for a minute!” she said in a hurried whisper. “He's mad! Don't you know he's mad? He has a fever — nervous fever. The doctor told me so. Go, run after him ...”

74.25.oldText: Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not fifty paces ahead of him.

74.26.oldText: “What do you want?” Ivan turned quickly on Alyosha, seeing him running after him. “She told you to catch up with me, because I'm mad. I know it all by heart,” he added irritably.

74.27.oldText: “She's mistaken, of course; but she's right that you are ill,” Alyosha said. “I was just now looking at your face. You look very ill, Ivan.”

74.28.oldText: Ivan walked on without stopping. Alyosha followed him.

74.29.oldText: “And do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how people go out of their minds?” Ivan asked in a voice that had suddenly gone quiet, without a trace of irritation, with a note of the simplest curiosity.

74.30.oldText: “No, I don't. I suppose there are all kinds of insanity.”

74.31.oldText: “And can one observe that one's going mad oneself?”

74.32.oldText: “I imagine one can't see oneself clearly in such circumstances,” Alyosha answered, surprised.

74.33.oldText: Ivan paused for half a minute.

74.34.oldText: “If you want to talk with me, please change the subject,” he said suddenly.

74.35.oldText: “Oh — while I think of it, I have a letter for you,” Alyosha said timidly, and he took Lise's note from his pocket and held it out to Ivan. They were just under a lamppost. Ivan recognized the handwriting at once.

74.36.oldText: “Ah, from that little demon!” he laughed maliciously, and, without opening the envelope, he tore it into pieces and threw them into the air. The scraps scattered on the wind.

74.37.oldText: “She's not sixteen yet, I believe, and already offering herself,” he said contemptuously, striding off down the street again.

74.38.oldText: “How do you mean, offering herself?” Alyosha exclaimed.

74.39.oldText: “As wanton women offer themselves, to be sure.”

74.40.oldText: “How can you, Ivan, how can you?” Alyosha cried warmly, in a grieved voice. “She's a child; you're insulting a child! She's ill; she's very ill, too. She's perhaps on the verge of insanity. I had hoped to hear something from you ... that would save her.”

74.41.oldText: “You'll hear nothing from me. If she's a child, I'm not her nurse. Be quiet, Alexey. Don't keep harping on her. I'm not even thinking about it.”

74.42.oldText: They were silent again for a moment.
