74.43.oldText: “She'll be praying all night now to the Mother of God to show her how to act tomorrow at the trial,” he said sharply and angrily again.

74.45.oldText: “Yes. Whether she's to save Mitya or ruin him. She'll pray for light from above. She can't make up her own mind, you see. She hasn't had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nurse, too. She wants me to sing her lullabies.”

74.46.oldText: “Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” Alyosha said sadly.

74.47.oldText: “Perhaps; but I'm not very keen on her.”

74.48.oldText: “She's suffering. Why do you ... sometimes say things to her that give her hope?” Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. “I know you've given her hope. Forgive me for speaking to you like this,” he added.

74.49.oldText: “I can't behave with her as I ought — break off completely and tell her so straight out,” Ivan said, irritably. “I have to wait until sentence is passed on the murderer. If I break off with her now, she'll avenge herself on me by ruining that scoundrel at the trial tomorrow, because she hates him and knows she hates him. It's all a lie — lie upon lie! As long as I don't break off with her, she goes on hoping, and she won't ruin that monster, knowing how I want to get him out of trouble. If only that damned verdict would come!”

74.50.oldText: The words “murderer” and “monster” echoed painfully in Alyosha's heart.

74.51.oldText: “But how can she ruin Mitya?” he asked, pondering Ivan's words. “What evidence can she give that would ruin Mitya?”

74.52.oldText: “You don't know about that yet. She has a document in her hands, in Mitya's own handwriting, that proves conclusively that he murdered Fyodor Pavlovitch.”

74.54.oldText: “Why is it impossible? I've read it myself.”

74.55.oldText: “There can't be such a document!” Alyosha repeated warmly. “There can't be, because he's not the murderer. It wasn't he who killed father — not he!”

74.57.oldText: “Who is the murderer, then, in your opinion?” he asked, with apparent coldness. There was even a supercilious note in his voice.

74.58.oldText: “You know who,” Alyosha pronounced in a low, penetrating voice.

74.59.oldText: “Who? You mean that myth about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”

74.60.oldText: Alyosha suddenly felt himself trembling all over.

74.61.oldText: “You know who,” broke helplessly from him. He could scarcely breathe.

74.62.oldText: “Who? Who?” Ivan cried, almost fiercely. All his restraint suddenly vanished.

74.63.oldText: “I only know one thing,” Alyosha went on, still almost in a whisper. “_It wasn't you_ who killed father.”

74.64.oldText: “‘Not you'! What do you mean by ‘not you'?” Ivan was thunderstruck.

74.65.oldText: “It wasn't you who killed father, not you!” Alyosha repeated firmly.

74.66.oldText: The silence lasted for half a minute.

74.67.oldText: “I know I didn't. Are you raving?” Ivan said, with a pale, distorted smile. His eyes were riveted on Alyosha. They were standing again under a lamppost.

74.68.oldText: “No, Ivan. You've told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”

74.69.oldText: “When did I say so? I was in Moscow. When have I said so?” Ivan faltered helplessly.

74.70.oldText: “You've said it to yourself many times, when you've been alone during these two dreadful months,” Alyosha went on softly and distinctly as before. Yet he was speaking now, as it were, not of himself, not of his own will, but obeying some irresistible command. “You've accused yourself and confessed to yourself that you are the murderer and no one else. But you didn't do it: you're mistaken: you are not the murderer. Do you hear? It was not you! God has sent me to tell you so.”

74.71.oldText: They were both silent. The silence lasted a whole long minute. They were both standing still, gazing into each other's eyes. They were both pale. Suddenly Ivan began trembling all over and clutched Alyosha's shoulder.

74.72.oldText: “You've been in my room!” he whispered hoarsely. “You've been there at night, when he came. Confess ... have you seen him, have you seen him?”

74.73.oldText: “Who do you mean — Mitya?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.

74.74.oldText: “Not him, damn the monster!” Ivan shouted, in a frenzy. “Do you know that he visits me? How did you find out? Speak!”

74.75.oldText: “Who is _he_? I don't know who you're talking about,” Alyosha faltered, beginning to feel alarmed.

74.76.oldText: “Yes, you do know ... or how could you — ? It's impossible that you don't know.”

74.77.oldText: Suddenly he seemed to check himself. He stood still and appeared to be thinking. A strange grin twisted his lips.

74.78.oldText: “Brother,” Alyosha began again, in a shaking voice, “I've said this to you because you'll believe my word, I know it. I tell you, once and for all — it's not you. You hear, once for all! God has put it into my heart to say this to you, even though it may make you hate me from this hour on.”

74.79.oldText: But by now Ivan had apparently regained his self-control.

74.80.oldText: “Alexey Fyodorovitch,” he said, with a cold smile, “I can't stand prophets and epileptics — messengers from God especially — and you know that only too well. I break off all relations with you from this moment, and probably forever. I beg you to leave me at this turning. That's the way to your lodgings too. You'd better be especially careful not to come near me today! Do you hear?”

74.81.oldText: He turned and walked on with a firm step, not looking back.

74.82.oldText: “Brother,” Alyosha called after him, “if anything happens to you today, turn to me before anyone!”

74.83.oldText: But Ivan made no reply. Alyosha stood under the lamppost at the crossroads until Ivan had vanished into the darkness. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan were in lodgings; neither of them was willing to live in Fyodor Pavlovitch's empty house. Alyosha had a furnished room in the house of some working people. Ivan lived some distance away. He had taken a roomy and fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house that belonged to a well-to-do lady, the widow of an official. But his only attendant was a deaf and rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six in the evening and got up at six in the morning. Ivan had become remarkably indifferent to his comforts of late, and very fond of being alone. He did everything for himself in the one room he lived in, and rarely set foot in any of the other rooms of his apartment.

74.84.oldText: He reached the gate of the house and had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He felt himself trembling all over with anger. Suddenly he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse, and walked with rapid steps in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a tiny, slanting wooden house, almost a hut, where Marya Kondratyevna — the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch's kitchen for soup and to whom Smerdyakov had once sung his songs and played the guitar — was now lodging. She had sold their little house and was now living here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill — almost dying — had been with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch's death. It was to him Ivan was going now, drawn by a sudden and irresistible prompting.

75.0.oldText: This was the third time Ivan had been to see Smerdyakov since his return from Moscow. The first time he had seen him and talked with him was the day he arrived; he had visited him once more a fortnight later. But his visits had ended with that second one, so that it was now over a month since he had seen him. And he had heard scarcely anything about him.

75.1.oldText: Ivan had only returned five days after his father's death, so he was not present at the funeral, which had taken place the day before he came back. The cause of his delay was that Alyosha, not knowing his Moscow address, had had to apply to Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph to him, and she, not knowing his address either, telegraphed her sister and aunt, reckoning that Ivan would go to see them as soon as he reached Moscow. But he didn't go to them until four days after his arrival. When he got the telegram, he had, of course, set off post-haste to our town. The first to meet him was Alyosha, and Ivan was greatly surprised to find that, contrary to the general opinion of the town, Alyosha refused to entertain any suspicion against Mitya and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later on, after seeing the police captain and the prosecutor, and hearing the details of the charge and the arrest, he was still more surprised at Alyosha, and put his opinion down to exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, of whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond.

75.2.oldText: By the way, let us say a word or two about Ivan's feelings toward his brother Dmitri. He positively disliked him; at most, he sometimes felt a compassion for him, and even that was mixed with great contempt, almost revulsion. Mitya's whole personality, even his appearance, was extremely unattractive to him. Ivan looked with indignation on Katerina Ivanovna's love for his brother. Yet he went to see Mitya on his first day back, and that interview, far from shaking his belief in Mitya's guilt, positively strengthened it. He found his brother agitated, nervously excited. Mitya had been talkative, but very distracted and incoherent. He used violent language, accused Smerdyakov, and was fearfully muddled. He talked mostly about the three thousand roubles which he said had been “stolen” from him by his father.

75.3.oldText: “The money was mine, it was my money,” Mitya kept repeating. “Even if I had stolen it, I would have had the right.”

75.4.oldText: He hardly contested the evidence against him, and when he did try to turn a fact to his advantage, it was in an absurd and incoherent way. He hardly seemed to wish to defend himself to Ivan or anyone else. Quite the contrary — he was angry and proudly scornful of the charges against him; he kept firing up and abusing everyone. He only laughed contemptuously at Grigory's evidence about the open door, and declared that it was “the devil that opened it.” But he couldn't bring forward any coherent explanation of the fact. He even succeeded in insulting Ivan during their first meeting, telling him sharply that it was not for people who declared that “everything was lawful” to suspect and question him. Altogether he was anything but friendly with Ivan on that occasion. Immediately after that interview with Mitya, Ivan went for the first time to see Smerdyakov.

75.5.oldText: On the train coming from Moscow, he had kept thinking of Smerdyakov and of his last conversation with him the evening before he'd gone away. Many things seemed puzzling and suspicious to him. But when he gave his evidence to the investigating lawyer, Ivan said nothing for the time being about that conversation. He put that off until he had seen Smerdyakov, who was at the time in the hospital.

75.6.oldText: Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, confidently asserted in reply to Ivan's persistent questions that Smerdyakov's epileptic attack was unmistakably genuine, and they were surprised that Ivan should ask whether he might have been shamming on the day of the catastrophe. They gave him to understand that the attack had been an exceptional one, the fits persisting and recurring several times, so that the patient's life had positively been in danger, and only now, after remedies had been applied, could they state with confidence that the patient would survive. “Though it might well be,” Doctor Herzenstube added, “that his reason will be impaired for a considerable period, if not permanently.” On Ivan's asking impatiently whether that meant Smerdyakov was now mad, they told him that this wasn't yet the case in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities could be observed. Ivan decided to find out for himself what those abnormalities were.

75.7.oldText: At the hospital he was immediately allowed to see the patient. Smerdyakov was lying on a truckle bed in a separate ward. There was only one other bed in the room, and in it lay a tradesman of the town, swollen with dropsy, who was obviously near death; he could be no hindrance to their conversation. Smerdyakov grinned uncertainly on seeing Ivan, and for the first instant seemed nervous. So at least Ivan fancied. But that was only momentary. For the rest of the time Ivan was struck, on the contrary, by Smerdyakov's composure. From the first glance Ivan had no doubt that he was very ill. He was very weak; he spoke slowly, seeming to move his tongue with difficulty; he was much thinner and sallower. Throughout the interview, which lasted twenty minutes, he kept complaining of headache and of pain in all his limbs. His thin emasculate face seemed to have grown so tiny; his hair was ruffled, and his crest of curls in front stood up in a thin tuft. But in the left eye, which was screwed up and seemed to be insinuating something, Smerdyakov showed himself unchanged. “It's always worth while speaking to a clever man.” Ivan was reminded of that at once. He sat down on the stool at his feet. Smerdyakov, with painful effort, shifted his position in bed, but he was not the first to speak. He remained mute, and didn't even look much interested.

75.8.oldText: “Can you talk to me?” Ivan asked. “I won't tire you much.”

75.9.oldText: “Certainly I can,” Smerdyakov mumbled, in a faint voice. “Has your honor been back long?” he added patronizingly, as though encouraging a nervous visitor.

75.10.oldText: “I only arrived today. To see the mess you're all in here.”

75.12.oldText: “Why do you sigh? You knew about it all along,” Ivan blurted out.

75.13.oldText: Smerdyakov was stolidly silent for a while.

75.14.oldText: “How could I help knowing? It was clear beforehand. But how could I tell it would turn out like that?”

75.15.oldText: “What would turn out? Don't prevaricate! You foretold you'd have a fit — on the way down to the cellar, you remember. You mentioned the very spot.”

75.16.oldText: “Have you said so at the examination yet?” Smerdyakov asked with composure.

75.18.oldText: “No, I haven't yet — but I certainly shall. You must explain a great deal to me, my man; and let me tell you, I'm not going to let you play with me!”

75.19.oldText: “Why should I play with you, when I put my whole trust in you, as in God Almighty?” said Smerdyakov, with the same composure, only closing his eyes for a moment.

75.20.oldText: “In the first place,” Ivan began, “I know that epileptic fits can't be predicted beforehand. I've inquired; don't try to take me in. You can't foretell the day and the hour. How is it you told me the day and the hour beforehand, and about the cellar, too? How could you tell you would fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, if you didn't sham a fit on purpose?”

75.21.oldText: “I had to go to the cellar anyway — several times a day, in fact,” Smerdyakov drawled deliberately. “I fell from the garret in just the same way a year ago. It's quite true you can't predict the day and hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a presentiment of it.”

75.23.oldText: “As to my epilepsy, sir, you had much better ask the doctors here. You can ask them whether it was a real fit or a sham; it's no use my saying any more about it.”

75.24.oldText: “And the cellar? How could you know beforehand about the cellar?”

75.25.oldText: “You don't seem able to let go of that cellar! As I was going down to the cellar, I was in terrible dread and doubt. What frightened me most was losing you and being left without defense in the whole world. So I went down into the cellar thinking, ‘Here, it'll come on any moment, it'll strike me down any moment — will I fall?' And it was through this fear that I suddenly felt the spasm that always comes ... and so I went flying. All of that, and all of our previous conversation at the gate the evening before, when I told you how frightened I was and spoke of the cellar — I told all of it to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it's all been written down in the protocol. And the doctor here, Mr. Varvinsky, insisted to all of them that it was the very thought of it that brought it on, the apprehension that I might fall. It was just then that the fit seized me. And so they've written it down, that this is how it must have happened, simply out of my fear.”

75.26.oldText: As he finished, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as though exhausted.

75.27.oldText: “So you've said all that in your testimony?” Ivan said, somewhat taken aback. He had meant to frighten him with the threat of repeating their conversation, and it turned out Smerdyakov had already reported all of it himself.

75.28.oldText: “What have I to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov pronounced firmly.

75.29.oldText: “And have you told them every word of our conversation at the gate?”

75.31.oldText: “And did you tell them that you can sham fits, as you boasted then?”

75.32.oldText: “No, I didn't tell them that either.”

75.33.oldText: “Tell me now, why did you send me to Tchermashnya that time?”

75.34.oldText: “I was afraid you'd go off to Moscow; Tchermashnya is nearer, anyway.”

75.35.oldText: “You're lying; you suggested going away yourself; you told me to get out of the way of trouble.”

75.36.oldText: “That was simply out of affection and my sincere devotion to you, foreseeing trouble in the house, wanting to spare you. Only I wanted to spare myself even more. That's why I told you to get out of harm's way, so you might understand that there would be trouble in the house, and would stay at home to protect your father.”

75.37.oldText: “You might have said it more directly, you blockhead!” Ivan suddenly fired up.

75.38.oldText: “How could I have said it more directly back then? It was just my fear that made me speak, and you might have gotten angry, too. Of course, I might well have worried that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and carry away that money, because he considered it as good as his own; but who could have told that it would end in a murder like this? I thought he'd only carry off the three thousand that lay under the master's mattress in the envelope — and you see, he's murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”

75.39.oldText: “But if you yourself say it couldn't be guessed, how was I supposed to have guessed it and stayed home? You're contradicting yourself!” Ivan said, pondering.

75.40.oldText: “You might have guessed from my sending you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow.”

75.41.oldText: “How could I have guessed it from that?”

75.42.oldText: Smerdyakov seemed much exhausted, and again he was silent for a minute.

75.43.oldText: “You might have guessed from the fact of my asking you not to go to Moscow but to Tchermashnya, that I wanted you nearer, because Moscow's a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you weren't far away, wouldn't be so bold. And if anything had happened, you could have come to protect me too, because I warned you of Grigory Vassilyevitch's illness, and that I was afraid of having a fit. And when I explained those knocks to you, by which someone could get in to the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you'd guess yourself he was bound to do something, and so wouldn't go to Tchermashnya at all, but would stay.”

75.44.oldText: “He talks very coherently,” Ivan thought, “though he does mumble; what's the derangement of his faculties that Herzenstube talked of?”

75.45.oldText: “You're being cunning with me, damn you!” he exclaimed, getting angry.

75.46.oldText: “But I thought at the time that you quite guessed,” Smerdyakov parried with the simplest air.

75.47.oldText: “If I'd guessed, I would have stayed,” Ivan cried.

75.48.oldText: “Why, I thought it was because you'd guessed that you went away in such a hurry, only to get out of trouble, only to run away and save yourself in your fright.”

75.49.oldText: “You think everyone is as great a coward as yourself?”

75.50.oldText: “Forgive me, I thought you were like me.”

75.51.oldText: “Of course, I ought to have guessed,” Ivan said, agitated. “And I did guess there was some mischief brewing on your part ... only you're lying, you're lying again,” he cried, suddenly remembering. “Do you remember how you came up to the carriage and said to me, ‘It's always worth while speaking to a clever man'? So you were glad I was going away, since you praised me?”

75.52.oldText: Smerdyakov sighed again and again. A trace of color came into his face.

75.53.oldText: “If I was pleased,” he said rather breathlessly, “it was simply because you agreed not to go to Moscow, but to Tchermashnya. Because it was nearer, at any rate. Only when I said those words to you, it was not by way of praise, but of reproach. You didn't understand it.”

75.55.oldText: “Why, that foreseeing such a calamity, you deserted your own father, and wouldn't protect us, because I might have been taken up at any time for stealing that three thousand.”

75.56.oldText: “Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait — did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?”

75.57.oldText: “I told them everything just as it was.”

75.59.oldText: “If I thought of anything back then,” he began again, “it was solely of some wickedness on your part. Dmitri might kill him, but that he would steal — I didn't believe that back then. But I was prepared for any wickedness from you. You told me yourself you could sham a fit. What did you say that for?”

75.60.oldText: “It was just out of my simplicity — and I've never shammed a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it then to show off to you. It was just foolishness. I liked you so much at the time, and was open-hearted with you.”

75.61.oldText: “My brother directly accuses you of the murder and the theft.”

75.62.oldText: “What else is there left for him to do?” Smerdyakov said, with a bitter grin. “And who'll believe him with all the proofs against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say after that? But never mind him! He's trembling to save himself.”

75.63.oldText: He slowly stopped speaking; then suddenly, as if on reflection, added:

75.64.oldText: “And look here again. He wants to throw it on me and make out it's the work of my hands — I've heard that already. But as to my being clever at shamming a fit: would I have told you beforehand I could sham one, if I really had had such a design on your father? If I'd been planning such a murder, could I have been such a fool as to give such evidence against myself in advance? And to his son, too! Upon my word! Is that likely? As if such a thing could be — it's never happened. No one hears this talk of ours now except Providence itself, and if you were to tell of it to the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch, you might defend me completely by doing so, because who would be likely to be such a criminal if he's so open-hearted in advance? Anyone can see that.”

75.65.oldText: “Well —” and Ivan got up to cut the conversation short, struck by Smerdyakov's last argument. “I don't suspect you at all, and I think it's absurd, in fact, to suspect you. On the contrary, I'm grateful to you for setting my mind at rest. Now I'm going, but I'll come again. Meanwhile, good-bye. Get well. Is there anything you want?”

75.66.oldText: “I'm very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn't forget me, and provides me with whatever I need, out of her kindness. Good people visit me every day.”

75.67.oldText: “Good-bye. But I won't mention your being able to sham a fit, and I don't advise you to either,” something made Ivan say suddenly.

75.68.oldText: “I quite understand. And if you don't speak of that, I'll say nothing of that conversation of ours at the gate.”

75.69.oldText: Then it happened that Ivan went out, and only after going a dozen steps along the corridor did he suddenly feel that there was an insulting significance in Smerdyakov's last words. He was almost on the point of turning back, but it was only a passing impulse, and muttering, “Nonsense!” he walked out of the hospital.

75.70.oldText: His chief feeling was one of relief at the fact that it was Mitya, not Smerdyakov, who had committed the murder, though you might have expected him to feel the opposite. He didn't want to analyze the reason for this feeling, and even felt a positive revulsion at prying into his own sensations. He felt as though he wanted to hurry up and forget something. In the following days he became convinced of Mitya's guilt as he learned the full weight of evidence against him. There was evidence from people of no importance — Fenya and her mother, for instance — but the effect of it was almost overpowering. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern, and at Plotnikov's shop, as well as the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence seemed conclusive. It was the details that were so damning. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers almost as much as Grigory's evidence about the open door. Grigory's wife, Marfa, in answer to Ivan's questions, declared that Smerdyakov had been lying all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed,” and that although she was a sound sleeper, she had woken several times and heard him moaning. “He was moaning the whole time, moaning continually.”

75.71.oldText: Talking to Herzenstube and giving it as his opinion that Smerdyakov was not mad, only rather weak, Ivan only drew from the old man a subtle smile.

75.72.oldText: “Do you know how he spends his time now?” he asked. “Learning lists of French words by heart. He has an exercise book under his pillow with the French words written out in Russian letters for him by someone — he he he!”

75.73.oldText: Ivan ended by dismissing all doubts. He couldn't think of Dmitri without repulsion. Only one thing was strange, however. Alyosha kept insisting that Dmitri was not the murderer, and that “in all probability” Smerdyakov was. Ivan always felt that Alyosha's opinion meant a great deal to him, and so he was astonished at it now. Another strange thing was that Alyosha made no attempt to talk about Mitya with Ivan — he never brought up the subject and only answered his questions. This, too, struck Ivan particularly.

75.74.oldText: But he was very much preoccupied at that time with something quite apart from all that. On his return from Moscow, he had abandoned himself hopelessly to his mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin to speak of this new passion of Ivan's, which left its mark on all the rest of his life: that would make the subject of another novel, which I may perhaps never write. But I cannot omit to mention here that when Ivan, on leaving Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha, as I have already related, told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie: he loved her madly, though at times he hated her so that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to bring about this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she rushed on Ivan's return to meet him as her one salvation. She was hurt, insulted, humiliated in her feelings. And here the man had come back to her who had loved her so ardently before (oh, she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she considered so superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl didn't abandon herself altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. She was constantly tormented at the same time by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were many) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had called to Alyosha “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything. But of all this, later.

75.75.oldText: He did, in fact, for a time almost forget Smerdyakov's existence, and yet, a fortnight after his first visit to him, he began to be haunted by the same strange thoughts as before. It's enough to say that he was constantly asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch's house, he had crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened to hear what his father was doing downstairs. Why had he recalled that afterwards with revulsion? Why, the next morning, had he been suddenly so depressed on the journey? Why, as he reached Moscow, had he said to himself, “I am a scoundrel”? And now he almost felt that these tormenting thoughts would even make him forget Katerina Ivanovna, so completely did they take hold of him again. It was just after feeling this that he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once, and put a question to him:

75.76.oldText: “Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterwards I told you in the yard that I reserved ‘the right to desire'? Tell me — did you think then that I desired father's death or not?”

75.77.oldText: “I did think so,” Alyosha answered softly.

75.78.oldText: “It was so, too; it was not a matter of guessing. But didn't you also fancy then that what I wished was just that ‘one reptile should devour another'; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even prepared to help bring that about?”

75.79.oldText: Alyosha turned rather pale, and looked silently into his brother's face.

75.80.oldText: “Speak!” Ivan cried. “I want above all to know what you thought then. I want the truth, the truth!”

75.81.oldText: He drew a deep breath, looking angrily at Alyosha before the answer came.

75.82.oldText: “Forgive me, I did think that too, at the time,” Alyosha whispered, and he didn't add one softening phrase.

75.83.oldText: “Thanks,” Ivan snapped, and, leaving Alyosha, he walked quickly on his way. From that time Alyosha noticed that Ivan began obviously avoiding him and seemed even to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha gave up going to see him. Immediately after that meeting with him, Ivan didn't go home but went straight to Smerdyakov again.

76.0.oldText: By that time Smerdyakov had been discharged from the hospital. Ivan knew his new lodging — the dilapidated little wooden house, divided in two by a passage, on one side of which lived Marya Kondratyevna and her mother, and on the other, Smerdyakov. No one knew on what terms he was living with them, whether as a friend or as a lodger. It was supposed afterwards that he had come to stay with them as Marya Kondratyevna's betrothed, and was living there for a time without paying for board or lodging. Both mother and daughter had the greatest respect for him and looked on him as far superior to themselves.

76.1.oldText: Ivan knocked, and when the door was opened, he went straight into the passage. By Marya Kondratyevna's directions, he went straight to the better room on the left, occupied by Smerdyakov. There was a tiled stove in the room, and it was extremely hot. The walls were gay with blue paper, which was rather worn, however, and in the cracks under it cockroaches swarmed in amazing numbers, so that there was a continual rustling from them. The furniture was very scanty: two benches against each wall, and two chairs by the table. The plain wooden table was covered with a cloth patterned in pink. There was a pot of geranium on each of the two little windows. In the corner there was a case of icons. On the table stood a little copper samovar, heavily dented, and a tray with two cups. But Smerdyakov had finished his tea and the samovar was out. He was sitting at the table on a bench. He was looking at an exercise book and slowly writing with a pen. There was a bottle of ink beside him and a flat iron candlestick with a composite candle. Ivan saw at once from Smerdyakov's face that he had completely recovered from his illness. His face looked fresher, fuller, his hair stood up jauntily in front and was plastered down at the sides. He was sitting in a parti-colored, wadded dressing gown, rather dirty and frayed. He had spectacles on his nose, which Ivan had never seen him wearing before. This trifling circumstance suddenly redoubled Ivan's anger: “A creature like that, wearing spectacles!”

76.2.oldText: Smerdyakov slowly raised his head and looked intently at his visitor through his spectacles; then he slowly took them off and rose from the bench — but not at all respectfully, almost lazily, doing the bare minimum required by common civility. All of this struck Ivan at once; he took it all in and noted it immediately — most of all the look in Smerdyakov's eyes, positively malicious, churlish, and haughty. “What do you want to intrude for?” it seemed to say; “we settled everything then; why have you come again?” Ivan could scarcely control himself.

76.3.oldText: “It's hot here,” he said, still standing, and unbuttoned his overcoat.

76.5.oldText: Ivan took off his coat and threw it onto a bench with trembling hands. He took a chair, moved it quickly to the table, and sat down. Smerdyakov managed to sit down on his bench in front of him.

76.6.oldText: “To begin with, are we alone?” Ivan asked sternly and impulsively. “Can they overhear us in there?”

76.7.oldText: “No one can hear anything. You've seen for yourself: there's a passage.”

76.8.oldText: “Listen, my good fellow. What was it you babbled as I was leaving the hospital — that if I said nothing about your faculty of shamming fits, you wouldn't tell the investigating lawyer all of our conversation at the gate? What do you mean by _all_? What could you mean by it? Were you threatening me? Have I entered into some sort of compact with you? Do you suppose I'm afraid of you?”

76.9.oldText: Ivan said this in a perfect fury, giving him to understand, with obvious intention, that he scorned any subterfuge or indirectness and meant to lay his cards on the table. Smerdyakov's eyes gleamed resentfully, his left eye winked, and he at once gave his answer, with his customary composure and deliberation. “You want to have it all above board — very well, you shall have it,” he seemed to say.

76.10.oldText: “This is what I meant then, and this is why I said that: that you, knowing beforehand of this murder of your own parent, left him to his fate, and that people mustn't, after that, come to any ugly conclusion about your feelings — and perhaps about something else too — that's what I promised not to tell the authorities.”

76.11.oldText: Though Smerdyakov spoke without haste and was obviously controlling himself, there was something in his voice — determined and emphatic, resentful and insolently defiant. He stared impudently at Ivan. A mist passed before Ivan's eyes for a moment.

76.12.oldText: “How? What? Are you out of your mind?”

76.13.oldText: “I'm perfectly in possession of all my faculties.”

76.14.oldText: “Do you suppose I _knew_ of the murder?” Ivan cried at last, and he brought his fist violently down on the table. “What do you mean by ‘something else, too'? Speak, scoundrel!”

76.15.oldText: Smerdyakov was silent, still watching Ivan with the same insolent stare.

76.16.oldText: “Speak, you stinking rogue — what is that ‘something else, too'?”

76.17.oldText: “The ‘something else' I meant was that you probably also wanted your parent's death very much.”

76.18.oldText: Ivan jumped up and struck him with all his might on the shoulder, so that he fell back against the wall. In an instant his face was bathed in tears. Saying, “It's a shame, sir, to strike a sick man,” he dried his eyes with a very dirty blue check handkerchief and sank into quiet weeping. A minute passed.

76.19.oldText: “That's enough. Stop,” Ivan said peremptorily, sitting down again. “Don't try my patience any further.”

76.20.oldText: Smerdyakov took the rag from his eyes. Every line of his puckered face reflected the insult he had just received.

76.21.oldText: “So you thought then, you scoundrel, that together with Dmitri I meant to kill my father?”

76.22.oldText: “I didn't know what thoughts were in your mind then,” Smerdyakov said resentfully, “and so I stopped you at the gate to sound you out on that very point.”

76.24.oldText: “Why, that very thing — whether you wanted your father to be murdered, or not.”

76.25.oldText: What infuriated Ivan more than anything was the aggressive, insolent tone Smerdyakov persistently kept.

76.26.oldText: “It was you who murdered him?” he suddenly cried.

76.28.oldText: “You know perfectly well for a fact that it wasn't I who murdered him. And I should have thought there was no need for a sensible man to bring it up again.”

76.29.oldText: “But why, why did you have such a suspicion about me at the time?”

76.30.oldText: “As you already know, it was simply from fear. Because I was in such a position, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I resolved to sound you out too, because I thought that if you wanted the same as your brother, then the business was as good as settled, and I'd be crushed like a fly, too.”

76.31.oldText: “Look here — you didn't say that a fortnight ago.”

76.32.oldText: “I meant the same thing when I talked to you in the hospital, only I thought you'd understand without wasting words, and that a sensible man like you wouldn't care to talk of it openly.”

76.33.oldText: “What next! Come — answer, answer, I insist: what was it ... what could I have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean little soul?”

76.34.oldText: “As for the murder, you couldn't have done it yourself and didn't want to; but as for wanting someone else to do it — that was just what you did want.”

76.35.oldText: “And how coolly, how coolly he speaks! But why should I have wanted it? What grounds had I for wanting it?”

76.36.oldText: “What grounds had you? What about the inheritance?” said Smerdyakov sarcastically, and, as it were, vindictively. “Why, after your parent's death there was at least forty thousand to come to each of you, very likely more; but if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady then, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she'd have had all his capital made over to her the moment they were married, because she's plenty of sense, so that your parent wouldn't have left the three of you two roubles between you. And were they far from a wedding? Not a hair's breadth: that lady had only to lift her little finger and he'd have run after her to the church, tongue hanging out.”

76.37.oldText: Ivan restrained himself with painful effort.

76.38.oldText: “Very good,” he observed at last. “You see, I haven't jumped up, I haven't knocked you down, I haven't killed you. Go on. So, according to you, I had fixed on Dmitri to do it; I was counting on him?”

76.39.oldText: “How could you help counting on him? If he killed him, then he'd lose all the rights of a nobleman, his rank and property, and be sent off to exile; so his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts, and you'd each have not forty, but sixty thousand. There's no doubt you were counting on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

76.40.oldText: “What I have to put up with from you! Listen, scoundrel — if I'd been counting on anyone then, it would have been on you, not on Dmitri, and I swear I did expect some wickedness from you at the time. I remember my impression!”

76.41.oldText: “I thought so too, for a minute at the time — that you were counting on me as well,” Smerdyakov said, with a sarcastic grin. “So it was just by that, more than anything, that you showed me what was in your mind. Because if you had a foreboding about me and yet went away, you were as good as saying to me, ‘You can murder my parent, I won't hinder you!'”

76.42.oldText: “You scoundrel! So that's how you understood it!”

76.43.oldText: “It was that whole business of going to Tchermashnya. Why! You were meaning to go to Moscow and refused all your father's entreaties to go to Tchermashnya — and then on a foolish word from me, you consented at once! What reason had you to agree to Tchermashnya? Since you went to Tchermashnya with no reason, simply at my word, it shows you must have expected something from me.”

76.44.oldText: “No, I swear I didn't!” Ivan shouted, grinding his teeth.

76.45.oldText: “You didn't? Then you ought, as your father's son, to have had me hauled to the lock-up and thrashed at once for saying what I did ... or at the very least, given me a punch in the face on the spot; but you weren't the least bit angry, if you please, and at once in a friendly way acted on my foolish word and went away, which was utterly absurd, because you ought to have stayed to save your parent's life. How could I help drawing my conclusions?”

76.46.oldText: Ivan sat scowling, both his fists convulsively pressed on his knees.

76.47.oldText: “Yes, I am sorry I didn't punch you in the face,” he said with a bitter smile. “I couldn't have dragged you off to the lock-up at that point. Who would have believed me, and what charge could I have brought against you? But the punch in the face ... oh, I'm sorry I didn't think of it. Though blows are forbidden, I would have pounded your ugly face to a pulp.”

76.49.oldText: “In the ordinary occasions of life,” he said in the same complacent, sententious tone in which he had taunted Grigory and argued with him about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch's table, “in the ordinary occasions of life, blows on the face are forbidden nowadays by law, and people have given them up; but in exceptional occasions of life, people still fly to blows — not only among us, but all over the world, be it the fullest Republic of France, just as in the time of Adam and Eve, and they never will leave off — but you, even in an exceptional case, didn't dare.”

76.50.oldText: “What are you learning French words for?” Ivan nodded toward the exercise book lying on the table.

76.51.oldText: “Why shouldn't I learn them to improve my education, in case I should chance to go one day to those happy parts of Europe?”

76.52.oldText: “Listen, monster.” Ivan's eyes flashed and he trembled all over. “I'm not afraid of your accusations; you can say what you like about me, and if I don't beat you to death, it's simply because I suspect you of that crime and I'll drag you to justice. I'll unmask you.”

76.53.oldText: “To my mind, you'd better keep quiet — because what can you accuse me of, considering my complete innocence? And who would believe you? Only if you begin, I'll tell everything too, because I must defend myself.”

76.54.oldText: “Do you think I'm afraid of you now?”

76.55.oldText: “If the court doesn't believe everything I've just said to you, the public will, and you'll be ashamed.”

76.56.oldText: “That's as much as to say, ‘It's always worth while speaking to a sensible man,' eh?” Ivan snarled.

76.57.oldText: “You hit the mark exactly. And you'd better be sensible.”

76.58.oldText: Ivan got up, shaking all over with indignation, put on his coat, and without replying further to Smerdyakov, without even looking at him, walked quickly out of the cottage. The cool evening air refreshed him. There was a bright moon in the sky. A nightmare of ideas and sensations filled his soul. “Shall I go right now and give information against Smerdyakov? But what information can I give? He is not guilty, anyway. On the contrary, he'll accuse me. And in fact, why did I set off for Tchermashnya that day? What for? What for?” Ivan asked himself. “Yes, of course, I was expecting something and he's right ...” And he remembered for the hundredth time how, on the last night in his father's house, he had listened on the stairs. But he remembered it now with such anguish that he stood still on the spot as though he had been stabbed. “Yes, I expected it then — that's true! I wanted the murder, I did want the murder! Did I want the murder? Did I want it? I must kill Smerdyakov! If I don't dare kill Smerdyakov now, life is not worth living!”

76.59.oldText: Ivan didn't go home, but went straight to Katerina Ivanovna and alarmed her by his appearance. He was like a madman. He repeated all his conversation with Smerdyakov, every syllable of it. He couldn't be calmed, however much she tried to soothe him: he kept pacing around the room, speaking strangely, disconnectedly. At last he sat down, put his elbows on the table, leaned his head in his hands, and pronounced this strange sentence: “If it's not Dmitri, but Smerdyakov who's the murderer, I share his guilt, because I put him up to it. Whether I did, I don't know yet. But if he's the murderer, and not Dmitri, then, of course, I am the murderer too.”

76.60.oldText: When Katerina Ivanovna heard that, she got up from her seat without a word, went to her writing table, opened a box standing on it, took out a sheet of paper, and laid it in front of Ivan. This was the document of which Ivan later spoke to Alyosha as a “conclusive proof” that Dmitri had killed his father. It was the letter Mitya had written to Katerina Ivanovna when he was drunk, on the very evening he met Alyosha at the crossroads on his way to the monastery, after the scene at Katerina Ivanovna's when Grushenka had insulted her. Then, parting from Alyosha, Mitya had rushed to Grushenka. I don't know whether he saw her, but that evening he had been at the “Metropolis,” where he got thoroughly drunk. Then he asked for pen and paper and wrote a document of weighty consequence to himself. It was a wordy, disconnected, frantic letter — a drunken letter, in fact. It was like the talk of a drunken man who, on his return home, begins with extraordinary heat telling his wife or one of the household how he has just been insulted, what a rascal had just insulted him, what a fine fellow he is on the other hand, and how he'll pay that scoundrel out — all at great length, with great excitement and incoherence, with drunken tears and blows on the table. The letter was written on a dirty sheet of ordinary paper of the cheapest kind. It had been provided by the tavern, and there were figures scrawled on the back of it. There was clearly not enough space for his drunken verbosity, and Mitya not only filled the margins but wrote the last line straight across the rest. The letter ran as follows:

76.61.oldText: FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand, and farewell, woman of great wrath — but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! Tomorrow I'll try to get it from everyone, and if I can't borrow it, I give you my word of honor I'll go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I'll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, because I've been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No — better not forgive me, you'll be happier and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, because I love another woman, and you got to know her too well today — how can you forgive? I will murder the man who's robbed me! I'll leave you all and go to the East to see no one again. Not _her_ either, because you're not my only tormentor — she is too. Farewell! P.S. — I write my curse, but I adore you! I hear it in my heart. One string is left, and it vibrates. Better tear my heart in two! I'll kill myself — but first of all that cur. I'll tear three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though I've been a scoundrel to you, I am not a thief! You can expect three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, tied with pink ribbon. I'm not a thief, but I'll murder my thief. Katya, don't look disdainful. Dmitri is not a thief! But a murderer! He has murdered his father and ruined himself to hold his ground rather than endure your pride. And he doesn't love you. P.P.S. — I kiss your feet, farewell! P.P.P.S. — Katya, pray to God that someone gives me the money. Then I won't be steeped in gore, and if no one does — I will be! Kill me!

76.63.oldText: When Ivan read this “document,” he was convinced. So then it was his brother, not Smerdyakov. And if not Smerdyakov, then not he, Ivan. This letter immediately took on in his eyes the form of a logical proof. There could no longer be the slightest doubt of Mitya's guilt. The suspicion never occurred to Ivan, by the way, that Mitya might have committed the murder in conjunction with Smerdyakov; and indeed, such a theory didn't fit the facts. Ivan was completely reassured. The next morning he only thought of Smerdyakov and his gibes with contempt. A few days later he positively wondered how he could have been so horribly distressed at his suspicions. He resolved to dismiss him with contempt and forget him. So passed a month. He made no further inquiry about Smerdyakov, but twice he happened to hear that he was very ill and out of his mind.

76.64.oldText: “He'll end in madness,” the young doctor Varvinsky observed about him, and Ivan remembered this. During the last week of that month Ivan himself began to feel very ill. He went to consult the Moscow doctor Katerina Ivanovna had sent for just before the trial. And just at that time his relations with Katerina Ivanovna became acutely strained. They were like two enemies in love with each other. Katerina Ivanovna's “returns” to Mitya — that is, her brief but violent revulsions of feeling in his favor — drove Ivan to perfect frenzy. Strange to say, until that last scene described above, when Alyosha came from Mitya to Katerina Ivanovna, Ivan had never once during that month heard her express a doubt of Mitya's guilt, in spite of those “returns” that were so hateful to him. It is remarkable, too, that while he felt he hated Mitya more and more every day, he realized it was not on account of Katya's “returns” that he hated him, but precisely _because he was the murderer of his father_. He was conscious of this and fully acknowledged it to himself.

76.65.oldText: Nevertheless, he went to see Mitya ten days before the trial and proposed to him a plan of escape — a plan he had obviously been thinking over for a long time. He was partly impelled to do this by a sore spot still left in his heart from a phrase of Smerdyakov's: that it was to his, Ivan's, advantage that his brother should be convicted, because that would raise his inheritance and Alyosha's from forty to sixty thousand roubles. He resolved to sacrifice thirty thousand on arranging Mitya's escape. On his return from seeing him, he was very mournful and dispirited; he suddenly began to feel that he was anxious for Mitya's escape not only to heal that sore spot by sacrificing thirty thousand, but for another reason. “Is it because I am just as much a murderer at heart?” he asked himself. Something very deep down seemed to be burning and festering in his soul. His pride above all suffered cruelly all that month. But of that later.

76.66.oldText: When, after his conversation with Alyosha, Ivan suddenly decided, with his hand on the bell of his lodging, to go to Smerdyakov, he obeyed a sudden and peculiar impulse of indignation. He suddenly remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had only just cried out to him in Alyosha's presence: “It was you, you, who persuaded me of his” (that is, Mitya's) “guilt!” Ivan was thunderstruck when he recalled it. He had never once tried to persuade her that Mitya was the murderer; on the contrary, he had suspected himself in her presence, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov. It was _she_, she, who had produced that “document” and proved his brother's guilt. And now she suddenly exclaimed, “I've been at Smerdyakov's myself!” When had she been there? Ivan had known nothing of it. So she was not so sure of Mitya's guilt after all! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what, had he said to her? His heart burned with violent anger. He could not understand how he could, half an hour earlier, have let those words pass and not cried out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off to Smerdyakov. “I shall kill him this time, perhaps,” he thought on the way.

77.0.oldText: When he was halfway there, the keen dry wind that had been blowing early that morning rose again, and a fine dry snow began to fall thickly. It didn't lie on the ground, but was whirled about by the wind, and soon there was a regular snowstorm. There were scarcely any lampposts in the part of town where Smerdyakov lived. Ivan strode alone in the darkness, unconscious of the storm, instinctively picking his way. His head ached and there was a painful throbbing in his temples. He felt his hands twitching convulsively. Not far from Marya Kondratyevna's cottage, Ivan suddenly came upon a solitary drunken little peasant. He was wearing a coarse, patched coat, and walking in zigzags, grumbling and swearing to himself. Then suddenly he would begin singing in a husky, drunken voice:

77.1.oldText: “Ach, Vanka's gone to Petersburg; I won't wait till he comes back.”

77.2.oldText: But he broke off every time at the second line and started swearing again; then he would start the same song again. Ivan felt an intense hatred for him before he'd even thought about him. Suddenly he realized his presence and felt an irresistible urge to knock him down. At that moment they met, and the peasant, with a violent lurch, fell full tilt against Ivan, who pushed him back furiously. The peasant went flying backwards and fell like a log on the frozen ground. He gave one plaintive “O-oh!” and then was silent. Ivan stepped up to him. He was lying on his back, without movement or consciousness. “He'll freeze to death,” Ivan thought, and he went on his way to Smerdyakov's.

77.3.oldText: In the passage, Marya Kondratyevna, who ran out to open the door with a candle in her hand, whispered that Smerdyakov was very ill. “It's not that he's laid up, but he seems not himself, and he even told us to take the tea away; he wouldn't have any.”

77.4.oldText: “Why — does he make a row?” Ivan asked coarsely.

77.5.oldText: “Oh dear, no, quite the contrary, he's very quiet. Only please don't talk to him too long,” Marya Kondratyevna begged him. Ivan opened the door and stepped into the room.

77.6.oldText: It was overheated as before, but there were changes in the room. One of the benches at the side had been removed, and in its place had been put a large old mahogany leather sofa, on which a bed had been made up with fairly clean white pillows. Smerdyakov was sitting on the sofa, wearing the same dressing gown. The table had been brought out in front of the sofa, so that there was hardly room to move. On the table lay a thick book in a yellow cover, but Smerdyakov was not reading it. He seemed to be sitting there doing nothing. He met Ivan with a slow, silent gaze and seemed not at all surprised at his coming. There was a great change in his face; he was much thinner and sallower. His eyes were sunken and there were blue marks under them.

77.7.oldText: “Why, you really are ill?” Ivan stopped short. “I won't keep you long, I won't even take off my coat. Where can one sit down?”

77.8.oldText: He went to the other end of the table, moved a chair up, and sat down on it.

77.9.oldText: “Why are you looking at me without speaking? I've only come with one question, and I swear I won't leave without an answer. Has the young lady, Katerina Ivanovna, been to see you?”

77.10.oldText: Smerdyakov still remained silent, looking quietly at Ivan as before. Suddenly, with a motion of his hand, he turned his face away.

77.11.oldText: “What's the matter with you?” Ivan cried.

77.14.oldText: “Yes, she has. It's no matter to you. Leave me alone.”

77.15.oldText: “No, I won't leave you alone. Tell me, when was she here?”

77.16.oldText: “Why, I'd quite forgotten about her,” Smerdyakov said, with a scornful smile, and turning his face to Ivan again, he stared at him with a look of frenzied hatred, the same look he had fixed on him at their last meeting, a month before.

77.17.oldText: “You seem very ill yourself, your face is sunken; you don't look like yourself,” he said to Ivan.

77.18.oldText: “Never mind my health, tell me what I ask you.”

77.19.oldText: “But why are your eyes so yellow? The whites are quite yellow. Are you so worried?” He smiled contemptuously, and suddenly laughed outright.

77.20.oldText: “Listen — I've told you I won't leave without an answer!” Ivan cried, intensely irritated.

77.21.oldText: “Why do you keep pestering me? Why do you torment me?” Smerdyakov said, with a look of suffering.

77.22.oldText: “Damn it! I've nothing to do with you. Just answer my question, and I'll go.”

77.23.oldText: “I've no answer to give you,” Smerdyakov said, looking down again.

77.24.oldText: “You may be sure I'll make you answer!”

77.25.oldText: “Why are you so uneasy?” Smerdyakov stared at him, not merely with contempt but almost with revulsion. “Is this because the trial begins tomorrow? Nothing will happen to you; can't you believe that at last? Go home, go to bed, and sleep in peace; don't be afraid of anything.”

77.26.oldText: “I don't understand you ... What have I to be afraid of tomorrow?” Ivan said in astonishment, and suddenly a chill breath of fear did pass over his soul. Smerdyakov measured him with his eyes.

77.27.oldText: “You don't understand?” he drawled reproachfully. “It's a strange thing for a sensible man to want to put on such a farce!”

77.28.oldText: Ivan looked at him speechless. The startling, incredibly supercilious tone of this man who had once been his valet was extraordinary in itself. He had not taken such a tone even at their last meeting.

77.29.oldText: “I'm telling you, you've nothing to be afraid of. I won't say anything about you; there's no proof against you. I say — how your hands are trembling! Why are your fingers twitching like that? Go home, _you_ did not murder him.”

77.31.oldText: “I know it wasn't I,” he faltered.

77.32.oldText: “Do you?” Smerdyakov caught him up again.

77.33.oldText: Ivan jumped up and seized him by the shoulder.

77.34.oldText: “Tell me everything, you viper! Tell me everything!”

77.35.oldText: Smerdyakov wasn't in the least scared. He only riveted his eyes on Ivan with insane hatred.

77.36.oldText: “Well, it was you who murdered him, if that's it,” he whispered furiously.

77.37.oldText: Ivan sank back into his chair, as though pondering something. He laughed malignantly.

77.38.oldText: “You mean my going away. What you talked about last time?”

77.39.oldText: “You stood before me last time and understood it all, and you understand it now.”

77.40.oldText: “All I understand is that you're mad.”

77.41.oldText: “Aren't you tired of it? Here we are, face to face; what's the use of going on keeping up the farce for each other? Are you still trying to throw it all on me, to my face? _You_ murdered him; you are the real murderer. I was only your instrument, your faithful servant, and it was following your words that I did it.”

77.42.oldText: “_Did_ it? Why — did you murder him?” Ivan turned cold.

77.43.oldText: Something seemed to give way in his brain, and he shuddered all over with a cold shiver. Then Smerdyakov himself looked at him in wonder; probably the genuineness of Ivan's horror struck him.

77.44.oldText: “You don't mean to say you really didn't know?” he faltered mistrustfully, looking with a forced smile into his eyes. Ivan still gazed at him, and seemed unable to speak.

77.45.oldText: Ach, Vanka's gone to Petersburg; I won't wait till he comes back —

77.47.oldText: “Do you know, I'm afraid you're a dream, a phantom sitting before me,” he muttered.

77.48.oldText: “There's no phantom here, only us two — and one other. No doubt he's here, that third, between us.”

77.49.oldText: “Who is he? Who is here? What third person?” Ivan cried in alarm, looking about him, his eyes searching every corner.

77.50.oldText: “That third is God Himself — Providence. He is the third beside us now. Only don't look for Him, you won't find Him.”

77.51.oldText: “It's a lie that you killed him!” Ivan cried madly. “You're mad, or teasing me again!”

77.52.oldText: Smerdyakov, as before, watched him curiously, with no sign of fear. He could still scarcely get over his incredulity; he still imagined that Ivan knew everything and was trying to “throw it all on him to his face.”

77.53.oldText: “Wait a minute,” he said at last in a weak voice, and suddenly, lifting his left leg from under the table, he began turning up his trouser leg. He was wearing long white stockings and slippers. Slowly he took off his garter and fumbled to the bottom of his stocking. Ivan gazed at him, and suddenly shuddered in a paroxysm of terror.

77.54.oldText: “He's mad!” he cried, and jumping up quickly, he drew back, so that he knocked his back against the wall and stood up against it, stiff and straight. He looked with insane terror at Smerdyakov, who, entirely unaffected by his terror, continued fumbling in his stocking, as though making an effort to grip something with his fingers and pull it out. At last he got hold of it and began pulling it out. Ivan saw that it was a piece of paper, or perhaps a roll of papers. Smerdyakov pulled it out and laid it on the table.

77.57.oldText: “Kindly look at it,” Smerdyakov answered, still in the same low tone.

77.58.oldText: Ivan stepped up to the table, picked up the roll of paper, and began unfolding it, but suddenly he drew back his fingers, as if from contact with a loathsome reptile.

77.59.oldText: “Your hands keep twitching,” Smerdyakov observed, and he deliberately unfolded the bundle himself. Under the wrapper were three packets of hundred-rouble notes.

77.60.oldText: “They're all here, all the three thousand roubles; you needn't count them. Take them,” Smerdyakov suggested to Ivan, nodding at the notes. Ivan sank back into his chair. He was as white as a handkerchief.

77.61.oldText: “You frightened me ... with your stocking,” he said, with a strange grin.

77.63.oldText: “No, I didn't know. I kept thinking of Dmitri. Brother, brother! Ach!” He suddenly clutched his head in both hands.

77.64.oldText: “Listen. Did you kill him alone? With my brother's help or without?”

77.65.oldText: “It was only with you, with your help, that I killed him; Dmitri Fyodorovitch is completely innocent.”

77.66.oldText: “All right, all right. Talk about me later. Why do I keep trembling? I can't speak properly.”

77.67.oldText: “You were bold enough back then. You said ‘everything was lawful,' and now how frightened you are,” Smerdyakov muttered in surprise. “Won't you have some lemonade? I'll ask for some at once. It's very refreshing. Only I must hide this first.”

77.68.oldText: And again he gestured at the notes. He was about to get up and call at the door to Marya Kondratyevna to make some lemonade and bring it in, but, looking for something to cover the notes so she wouldn't see them, he first took out his handkerchief; and since it turned out to be very dirty, he took up the big yellow book Ivan had noticed at first lying on the table, and put it over the notes. The book was _The Sayings of the Holy Father Isaac the Syrian_. Ivan read it mechanically.

77.69.oldText: “I won't have any lemonade,” he said. “Talk of me later. Sit down and tell me how you did it. Tell me all about it.”

77.70.oldText: “You'd better take off your greatcoat, or you'll be too hot.” Ivan, as if the thought had only just occurred to him, took off his coat and, without getting up from his chair, threw it on the bench.

77.72.oldText: He seemed calmer. He waited, feeling sure Smerdyakov would tell him _everything_ about it.

77.73.oldText: “How it was done?” Smerdyakov sighed. “It was done in the most natural way, following your very words.”

77.74.oldText: “Of my words later,” Ivan broke in again, apparently with complete self-possession, firmly uttering his words and not shouting as before. “Just tell me in detail how you did it. Everything, as it happened. Don't leave anything out. The details, above everything, the details, I beg you.”

77.75.oldText: “You had gone, and then I fell into the cellar.”

77.76.oldText: “In a real fit, or a sham one?”

77.77.oldText: “A sham one, naturally. I shammed it all. I went quietly down the steps to the very bottom and lay down quietly, and as I lay down I gave a scream, and struggled, until they carried me out.”

77.78.oldText: “Wait! And were you shamming all along afterwards, and in the hospital?”

77.79.oldText: “No, not at all. The next morning, before they took me to the hospital, I had a real attack and a more violent one than I've had for years. For two days I was completely unconscious.”

77.81.oldText: “They laid me on the bed. I knew I'd be on the other side of the partition, because whenever I was ill, Marfa Ignatyevna used to put me there, near them. She's always been very kind to me, ever since I was born. At night I moaned, but quietly. I kept expecting Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come.”

77.83.oldText: “Not to me. I expected him to come into the house, because I had no doubt he'd come that night — because without me there, and getting no news, he'd be sure to come and climb over the fence as he used to and do something.”

77.85.oldText: “Then nothing would have happened. I would never have brought myself to it without him.”

77.86.oldText: “All right, all right ... speak more intelligibly, don't hurry; above all, don't leave anything out!”

77.87.oldText: “I expected him to kill Fyodor Pavlovitch. I thought that was certain, because I had prepared him for it ... during the last few days. He knew about the knocks, that was the main thing. With his suspiciousness and the fury that had been building in him all those days, he was bound to get into the house by means of those taps. That was inevitable, so I was expecting him.”

77.88.oldText: “Wait,” Ivan interrupted; “if he had killed him, he would have taken the money and carried it away; you must have considered that. What would you have gotten out of it afterwards? I don't see.”

77.89.oldText: “But he would never have found the money. That was only what I told him, that the money was under the mattress. But that wasn't true. It had been kept in a box. And afterwards I suggested to Fyodor Pavlovitch, since I was the only person he trusted, that he hide the envelope with the notes in the corner behind the icons, because no one would have guessed that place, especially if they came in a hurry. So that's where the envelope lay, in the corner behind the icons. It would have been absurd to keep it under the mattress — the box, at any rate, could be locked. But everyone believed it was under the mattress. A stupid thing to believe. So if Dmitri Fyodorovitch had committed the murder, finding nothing, he would either have run away in a hurry, afraid of every sound, as always happens with murderers, or he would have been arrested. So I could always have climbed up to the icons and taken the money away the next morning or even that same night, and it would have all been pinned on Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I could count on that.”

77.90.oldText: “But what if he didn't kill him, just knocked him down?”

77.91.oldText: “If he didn't kill him, of course I wouldn't have ventured to take the money, and nothing would have happened. But I calculated that he'd beat him senseless, and I'd have time to take it then, and afterwards I'd make out to Fyodor Pavlovitch that no one but Dmitri Fyodorovitch had taken the money after beating him.”

77.92.oldText: “Stop ... I'm getting mixed up. Then it was Dmitri after all who killed him; you only took the money?”

77.93.oldText: “No, he didn't kill him. Well, I might as well have told you now that he was the murderer. But I don't want to lie to you now, because ... because if you really haven't understood till now, as I see for myself, and aren't pretending so as to throw your guilt on me to my very face, you are still responsible for all of it, since you knew of the murder and charged me to do it, and went away knowing all about it. And so I want to prove to your face this evening that you are the only real murderer in the whole affair, and I am not the real murderer, though I did kill him. You are the rightful murderer.”

77.94.oldText: “Why, why, am I a murderer? Oh God!” Ivan cried, unable to restrain himself at last, and forgetting that he had put off discussing himself until the end of the conversation. “You still mean that Tchermashnya? Wait — tell me, why did you want my consent, if you really took Tchermashnya as consent? How do you explain that now?”

77.95.oldText: “Assured of your consent, I knew you wouldn't have made an outcry over those three thousand being lost, even if I'd been suspected instead of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, or as his accomplice; on the contrary, you'd have protected me from others. And when you came into your inheritance, you'd have rewarded me when you could, all the rest of your life. Because you'd have received your inheritance through me, seeing that if he had married Agrafena Alexandrovna, you wouldn't have had a farthing.”

77.96.oldText: “Ah! So you intended to worry me all my life afterwards,” Ivan snarled. “And what if I hadn't gone away then, but had informed on you?”

77.97.oldText: “What could you have informed them of? That I persuaded you to go to Tchermashnya? That's all nonsense. Besides, after our conversation you'd either have gone away or have stayed. If you had stayed, nothing would have happened. I would have known you didn't want it done, and I wouldn't have attempted anything. Since you went away, it meant you'd assured me that you wouldn't dare inform against me at the trial, and that you'd overlook my having the three thousand. And, indeed, you couldn't have prosecuted me afterwards, because in that case I'd have told it all in court — not that I had stolen the money or killed him, I wouldn't have said that — but that you'd put me up to the theft and the murder, though I hadn't consented to it. That's why I needed your consent, so that you couldn't have cornered me later, for what proof could you have had? I could always have cornered you, revealing your eagerness for your father's death, and I tell you, the public would have believed it all, and you'd have been ashamed the rest of your life.”

77.98.oldText: “Was I so eager, was I?” Ivan snarled again.

77.99.oldText: “To be sure you were, and by your consent you silently sanctioned my doing it.” Smerdyakov looked resolutely at Ivan. He was very weak and spoke slowly and wearily, but some hidden inner force drove him on. He evidently had some design. Ivan felt that.

77.100.oldText: “Go on,” he said. “Tell me what happened that night.”

77.101.oldText: “What more is there to tell? I lay there and I thought I heard the master shout. And before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and he suddenly gave a scream, and then all was silence and darkness. I lay there waiting, my heart pounding; I couldn't bear it. At last I got up, went out. I saw the window on the left, into the garden, was open, and I stepped to the left to listen whether he was sitting there alive, and I heard the master moving about, sighing, so I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!' I thought. I went to the window and shouted to the master, ‘It's I.' And he shouted to me, ‘He's been, he's been; he's run away.' He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He's killed Grigory!' ‘Where?' I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,' he pointed. He was whispering, too. ‘Wait a moment,' I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there I came upon Grigory Vassilyevitch lying by the wall, covered with blood, senseless. So it's true that Dmitri Fyodorovitch has been here, was the thought that came into my head, and I determined on the spot to make an end of it, since Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he were alive, would see nothing of it lying there senseless. The only risk was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the moment, but the longing to get it done came over me, till I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window to the master and said, ‘She's here, she's come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, wants to be let in.' And he started like a baby. ‘Where is she?' he positively gasped, but couldn't believe it. ‘She's standing there,' I said. ‘Open up.' He looked out of the window at me, half believing, half distrustful, but afraid to open. ‘Why, he's afraid of me now,' I thought. And it was funny. It struck me to knock on the window frame those taps we'd agreed upon as a signal that Grushenka had come, in his presence, right before his eyes. He didn't seem to believe my word, but as soon as he heard the taps, he ran at once to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the way to prevent me passing. ‘Where is she? Where is she?' He looked at me, all of a tremble. ‘Well,' I thought, ‘if he's that frightened of me, it's a bad lookout!' And my legs went weak with fright that he wouldn't let me in, or would call out, or Marfa Ignatyevna would come running up, or something else might happen. I don't remember now, but I must have stood pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she's there, there, under the window; how is it you don't see her?' I said. ‘Bring her, then, bring her.' ‘She's afraid,' I said; ‘she was frightened at the noise, she's hiding in the bushes; go and call to her yourself from the study.' He ran to the window, put the candle in the window. ‘Grushenka,' he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you here?' Though he cried that, he didn't want to lean out of the window, he didn't want to move away from me, because he was panic-stricken; he was so frightened he didn't dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, here she is,' I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out of it. ‘Here she is; she's in the bush, laughing at you, don't you see her?' He suddenly believed it; he was all of a shake — he was awfully crazy about her — and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up that iron paperweight from his table; do you remember, weighing about three pounds? I swung it and hit him on the top of the skull with the corner of it. He didn't even cry out. He just sank down suddenly, and I hit him again and a third time. And the third time I knew I'd broken his skull. He suddenly rolled onto his back, face upwards, covered in blood. I looked myself over. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight, put it back, went up to the icons, took the money out of the envelope, and flung the envelope on the floor and the pink ribbon beside it. I went out into the garden, all of a tremble, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it — you know the one. I'd marked it long before and put a rag and a piece of paper ready in it. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and stuffed it deep down in the hole. And there it stayed for over a fortnight. I took it out later, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed, lay down, and thought, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may go badly for me, but if he isn't killed and recovers, it'll be first-rate, because he'll bear witness that Dmitri Fyodorovitch has been here, and so he must have killed him and taken the money.' Then I started groaning with suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as possible. At last she got up and rushed to me, but when she saw Grigory Vassilyevitch was not there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. And that set it all going and set my mind at rest.”

77.102.oldText: He stopped. Ivan had listened all the while in dead silence, without stirring or taking his eyes off him. As he told his story, Smerdyakov glanced at him from time to time, but for the most part kept his eyes averted. When he had finished, he was evidently agitated and was breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face. But it was impossible to tell whether it was remorse he was feeling, or something else.

77.103.oldText: “Wait,” Ivan cried, pondering. “What about the door? If he only opened the door to you, how could Grigory have seen it open before? Because Grigory saw it before you went out.”

77.104.oldText: It was remarkable that Ivan was speaking quite amicably, in a different tone, not angry as before, so that if anyone had opened the door at that moment and peeped in at them, he would certainly have concluded they were talking peaceably about some ordinary, though interesting, subject.

77.105.oldText: “As for that door and Grigory Vassilyevitch's having seen it open, that's only his fancy,” Smerdyakov said, with a wry smile. “He's not a man, I assure you, but an obstinate mule. He didn't see it, but fancied he had seen it, and there's no shaking him. It's just our luck he took that idea into his head, because after that they can't fail to convict Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

77.106.oldText: “Listen ...” Ivan said, beginning to seem bewildered again and making an effort to grasp something. “Listen. There are a lot of questions I want to ask you, but I keep forgetting them ... I keep forgetting and getting mixed up. Yes. Tell me this at least — why did you open the envelope and leave it on the floor? Why didn't you simply carry off the envelope? When you were telling me, I got the impression you spoke of it as though it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can't understand.”

77.107.oldText: “I did that for a good reason. Because if a man had known all about it, as I did for instance — if he'd seen those notes before, and perhaps had put them in that envelope himself, and had seen the envelope sealed up and addressed with his own eyes — if such a man had done the murder, what would have made him tear open the envelope afterwards, especially in such desperate haste, since he'd know for certain the notes must be in the envelope? No — if the robber had been someone like me, he'd simply have put the envelope straight in his pocket and gotten away with it as fast as he could. But it would be quite different with Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He only knew about the envelope by hearsay; he'd never seen it, and if he'd found it, for instance, under the mattress, he'd have torn it open as quickly as possible to make sure the notes were inside. And he'd have thrown the envelope down without stopping to think that it would be evidence against him. Because he wasn't an habitual thief and had never directly stolen anything before, being a gentleman born, and if he did bring himself to steal, it wouldn't be proper stealing but simply taking what was his own, since he'd told the whole town he meant to before, and had even bragged out loud before everyone that he'd go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn't say that openly to the prosecutor while I was being examined — quite the contrary, I brought him to it by a hint, as though I didn't see it myself, and as though he'd thought of it himself and I hadn't prompted him; so that Mr. Prosecutor's mouth positively watered at my suggestion.”

77.108.oldText: “But can you really have thought of all that on the spot?” Ivan cried, overcome with astonishment. He looked at Smerdyakov again with alarm.

77.109.oldText: “Mercy on us! Could anyone think of it all in such a desperate hurry? It was all thought out beforehand.”

77.110.oldText: “Well ... well, it was the devil who helped you!” Ivan cried again. “No — you're not a fool, you're far cleverer than I thought.”

77.111.oldText: He got up, obviously intending to walk across the room. He was in terrible distress. But since the table blocked his way, and there was hardly room to pass between the table and the wall, he only turned where he stood and sat down again. Perhaps the impossibility of moving irritated him, because he suddenly cried out almost as furiously as before.
