77.112.oldText: “Listen, you miserable, contemptible creature! Don't you understand that if I haven't killed you, it's simply because I'm keeping you to answer tomorrow at the trial. God sees,” Ivan raised his hand, “perhaps I too was guilty; perhaps I really had a secret desire for my father's ... death, but I swear I wasn't as guilty as you think, and perhaps I didn't urge you on at all. No, no, I didn't urge you on! But no matter — I'll give evidence against myself tomorrow at the trial. I'm determined to! I'll tell everything, everything. But we'll appear together. And whatever you may say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I'll face it; I'm not afraid of you. I'll confirm it all myself! But you must confess, too! You must, you must; we'll go together. That's how it shall be!”

77.113.oldText: Ivan said this solemnly and resolutely, and from his flashing eyes alone it could be seen that it would be so.

77.114.oldText: “You're ill, I see; you are quite ill. Your eyes are yellow,” Smerdyakov observed, without the least irony, with apparent sympathy in fact.

77.115.oldText: “We'll go together,” Ivan repeated. “And if you won't go, no matter, I'll go alone.”

77.117.oldText: “There'll be nothing of the sort, and you won't go,” he concluded at last positively.

77.118.oldText: “You don't understand me,” Ivan exclaimed reproachfully.

77.119.oldText: “You'll be too much ashamed if you confess it all. And what's more, it will be no use at all, because I'll say straight out that I never said anything of the sort to you, and that you're either ill (and it looks like it, too), or that you're so sorry for your brother that you're sacrificing yourself to save him, and have invented it all against me, because you've always thought no more of me than if I were a fly. And who will believe you, and what single proof have you got?”

77.120.oldText: “Listen — you showed me those notes just now to convince me.”

77.121.oldText: Smerdyakov lifted the book off the notes and laid it aside.

77.123.oldText: “Of course, I'll take it. But why do you give it to me, if you committed the murder for its sake?” Ivan looked at him with great surprise.

77.124.oldText: “I don't want it,” Smerdyakov said in a shaking voice, with a gesture of refusal. “I did have an idea of starting a new life with that money, in Moscow or, better still, abroad. I did dream of it, chiefly because ‘all things are lawful.' That was quite right, what you taught me, because you talked a lot to me about that. For if there's no everlasting God, there's no such thing as virtue, and there's no need of it. You were right there. So that's how I looked at it.”

77.125.oldText: “Did you come to that yourself?” Ivan asked, with a wry smile.

77.127.oldText: “And now, I suppose, you believe in God, since you're giving back the money?”

77.129.oldText: “Then why are you giving it back?”

77.130.oldText: “Leave off ... that's enough!” Smerdyakov waved his hand again. “You used to say yourself that everything was lawful, so why are you so upset now, too? You even want to go and give evidence against yourself. Only there'll be nothing of the sort! You won't go to give evidence,” Smerdyakov decided with conviction.

77.132.oldText: “It's impossible. You're very clever. You're fond of money, I know that. You like to be respected, too, because you're very proud; you're far too fond of female charms, too, and you mind most of all about living in undisturbed comfort, without having to depend on anyone — that's what you care about most. You won't want to spoil your life forever by taking such a disgrace on yourself. You're like Fyodor Pavlovitch — you're more like him than any of his children; you have the same soul as he had.”

77.133.oldText: “You're not a fool,” Ivan said, seeming struck. The blood rushed to his face. “You're serious now!” he observed, looking suddenly at Smerdyakov with a different expression.

77.134.oldText: “It was your pride that made you think me a fool. Take the money.”

77.135.oldText: Ivan took the three rolls of notes and put them in his pocket without wrapping them in anything.

77.136.oldText: “I'll show them in court tomorrow,” he said.

77.137.oldText: “Nobody will believe you, as you have plenty of money of your own; you may simply have taken it out of your cash box and brought it to the court.”

77.139.oldText: “I repeat,” he said, “the only reason I haven't killed you is that I need you for tomorrow, remember that — don't forget it!”

77.140.oldText: “Well, kill me. Kill me now,” Smerdyakov said, all at once looking strangely at Ivan. “You won't dare do that either!” he added, with a bitter smile. “You won't dare to do anything, you, who used to be so bold!”

77.141.oldText: “Till tomorrow,” Ivan cried, and moved to go out.

77.142.oldText: “Wait a moment ... Show me those notes again.”

77.143.oldText: Ivan took out the notes and showed them to him. Smerdyakov looked at them for ten seconds.

77.144.oldText: “Well, you can go,” he said, with a wave of his hand. “Ivan Fyodorovitch!” he called after him again.

77.145.oldText: “What do you want?” Ivan turned without stopping.

77.147.oldText: “Till tomorrow!” Ivan cried again, and he walked out of the cottage.

77.148.oldText: The snowstorm was still raging. He walked the first few steps boldly, but suddenly began to stagger. “It's something physical,” he thought with a grin. Something like joy was springing up in his heart. He was conscious of boundless resolution; he would put an end to the wavering that had so tortured him of late. His determination was fixed, “and now it will not be changed,” he thought with relief. At that moment he stumbled against something and almost fell. Stopping short, he made out at his feet the peasant he had knocked down, still lying senseless and motionless. The snow had almost covered his face. Ivan seized him and lifted him in his arms. Seeing a light in the little house to the right, he went up, knocked at the shutters, and asked the man to whom the house belonged to help him carry the peasant to the police station, promising him three roubles. The man got ready and came out. I won't describe in detail how Ivan succeeded in bringing the peasant to the police station and arranging for a doctor to see him at once, providing with a generous hand for the expenses. Suffice it to say that this business took a whole hour, but Ivan was well content with it. His mind wandered and worked incessantly.

77.149.oldText: “If I hadn't taken my decision so firmly for tomorrow,” he reflected with satisfaction, “I wouldn't have stayed a whole hour to look after the peasant, but should have passed by, without caring about his freezing. I'm quite capable of watching myself, by the way,” he thought at the same instant, with still greater satisfaction, “although they've decided that I'm going out of my mind!”

77.150.oldText: Just as he reached his own house he stopped short, asking himself suddenly whether he hadn't better go at once to the prosecutor and tell him everything. He decided the question by turning back to the house. “Everything together, tomorrow!” he whispered to himself, and, strange to say, almost all his gladness and self-satisfaction passed in one instant.

77.151.oldText: As he entered his room, he felt something like a touch of ice on his heart, like a recollection or, more exactly, a reminder of something agonizing and revolting that was in the room now, at that moment, and had been there before. He sank wearily onto his sofa. The old woman brought him a samovar; he made tea, but did not touch it. He sat on the sofa and felt giddy. He felt ill and helpless. He was beginning to doze off, but got up uneasily and walked across the room to shake off his drowsiness. At moments he imagined he was delirious, but it was not illness he was thinking of most. Sitting down again, he began looking around, as though searching for something. This happened several times. At last his eyes fastened intently on one point. Ivan smiled, but an angry flush suffused his face. He sat for a long time in his place, his head propped on both arms, though he looked sideways at the same point, at the sofa that stood against the opposite wall. There was evidently something there — some object — that was irritating him, worrying him, tormenting him.

78.0.oldText: I am not a doctor, yet I feel the moment has come when I must inevitably give the reader some account of the nature of Ivan's illness. Anticipating events, I can say at least one thing: at that moment he was on the very eve of an attack of brain fever. Though his health had long been affected, it had offered stubborn resistance to the fever which in the end gained complete mastery over it. Though I know nothing of medicine, I venture to suggest that he really had, perhaps by a terrible effort of will, succeeded in delaying the attack for a time, hoping, of course, to stave it off entirely. He knew he was unwell, but he loathed the thought of being ill at that fatal time, at the approaching crisis in his life, when he needed all his wits about him, to say what he had to say boldly and resolutely and to “justify himself to himself.”

78.1.oldText: He had, however, consulted the new doctor, who had been brought from Moscow on a fantastic notion of Katerina Ivanovna's, already mentioned. After listening to him and examining him, the doctor came to the conclusion that Ivan was indeed suffering from some disorder of the brain, and was not at all surprised by an admission Ivan had reluctantly made. “Hallucinations are quite likely in your condition,” the doctor pronounced, “though it would be better to verify them ... you must take steps at once, without a moment's delay, or things will go badly with you.” But Ivan did not follow this judicious advice and did not take to his bed to be nursed. “I'm walking about, so I'm strong enough; if I drop, it'll be different then, anyone may nurse me who likes,” he decided, dismissing the subject.

78.2.oldText: And so he was sitting there, almost conscious himself of his delirium and, as I've already said, staring persistently at some object on the sofa across from him against the opposite wall. Someone appeared to be sitting there, though goodness knows how he'd gotten in, since he had not been in the room when Ivan had come into it on his return from Smerdyakov. This was a person — or, more accurately speaking, a Russian gentleman of a particular kind — no longer young, _qui faisait la cinquantaine_, as the French say, with rather long, still thick, dark hair slightly streaked with gray and a small pointed beard. He was wearing a brownish reefer jacket, rather shabby, but evidently made by a good tailor, and of a fashion at least three years old, one that had been discarded by smart and well-to-do people for the last two years. His linen and his long, scarf-like necktie were of a kind worn by people who aim at being stylish, but on closer inspection his linen was not very clean and his wide scarf was very threadbare. The visitor's check trousers were of excellent cut but too light in color, and too tight for the present fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat was quite out of keeping with the season.

78.3.oldText: In short, there was every appearance of gentility on straitened means. It looked as though the gentleman belonged to that class of idle landowners who used to flourish in the days of serfdom. He had unmistakably been, at some time, in good and fashionable society, had once had good connections, had perhaps even preserved them, but, after a gay youth, becoming gradually impoverished following the abolition of serfdom, he had sunk into the position of a poor relation of the best class, wandering from one good old friend to another and received by them for his companionable and accommodating disposition and because, after all, he was a gentleman who could be seated at any table — though, of course, not in the place of honor. Such gentlemen of accommodating temper and dependent position, who can tell a story, take a hand at cards, and have a distinct aversion to any duties forced upon them, are usually solitary creatures, either bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but in that case the children are always being brought up at a distance, at some aunt's, to whom the gentleman never alludes in good society, seemingly ashamed of the connection. They gradually lose sight of their children altogether, though at intervals they receive a birthday or Christmas letter from them, and sometimes even answer it.

78.4.oldText: The countenance of the unexpected visitor was not so much good-natured as accommodating, ready to assume any amiable expression as occasion might require. He had no watch, but he had a tortoiseshell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand was a massive gold ring set with a cheap opal.

78.5.oldText: Ivan was angrily silent and would not begin the conversation. The visitor waited and sat there exactly like a poor relation who has come downstairs from his room to keep his host company at tea, and was discreetly silent, seeing that his host was frowning and preoccupied. But he was ready for any affable conversation as soon as his host should begin it. Suddenly his face expressed sudden solicitude.

78.6.oldText: “I say,” he began to Ivan, “excuse me, I only mention it to remind you. You went to Smerdyakov's to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, but you came away without finding out anything about her — you probably forgot —”

78.7.oldText: “Ah, yes,” broke from Ivan, and his face grew gloomy with uneasiness. “Yes, I'd forgotten ... but it doesn't matter now, never mind, till tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. “And you,” he added, addressing his visitor, “I would have remembered that myself in a minute, because that was exactly what was tormenting me! Why do you interfere, as if I'd believe you put the thought in my head, and I hadn't remembered it myself?”

78.8.oldText: “Don't believe it, then,” said the gentleman, smiling amicably. “What's the good of believing against your will? Besides, proofs are no help toward believing, especially material proofs. Thomas believed not because he saw Christ risen, but because he wanted to believe before he saw. Look at the spiritualists, for instance. I am very fond of them ... only fancy — they imagine they're serving the cause of religion because the devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, of the existence of another world. The other world and material proofs — what next! And if it comes to that, does proving there's a devil prove there's a God? I want to join an idealist society; I'll lead the opposition in it; I'll say I'm a realist, but not a materialist, he he!”

78.9.oldText: “Listen,” Ivan suddenly got up from the table. “I seem to be delirious. I am delirious, in fact — talk any nonsense you like, I don't care! You won't drive me to fury, as you did last time. But I feel somehow ashamed. I want to walk around the room. I sometimes don't see you and don't even hear your voice, as I did last time, but I always guess what you're prating about, because it's I, _I myself speaking, not you_. Only I don't know whether I was dreaming last time or whether I really saw you. I'll wet a towel and put it on my head, and perhaps you'll vanish into air.”

78.10.oldText: Ivan went into the corner, took a towel, and did as he said, and with a wet towel on his head began walking up and down the room.

78.11.oldText: “I'm so glad you treat me so familiarly,” the visitor began.

78.12.oldText: “Fool,” Ivan laughed, “do you suppose I'd stand on ceremony with you? I'm in good spirits now, though I have a pain in my forehead ... and in the top of my head ... only please don't talk philosophy, as you did last time. If you can't take yourself off, talk of something amusing. Talk gossip — you're a poor relation, you ought to talk gossip. What a nightmare to have! But I'm not afraid of you. I'll get the better of you. I won't be taken to a madhouse!”

78.13.oldText: “_C'est charmant_, poor relation. Yes, I'm in my natural shape. For what am I on earth but a poor relation? By the way, I'm listening to you and am rather surprised to find that you're actually beginning to take me for something real, not simply your fancy, as you kept insisting last time —”

78.14.oldText: “Never for one minute have I taken you for reality,” Ivan cried with a sort of fury. “You're a lie, you're my illness, you're a phantom. It's only that I don't know how to destroy you, and I see I must suffer for a while. You are my hallucination. You are the incarnation of myself, but only of one side of me ... of my thoughts and feelings, but only the nastiest and stupidest of them. From that point of view you might be of interest to me, if I had time to waste on you —”

78.15.oldText: “Excuse me, excuse me — I'll catch you out. When you flew at Alyosha under the lamppost this evening and shouted to him, ‘You learned it from _him_! How do you know that _he_ visits me?' you were thinking of me then. So for one brief moment you did believe that I really exist,” the gentleman laughed blandly.

78.16.oldText: “Yes, that was a moment of weakness ... but I couldn't believe in you. I don't know whether I was asleep or awake last time. Perhaps I was only dreaming then, and didn't see you in reality at all —”

78.17.oldText: “And why were you so surly with Alyosha just now? He's a dear; I've treated him badly over Father Zossima.”

78.18.oldText: “Don't talk of Alyosha! How dare you, you flunkey!” Ivan laughed again.

78.19.oldText: “You scold me, but you laugh — that's a good sign. But you're much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours —”

78.20.oldText: “Don't speak of my resolution,” Ivan cried savagely.

78.21.oldText: “I understand, I understand. _C'est noble, c'est charmant_ — you're going to defend your brother and sacrifice yourself ... _C'est chevaleresque_.”

78.23.oldText: “I won't be altogether sorry, because then my object will be attained. If you kick me, you must believe in my reality, because people don't kick ghosts. Joking aside, it doesn't matter to me — scold if you like, though it's better to be a trifle more polite even to me. ‘Fool, flunkey!' What words!”

78.24.oldText: “Scolding you, I scold myself,” Ivan laughed again. “You are myself, myself, only with a different face. You just say what I'm thinking ... and are incapable of saying anything new!”

78.25.oldText: “If I'm like you in my way of thinking, it's all to my credit,” the gentleman declared, with delicacy and dignity.

78.26.oldText: “You choose out only my worst thoughts, and what's more, the stupid ones. You are stupid and vulgar. You are awfully stupid. No, I can't put up with you! What am I to do, what am I to do?” Ivan said through his clenched teeth.

78.27.oldText: “My dear friend, above all things I want to behave like a gentleman and to be recognized as such,” the visitor began in an excess of deprecating and simple-hearted pride, typical of a poor relation. “I am poor, but ... I won't say very honest, but ... it's an axiom generally accepted in society that I am a fallen angel. I really can't conceive how I can ever have been an angel. If I ever was, it must have been so long ago that there's no harm in forgetting it. Now I only prize the reputation of being a gentlemanly person, and I live as I can, trying to make myself agreeable. I love men genuinely — I've been greatly calumniated! Here, when I stay with you from time to time, my life gains a kind of reality, and that's what I like most. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastic, and so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything is circumscribed, here everything is formulated and geometrical, while we have nothing but indeterminate equations! I wander about here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I become superstitious. Please don't laugh, that's just what I like — becoming superstitious. I adopt all your habits here: I've grown fond of going to the public baths, would you believe it, and I go and steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once for all and irrevocably in the form of some merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing everything she believes. My ideal is to go to church and offer a candle in simple-hearted faith, upon my word it is. Then there would be an end to my sufferings. I've taken a fancy to being doctored, too; in the spring there was an outbreak of smallpox and I went and got vaccinated at a foundling hospital — if only you knew how I enjoyed myself that day. I subscribed ten roubles in the cause of the Slavs! But you're not listening. Do you know, you're not at all well this evening? I know you went yesterday to that doctor ... well, what about your health? What did the doctor say?”

78.29.oldText: “But you're clever, at any rate. You're scolding again? I didn't ask out of sympathy. You needn't answer. Now rheumatism has come on again —”

78.31.oldText: “You keep saying the same thing; but I had such an attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this day.”

78.33.oldText: “Why not, if I sometimes put on fleshly form? I put on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”

78.34.oldText: “What, what, Satan _sum et nihil humanum_ ... that's not bad for the devil!”

78.35.oldText: “I'm glad I've pleased you at last.”

78.36.oldText: “But you didn't get that from me.” Ivan stopped suddenly, as if struck. “That never entered my head — that's strange.”

78.37.oldText: “_C'est du nouveau, n'est-ce pas?_ This time I'll act honestly and explain it to you. Listen — in dreams, and especially in nightmares, whether from indigestion or anything else, a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such complex and realistic actuality, such events — even a whole world of events, woven into such a plot with such unexpected details, from the most exalted matters to the last button on a cuff — as I swear Leo Tolstoy has never invented. Yet such dreams are sometimes dreamt not by writers, but by the most ordinary people — officials, journalists, priests. The whole subject is a complete enigma. A statesman confessed to me, indeed, that all his best ideas came to him when he was asleep. Well, that's how it is now. Though I am your hallucination, yet, just as in a nightmare, I say original things that hadn't entered your head before. So I don't repeat your ideas, yet I'm only your nightmare, nothing more.”

78.38.oldText: “You're lying. Your aim is to convince me you exist apart and aren't my nightmare, and now you're asserting you are a dream.”

78.39.oldText: “My dear fellow, I've adopted a special method today — I'll explain it to you afterwards. Wait, where did I break off? Oh yes. I caught cold then, only not here but yonder.”

78.40.oldText: “Where is yonder? Tell me — will you be here long? Can't you go away?” Ivan exclaimed almost in despair. He stopped walking to and fro, sat down on the sofa, leaned his elbows on the table again, and held his head tight in both hands. He pulled the wet towel off and flung it away in vexation. It was evidently of no use.

78.41.oldText: “Your nerves are out of order,” the gentleman observed, with a carelessly easy, though perfectly polite, air. “You're angry with me even for being able to catch cold, though it happened in a most natural way. I was hurrying at the time to a diplomatic _soirée_ at the house of a lady of high rank in Petersburg who was angling for influence in the Ministry. Well, evening suit, white tie, gloves — though I was God knows where and had to fly through space to reach your earth. Of course, it took only an instant, but you know, a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes, and just imagine — in an evening suit with an open waistcoat. Spirits don't freeze, but when one's in fleshly form, well ... in brief, I didn't think, and off I set, and you know, in those ethereal spaces, in the water that is above the firmament, there's such a frost ... or rather, one can't call it frost — you can imagine, 150 degrees below zero! You know the game the village girls play — they invite the unwary to lick an axe in thirty degrees of frost: the tongue instantly freezes to it, and the dupe tears the skin off, so it bleeds. But that's only at 30 degrees; at 150 degrees I imagine it would be enough to put your finger on the axe and that would be the end of it ... if only there could be an axe there.”

78.42.oldText: “And can there be an axe there?” Ivan interrupted, carelessly and disdainfully. He was exerting himself to the utmost not to believe in the delusion and not to sink into complete insanity.

78.43.oldText: “An axe?” the guest interrupted in surprise.

78.44.oldText: “Yes — what would become of an axe there?” Ivan cried suddenly, with a sort of savage and insistent obstinacy.

78.45.oldText: “What would become of an axe in space? _Quelle idée!_ If it were to fall at any distance, it would, I think, begin flying around the earth without knowing why, like a satellite. The astronomers would calculate the rising and the setting of the axe; _Gatzuk_ would put it in his calendar, and that's all.”

78.46.oldText: “You're stupid, awfully stupid,” Ivan said peevishly. “Fib more cleverly, or I won't listen. You want to get the better of me by realism, to convince me that you exist, but I don't want to believe you exist! I won't believe it!”

78.47.oldText: “But I'm not fibbing, it's all the truth; the truth is, unhappily, hardly ever amusing. I see you persist in expecting something big of me, and perhaps something fine. That's a great pity, because I only give what I can —”

78.49.oldText: “Philosophy, indeed, when all my right side has gone numb and I'm moaning and groaning! I've tried the whole medical faculty: they diagnose beautifully, they have the whole of your disease at their fingertips, but they have no idea how to cure you. There was an enthusiastic little student here — ‘You may die,' he said, ‘but you'll know perfectly well what disease you're dying of!' And then the way they have of sending people to specialists! ‘We only diagnose,' they say, ‘go see such-and-such a specialist, he'll cure you.' The old-fashioned doctor who used to cure every sort of disease has completely disappeared, I assure you; now there are only specialists, and they all advertise in the newspapers. If there's anything wrong with your nose, they send you to Paris: there, they say, is a European specialist who cures noses. If you go to Paris, he'll look at your nose; I can only cure your right nostril, he'll tell you, because I don't cure the left nostril — that's not my specialty, but go to Vienna, there's a specialist there who will cure your left nostril. What are you to do? I fell back on popular remedies; a German doctor advised me to rub myself with honey and salt at the bathhouse. Solely to get an extra bath, I went, smeared myself all over, and it did me no good whatsoever. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. He sent me a book and some drops, bless him, and — only fancy — Hoff's malt extract cured me! I bought it by accident, drank a bottle and a half of it, and was ready to dance — it took it away completely. I made up my mind to write to the papers to thank him, I was prompted by a feeling of gratitude, and only fancy, it led to no end of a bother: not a single paper would take my letter. ‘It would be very reactionary,' they said. ‘No one will believe it. _Le diable n'existe point._ You'd better remain anonymous,' they advised me. What use is a letter of thanks if it's anonymous? I laughed with the men at the newspaper office. ‘It's reactionary to believe in God in our days,' I said, ‘but I'm the devil, so I may be believed in.' ‘We quite understand that,' they said. ‘Who doesn't believe in the devil? Yet it won't do — it might injure our reputation. As a joke, if you like.' But I thought, as a joke it wouldn't be very witty. So it wasn't printed. And do you know, I've felt sore about it to this day. My best feelings, gratitude for instance, are literally denied me simply on account of my social position.”

78.51.oldText: “God preserve me from that — but one can't help complaining sometimes. I'm a slandered man. You upbraid me every moment with being stupid. You can see you're young. My dear fellow, intelligence isn't the only thing! I have a naturally kind and merry heart. ‘I also write vaudevilles of all sorts.' You seem to take me for Hlestakov grown old, but my fate is a far more serious one. Before time was, by some decree I could never make out, I was predestined ‘to deny,' and yet I am genuinely good-hearted and not at all inclined to negation. ‘No, you must go and deny, without denial there's no criticism, and what would a journal be without a column of criticism?' Without criticism it would be nothing but one ‘hosannah.' But nothing but hosannah is not enough for life — the hosannah must be tried in the crucible of doubt, and so on, in the same style. But I don't meddle in that — I didn't create it, I'm not answerable for it. Well, they've chosen their scapegoat, they've made me write the column of criticism, and so life was made possible. We understand that comedy; I, for one, simply ask for annihilation. ‘No — live,' I'm told, ‘because there'd be nothing without you. If everything in the universe were sensible, nothing would happen. There would be no events without you, and there must be events.' So against the grain I serve to produce events and do what's irrational because I am commanded to. For all their indisputable intelligence, men take this farce as something serious, and that is their tragedy. They suffer, of course ... but then they live, they live a real life, not a fantastic one, because suffering is life. Without suffering, what would be the pleasure of it? It would be transformed into an endless church service — it would be holy, but tedious. But what about me? I suffer, but still, I don't live. I am x in an indeterminate equation. I'm a sort of phantom in life who has lost all beginning and end, and who has even forgotten his own name. You're laughing — no, you're not laughing, you're angry again. You're forever angry, all you care about is intelligence, but I repeat again that I would give away all this super-stellar life, all the ranks and honors, simply to be transformed into the soul of a merchant's wife weighing eighteen stone and to set candles at God's shrine.”

78.52.oldText: “Then even you don't believe in God?” Ivan said, with a smile of hatred.

78.53.oldText: “What can I say? — that is, if you're in earnest —”

78.54.oldText: “Is there a God, or not?” Ivan cried with the same savage intensity.

78.55.oldText: “Ah, then you're in earnest! My dear fellow, upon my word, I don't know. There — I've said it now!”

78.56.oldText: “You don't know, but you see God? No, you are not someone apart, you are myself, you are I and nothing more! You are rubbish, you are my fancy!”

78.57.oldText: “Well, if you like, I have the same philosophy as you — that would be true. _Je pense, donc je suis_, I know that for a fact; all the rest, all these worlds, God and even Satan — all that is not proved, to my mind. Does all that exist of itself, or is it only an emanation of myself, a logical development of my ego which alone has existed forever: but I hurry to stop, for I believe you're about to jump up and hit me.”

78.58.oldText: “You'd better tell me some anecdote!” Ivan said miserably.

78.59.oldText: “There is an anecdote precisely on our subject, or rather a legend, not an anecdote. You reproach me with unbelief, you see, you say, yet you don't believe. But, my dear fellow, I'm not the only one like that. We're all in a muddle over there now, and all through your science. Once there used to be atoms, five senses, four elements, and then everything hung together somehow. There were atoms even in the ancient world, but since we've learned that you've discovered the chemical molecule and protoplasm and the devil knows what, we've had to lower our crest. There's a regular muddle, and above all, superstition, scandal; there's as much scandal among us as among you, you know — a little more, in fact — and spying, indeed, because we have our secret police department where private information is received. Well, this wild legend belongs to our middle ages — not yours, but ours — and no one believes it even among us, except the old ladies of eighteen stone (not your old ladies I mean, but ours). We have everything you have, I'm revealing one of our secrets out of friendship for you, though it's forbidden. This legend is about Paradise. There was, they say, here on earth a thinker and philosopher. He rejected everything — ‘laws, conscience, faith,' and, above all, the future life. He died; he expected to go straight to darkness and death, and he found a future life before him. He was astounded and indignant. ‘This is against my principles!' he said. And he was punished for that ... that is, you must excuse me, I'm just repeating what I heard myself, it's only a legend ... he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in the dark (we've adopted the metric system, you know), and when he had finished that quadrillion, the gates of heaven would be opened to him and he would be forgiven —”

78.60.oldText: “And what tortures do you have in the other world besides the quadrillion kilometers?” Ivan asked, with a strange eagerness.

78.61.oldText: “What tortures? Ah, don't ask. In the old days we had all sorts, but now they've taken chiefly to moral punishments — ‘the stings of conscience' and all that nonsense. We got that too from you, from the softening of your manners. And who's the better for it? Only those who have no conscience, because how can they be tortured by conscience when they have none? But decent people, who have conscience and a sense of honor, suffer for it. Reforms, when the ground hasn't been prepared for them, especially if they're institutions copied from abroad, do nothing but mischief! The ancient fire was better. Well, this man, who was sentenced to the quadrillion kilometers, stood still, looked around him, and lay down across the road. ‘I won't go, I refuse on principle!' Take the soul of an enlightened Russian atheist and mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked for three days and nights in the belly of the whale, and you get the character of that thinker who lay across the road.”

78.63.oldText: “Well, I suppose there was something to lie on. You're not laughing?”

78.64.oldText: “Bravo!” Ivan cried, still with the same strange eagerness. Now he was listening with an unexpected curiosity. “Well, is he still lying there?”

78.65.oldText: “That's the point — that he isn't. He lay there for almost a thousand years, and then he got up and went on.”

78.66.oldText: “What an ass!” Ivan cried, laughing nervously and still seeming to be pondering something intently. “Does it make any difference whether he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take a billion years to walk it?”

78.67.oldText: “Much more than that. I haven't got a pencil and paper or I could work it out. But he got there long ago, and that's where the story begins.”

78.68.oldText: “What — he got there? But how did he come by the billion years to do it?”

78.69.oldText: “Why, you keep thinking of our present earth! But our present earth may have been repeated a billion times. Why, it's become extinct, been frozen, cracked, broken to bits, disintegrated into its elements, again ‘the water above the firmament,' then again a comet, again a sun, again from the sun it becomes earth — and the same sequence may have been repeated endlessly and in exactly the same way down to every detail — most unseemly and insufferably tedious —”

78.71.oldText: “Why, the moment the gates of Paradise opened and he walked in, before he'd been there two seconds by his watch (though to my thinking, his watch must have long since dissolved into its elements on the way), he cried out that those two seconds were worth walking not a quadrillion kilometers but a quadrillion of quadrillions, raised to the quadrillionth power! In fact, he sang ‘hosannah' and overdid it so that some persons there of lofty ideas wouldn't shake hands with him at first — he'd become too rapidly reactionary, they said. The Russian temperament. I repeat, it's a legend. I give it for what it's worth. So that's the sort of ideas we still have on such subjects, even now.”

78.72.oldText: “I've caught you!” Ivan cried, with an almost childish delight, as though he'd succeeded in remembering something at last. “That anecdote about the quadrillion years — I made up myself! I was seventeen then, I was at the high school. I made up that anecdote and told it to a schoolfellow called Korovkin, it was at Moscow. The anecdote is so characteristic that I couldn't have taken it from anywhere. I thought I'd forgotten it ... but I've unconsciously recalled it — I recalled it myself — it was not you telling it! Thousands of things are unconsciously remembered like that, even when people are being taken to execution ... it's come back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You are a dream, not a living creature!”

78.73.oldText: “From the vehemence with which you deny my existence,” the gentleman laughed, “I'm convinced that you believe in me.”

78.74.oldText: “Not in the slightest! I haven't a hundredth part of a grain of faith in you!”

78.75.oldText: “But you have the thousandth part of a grain. Homeopathic doses are perhaps the strongest. Confess that you have faith even to the ten-thousandth part of a grain.”

78.76.oldText: “Not for one minute,” Ivan cried furiously. “But I would like to believe in you,” he added strangely.

78.77.oldText: “Aha! There's an admission! But I'm good-natured. I'll come to your assistance again. Listen — it was I who caught you, not you me. I told you your own anecdote, the one you'd forgotten, on purpose, so as to destroy your faith in me completely.”

78.78.oldText: “You're lying. The object of your visit is to convince me of your existence!”

78.79.oldText: “Just so. But hesitation, suspense, the conflict between belief and disbelief — is sometimes such torture to a conscientious man, such as yourself, that it's better to hang oneself at once. Knowing that you're inclined to believe in me, I administered some disbelief by telling you that anecdote. I lead you by turns to belief and disbelief, and I have my motive in it. It's the new method. As soon as you disbelieve in me completely, you'll begin assuring me to my face that I'm not a dream but a reality. I know you. Then I shall have attained my object, which is an honorable one. I shall sow in you only a tiny grain of faith, and it will grow into an oak tree — and such an oak tree that, sitting on it, you will long to enter the ranks of ‘the hermits in the wilderness and the saintly women,' because that's what you're secretly longing for. You'll dine on locusts, you'll wander into the wilderness to save your soul!”

78.80.oldText: “Then it's for the salvation of my soul you're working, is it, you scoundrel?”

78.81.oldText: “One must do a good work sometimes. How ill-humored you are!”

78.82.oldText: “Fool! Did you ever tempt those holy men who ate locusts and prayed seventeen years in the wilderness till they were overgrown with moss?”

78.83.oldText: “My dear fellow, I've done nothing else. One forgets the whole world and all the worlds, and sticks to one such saint, because he is a very precious diamond. One such soul, you know, is sometimes worth a whole constellation. We have our system of reckoning, you know. The conquest is priceless! And some of them, on my word, are not inferior to you in culture, though you won't believe it. They can contemplate such depths of belief and disbelief at the same moment that sometimes it really seems they're within a hair's breadth of being ‘turned upside down,' as the actor Gorbunov says.”

78.84.oldText: “Well, did you get your nose pulled?”[8]

78.85.oldText: “My dear fellow,” the visitor observed sententiously, “it's better to get off with your nose pulled than without a nose at all. As an afflicted marquis observed not long ago (he must have been treated by a specialist) in confession to his spiritual father — a Jesuit. I was present, it was simply charming. ‘Give me back my nose!' he said, and he beat his breast. ‘My son,' said the priest evasively, ‘all things are accomplished in accordance with the inscrutable decrees of Providence, and what seems a misfortune sometimes leads to extraordinary, though unapparent, benefits. If stern destiny has deprived you of your nose, it's to your advantage that no one can ever pull you by your nose.' ‘Holy father, that's no comfort,' cried the despairing marquis. ‘I'd be delighted to have my nose pulled every day of my life, if it were only in its proper place.' ‘My son,' sighs the priest, ‘you can't expect every blessing at once. This is murmuring against Providence, who, even in this, has not forgotten you, because if you repine as you repined just now, declaring you'd be glad to have your nose pulled for the rest of your life, your desire has already been fulfilled indirectly, for when you lost your nose, you were led by the nose.'”

78.87.oldText: “My dear friend, I only wanted to amuse you. But I swear that's genuine Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it all happened word for word as I've told you. It happened recently and gave me a great deal of trouble. The unhappy young man shot himself that very night when he got home. I was by his side till the very last moment. Those Jesuit confessionals are really my most delightful diversion at melancholy moments. Here's another incident that happened only the other day. A little blonde Norman girl of twenty — a buxom, unsophisticated beauty that would make your mouth water — comes to an old priest. She bends down and whispers her sin into the grating. ‘Why, my daughter, have you fallen again already?' the priest cries. ‘O Sancta Maria, what do I hear! Not the same man this time, how long is this going on? Aren't you ashamed!' ‘_Ah, mon père_,' the sinner answers, with tears of penitence, ‘_ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!_' Fancy, such an answer! I drew back. It was the cry of nature, better than innocence itself, if you like. I absolved her sin on the spot and was turning to go, but I was forced to turn back. I heard the priest at the grating making an appointment with her for the evening — though he was an old man, hard as flint, he fell in an instant! It was nature, the truth of nature asserting its rights! What, you're turning up your nose again? Angry again? I don't know how to please you —”

78.88.oldText: “Leave me alone, you're beating on my brain like a haunting nightmare,” Ivan moaned miserably, helpless before his apparition. “I'm bored with you, agonizingly and insufferably. I'd give anything to be able to shake you off!”

78.89.oldText: “I repeat — moderate your expectations, don't demand of me ‘everything great and noble,' and you'll see how well we'll get on,” the gentleman said impressively. “You're really angry with me for not having appeared to you in a red glow, with thunder and lightning, with scorched wings, but have shown myself in such a modest form. You're wounded, in the first place, in your aesthetic feelings, and, secondly, in your pride. How could such a vulgar devil visit such a great man as you! Yes, there's that romantic strain in you, the one that was so derided by Byelinsky. I can't help it, young man; as I got ready to come to you, I did, as a joke, think of appearing in the figure of a retired general who had served in the Caucasus, with a star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat. But I was positively afraid to do it, because you'd have thrashed me for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat, instead of at least the Polar Star or the Sirius. And you keep saying I'm stupid, but, mercy on us, I make no claim to be your equal in intelligence. Mephistopheles declared to Faust that he desired evil, but did only good. Well, he can say what he likes; it's quite the opposite with me. I am perhaps the one man in all creation who loves the truth and genuinely desires good. I was there when the Word, who died on the Cross, rose up into heaven bearing on His bosom the soul of the penitent thief. I heard the glad shrieks of the cherubim singing and shouting hosannah, and the thunderous rapture of the seraphim which shook heaven and all creation, and I swear to you by all that's sacred, I longed to join the choir and shout hosannah with them all. The word had almost escaped me, had almost broken from my lips ... you know how susceptible and aesthetically impressionable I am. But common sense — oh, a most unhappy trait in my character — kept me in due bounds, and I let the moment pass! Because what, I reflected, what would have happened after my hosannah? Everything on earth would have been extinguished at once and no events could have occurred. And so, solely from a sense of duty and my social position, I was forced to suppress the good moment and to stick to my nasty task. Somebody takes all the credit of what's good for Himself, and nothing but nastiness is left to me. But I don't envy the honor of a life of idle imposture, I'm not ambitious. Why am I, of all creatures in the world, doomed to be cursed by all decent people and even to be kicked, because if I put on mortal form I am bound to take such consequences sometimes? I know, of course, there's a secret in it, but they won't tell me the secret for anything, because then perhaps, seeing the meaning of it, I might bawl hosannah, and the indispensable minus would disappear at once, and good sense would reign supreme throughout the whole world. And that, of course, would mean the end of everything, even of magazines and newspapers, for who would take them in? I know that in the end of all things I will be reconciled. I too shall walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But till that happens I am sulking and fulfill my destiny though it's against the grain — that is, to ruin thousands for the sake of saving one. How many souls have had to be ruined and how many honorable reputations destroyed for the sake of that one righteous man, Job, over whom they made such a fool of me in the old days! Yes, until the secret is revealed, there are two sorts of truths for me — one, their truth, yonder, which I know nothing about so far, and the other my own. And there's no knowing which will turn out the better. Are you asleep?”

78.90.oldText: “I might well be,” Ivan groaned angrily. “All my stupid ideas — outgrown, thrashed out long ago and flung aside like a dead carcass — you present to me as something new!”

78.91.oldText: “There's no pleasing you! And I thought I'd fascinate you with my literary style. That hosannah in the skies really wasn't bad, was it? And then that ironic tone _à la_ Heine, eh?”

78.92.oldText: “No, I was never such a flunkey! How then could my soul beget a flunkey like you?”

78.93.oldText: “My dear fellow, I know a most charming and attractive young Russian gentleman, a young thinker and a great lover of literature and art, the author of a promising poem entitled _The Grand Inquisitor_. I was only thinking of him!”

78.94.oldText: “I forbid you to speak of _The Grand Inquisitor_,” Ivan cried, crimson with shame.

78.95.oldText: “And the _Geological Cataclysm_. Do you remember? That was a poem, now!”

78.96.oldText: “Hold your tongue, or I'll kill you!”

78.97.oldText: “You'll kill me? No, excuse me, I will speak. I came to treat myself to that pleasure. Oh, I love the dreams of my ardent young friends, quivering with eagerness for life! ‘There are new men,' you decided last spring, when you were meaning to come here. ‘They propose to destroy everything and begin with cannibalism. Stupid fellows! They didn't ask my advice! I maintain that nothing needs to be destroyed, that we only need to destroy the idea of God in man — that's how we have to set to work. It's that, that we must begin with. Oh, blind race of men who have no understanding! As soon as men have all of them denied God — and I believe that period, analogous to geological periods, will come to pass — the old conception of the universe will fall of itself, without cannibalism, and, what's more, the old morality, and everything will begin anew. Men will unite to take from life all it can give, but only for joy and happiness in the present world. Man will be lifted up with a spirit of divine Titanic pride and the man-god will appear. From hour to hour extending his conquest of nature infinitely by his will and his science, man will feel such lofty joy from hour to hour in doing it that it will make up for all his old dreams of the joys of heaven. Everyone will know that he is mortal and will accept death proudly and serenely like a god. His pride will teach him that it's useless to repine at life's being a moment, and he will love his brother without need of reward. Love will be sufficient only for a moment of life, but the very consciousness of its momentariness will intensify its fire, which is now dissipated in dreams of eternal love beyond the grave' — and so on and so on in the same style. Charming!”

78.98.oldText: Ivan sat with his eyes on the floor and his hands pressed to his ears, but he began trembling all over. The voice continued.

78.99.oldText: “The question now is, my young thinker reflected, is it possible that such a period will ever come? If it does, everything is determined and humanity is settled forever. But since, owing to man's inveterate stupidity, this can't come about for at least a thousand years, anyone who recognizes the truth even now may legitimately order his life as he pleases, on the new principles. In that sense, ‘all things are lawful' for him. What's more, even if this period never comes to pass, since there's no God and no immortality anyway, the new man may well become the man-god, even if he's the only one in the whole world, and, promoted to his new position, he may lightheartedly overstep all the barriers of the old morality of the old slave-man, if necessary. There is no law for God. Where God stands, the place is holy. Where I stand will be at once the foremost place — ‘all things are lawful,' and that's the end of it! That's all very charming; but if you want to swindle, why do you need a moral sanction for doing it? But that's our modern Russian all over. He can't bring himself to swindle without a moral sanction. He's so in love with truth —”

78.100.oldText: The visitor talked, obviously carried away by his own eloquence, speaking louder and louder and looking ironically at his host. But he did not succeed in finishing; Ivan suddenly snatched a glass from the table and flung it at the orator.

78.101.oldText: “_Ah, mais c'est bête enfin_,” the latter cried, jumping up from the sofa and shaking the drops of tea off himself. “He remembers Luther's inkstand! He takes me for a dream and throws glasses at a dream! It's just like a woman! I suspected you were only pretending to stop up your ears.”

78.102.oldText: A loud, persistent knocking was suddenly heard at the window. Ivan jumped up from the sofa.

78.103.oldText: “Do you hear? You'd better open it,” the visitor cried. “It's your brother Alyosha with the most interesting and surprising news, I'll bet!”

78.104.oldText: “Be silent, deceiver — I knew it was Alyosha, I felt he was coming, and of course he hasn't come for nothing; of course he brings ‘news,'” Ivan exclaimed frantically.

78.105.oldText: “Open, open to him. There's a snowstorm, and he's your brother. _Monsieur sait-il le temps qu'il fait? C'est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors._”

78.106.oldText: The knocking continued. Ivan wanted to rush to the window, but something seemed to fetter his arms and legs. He strained every effort to break his chains, but in vain. The knocking at the window grew louder and louder. At last the chains were broken and Ivan leapt up from the sofa. He looked around him wildly. Both candles had almost burned out, the glass he had just thrown at his visitor stood in front of him on the table, and there was no one on the sofa opposite. The knocking on the window frame went on persistently, but it was by no means as loud as it had seemed in his dream; on the contrary, it was quite subdued.

78.107.oldText: “It was not a dream! No, I swear it was not a dream, it all just happened!” Ivan cried. He rushed to the window and opened the movable pane.

78.108.oldText: “Alyosha, I told you not to come,” he cried fiercely to his brother. “In two words, what do you want? In two words, do you hear?”

78.110.oldText: “Come round to the steps, I'll open at once,” Ivan said, going to open the door to Alyosha.

79.0.oldText: Alyosha came in and told Ivan that a little over an hour ago Marya Kondratyevna had run to his rooms and told him Smerdyakov had taken his own life. “I went in to clear away the samovar, and he was hanging from a nail in the wall.” On Alyosha's inquiring whether she had informed the police, she answered that she had told no one, “but I flew straight to you, I've run all the way.” She seemed perfectly crazy, Alyosha reported, and was shaking like a leaf. When Alyosha had run with her to the cottage, he found Smerdyakov still hanging. On the table lay a note: “I destroy my life of my own will and desire, so as to throw no blame on anyone.” Alyosha left the note on the table and went straight to the police captain and told him all about it. “And from him I've come straight to you,” Alyosha said in conclusion, looking intently into Ivan's face. He hadn't taken his eyes off him while he told his story, as though struck by something in his expression.

79.1.oldText: “Brother,” he cried suddenly, “you must be terribly ill. You look and don't seem to understand what I'm telling you.”

79.2.oldText: “It's a good thing you came,” Ivan said, as though brooding, not hearing Alyosha's exclamation. “I knew he had hanged himself.”

79.4.oldText: “I don't know. But I knew. Did I know? Yes, he told me. He told me so just now.”

79.5.oldText: Ivan stood in the middle of the room, and still spoke in the same brooding tone, looking at the floor.

79.6.oldText: “Who is _he_?” Alyosha asked, involuntarily looking around.

79.8.oldText: Ivan raised his head and smiled softly.

79.9.oldText: “He was afraid of you, of a dove like you. You're a ‘pure cherub.' Dmitri calls you a cherub. Cherub! ... the thunderous rapture of the seraphim. What are seraphim? Perhaps a whole constellation. But perhaps that constellation is only a chemical molecule. There's a constellation of the Lion and the Sun. Don't you know it?”

79.10.oldText: “Brother, sit down,” Alyosha said in alarm. “For goodness' sake, sit down on the sofa! You're delirious; put your head on the pillow, that's right. Would you like a wet towel on your head? Perhaps it will do you good.”

79.11.oldText: “Give me the towel — it's there on the chair. I just threw it down there.”

79.12.oldText: “It's not here. Don't worry yourself. I know where it is — here,” Alyosha said, finding a clean towel, folded up and unused, by Ivan's dressing table in the other corner of the room. Ivan looked strangely at the towel: recollection seemed to come back to him for an instant.

79.13.oldText: “Wait —” he got up from the sofa. “An hour ago I took that new towel from there and wetted it. I wrapped it around my head and threw it down here. How is it dry? There was no other.”

79.14.oldText: “You put that towel on your head?” Alyosha asked.

79.15.oldText: “Yes, and walked up and down the room an hour ago. Why have the candles burned down so? What's the time?”

79.17.oldText: “No, no, no!” Ivan cried suddenly. “It was not a dream. He was here; he was sitting here, on that sofa. When you knocked at the window, I threw a glass at him ... this one. Wait a minute. I was asleep last time, but this dream wasn't a dream. It's happened before. I have dreams now, Alyosha ... yet they're not dreams, but reality. I walk about, talk, and see ... though I'm asleep. But he was sitting here, on that sofa there. He's frightfully stupid, Alyosha, frightfully stupid.” Ivan laughed suddenly and began pacing about the room.

79.18.oldText: “Who's stupid? Who are you talking about, brother?” Alyosha asked anxiously again.

79.19.oldText: “The devil! He's taken to visiting me. He's been here twice, almost three times. He taunted me with being angry that he was a simple devil, and not Satan, with scorched wings, in thunder and lightning. But he isn't Satan: that's a lie. He's an impostor. He's just a devil — a paltry, trivial devil. He goes to the bathhouse. If you undressed him, you'd be sure to find he had a tail, long and smooth, like a Danish dog's, a yard long, dun-colored. Alyosha, you're cold. You've been in the snow. Would you like some tea? What? Is it cold? Shall I tell her to bring some? _C'est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors._ ...”

79.20.oldText: Alyosha ran to the washstand, wetted the towel, persuaded Ivan to sit down again, and put the wet towel around his head. He sat down beside him.

79.21.oldText: “What were you telling me just now about Lise?” Ivan began again. (He was becoming very talkative.) “I like Lise. I said something nasty about her. It was a lie. I like her. I'm afraid of Katya tomorrow. I'm more afraid of her than of anything. Because of the future. She'll cast me off tomorrow and trample me underfoot. She thinks that I'm ruining Mitya out of jealousy on her account! Yes, she thinks that! But it's not so. Tomorrow the cross, but not the gallows. No, I shan't hang myself. Do you know, I could never commit suicide, Alyosha. Is it because I'm base? I'm not a coward. Is it from love of life? How did I know that Smerdyakov had hanged himself? Yes, it was _he_ who told me so.”

79.22.oldText: “And you're quite convinced someone has been here?” Alyosha asked.

79.23.oldText: “Yes, on that sofa in the corner. You would have driven him away. You did drive him away: he disappeared when you arrived. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know that I loved your face? And _he_ is myself, Alyosha. All that's base in me, all that's mean and contemptible. Yes, I'm a romantic. He guessed it ... though it's a libel. He's frightfully stupid; but it's to his advantage. He has cunning, animal cunning — he knew how to infuriate me. He kept taunting me about believing in him, and that was how he made me listen to him. He fooled me like a boy. He told me a great deal that was true about myself, though. I'd never have admitted it to myself. Do you know, Alyosha,” Ivan added in an intensely earnest and confidential tone, “I'd be awfully glad to think that it was _he_, and not I.”

79.24.oldText: “He has worn you out,” Alyosha said, looking compassionately at his brother.

79.25.oldText: “He's been teasing me. And you know, he does it so cleverly, so cleverly. ‘Conscience! What is conscience? I make it up for myself. Why am I tormented by it? From habit. From the universal habit of mankind over the last seven thousand years. So let us give it up, and we shall be gods.' It was he who said that, it was he who said that!”

79.26.oldText: “And not you, not you?” Alyosha couldn't help crying, looking frankly at his brother. “Never mind him, anyway; have done with him and forget him. And let him take with him all that you curse now, and never come back!”

79.27.oldText: “Yes, but he's spiteful. He laughed at me. He was impudent, Alyosha,” Ivan said, with a shudder of offense. “But he was unfair to me, unfair about lots of things. He told lies about me to my face. ‘Oh, you're going to perform an act of heroic virtue: to confess you murdered your father, that the valet murdered him at your instigation.'”

79.28.oldText: “Brother,” Alyosha put in, “restrain yourself. It was not you who murdered him. It's not true!”

79.29.oldText: “That's what he says, he, and he knows it. ‘You're going to perform an act of heroic virtue, and you don't believe in virtue; that's what tortures you and makes you angry, that's why you're so vindictive.' He said that to me about me and he knows what he says.”

79.30.oldText: “It's you saying that, not he,” Alyosha exclaimed mournfully, “and you say it because you're ill and delirious, tormenting yourself.”

79.31.oldText: “No, he knows what he says. ‘You're going out of pride,' he says. ‘You'll stand up and say it was I who killed him, and why do you writhe with horror? You are lying! I despise your opinion, I despise your horror!' He said that about me. ‘And do you know you're longing for their praise — “he's a criminal, a murderer, but what a generous soul; he wanted to save his brother and he confessed.”' That's a lie, Alyosha!” Ivan cried suddenly, his eyes flashing. “I don't want the low rabble to praise me, I swear I don't! That's a lie! That's why I threw the glass at him and it broke against his ugly face.”

79.32.oldText: “Brother, calm yourself, stop!” Alyosha entreated him.

79.33.oldText: “Yes, he knows how to torment a man. He's cruel,” Ivan went on, not heeding. “I had an inkling from the first what he'd come for. ‘Granting that you're going out of pride, still you had the hope that Smerdyakov might be convicted and sent to Siberia, and Mitya would be acquitted, while you'd only be punished with moral condemnation' (‘Do you hear?' he laughed at that) — ‘and some people will praise you. But now Smerdyakov's dead, he's hanged himself, and who'll believe you alone? But still you're going, you're going, you'll go all the same, you've decided to go. What are you going for now?' That's awful, Alyosha. I can't stand such questions. Who dare ask me such questions?”

79.34.oldText: “Brother,” Alyosha put in — his heart sank with terror, but he still seemed to hope to bring Ivan to reason — “how could he have told you of Smerdyakov's death before I came, when no one knew of it and there wasn't time for anyone to know of it?”

79.35.oldText: “He told me,” Ivan said firmly, refusing to admit a doubt. “It was all he did talk about, if it comes to that. ‘And it would be all right if you believed in virtue,' he said. ‘No matter if they disbelieve you, you're going for the sake of principle. But you're a little pig like Fyodor Pavlovitch, and what do you want with virtue? Why do you want to go meddling, if your sacrifice is of no use to anyone? Because you don't know yourself why you go! Oh, you'd give a great deal to know yourself why you go! And have you made up your mind? You haven't made up your mind. You'll sit all night deliberating whether to go or not. But you will go; you know you'll go. You know that whichever way you decide, the decision doesn't depend on you. You'll go because you won't dare not to go. Why won't you dare? You must guess that for yourself. That's a riddle for you!' He got up and went away. You came, and he went. He called me a coward, Alyosha! _Le mot de l'énigme_ is that I am a coward. ‘It is not for such eagles to soar above the earth.' It was he who added that — he! And Smerdyakov said the same. He must be killed! Katya despises me. I've seen that for a month now. Even Lise will begin to despise me! ‘You're going in order to be praised.' That's a brutal lie! And you despise me too, Alyosha. Now I'm going to hate you again! And I hate the monster too! I hate the monster! I don't want to save the monster. Let him rot in Siberia! He's begun singing a hymn! Oh, tomorrow I'll go, stand before them, and spit in their faces!”

79.36.oldText: He jumped up in a frenzy, flung off the towel, and fell to pacing up and down the room again. Alyosha recalled what he had just said. “I seem to be sleeping awake. I walk, I speak, I see, but I am asleep.” It seemed to be just like that now. Alyosha didn't leave him. The thought passed through his mind to run for a doctor, but he was afraid to leave his brother alone: there was no one he could leave him with. Gradually, Ivan lost consciousness completely at last. He still went on talking, talking incessantly, but quite incoherently, and even articulated his words with difficulty. Suddenly he staggered violently, but Alyosha was in time to support him. Ivan let him lead him to his bed. Alyosha undressed him somehow and put him to bed. He sat watching over him for another two hours. The sick man slept soundly, without stirring, breathing softly and evenly. Alyosha took a pillow and lay down on the sofa without undressing.

79.37.oldText: As he fell asleep he prayed for Mitya and Ivan. He began to understand Ivan's illness. “The anguish of a proud determination. An earnest conscience!” God, in Whom he disbelieved, and His truth were gaining mastery over his heart, which still refused to submit. “Yes,” the thought floated through Alyosha's head as it lay on the pillow, “yes, if Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan's evidence; but he'll go and give it.” Alyosha smiled softly. “God will conquer!” he thought. “He'll either rise up in the light of truth, or ... he'll perish in hate, revenging on himself and on everyone his having served the cause he does not believe in,” Alyosha added bitterly, and again he prayed for Ivan.

80.0.oldText: At ten o'clock in the morning of the day following the events I've just described, the trial of Dmitri Karamazov began in our district court.

80.1.oldText: I hasten to emphasize that I am far from considering myself capable of reporting everything that took place at the trial in full detail, or even in the actual order of events. I imagine that to mention everything with full explanation would fill a volume, even a very large one. And so I trust I may not be reproached for confining myself to what struck me. I may have chosen what was actually of secondary importance as the most interesting, and may have omitted the most prominent and essential details. But I see I'd do better not to apologize. I'll do my best, and the reader will see for himself that I've done all I could.

80.2.oldText: And to begin with, before we enter the court, I'll mention what surprised me most that day. As it turned out later, everyone was surprised by it as well. We all knew that the affair had aroused great interest, that everyone was burning with impatience for the trial to begin, that for the last two months it had been a subject of talk, conjecture, exclamation, and surmise in local society. Everyone knew, too, that the case had become known throughout Russia, but we had not imagined it had aroused such burning, such intense interest in everyone, not only among ourselves but all over Russia. This became evident at the trial that day.

80.3.oldText: Visitors had arrived not only from the chief town of our province but from several other Russian towns, as well as from Moscow and Petersburg. Among them were lawyers, ladies, and even several distinguished personages. Every ticket of admission had been snatched up. A special area behind the table where the three judges sat was set apart for the most distinguished and important of the male visitors; a row of armchairs had been placed there — something exceptional, which had never been allowed before. A large proportion — no less than half — of the public were ladies. There were so many lawyers from all over that they didn't know where to seat them all, since every ticket had long since been eagerly sought out and distributed. I saw at the end of the room, behind the platform, a special partition hurriedly put up, behind which all these lawyers were admitted, and they thought themselves lucky to have standing room there, for all chairs had been removed for the sake of space, and the crowd behind the partition stood throughout the case closely packed, shoulder to shoulder.

80.4.oldText: Some of the ladies, especially those who had come from a distance, appeared in the gallery very smartly dressed, but the majority of the ladies were oblivious even of their dress. Their faces betrayed hysterical, intense, almost morbid curiosity. A peculiar fact — established afterwards by many observations — was that almost all the ladies, or at least the vast majority of them, were on Mitya's side and in favor of his being acquitted. This was perhaps chiefly due to his reputation as a conqueror of female hearts. It was known that two rival women would appear in the case. One of them — Katerina Ivanovna — was an object of general interest. All sorts of extraordinary tales were told about her, amazing anecdotes of her passion for Mitya in spite of his crime. Her pride and her “aristocratic connections” were particularly insisted upon (she had called on scarcely anyone in the town). People said she intended to petition the government for leave to accompany the criminal to Siberia and to be married to him somewhere in the mines. The appearance of Grushenka in court was awaited with no less impatience. The public was looking forward with anxious curiosity to the meeting of the two rivals — the proud aristocratic girl and “the hetaira.” But Grushenka was a more familiar figure to the ladies of the district than Katerina Ivanovna. They had already seen “the woman who had ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his unhappy son,” and all, almost without exception, wondered how father and son could be so in love with “such a very common, ordinary Russian girl, who wasn't even pretty.”

80.5.oldText: In short, there was a great deal of talk. I know for a fact that there were several serious family quarrels on Mitya's account in our town. Many ladies quarreled violently with their husbands over differences of opinion about the dreadful case, and it was only natural that the husbands of these ladies, far from being favorably disposed to the prisoner, should enter the court bitterly prejudiced against him. In fact, one may say pretty certainly that the masculine, as distinct from the feminine, part of the audience was biased against the prisoner. There were numbers of severe, frowning, even vindictive faces. Mitya, indeed, had managed to offend many people during his stay in town. Some of the visitors were, of course, in excellent spirits and quite unconcerned about the fate of Mitya personally. But all were interested in the trial, and the majority of the men were certainly hoping for the criminal's conviction, except perhaps the lawyers, who were more interested in the legal than in the moral aspect of the case.

80.6.oldText: Everyone was excited at the presence of the celebrated lawyer Fetyukovitch. His talent was well known, and this was not the first time he had defended notorious criminal cases in the provinces. And whenever he defended them, such cases became celebrated and long remembered all over Russia. There were stories, too, about our prosecutor and about the President of the Court. It was said that Ippolit Kirillovitch was in a tremor at meeting Fetyukovitch, and that they had been enemies from the beginning of their careers in Petersburg; that although our sensitive prosecutor — who always believed he had been wronged by someone in Petersburg because his talents had not been properly appreciated — was keenly excited over the Karamazov case, and was even dreaming of rebuilding his flagging fortunes by means of it, Fetyukovitch, they said, was his one anxiety. But these rumors were not quite just. Our prosecutor was not one of those men who lose heart in the face of danger. On the contrary, his self-confidence grew with the increase of danger. It must be noted that our prosecutor was in general too hasty and morbidly impressionable. He would put his whole soul into some case and work at it as though his whole fate and entire fortune depended on its outcome. This was the subject of some ridicule in the legal world, because precisely by this trait our prosecutor had gained a wider notoriety than could have been expected from his modest position. People laughed particularly at his passion for psychology. In my opinion, they were wrong, and our prosecutor, I believe, was a character of greater depth than was generally supposed. But with his delicate health he had failed to make his mark at the outset of his career, and had never made up for it later.

80.7.oldText: As for the President of our Court, I can only say that he was a humane and cultured man, with a practical knowledge of his work and progressive views. He was rather ambitious, but not greatly concerned about his future career. The great aim of his life was to be a man of advanced ideas. He was, too, a man of connections and property. He felt, as we learned afterwards, rather strongly about the Karamazov case, but from a social, not a personal standpoint. He was interested in it as a social phenomenon, in its classification and character as a product of our social conditions, as typical of the national character, and so on, and so on. His attitude to the personal aspect of the case, to its tragic significance and the persons involved in it, including the prisoner, was rather indifferent and abstract, as was perhaps fitting, indeed.

80.8.oldText: The court was packed and overflowing long before the judges made their appearance. Our court is the best hall in town — spacious, lofty, and good for sound. On the right of the judges, who were on a raised platform, a table and two rows of chairs had been set ready for the jury. On the left was the place for the prisoner and the counsel for the defense. In the middle of the court, near the judges, was a table with the “material proofs.” On it lay Fyodor Pavlovitch's white silk dressing gown, stained with blood; the fatal brass pestle with which the supposed murder had been committed; Mitya's shirt, with a bloodstained sleeve; his coat, stained with blood in patches over the pocket in which he had put his handkerchief; the handkerchief itself, stiff with blood and by now quite yellow; the pistol Mitya had loaded at Perhotin's with a view to suicide, which had been taken from him on the sly at Mokroe by Trifon Borissovitch; the envelope in which the three thousand roubles had been put ready for Grushenka; the narrow pink ribbon with which it had been tied; and many other items I don't remember. In the body of the hall, at some distance, came the seats for the public. But in front of the balustrade a few chairs had been placed for witnesses who remained in the court after giving their evidence.

80.9.oldText: At ten o'clock the three judges arrived — the President, one honorary justice of the peace, and one other. The prosecutor, of course, entered immediately after. The President was a short, stout, thick-set man of fifty, with a dyspeptic complexion, dark hair turning gray and cut short, and a red ribbon — of what Order I don't remember. The prosecutor struck me, and the others too, as looking particularly pale, almost green. His face seemed to have grown suddenly thinner, perhaps overnight, for I had seen him looking as usual only two days before. The President began by asking the court whether all the jury were present.

80.10.oldText: But I see I can't go on like this, partly because some things I didn't hear, others I didn't notice, and others I've forgotten — but most of all because, as I've said, I have literally no time or space to mention everything that was said and done. I only know that neither side objected to very many of the jurymen. I remember the twelve jurymen — four were petty officials of the town, two were merchants, and six were peasants and artisans of the town. I remember, long before the trial, questions were continually asked with some surprise, especially by ladies: “Can such a delicate, complex, and psychological case be submitted for decision to petty officials and even peasants?” and “What can an official — still more, a peasant — understand of such an affair?” All four officials on the jury were, in fact, men of no consequence and of low rank. Except one who was rather younger, they were gray-headed men, little known in society, who had vegetated on a pitiful salary, and who probably had elderly, unpresentable wives and crowds of children — perhaps even without shoes and stockings. At most, they spent their leisure over cards and, of course, had never read a single book. The two merchants looked respectable, but were strangely silent and stolid. One of them was clean-shaven and dressed in European style; the other had a small gray beard, and wore a red ribbon with some kind of medal on it around his neck. There's no need to speak of the artisans and the peasants. The artisans of Skotoprigonyevsk are almost peasants, and even work the land. Two of them also wore European dress, and perhaps for that reason looked dirtier and more uninviting than the others. So that one might well wonder, as I did as soon as I'd looked at them, “what men like this could possibly make of such a case?” Yet their faces made a strangely imposing, almost menacing, impression — they were stern and frowning.

80.11.oldText: At last the President opened the case of the murder of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. I don't quite remember how he described him. The court usher was told to bring in the prisoner, and Mitya made his appearance. There was a hush throughout the court. You could have heard a fly. I don't know how it was with others, but Mitya made a most unfavorable impression on me. He looked an awful dandy in a brand-new frock coat. I heard afterwards that he had ordered it in Moscow expressly for the occasion from his own tailor, who had his measurements. He wore immaculate black kid gloves and exquisite linen. He walked in with his yard-long strides, looking stiffly straight ahead, and sat down in his place with a most unperturbed air.

80.12.oldText: At the same moment the counsel for the defense, the celebrated Fetyukovitch, entered, and a sort of subdued hum passed through the court. He was a tall, spare man, with long thin legs, extremely long, thin, pale fingers, a clean-shaven face, demurely brushed, rather short hair, and thin lips that were at times curved into something between a sneer and a smile. He looked about forty. His face would have been pleasant, if not for his eyes, which, in themselves small and inexpressive, were set remarkably close together, with only the thin, long nose as a dividing line between them. In fact, there was something strikingly birdlike about his face. He was in evening dress and a white tie.

80.13.oldText: I remember the President's first questions to Mitya, about his name, his profession, and so on. Mitya answered sharply, and his voice was so unexpectedly loud that it made the President start and look at the prisoner in surprise. Then followed a list of persons who were to take part in the proceedings — that is, of the witnesses and experts. It was a long list. Four of the witnesses were absent — Miüsov, who had given evidence at the preliminary inquiry but was now in Paris; Madame Hohlakov and Maximov, who were absent due to illness; and Smerdyakov, through his sudden death, of which an official statement from the police was presented. The news of Smerdyakov's death produced a sudden stir and whisper in the court. Many of the audience, of course, had not heard of the sudden suicide. What struck people most was Mitya's sudden outburst. As soon as the statement of Smerdyakov's death was made, he cried out loud from his place:
